title: _External_ Data Request for Land Development Workgroup.msg
subject: [External] Data Request for Land Development Workgroup
body:
Hi Stephanie,

Here is some language that might be helpful for your email to the Land Development Group. OSEJ would like to initiate most external contacts for the formal RWER, so the description below is more focused  the County’s technical tasks.  Since Max will already be in attendance he will be available to be the point person on this.

The County is currently evaluating the feasibility of storm drain diversions to water recycling facilities. As such, we are looking to map (via GIS data) local sewer networks and sewersheds draining to water recycling facilities (both direct potable reuse and recycled water [“purple pipe”]). We are also interested in mapping the service areas for all local direct potable reuse facilities, water recycling facilities, and desalination facilities. It would be very helpful if each representative could provide a publicly available data source or identify a subject matter expert (and provide contact information) for more information on obtaining this data.

We will most likely also need to reach out to specific water districts/agencies, but this could be a very helpful start!

Thanks,
Megan

title: _External_ RE_ Conversation with Sub Consultant UCSD - Regional Water Equity Report.msg
subject: [External] RE: Conversation with Sub Consultant UCSD - Regional Water Equity Report
body:
Hi Stephanie,

I just connected with our UCSD subcontractor over the phone and conveyed the messages below. They understand their requested role moving forward. However, it was verbally stated that they may prefer to terminate their contract early, prior to completing the literature review. We should discuss how that would impact the project and how we can help move things ahead smoothly.

It looks like I missed you this afternoon, and I am out tomorrow, but I will reconnect with you on Monday.

Ken, as the Project Director, is also in the loop on this.

Thank you,

Megan

Megan M. Otto, PE (CA)

Direct: 619.810.4043

From: Gaines, Stephanie <Stephanie.Gaines@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Sent: Wednesday, April 26, 2023 4:51 PM
To: Megan Otto <MMOtto@Geosyntec.com>
Subject: Conversation with Sub Consultant UCSD - Regional Water Equity Report

CAUTION: This email originated from outside of the organization. Do not click links or open attachments unless you recognize the sender and know the content is safe. If you have any suspicion, please confirm with the sender verbally that this email is authentic. If you suspect fraud, click "Phish Alert Report."

Hi Megan,

Thank you for taking the time today to discuss the difficulties we have experienced with the sub-consultant from UCSD for the Regional Water Equity Report project, specifically the primary contact from UCSD, Julie Beth Hinds. We would like to request that you have a conversation with the subconsultant about her inappropriate behavior and method of communication toward one of our County staff, Elise Ruiz, that occurred during two planning meetings, March 31, 2023, and April 13th, 2023. Elise experienced harassing behavior from UCSD’s mode of communication toward her, which left her feeling unsafe in the working space while leading meetings that were intended to collaboratively develop the agenda and program for the Water Assembly (held April 26, 2023). I know difficult conversations are never easy; the County has a zero-tolerance policy for harassment and that all staff, consultants and subcontractors engage with one another professionally and ethically.

Since we have more outreach meetings and work to conduct, for the remainder of the project, the County prefers to engage directly with Geosyntec on the RWER project and work products, and that Geosyntec not include the subconsultant from UCSD in future meetings but communicate and meet with them separately to finish the scoped literature review task.

Could you also please follow up with me after your conversation with UCSD, let me know what the agreed upon outcomes are, and that they understand their role, moving forward?

Thank you again – please reach out to me if you want to discuss this further.

Best,

 <https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/sdc/dpw/watersheds/GI-Projects/GSCWplan/> Stephanie Gaines

Project Manager | Watershed Structural Projects & Development Support

Office: Monday, Wednesday & Alternate Fridays (7:30-4:30)

Teleworking: Tuesday, Thursday & Alternate Fridays (7:00 – 4:00)

Hi Stephanie,

Thank you for coordinating this very useful dataset! We do have a few follow-up items below - let us know if you would like to discuss any of them. I am also looping Max and Mike in.

General Requests:

  1.  Are similar data available for all facilities, beyond the top 20? Depending on how the prioritization comes out, we may want to take a look at the other facilities’ water use.
  2.  If easily available, we would certainly welcome additional data (~5 years) to allow for the potential consideration of trends, but we can also make do with the last 3 years.
  3.  A contact person and email address for each site would be excellent for questions down the road.

Dataset-Specific Questions:

  1.  Can we assume that “Irrigation Water” reflects potable supply, while “Recycled Water” reflects recycled water for irrigation? Are there any instances of on-site greywater capture and use for either irrigation or interior use (e.g., toilet flushing)?
  2.  If you un-filter the Recycled Water tab it includes six sites, which may still be on the low side? As you noted, it would be helpful if DGS is able to confirm that these are the only recycled water using sites.
  3.  The Irrigation Water tab entries include a "Department" column. Can this be added to all sites?
  4.  Are the potable and irrigation water values in acre-feet? The recycled water tab has units, but not the others.
  5.  In some cases, the Recycled Water tab includes multiple account numbers for a single site. Some sites also have duplicated values (e.g., 4S Ranch Homestead Park for June 2022, under the same account number). Does this reflect multiple meters at that site or should some of these rows be removed/modified?
  6.  Some sites lack data for certain months across all three sets of data tabs (Potable, Irrigation, Recycled) – I’m guessing some of this is due to rain delays, but the absence of potable water use may indicate an error?
  7.  Will the CPNs link these sites to the facilities dataset that we are working to get through the DGS GIS team? This would help us tie the provided sites without exact addresses to the specific parcel to eb evaluated. If not, we would request full addresses for all sites. Examples include:

Hi Stephanie,

Thank you for coordinating this very useful dataset! We do have a few follow-up items below - let us know if you would like to discuss any of them. I am also looping Max and Mike in.

General Requests:

  1.  Are similar data available for all facilities, beyond the top 20? Depending on how the prioritization comes out, we may want to take a look at the other facilities’ water use.
  2.  If easily available, we would certainly welcome additional data (~5 years) to allow for the potential consideration of trends, but we can also make do with the last 3 years.
  3.  A contact person and email address for each site would be excellent for questions down the road.

Dataset-Specific Questions:

  1.  Can we assume that “Irrigation Water” reflects potable supply, while “Recycled Water” reflects recycled water for irrigation? Are there any instances of on-site greywater capture and use for either irrigation or interior use (e.g., toilet flushing)?
  2.  If you un-filter the Recycled Water tab it includes six sites, which may still be on the low side? As you noted, it would be helpful if DGS is able to confirm that these are the only recycled water using sites.
  3.  The Irrigation Water tab entries include a "Department" column. Can this be added to all sites?
  4.  Are the potable and irrigation water values in acre-feet? The recycled water tab has units, but not the others.
  5.  In some cases, the Recycled Water tab includes multiple account numbers for a single site. Some sites also have duplicated values (e.g., 4S Ranch Homestead Park for June 2022, under the same account number). Does this reflect multiple meters at that site or should some of these rows be removed/modified?
  6.  Some sites lack data for certain months across all three sets of data tabs (Potable, Irrigation, Recycled) – I’m guessing some of this is due to rain delays, but the absence of potable water use may indicate an error?
  7.  Will the CPNs link these sites to the facilities dataset that we are working to get through the DGS GIS team? This would help us tie the provided sites without exact addresses to the specific parcel to eb evaluated. If not, we would request full addresses for all sites. Examples include:

General Requests:

  1.  Are similar data available for all facilities, beyond the top 20? Depending on how the prioritization comes out, we may want to take a look at the other facilities’ water use.
  2.  If easily available, we would certainly welcome additional data (~5 years) to allow for the potential consideration of trends, but we can also make do with the last 3 years.
  3.  A contact person and email address for each site would be excellent for questions down the road.

Dataset-Specific Questions:

  1.  Can we assume that “Irrigation Water” reflects potable supply, while “Recycled Water” reflects recycled water for irrigation? Are there any instances of on-site greywater capture and use for either irrigation or interior use (e.g., toilet flushing)?

  3.  The Irrigation Water tab entries include a "Department" column. Can this be added to all sites?
  4.  Are the potable and irrigation water values in acre-feet? The recycled water tab has units, but not the others.
  5.  In some cases, the Recycled Water tab includes multiple account numbers for a single site. Some sites also have duplicated values (e.g., 4S Ranch Homestead Park for June 2022, under the same account number). Does this reflect multiple meters at that site or should some of these rows be removed/modified?
  6.  Some sites lack data for certain months across all three sets of data tabs (Potable, Irrigation, Recycled) – I’m guessing some of this is due to rain delays, but the absence of potable water use may indicate an error?
  7.  Will the CPNs link these sites to the facilities dataset that we are working to get through the DGS GIS team? This would help us tie the provided sites without exact addresses to the specific parcel to eb evaluated. If not, we would request full addresses for all sites. Examples include:

Subject: [External] RE: RWER - Follow-Up Items

Hi Stephanie,

Thank you for coordinating this very useful dataset! We do have a few follow-up items below - let us know if you would like to discuss any of them. I am also looping Max and Mike in.

General Requests:

  1.  Are similar data available for all facilities, beyond the top 20? Depending on how the prioritization comes out, we may want to take a look at the other facilities’ water use.
  2.  If easily available, we would certainly welcome additional data (~5 years) to allow for the potential consideration of trends, but we can also make do with the last 3 years.
  3.  A contact person and email address for each site would be excellent for questions down the road.

Dataset-Specific Questions:

  1.  Can we assume that “Irrigation Water” reflects potable supply, while “Recycled Water” reflects recycled water for irrigation? Are there any instances of on-site greywater capture and use for either irrigation or interior use (e.g., toilet flushing)?
  2.  If you un-filter the Recycled Water tab it includes six sites, which may still be on the low side? As you noted, it would be helpful if DGS is able to confirm that these are the only recycled water using sites.
  3.  The Irrigation Water tab entries include a "Department" column. Can this be added to all sites?
  4.  Are the potable and irrigation water values in acre-feet? The recycled water tab has units, but not the others.
  5.  In some cases, the Recycled Water tab includes multiple account numbers for a single site. Some sites also have duplicated values (e.g., 4S Ranch Homestead Park for June 2022, under the same account number). Does this reflect multiple meters at that site or should some of these rows be removed/modified?
  6.  Some sites lack data for certain months across all three sets of data tabs (Potable, Irrigation, Recycled) – I’m guessing some of this is due to rain delays, but the absence of potable water use may indicate an error?
  7.  Will the CPNs link these sites to the facilities dataset that we are working to get through the DGS GIS team? This would help us tie the provided sites without exact addresses to the specific parcel to eb evaluated. If not, we would request full addresses for all sites. Examples include:

Cc: Aghassi, Sarah <Sarah.Aghassi@sdcounty.ca.gov>; Alfaro, Suedy <Suedy.Alfaro@sdcounty.ca.gov>; Murray, Heather <Heather.Murray@sdcounty.ca.gov>; Lawson, Jennifer <Jennifer.Lawson@sdcounty.ca.gov>; Lopez, Lydia <Lydia.Lopez@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Subject: Regional Water Equity Report/UCSD

Greetings Ken,

Thank you for making time to connect with me earlier today. This email is intended to summarize our conversation; please let me know if you have any corrections.

As you know, Geosyntec has subcontracted an aspect of work for the County of San Diego’s Regional Water Equity Report to UCSD. It was brought to my attention that a staff member from UCSD has been acting in an unprofessional manner, using hostile and discriminatory language toward a County employee and making them feel uncomfortable and unsafe due to the outbursts. This behavior is not tolerated by the County, and we appreciate your timely attention to remove any direct contact between UCSD staff and County employees moving forward. As UCSD is not a primary member of the project team, it is not anticipated that this change will compromise the quality of product that Geosyntec is providing to the Report.

During the County’s investigation of the situation, one of Geosyntec’s staff shared that she, too, felt targeted by the UCSD staff’s behavior and comments. As she is a Geosyntec employee, we expect that your office will perform whatever investigation you deem necessary.

We do hope that Geosyntec will communicate with UCSD the reasons for the change, so that the individual might be held accountable by their employer and get the help that they need.

I appreciate your help in addressing this matter.

Sincerely~

eden

Good afternoon Stephanie,

Pursuant to our conversation this afternoon UCSD would like to formalize a request for a minor scope amendment to reflect the change in focus and technical content of the Regional Water Equity Report convening slated for Wednesday, April 26th.  As the focus of the meeting will no longer be based on the contents of the drought impact literature review being conducted by UCSD, and as the need for and focus of presentation content and public information has changed, we would like to request approval of the following:

1. UCSD will focus on completion of a technical presentation highlighting preliminary findings of the literature review, submitted in powerpoint format by Friday, April 14th for editing and translation.  It is our understanding that the length of the presentation may be anywhere from ten minutes to roughly one hour, depending on the County’s selection of additional presenters with technical content.

2.  UCSD will complete a summary of the technical presentation for the public meeting.  This will be a graphic-rich handout in print and web-compatible format (likely powerpoint) by Friday, April 14th, offering key information and links in a form suitable for the general public and with links for further information to technical sources.

3.  For the meeting itself, UCSD will NOT be responsible for agendas, printing, name tags, etc.  as it is our understanding that Murakawa Communications has been contracted to supply these materials.  UCSD will have roughly ten (10) students present to assist with sign-in, logistics, polling, and collecting public comments.  UCSD’s students will have (10) iPads with them, with connectivity suitable for use for PollEverywhere questions for those without devices.

3.  UCSD will resume work on the literature review after the meeting, adding a review of available water rate information for San Diego and Imperial Counties and the bi-national region.  The meeting summary likewise will be completed.

Thank you Stephanie for your support and leadership!

Sincerely,

JB

title: RE_ Regional Water Equity - Water Assembly Planning Agenda.msg
subject: RE: Regional Water Equity - Water Assembly Planning Agenda
body:
Hi Stephanie and Crystal,

We had a productive meeting with the planning committee for the Water Assembly on April 26th. During today's meeting, we met with Murakawa (event planning/facilitator consultant team), Geosyntec, and JB.

We discussed that an important focus of this project, for current events and moving forward, will be the appropriate addressment of the state drought status. This effort will be supported by a 10-minute technical speaker to elaborate specifically on current drought data, and these recommendations have been made by JB from Scripps Institute of Oceanography:

1.	Jeffrey Mount <https://www.ppic.org/person/jeffrey-mount/> , Public Policy Institute of California (first choice)

He could speak to the drought in terms of long-term trends, provide context for this year, and discuss what is on the horizon, first from a State perspective, but also identifying challenges specific to the RWER region.

2.	Dr. F. Martin Ralph <https://mralph.scrippsprofiles.ucsd.edu/> , Director, Center for Western Weather Extremes <https://cw3e.ucsd.edu/> , Scripps Institute of Oceanography

Local technical expert on the physical process related to extremes in precipitation, climate projections, etc.

3.	Luca Delle Monache <https://ldellemonache.scrippsprofiles.ucsd.edu/> , Deputy Director, Center for Western Weather Extremes, Scripps Institute of Oceanography
4.	Tom Corringham, Research Economist, Center for Western Weather Extremes <https://cw3e.ucsd.edu/> , Scripps Institute of Oceanography

I will reach out to these individuals and request their presentation efforts, however given the tight timeline, it would be helpful to recruit any suggestions DPW may have to fill this role. If you may have any internal County folks or connections who may be able to speak to the drought status and educate the public on this matter, please feel free to reach out to them. Our goal is to have this individual onboard, create a presentation (I can edit the format, we just need context/visuals), and agree to participate in ~15 minute presentation to have material ready by 4/14.

Thanks and have a great weekend!

Elise

I agree – on both fronts!

Ken was so kind and constructive on our conversation, and I definitely understand how h and the Geosyntec team bring great contributions to this project.

The types of considerations that he raised are so valuable – especially for those that are experiencing them firsthand or want to better understand the bigger picture constraints.

Sent: Wednesday, May 17, 2023 4:15 PM
To: Brukman, Eden <Eden.Brukman@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Subject: RE: Regional Water Equity Report/UCSD

Hi Eden,

Ken is the nicest person, really! I’ve worked with him since about 2008, and we’ve always had very positive interactions and outcomes. I have been talking with Megan about bringing the remainder of the “UCSD” task in-house, too, and think that would be the best option for us.

I tend to agree, too, that including information on impacts realized by smaller water agencies, water rights, and potentially historic perspectives, would benefit this project; I believe some of the water history, and water stories included in our IRWM planning document for the San Diego Region could be a resource for these topics, and may not need much additional work to ‘flesh out’ and fit within our final report. We can certainly discuss that possibility during our Friday call.

Thanks again for follow up and helping us resolve this issue.

Best,

Stephanie Gaines

PM, DPW WPP

619-964-8337

Me too. We had a very positive conversation. He also mentioned that Geosyntec had proposed to UCSD the prospect of including some references to water access/drivers impacting availability, such as small water agencies and historic water rights issues… Apparently, UCSD staff were strongly opposed to the inclusion of such information, but Geosyntec feels that the situations and their ripple effects (forgive the pun ??) are worth including – even if on a more anecdotal level. I’d be curious to understand your inclination.

Also, Ken noted that there is little, if any, remaining needed deliverables from UCSD and they’d prefer to bring the remainder in-house. I suggested that he connect with you, but that on the surface I saw no glaring concerns with that proposal.

smiles,

eden

Greetings Ken,

Thank you for making time to connect with me earlier today. This email is intended to summarize our conversation; please let me know if you have any corrections.

As you know, Geosyntec has subcontracted an aspect of work for the County of San Diego’s Regional Water Equity Report to UCSD. It was brought to my attention that a staff member from UCSD has been acting in an unprofessional manner, using hostile and discriminatory language toward a County employee and making them feel uncomfortable and unsafe due to the outbursts. This behavior is not tolerated by the County, and we appreciate your timely attention to remove any direct contact between UCSD staff and County employees moving forward. As UCSD is not a primary member of the project team, it is not anticipated that this change will compromise the quality of product that Geosyntec is providing to the Report.

During the County’s investigation of the situation, one of Geosyntec’s staff shared that she, too, felt targeted by the UCSD staff’s behavior and comments. As she is a Geosyntec employee, we expect that your office will perform whatever investigation you deem necessary.

We do hope that Geosyntec will communicate with UCSD the reasons for the change, so that the individual might be held accountable by their employer and get the help that they need.

I appreciate your help in addressing this matter.

Sincerely~

eden

Hi Stephanie,

Thank you for coordinating this very useful dataset! We do have a few follow-up items below - let us know if you would like to discuss any of them. I am also looping Max and Mike in.

General Requests:

  1.  Are similar data available for all facilities, beyond the top 20? Depending on how the prioritization comes out, we may want to take a look at the other facilities’ water use.
  2.  If easily available, we would certainly welcome additional data (~5 years) to allow for the potential consideration of trends, but we can also make do with the last 3 years.
  3.  A contact person and email address for each site would be excellent for questions down the road.

Dataset-Specific Questions:

  1.  Can we assume that “Irrigation Water” reflects potable supply, while “Recycled Water” reflects recycled water for irrigation? Are there any instances of on-site greywater capture and use for either irrigation or interior use (e.g., toilet flushing)?
  2.  If you un-filter the Recycled Water tab it includes six sites, which may still be on the low side? As you noted, it would be helpful if DGS is able to confirm that these are the only recycled water using sites.
  3.  The Irrigation Water tab entries include a "Department" column. Can this be added to all sites?
  4.  Are the potable and irrigation water values in acre-feet? The recycled water tab has units, but not the others.
  5.  In some cases, the Recycled Water tab includes multiple account numbers for a single site. Some sites also have duplicated values (e.g., 4S Ranch Homestead Park for June 2022, under the same account number). Does this reflect multiple meters at that site or should some of these rows be removed/modified?
  6.  Some sites lack data for certain months across all three sets of data tabs (Potable, Irrigation, Recycled) – I’m guessing some of this is due to rain delays, but the absence of potable water use may indicate an error?

Cc: Maxwell Dugan <MDugan@Geosyntec.com>; Michael Escobar <Michael.Escobar@Geosyntec.com>
Subject: [External] RE: RWER - Follow-Up Items

Hi Stephanie,

Thank you for coordinating this very useful dataset! We do have a few follow-up items below - let us know if you would like to discuss any of them. I am also looping Max and Mike in.

General Requests:

  1.  Are similar data available for all facilities, beyond the top 20? Depending on how the prioritization comes out, we may want to take a look at the other facilities’ water use.
  2.  If easily available, we would certainly welcome additional data (~5 years) to allow for the potential consideration of trends, but we can also make do with the last 3 years.
  3.  A contact person and email address for each site would be excellent for questions down the road.

Dataset-Specific Questions:

  1.  Can we assume that “Irrigation Water” reflects potable supply, while “Recycled Water” reflects recycled water for irrigation? Are there any instances of on-site greywater capture and use for either irrigation or interior use (e.g., toilet flushing)?
  2.  If you un-filter the Recycled Water tab it includes six sites, which may still be on the low side? As you noted, it would be helpful if DGS is able to confirm that these are the only recycled water using sites.
  3.  The Irrigation Water tab entries include a "Department" column. Can this be added to all sites?
  4.  Are the potable and irrigation water values in acre-feet? The recycled water tab has units, but not the others.
  5.  In some cases, the Recycled Water tab includes multiple account numbers for a single site. Some sites also have duplicated values (e.g., 4S Ranch Homestead Park for June 2022, under the same account number). Does this reflect multiple meters at that site or should some of these rows be removed/modified?
  6.  Some sites lack data for certain months across all three sets of data tabs (Potable, Irrigation, Recycled) – I’m guessing some of this is due to rain delays, but the absence of potable water use may indicate an error?
  7.  Will the CPNs link these sites to the facilities dataset that we are working to get through the DGS GIS team? This would help us tie the provided sites without exact addresses to the specific parcel to eb evaluated. If not, we would request full addresses for all sites. Examples include:

Subject: [External] RWER - Task 4.A - Draft Memorandum

Good evening,

title: _External_ CASQA Abstract Consideration - Regional Water Equity Project Initial Research.msg
subject: [External] CASQA Abstract Consideration - Regional Water Equity Project Initial Research
body:
Hi Murtaza and Elise,

The statewide annual California Stormwater Quality Association (CASQA) conference<https://www.casqa.org/events/annual-conference/conference-overview> is being hosted in San Diego this fall (September 11-13th). The conference has a theme relevant to the RWER work (“Rain Ready California: Protecting and Collecting Water for Our Future”). We were thinking it would be a great opportunity to submit an abstract highlighting the project’s initial research on regional water supply projects and programs, plus the outcomes of the interviews, while highlighting the equity considerations in assessing potential enhancements. We would steer clear of sharing the official report, as it would be drafted around that time, but the intent and preliminary work would be really valuable to share with other municipalities and conference attendees with similar objectives.

We are also in coordination with Stephanie Gaines regarding a potential second abstract on the more technical tasks - the County’s potential diversion, capture/use, and infiltration project planning.

Let us know what you think – the abstract is due next Monday so we would draft it for your review in the next couple of days. We would of course love to have you join the presentation, if you are interested.

Thanks,
Megan

body:
Hi all,

The biweekly meeting notes have been uploaded to Sharepoint.

I also wanted to clarify on yesterday’s focus area discussion – there are five focus areas within the region, including: 1) Western San Diego County (a proxy for the SDCWA-connected agencies), Eastern San Diego County (all remaining parts SD County that are not connected to SDCWA, with the exception of the Tribal Nations), Tribal Nations (in both SD and Imperial Counties), Imperial County, and the Border Communities. Apologies for that confusion. We will be sure that the RWER makes that very clear upfront.

Below is a summary of ongoing action items:

1.	Geosyntec

subject: [External] RWER Task 3.B - Facilities Inventory and Screening Submittal
cc: Megan Otto <MMOtto@Geosyntec.com>; Maxwell Dugan <MDugan@Geosyntec.com>;	Jodie Montano <JMontano@Geosyntec.com>
body:
Hi Stephanie,

The Task 3.B deliverable is on Sharepoint in the Task 3.B folder <https://projectsitesb.geosyntec.com/8/SW033129-0547/_layouts/15/start.aspx#/SitePages/Home.aspx?RootFolder=%2F8%2FSW033129-0547%2FShared%20Documents%2FTask%203%20-%20SW%20Capture%20and%20Use%20at%20County%20Parks%20and%20Facilities%2FTask%203B%20Deliverable&FolderCTID=0x012000BB8DC2F928EF0944BBEB156EFA200989&View=%7B09ED6256-943F-4252-81B3-27AB4979A7B9%7D> . As discussed on the call today, the table presents the attributes associated with each County facility, supporting the potential infiltration and diversion screening as well as the next Task 3.C’s prioritization and identification of potential project opportunities. These facilities are compiled from the Task 3.A deliverable and include the additional facilities you sent on 7/3 from the missing data we identified during that task. The following two tabs are included for the Task 3.B deliverable:

*	Attributes, Rationale, and Desc: This tab provides the rationale, sources, and description of the various attributes added to each facility.
*	FAC_INF_DIV_CAP_RESULTS: This tab provides the attribute results for each facility, along with the infiltration and diversion screening results. The initial screening criteria for feasible infiltration and diversion for water supply in Columns O and P are listed below. Onsite Capture and Use screening will be shown during Task 3.C. Additionally, we have included if the parcel overlaps with a SWCFS Parcel, has dry weather flows at MS4 outfalls within 500ft sourced from WSP, and has water demands based on the data provided by the County in May.

Task 3.C will identify the potential project opportunities based on additional applied criteria to rule out areas not ideal for infiltration, diversion, or onsite capture and use (e.g., not within 40ft of septic parcels or 100ft of contamination sites, already has recycled water etc.). and include the weights and resulting scores for each of the facilities along with the prioritized list based on the prioritization framework.

It would be helpful to know if you would like us to remove leased facilities or if there are any other facilities we should remove prior to the prioritization and identification of potential project opportunities. Additionally, let us know if you would like us to include any other attributes for these facilities to support Task 3.C. Please provide this information by July 21 if possible.

1.	Infiltration

	a.	Infiltration screening

		*	Groundwater basins within 1-mile buffer, or;
		*	Within 1-Mile of a drinking well, but outside 150 feet of a drinking well, and;
		*	Permeable geology (Alluvium, Basalt, Conglomerate, Sandstone), and;
		*	Slopes <15%.

2.	Diversion

	a.	Diversion screening

		*	Within sewershed to recycled water treatment plant

Please let us know if you have questions!

Thank you!

title: Conversation with Sub Consultant UCSD - Regional Water Equity Report.msg
subject: Conversation with Sub Consultant UCSD - Regional Water Equity Report
body:
Hi Megan,

Thank you for taking the time today to discuss the difficulties we have experienced with the sub-consultant from UCSD for the Regional Water Equity Report project, specifically the primary contact from UCSD, Julie Beth Hinds. We would like to request that you have a conversation with the subconsultant about her inappropriate behavior and method of communication toward one of our County staff, Elise Ruiz, that occurred during two planning meetings, March 31, 2023, and April 13th, 2023. Elise experienced harassing behavior from UCSD's mode of communication toward her, which left her feeling unsafe in the working space while leading meetings that were intended to collaboratively develop the agenda and program for the Water Assembly (held April 26, 2023). I know difficult conversations are never easy; the County has a zero-tolerance policy for harassment and that all staff, consultants and subcontractors engage with one another professionally and ethically.

Since we have more outreach meetings and work to conduct, for the remainder of the project, the County prefers to engage directly with Geosyntec on the RWER project and work products, and that Geosyntec not include the subconsultant from UCSD in future meetings but communicate and meet with them separately to finish the scoped literature review task.

Could you also please follow up with me after your conversation with UCSD, let me know what the agreed upon outcomes are, and that they understand their role, moving forward?

Thank you again - please reach out to me if you want to discuss this further.

Best,

Subject: Task - FAQs for Water Equity Report

Hi Chris,

I need some help developing a set of FAQs for the upcoming Water Assembly (outreach) for the Water Equity Report. It's ok to develop more questions that fewer, and copy existing FAQs we have developed, as we plan to refine the list during an upcoming meeting.

The attached "fact sheet" is draft (so isn't for distribution yet) but includes a few dot-points that can provide you some context for the type of information we'll share during the Water Assembly. The FAQs we discussed developing would be considered "low handing fruit" (not complex questions or in the weeds) and focus on questions we anticipate stakeholders may ask on local water needs, water equity, reliability, and supply including stormwater harvesting or capture/reuse.

We have FAQs on our website, and the IRWM program website www.sdirwmp.org <http://www.sdirwmp.org> ; these would be a good starting point. Of course, if you need further guidance, please reach out to me; we need a draft by Tuesday of next week (mid-day would be great).

Best,

subject: OSEJ/DPW Regional Water Equity Report - Review of Affordable Housing Piece
body:
Good afternoon Anita, David, and Felipe,

It was a pleasure to meet you yesterday and discuss the Regional Water Equity effort! We are very appreciative of your time and insight on the Affordable Housing topic of the comprehensive report for this effort. As a reminder, the first draft of the Affordable Housing piece will be available as early as August 4th, and review will occur through August 18th.

As I mentioned yesterday, this work is conducted by LeSar and ARUP, and I wanted to share their outline of the research so far, as well as the summary of the stakeholder interviews for your reference.

Additionally, I've attached the project factsheet in case you are interested in the overall project topics, and the Deep Dive flyer for our virtual outreach events. Please feel free to let me know if you have any questions or would like to discuss this effort overall. I am happy to be a resource to you and your team, and thank you again for your time to review this report.

All the best,

Elise Ruiz, Group Program Manager

The contract years for both contracts end on May 31st. New capacity is available June 1st.

For either contract, it may be possible to “partially encumber” funding for a new task order prior to the end of the contract year, and then encumber the rest of the funds needed in the new contract year. Subject: RE: New Task Orders

Hi Stephanie,
The contract years for both contracts end on May 31st. New capacity is available June 1st.

For either contract, it may be possible to “partially encumber” funding for a new task order prior to the end of the contract year, and then encumber the rest of the funds needed in the new contract year. Something similar was done for the green streets master plan task order. I’m not sure if this is common practice, or if it could be done as easily with a PER.

This would require coordination with Danielle. When this was been done before, we waited until the very end of the contract year to encumber funds and use up remaining capacity. Something to discuss.

-Chris

Subject: RE: New Task Orders

Hi Stephanie,
The contract years for both contracts end on May 31st. New capacity is available June 1st.

For either contract, it may be possible to “partially encumber” funding for a new task order prior to the end of the contract year, and then encumber the rest of the funds needed in the new contract year. Something similar was done for the green streets master plan task order. I’m not sure if this is common practice, or if it could be done as easily with a PER.

This would require coordination with Danielle. When this was been done before, we waited until the very end of the contract year to encumber funds and use up remaining capacity. Something to discuss.

-Chris

Subject: RE: New Task Orders

Hi Stephanie,

The contract years for both contracts end on May 31st. New capacity is available June 1st.

For either contract, it may be possible to "partially encumber" funding for a new task order prior to the end of the contract year, and then encumber the rest of the funds needed in the new contract year. Something similar was done for the green streets master plan task order. I'm not sure if this is common practice, or if it could be done as easily with a PER.

This would require coordination with Danielle. When this was been done before, we waited until the very end of the contract year to encumber funds and use up remaining capacity. Something to discuss.

-Chris

subject: [External] RWER - Task 4B Deliverable
body:
Hi Stephanie,

The Task 4B deliverable is on Sharepoint in the Task 4.B folder <https://projectsitesb.geosyntec.com/8/SW033129-0547/_layouts/15/start.aspx#/SitePages/Home.aspx?RootFolder=%2F8%2FSW033129%2D0547%2FShared%20Documents%2FTask%204%20%2D%20SW%20Capture%20and%20Use%20along%20County%20Roads%2FTask%204%2EB%20Submittal&FolderCTID=0x012000BB8DC2F928EF0944BBEB156EFA200989&View=%7B09ED6256%2D943F%2D4252%2D81B3%2D27AB4979A7B9%7D> . The table presents the attributes associated with each road segment, supporting potential infiltration and diversion feasibility. The maps illustrate the screening processes and the locations of the top-ranked potential projects.

At this stage, it would be helpful to know if there are any highly ranked projects or areas that should be de-prioritized (e.g., a major project is already planned there, etc.). We can also look at the project you mentioned with the excess diversion capacity whenever you are able to send that info along.

Initial screening criteria included the following:

1.	Infiltration – ROW segments were prioritized based on the size of the MS4 drainage area (increased potential for capture), also needing to meet:

	a.	Infiltration feasibility

		*	Groundwater basins within 1-mile buffer, or;
		*	Within 1-Mile of a drinking well, but outside 150 feet of a drinking well, and;
		*	Permeable geology (Alluvium, Basalt, Conglomerate, Sandstone), and;
		*	Slopes <15%.

	b.	Intersects with buffered channels/culverts (100-ft) to represent the maximum feasible length for a connection from the storm drain to an infiltration system
	c.	Intersects MS4 outfall or MS4 drainage area
	d.	Excluding industrial land uses, per the CA Drywell Guidance <https://www.waterboards.ca.gov/water_issues/programs/stormwater/storms/docs/drywellguidance.pdf>

2.	Diversion - Prioritized based on average dry weather flow (gpd) over 6-year period of record for outfalls within 500-ft (from Power BI) (note that if multiple outfalls fell within that buffer, the highest flow was assumed). Also needing to meet:

	a.	Diversion feasibility

                                                               i.      Within sewershed to recycled water treatment plant

	b.	Intersects with buffered MS4 channel, culvert, or outfall (500-ft) to reflect the maximum feasible length for a diversion from the storm drain

General Notes

1.	To filter to the highest ranked projects, separately filter to exclude all “#N/A” in Columns J and K, for infiltration and diversion projects, respectively.
2.	High priority road segments are combined into “project opportunities”, grouped by community planning area, but within each project the road segments are not necessarily adjacent to one another. We will look further into this in the next stage.
3.	Diversion “project opportunities” are grouped by community planning area, but some can be further grouped by outfall. We will look further into this in the next stage.
4.	Both the infiltration and diversion opportunities along the ROW are contingent on being adjacent to existing MS4 conveyances (i.e., diversions from waterbodies are not evaluated). For this reason, fewer projects are identified in areas with less known/mapped infrastructure (e.g., Borrego).
5.	The next step will be scoring the top projects including the multi-benefit components.

Limitations

1.	Topography to be reviewed at the project scale (e.g., location of associated outfalls with respect to the ROW segments, the specific slope at the project location, etc.)
2.	Available width along ROW to be reviewed at the project scale
3.	Presence of septic systems to be reviewed at project scale, serving as an infiltration constraint
4.	While diversions have been identified in areas with sewer service and recycled water capabilities, the proximity of the ROW segment to the sewer main have not been confirmed, as sewer main infrastructure was not available for all locations. Similarly, the sewer capacity has not been confirmed.

Please let us know if you have questions about the assumptions above. We would also be happy to walk you through this and do a live zoom-in on each of the project opportunity areas in GIS.

Thanks,

Megan

title: _External_ RWER Task 4_C - ROW Prioritization Framework.msg
subject: [External] RWER Task 4.C - ROW Prioritization Framework
cc: Megan Otto <MMOtto@Geosyntec.com>; Maxwell Dugan <MDugan@Geosyntec.com>;	Lauren Case-McFate <Lauren.Case@Geosyntec.com>
body:
Hi Stephanie,

The Task 4.C deliverable is on Sharepoint in the Task 4.C folder. <https://projectsitesb.geosyntec.com/8/SW033129-0547/_layouts/15/start.aspx#/SitePages/Home.aspx?RootFolder=%2F8%2FSW033129-0547%2FShared%20Documents%2FTask%204%20-%20SW%20Capture%20and%20Use%20along%20County%20Roads%2FTask%204.C%20Submittal&FolderCTID=0x012000BB8DC2F928EF0944BBEB156EFA200989&View=%7B09ED6256-943F-4252-81B3-27AB4979A7B9%7D>  The Excel includes the attributes and potential project areas previously submitted under Task 3.B and consists of the ranking of the potential project areas based on the framework we discussed on the call yesterday.

The following tabs are included for the Task 4.C deliverable:

*	FAC_INF_DIV_RESULTS: This tab provides the attribute results for each segment along with the infiltration and diversion potential project opportunities and their scores (provided all the way on the right of the table). Scoring is based on the “Scoring Points Input” sheet.
*	Attributes, Rationale, and Desc: This tab provides the rationale, sources, and description of the various attributes added to each ROW (as previously submitted). We also included additional attributes to support the prioritization (“Additional Criteria for Prioritization”). “Project Opportunities” describes how project opportunities were identified. Additionally, the “Potential BMP Type” provides an attribute for whether the segment is feasible for an infiltration BMP (in cases where segments are feasible for infiltration, it may not be feasible based on surface soils or groundwater data). Additionally, the prioritization does not account for actual volume diverted, but rather proxies for volume expected for each water supply method.
*	Scoring Points Input: This tab provides the prioritization framework breakdown, including the various benefits, metrics, criteria, description, and points. You can change the point values in the yellow columns to change the percent contribution between categories. We have also included a very high level criteria for funding, based on the type of water supply method (infiltration, diversion, onsite capture and use). Note that we also changed the scoring to individually score each of the water supply methods to capture the 70%/10%/20% breakdown. So the points for each benefit may look a bit differently than the presentation you received yesterday.
*	Top Sites: This tab identifies the preliminary Top Project opportunities identified based on the highest scores. These have been grouped together based on physical location and their ranking. These have not been reviewed in detail for actual feasibility, but we plan to review the top sites in more detail during the next Task 4.D, which will also include a site visit. This list may change as we dive into the top project areas.

It would be great to receive your feedback on the following items by June 21:

*	Prioritization scheme and proposed percentage breakdown along with the specific criteria for each.
*	Any areas or segments you may want to exclude or look more into.
*	Any additional areas for potential surface ponding (if known).

Thank you!

DPR is the next frontier in sustainable water supply management. One of the biggest impediments to more widespread DPR is the lack of regulatory certainty – something that is beginning to change.

DPR rulemaking was recently completed in Colorado and is currently underway in several states including California, Arizona, and Florida. Cc: Ruiz, Elise <Elise.Ruiz@sdcounty.ca.gov>; Boerboom, Jacob <Jacob.Boerboom@sdcounty.ca.gov>; Shalini Vajjhala <shalini@refocuspartners.com>; Megan Otto <MMOtto@geosyntec.com>; Gaines, Stephanie <Stephanie.Gaines@sdcounty.ca.gov>; Stephanie Zinn <Stephanie.Zinn@geosyntec.com>
Subject: [External] Interview Follow Up - San Diego Regional Water Equity Project

Jordan, Kim, and Garrett

Thanks again for your participation in the interview for this project and hope all is well.  We do have a couple follow up questions we’d love your input on below.  These are not meant to take more than 10-15 minutes of your time and it would greatly benefit our analysis. Don't hesitate to reach out with any questions.

1. What do you see as the biggest risk(s) to the San Diego and Imperial region’s water supply portfolio with respect to long-term resilience? Based on info available in the SDIRWM (http://sdirwmp.org/pdf/SDIRWM_Final_2019_IRWM_Plan_compiled_2Jul19.pdf), residential water supply demand constitutes the largest (65%) demand, and population (residential) growth is also projected to increase. Some projections show that residential land use will grow by 56% by the year 2050 (from 2012 numbers). As such, I think that the biggest challenge to the water supply portfolio is residential population growth and associated increases in residential water supply demand. As the water demand increases along with population growth, there will also be compounding factors that may have negative effects on long-term water supply/portfolio resilience. These include economic volatility/strains that may affect how water is imported (infrastructure) and obtained (e.g., changes in agreements with Metropolitan Water District, Imperial Irrigation District, and other states/water supply networks along the Colorado river), climate change impacts to water supply locally as well as in distant source watersheds (e.g., Colorado river watersheds, and northern California snow pack), economic pressures to local agriculture growers related to cost of living increases, cost of water increases, climate change to plant growth/health, droughts, fires, and other changes that will make it more difficult to operate an agriculture operation locally. Other risks to the water supply portfolio include stakeholder support for funding/building water supply diversification, such as for local desal and water reclamation projects where some stakeholders may be averse to due to differing political/environmental protections perspectives.   The following snips are from the SDIRWM 2019 Plan.

2. Can you identify the top three water management projects types/solutions that you’d recommend the San Diego and Imperial region allocate more funding/effort towards? The top three project types that I feel will have the biggest regional impact to support water resiliency and which should have the majority of funding/efforts are desalination, regional water recycling, and conservation.

                                                         i.      Regional Water Recycling --> #1

                                                       ii.      Localized On-Site Reuse (Graywater) --> #2

                                                     iii.      Stormwater Capture and Reuse/Recycling -->#2

                                                     iv.      Desalination --> #1

                                                       v.      Storage Management - Increase Dam Capacity --> #4

                                                     vi.      Storage Management - Manage Groundwater Recharge --> #3

                                                   vii.      Conservation --> #1

3. Which of the following water supply solutions do you view at the “most at risk” in terms of being a reliable, long term source of water for the region? Which is “least at risk”?  Write “most risk” and “least risk” after two of the options below, and elaborate in 1-2 sentences on why.

                                                         i.      Regional Water Recycling --> I see this as an effective way to increase local water reliability, and this may be easier to accomplish than desal projects due to political/stakeholder support and/or opposition. E.g., some environmental groups may not support desal projects based on valuation of environmental impacts.

                                                       ii.      Localized On-Site Reuse (Graywater)

                                                     iii.      Stormwater Capture and Reuse/Recycling

                                                     iv.      Desalination --> I see this as potentially the most effective, positive impact for increasing local water supply resiliency. Desal should focus first on addressing brackish groundwater, then sea water. See diversification costs in snip, from the SDIRWM 2019 Plan.

                                                       v.      Storage Management - Increase Dam Capacity --> I think this is the most at-risk, and cannot be a reliable source of water for our region since increasing dam capacity does not directly result in improved water supply. Rather, the focus should be more on conservation, reuse, and desalination which would increase our local water supply/diversify our local portfolio. Conservation should include on-site water recycling, stormwater capture and use, and groundwater recharge practices.

                                                     vi.      Storage Management - Manage Groundwater Recharge
                                                   vii.      Conservation

Thank you in advance!

Ben

Good afternoon Heather,

I hope all is well and that you've been enjoying the start to summer!

I wanted to circle back on the previous conversations we've had about the comprehensive report that is being developed for the Board directed Regional Water Equity effort <https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/osej/waterequity/> , as we are preparing to begin the review process starting in August. I know I have mentioned a general timeline of the project for outreach and the comprehensive report, and we are now finalizing the next steps and wanted to confirm if you or anyone from your team would be available for support for review of the comprehensive report.

Our team would greatly appreciate your time to support as a technical reviewer for the draft "Water Sustainability" and "Stormwater Capture in Affordable Housing Units" chapters, which is being developed by Geosyntec and LeSar Development Consultants. Both of these chapters will have focus areas of recommended best practices, which include graywater reuse. We anticipate to receive the first draft by August 11 and review through August 16. These chapters will be added to the comprehensive report, which will be reviewed by Sarah Aghassi before going through public comment. I've summarized these requests and dates below:

Comprehensive Report Review

*       Review first draft of "Water Sustainability" and "Stormwater Capture in Affordable Housing Units" chapters August 11 - August 16

*       Review before DCAO review August 29 - September 5

*       Review after public comment October 15 - October 20

I've attached the project fact sheet for your reference. Please let me know if these dates work for you and your team, or if you would like more information on these efforts. I'm happy to answer any questions you may have or set up a call to talk through this more.

1 pm PT | 4 pm ET | (1 hour 15 minutes)
Free to WateReuse members

Join us for an informative webcast next month on Direct Potable Reuse (DPR) state policy.

DPR is the next frontier in sustainable water supply management. One of the biggest impediments to more widespread DPR is the lack of regulatory certainty – something that is beginning to change.

DPR rulemaking was recently completed in Colorado and is currently underway in several states including California, Arizona, and Florida. Wherever DPR regulations are under consideration, WateReuse Association State Sections and members are leading the charge. Together we have developed regulatory frameworks, secured legislation, and engaged with regulators to move processes forward. Join us to learn about the advocacy efforts that are moving DPR ahead across the country, the unique challenges and approaches to DPR in several states, and an update on the status of regulations.

title: RE_ Friday's quarterly meeting.msg
subject: RE: Friday's quarterly meeting
body:
For the first meeting, we'll discuss what we want to get out of the meetings.  Basically, the vision is for each group to share their progress towards their watershed's goals.  We'll start with what the watershed strategies says each group is doing, then each group can update everyone on status.  I'm hoping we'll create a simple list the first meeting, and then future meetings we can just quickly go through it together for each subsequent meeting.

It's meant to be high level, a quick check-in.  Each group to talk about 10 minutes, we'll identify any areas where we need to thread, and then we can wrap up with any next steps.  I don't think you'll need to prepare for it, I think everyone will know where tasks are at a high level, and any details can be researched/provided later if needed.

Christine A. Tolchin | Watershed Program Manager | Cell: 619-988-9748 |www.sdcounty.ca.gov/stormwater <http://www.sdcounty.ca.gov/stormwater>

Subject: FW: Geosyntec Capacity Requests

Hi Stephanie,

Jamie Milani is making two requests for additional capacity on the Geosyntec contract. Wanted to get your ok before proceeding. Info below:

1.	$35k increase to existing task order #23 (SLR P3).

subject: RE: RWER - Task 5 - Catalog of Recommendations for Scaling up Sustainable Agriculture Projects
attachments: RWER - Sustainable Agriculture Catalog JB Comments.docx
body:
Good afternoon all,

Thank you for the work on this! The County team has completed review and we've included a few high-level points after our review to pair with comments throughout the document.

Please reference these recommendations as you address overall comments:

*        Really great context setting in the first two pages. A recommendation is to add more at the end of the second page about what the columns are of the final table and why they matter. Such as, defining relative cost, relative difficulty to implement, etc. and what it is relative to and how it's been looked at specifically for the San Diego region.  Also, pre-viewing some of the strategies here would be an opportunity to introduce some of the methods and strategies (high-level).

*        Page 2 - please define these 10 categories, or provide examples on how this applies to our region to give some context before the individual tables.

*        Best practices tables provide overall/general strategies and awareness items. However, curious if some of the content from the tables on page 13 could be fused into the 10 tables to provide the local context on how a national best practice could be implemented/carried out at the regional level.

o   This may make the tables to big and complex - therefore, consider adding more context at the beginning that acknowledges recent and ongoing programs/activities, and practices

*        The best practices tables should really help set up the specific opportunities starting on page 18. However, there are a lot of terms/programs/approaches that are being referenced in the opportunities table for the first time and if someone isn't plugged into this industry, they may not know and be   able to follow (for example defining payment for ecosystem services).

*        We also need to know what "relative" means in the three headings? Relative to what - to national best practices or another factor? The San Diego region has unique geography and hydrology, as well as cost of water/land.

*        Please also define "drought resilience value" - and for "degree of difficulty" to implement?

*        Recommend an approach to streamline narration of Best Practice tables or provide an overview for the reader of what to expect when reading this section

*        Ensure we add "region" or "regionally" when mentioning "San Diego" to ensure reader understand we are talking about the region and not the City of San Diego

*        Page 7 - (more of a question) curious if anything came up about a slaughterhouse? The San Diego region currently does not have one and we get questions about this every so often - animals have to go up to riverside or LA county for this

*        Page 8 - intro -- farmers are the busiest and operate on such a small income - they do not have time to go to workshops and field trip days -- could this be compensated? Or how do we incentivize the education/training when we see not many go into farming

Thank you,

Elise

Subject: [External] RWER Task 4.C - ROW Prioritization Framework

Hi Stephanie,

The Task 4.C deliverable is on Sharepoint in the Task 4.C folder. <https://projectsitesb.geosyntec.com/8/SW033129-0547/_layouts/15/start.aspx#/SitePages/Home.aspx?RootFolder=%2F8%2FSW033129-0547%2FShared%20Documents%2FTask%204%20-%20SW%20Capture%20and%20Use%20along%20County%20Roads%2FTask%204.C%20Submittal&FolderCTID=0x012000BB8DC2F928EF0944BBEB156EFA200989&View=%7B09ED6256-943F-4252-81B3-27AB4979A7B9%7D>  The Excel includes the attributes and potential project areas previously submitted under Task 3.B and consists of the ranking of the potential project areas based on the framework we discussed on the call yesterday.

The following tabs are included for the Task 4.C deliverable:

*	FAC_INF_DIV_RESULTS: This tab provides the attribute results for each segment along with the infiltration and diversion potential project opportunities and their scores (provided all the way on the right of the table). Scoring is based on the "Scoring Points Input" sheet.
*	Attributes, Rationale, and Desc: This tab provides the rationale, sources, and description of the various attributes added to each ROW (as previously submitted). We also included additional attributes to support the prioritization ("Additional Criteria for Prioritization"). "Project Opportunities" describes how project opportunities were identified. Additionally, the "Potential BMP Type" provides an attribute for whether the segment is feasible for an infiltration BMP (in cases where segments are feasible for infiltration, it may not be feasible based on surface soils or groundwater data). Additionally, the prioritization does not account for actual volume diverted, but rather proxies for volume expected for each water supply method.
*	Scoring Points Input: This tab provides the prioritization framework breakdown, including the various benefits, metrics, criteria, description, and points. You can change the point values in the yellow columns to change the percent contribution between categories. We have also included a very high level criteria for funding, based on the type of water supply method (infiltration, diversion, onsite capture and use). Note that we also changed the scoring to individually score each of the water supply methods to capture the 70%/10%/20% breakdown. So the points for each benefit may look a bit differently than the presentation you received yesterday.
*	Top Sites: This tab identifies the preliminary Top Project opportunities identified based on the highest scores. These have been grouped together based on physical location and their ranking. These have not been reviewed in detail for actual feasibility, but we plan to review the top sites in more detail during the next Task 4.D, which will also include a site visit. This list may change as we dive into the top project areas.

It would be great to receive your feedback on the following items by June 21:

*	Prioritization scheme and proposed percentage breakdown along with the specific criteria for each.
*	Any areas or segments you may want to exclude or look more into.
*	Any additional areas for potential surface ponding (if known).

title: Regional Water Equity - Request for Report Review.msg
subject: Regional Water Equity - Request for Report Review
body:
Good afternoon Kimberly,

I hope all is well and that you've been enjoying the start to summer!

Thank you so much for your support in providing additional responses for the stakeholder interview questions for the Regional Water Equity effort <https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/osej/waterequity/> . We are now finalizing the next steps to prepare for the comprehensive report to begin reviewing the first draft in early August. I wanted to connect with you to see if you or anyone from your team would be available for support for review of the report?

Our team would greatly appreciate your time to support as a technical reviewer for the draft "Sustainable Agriculture" chapter, which is being developed by Geosyntec and Re:focus. This chapter will have focus areas of recommended best practices for sustainable farming. We anticipate to receive the first draft by August 11 and review through August 16. This chapter will be added to the comprehensive report, which will be reviewed by Sarah Aghassi before going through public comment. I've summarized these requests and dates below:

Comprehensive Report Review

*       Review first draft of "Sustainable Agriculture" chapter August 11 - August 16

*       Review before DCAO review August 29 - September 5

*       Review after public comment October 15 - October 20

I've attached the project fact sheet for your reference. Please let me know if these dates work for you and your team, or if you would like more information on these efforts. I'm happy to answer any questions you may have or set up a call to talk through this more.

Have a great weekend,

body:
Good afternoon and happy Friday – It is great to e-meet you, Melissa and Corey!

We really appreciate your interest in this effort, as we value insight from USGBC to help inform our research on the important topic of water sustainability.

We are currently in the phase of developing the comprehensive report with the support of our consulting team, and hosting outreach events to gather feedback from our communities. I want to share a few resources with you to give you some details about the Regional Water Equity effort.

*	I’ve attached a project fact sheet which gives background details on this effort, which was directed by our Board of Supervisors, and how we are researching focus area by topic.
*	Please check out the Regional Water Equity website <https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/sdc/lueg/osej/regional_water_equity_project.html>  as well to learn about what has been done so far and what steps we have planned next.

Would your team be available to meet for a 1-hour interview sometime in the next month? We can provide interview questions ahead of time so you can prepare. If you could provide some timeframes, I would happy to coordinate a meeting that would work best for your team’s availability. Again, thank you for your time to collaborate with us and we look forward to connecting!

All the best,

Elise Ruiz, Group Program Manager

Subject: RE: Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water

Hi Stephanie,

Below are my notes on the proposed regulations for Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water.

Regulatory Objective

To establish risk-based log reduction targets for the removal of pathogens such as enteric viruses, parasitic protozoa, and enteric bacteria for non-potable water sources (graywater, rainwater, stormwater, and blackwater), and non-potable end uses (toilet and urinal flushing, clothes washing, irrigation, and dust suppression).

Non-potable water sources

Non-potable end uses

*	Graywater
*	Rainwater
*	Stormwater
*	Blackwater

*	Toilet Flushing
*	Clothes Washing
*	Irrigation
*	Dust Suppression

Exclusions

Regulations do not apply to:

*	Untreated graywater systems that are used exclusively for subsurface irrigation
*	Untreated rainwater systems that are used exclusively for surface, subsurface, or drip irrigation
*	Municipal stormwater capture and use systems

What systems are subject to the new regulations?

An onsite treatment system is subject to the new regulations if:

*	It treats one or more of the following water sources, in whole or in part:

	*	Rainwater
	*	Stormwater
	*	Graywater, or
	*	Blackwater

*	The water sources are collected, treated, and used onsite
*	The treated water is used for non-potable purpose
*	It is connected to community sewer system as its only mean for disposal (blackwater system)

The regulations are intended for building-scale or district-scale (multiple buildings or campus) systems onsite reuse.

Risk-based Water Quality Standard

The goal is to achieve a (microbial) risk level of health protection from pathogens in onsite treated water of 1 in 10,000 infections per person per year. This is consistent with acceptable risk for EPA drinking water regulations and State of CA potable reuse regulations.

There will be two sets of log reduction targets for 1) indoor uses (toilet flushing, clothes washing) and 2) outdoor uses (irrigation, dust control, fire suppression, and car washing).

Schedule

The State Water Board is required to adopt the regulations by December 1, 2022. The Department of Housing and Community Development is required to develop and propose for adoption any necessary corresponding building standards to support the regulations adopted by the State Water Board by December 1, 2023.

The State Water Board’s website <https://www.waterboards.ca.gov/drinking_water/certlic/drinkingwater/onsite_nonpotable_reuse_regulations.html>  for the program offers no evidence that the regulation have been finalized. All procedural dates are listed as TBD.

Let me know if you have any questions you’d like me to look into.

Thanks,

Chris

Subject: RE: Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water

Hi Stephanie,

Below are my notes on the proposed regulations for Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water.

Regulatory Objective

To establish risk-based log reduction targets for the removal of pathogens such as enteric viruses, parasitic protozoa, and enteric bacteria for non-potable water sources (graywater, rainwater, stormwater, and blackwater), and non-potable end uses (toilet and urinal flushing, clothes washing, irrigation, and dust suppression).

Non-potable water sources

Non-potable end uses

*	Graywater
*	Rainwater
*	Stormwater
*	Blackwater

*	Toilet Flushing
*	Clothes Washing
*	Irrigation
*	Dust Suppression

Exclusions

Regulations do not apply to:

*	Untreated graywater systems that are used exclusively for subsurface irrigation
*	Untreated rainwater systems that are used exclusively for surface, subsurface, or drip irrigation
*	Municipal stormwater capture and use systems

What systems are subject to the new regulations?

An onsite treatment system is subject to the new regulations if:

*	It treats one or more of the following water sources, in whole or in part:

	*	Rainwater
	*	Stormwater
	*	Graywater, or
	*	Blackwater

*	The water sources are collected, treated, and used onsite
*	The treated water is used for non-potable purpose
*	It is connected to community sewer system as its only mean for disposal (blackwater system)

The regulations are intended for building-scale or district-scale (multiple buildings or campus) systems onsite reuse.

Risk-based Water Quality Standard

The goal is to achieve a (microbial) risk level of health protection from pathogens in onsite treated water of 1 in 10,000 infections per person per year. This is consistent with acceptable risk for EPA drinking water regulations and State of CA potable reuse regulations.

There will be two sets of log reduction targets for 1) indoor uses (toilet flushing, clothes washing) and 2) outdoor uses (irrigation, dust control, fire suppression, and car washing).

Schedule

The State Water Board is required to adopt the regulations by December 1, 2022. The Department of Housing and Community Development is required to develop and propose for adoption any necessary corresponding building standards to support the regulations adopted by the State Water Board by December 1, 2023.

The State Water Board’s website <https://www.waterboards.ca.gov/drinking_water/certlic/drinkingwater/onsite_nonpotable_reuse_regulations.html>  for the program offers no evidence that the regulation have been finalized. All procedural dates are listed as TBD.

Let me know if you have any questions you’d like me to look into.

Thanks,

Chris

Subject: RE: Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water

Hi Stephanie,

Below are my notes on the proposed regulations for Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water.

Regulatory Objective

To establish risk-based log reduction targets for the removal of pathogens such as enteric viruses, parasitic protozoa, and enteric bacteria for non-potable water sources (graywater, rainwater, stormwater, and blackwater), and non-potable end uses (toilet and urinal flushing, clothes washing, irrigation, and dust suppression).

Non-potable water sources

Non-potable end uses

*	Graywater
*	Rainwater
*	Stormwater
*	Blackwater

*	Toilet Flushing
*	Clothes Washing
*	Irrigation
*	Dust Suppression

Exclusions

Regulations do not apply to:

*	Untreated graywater systems that are used exclusively for subsurface irrigation
*	Untreated rainwater systems that are used exclusively for surface, subsurface, or drip irrigation
*	Municipal stormwater capture and use systems

What systems are subject to the new regulations?

An onsite treatment system is subject to the new regulations if:

*	It treats one or more of the following water sources, in whole or in part:

	*	Rainwater
	*	Stormwater
	*	Graywater, or
	*	Blackwater

*	The water sources are collected, treated, and used onsite
*	The treated water is used for non-potable purpose
*	It is connected to community sewer system as its only mean for disposal (blackwater system)

The regulations are intended for building-scale or district-scale (multiple buildings or campus) systems onsite reuse.

Risk-based Water Quality Standard

The goal is to achieve a (microbial) risk level of health protection from pathogens in onsite treated water of 1 in 10,000 infections per person per year. This is consistent with acceptable risk for EPA drinking water regulations and State of CA potable reuse regulations.

There will be two sets of log reduction targets for 1) indoor uses (toilet flushing, clothes washing) and 2) outdoor uses (irrigation, dust control, fire suppression, and car washing).

Schedule

The State Water Board is required to adopt the regulations by December 1, 2022. The Department of Housing and Community Development is required to develop and propose for adoption any necessary corresponding building standards to support the regulations adopted by the State Water Board by December 1, 2023.

The State Water Board’s website <https://www.waterboards.ca.gov/drinking_water/certlic/drinkingwater/onsite_nonpotable_reuse_regulations.html>  for the program offers no evidence that the regulation have been finalized. All procedural dates are listed as TBD.

Let me know if you have any questions you’d like me to look into.

Thanks,

Chris

Subject: [External] Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water

Kacen, Stephanie,

Here is some follow-up information from the Policy and Permitting Subcommittee call. The Division of Drinking Water is developing regulations for the Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water. This is a legislative mandate. California Water Code section 13558 requires the State Water Board to adopt regulations on or before December 1, 2022. I just checked the website, and the schedule is still listed as TBD.

There was a workshop earlier this year and several stormwater representatives participated asking a lot of questions about whether this will affect our capture and use projects. The outcome was including the following statement in the FAQ, which is somewhat reassuring, however this might be something to track as the underlying language in the legislation and the draft information shared remains confusing.

12. Will the proposed regulations apply to municipal stormwater capture and use systems? No. The regulations are intended for building-scale or district-scale (multiple buildings or campus) systems onsite reuse. Watershed-scale stormwater capture projects designed to collect and store watershed-wide runoff during dry or wet weather conditions would not fit into the definition of OTNWS since the collection of the source water (stormwater) and in many cases, the use, are not onsite.

See more info here:  https://www.waterboards.ca.gov/drinking_water/certlic/drinkingwater/onsite_nonpotable_reuse_regulations.html <https://www.waterboards.ca.gov/drinking_water/certlic/drinkingwater/onsite_nonpotable_reuse_regulations.html>

Subject: RWER Data Collection Support: Data for County-owned Land

Hi Krista,

I hope you’re doing well!  I’m working with the Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice (OSEJ) to develop the Regional Water Equity Report (RWER); our team is collecting data to support development of the report. We recently had a meeting with Fali Field, as well, to request GIS location data on County-owned facilities  (not leased). We’ll be receiving an excel data table with locations of owned facilities & CPNs, and she recommend I reach out to you to see if we could receive similar location and CPN data for county owned land. The purpose of this data collection is to identify sites that may be good candidates for stormwater capture, storage and reuse, and diversion projects.

Would you be able to provide the data for our currently owned land parcels? Ideally, we’d like to receive this data by the end of this week (June 2nd); would that be possible? I’m also happy to meet with you and provide more context on the project, and have included a bit of background on the report we’re developing the reason for the request.

Background

In September 2022, our Board directed staff to analyze drought management and water sustainability practices and to address our region’s reliance on water resources. The effort is binational and regional in scale and includes a comprehensive regional assessment of San Diego County, as well as interviews with Imperial County and water agencies in Tijuana to identify recommendations (projects) to support addressing the drought equitably. Proposed recommendations are to be aligned with California’s Water Supply Strategy, which includes creating new storage for water to capitalize on big storms, recycle/reuse water to enable safter use of wastewater that we currently discharge to the ocean, improve efficient water use and conservation and creating “new water” through stormwater capture/reuse, desalination, and diversification of supplies.

The OSEJ is leading this multi-county/binational effort, and DPW WPP is helping to collect data, among other tasks. We’re currently at the end of our data collection process and conducting stakeholder interviews with support of our consulting team. Data collection examples include identifying opportunities on county-owned land/facilities where stormwater capture/use and storage can be implemented, as well as opportunities for water diversion.

Best,

body:
Hi Stephanie,

For your review under Task 3.A, we have compiled the County facilities based on both the County Properties and Buildings data (collectively called “facilities”) provided by County staff. The intent is to confirm the use of these specific facilities in the screening under Task 3.B, meaning:

1.	That this list includes all facilities to be screened, no critical facilities are missing, and
2.	That this list does not include any facilities that should not be screened (e.g., leased sites, specific departments, etc.).

You can filter the table for the department, type of building, tenure (column BD, i.e., owned vs. leased), etc..

We also identified 21 missing geolocators (APNs, addresses) from the buildings file which are needed to locate them spatially and 57 APNs within both the Buildings and Properties files which are not identified in the base Parcel file (SDEP_SANGIS_PARCEL). The specific facilities with these missing parameters are shown in the attached Excel on “Notes” tab.

All files are also on SharePoint in the Task 3A Deliverable <https://projectsitesb.geosyntec.com/8/SW033129-0547/_layouts/15/start.aspx#/SitePages/Home.aspx?RootFolder=%2F8%2FSW033129%2D0547%2FShared%20Documents%2FTask%203%20%2D%20SW%20Capture%20and%20Use%20at%20County%20Parks%20and%20Facilities%2FTask%203A%20Deliverable&FolderCTID=0x012000BB8DC2F928EF0944BBEB156EFA200989&View=%7B09ED6256%2D943F%2D4252%2D81B3%2D27AB4979A7B9%7D>  folder.
