Subject: RE: Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water

Hi Stephanie,

Below are my notes on the proposed regulations for Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water.

Regulatory Objective

To establish risk-based log reduction targets for the removal of pathogens such as enteric viruses, parasitic protozoa, and enteric bacteria for non-potable water sources (graywater, rainwater, stormwater, and blackwater), and non-potable end uses (toilet and urinal flushing, clothes washing, irrigation, and dust suppression).

Non-potable water sources

Non-potable end uses

*	Graywater
*	Rainwater
*	Stormwater
*	Blackwater

*	Toilet Flushing
*	Clothes Washing
*	Irrigation
*	Dust Suppression

Exclusions

Regulations do not apply to:

*	Untreated graywater systems that are used exclusively for subsurface irrigation
*	Untreated rainwater systems that are used exclusively for surface, subsurface, or drip irrigation
*	Municipal stormwater capture and use systems

What systems are subject to the new regulations?

An onsite treatment system is subject to the new regulations if:

*	It treats one or more of the following water sources, in whole or in part:

	*	Rainwater
	*	Stormwater
	*	Graywater, or
	*	Blackwater

*	The water sources are collected, treated, and used onsite
*	The treated water is used for non-potable purpose
*	It is connected to community sewer system as its only mean for disposal (blackwater system)

The regulations are intended for building-scale or district-scale (multiple buildings or campus) systems onsite reuse.

Risk-based Water Quality Standard

The goal is to achieve a (microbial) risk level of health protection from pathogens in onsite treated water of 1 in 10,000 infections per person per year. This is consistent with acceptable risk for EPA drinking water regulations and State of CA potable reuse regulations.

There will be two sets of log reduction targets for 1) indoor uses (toilet flushing, clothes washing) and 2) outdoor uses (irrigation, dust control, fire suppression, and car washing).

Schedule

The State Water Board is required to adopt the regulations by December 1, 2022. The Department of Housing and Community Development is required to develop and propose for adoption any necessary corresponding building standards to support the regulations adopted by the State Water Board by December 1, 2023.

The State Water Board's website <https://www.waterboards.ca.gov/drinking_water/certlic/drinkingwater/onsite_nonpotable_reuse_regulations.html>  for the program offers no evidence that the regulation have been finalized. All procedural dates are listed as TBD.

Let me know if you have any questions you'd like me to look into.

Thanks,

Chris

Subject: [External] Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water

Kacen, Stephanie,

Here is some follow-up information from the Policy and Permitting Subcommittee call. The Division of Drinking Water is developing regulations for the Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water. This is a legislative mandate. California Water Code section 13558 requires the State Water Board to adopt regulations on or before December 1, 2022. I just checked the website, and the schedule is still listed as TBD.

There was a workshop earlier this year and several stormwater representatives participated asking a lot of questions about whether this will affect our capture and use projects. The outcome was including the following statement in the FAQ, which is somewhat reassuring, however this might be something to track as the underlying language in the legislation and the draft information shared remains confusing.

12. Will the proposed regulations apply to municipal stormwater capture and use systems? No. The regulations are intended for building-scale or district-scale (multiple buildings or campus) systems onsite reuse. Watershed-scale stormwater capture projects designed to collect and store watershed-wide runoff during dry or wet weather conditions would not fit into the definition of OTNWS since the collection of the source water (stormwater) and in many cases, the use, are not onsite.

See more info here:  https://www.waterboards.ca.gov/drinking_water/certlic/drinkingwater/onsite_nonpotable_reuse_regulations.html

Subject: RWER Data Collection Support: Data for County-owned Land

Hi Krista,

I hope you’re doing well!  I’m working with the Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice (OSEJ) to develop the Regional Water Equity Report (RWER); our team is collecting data to support development of the report. We recently had a meeting with Fali Field, as well, to request GIS location data on County-owned facilities  (not leased). We’ll be receiving an excel data table with locations of owned facilities & CPNs, and she recommend I reach out to you to see if we could receive similar location and CPN data for county owned land. The purpose of this data collection is to identify sites that may be good candidates for stormwater capture, storage and reuse, and diversion projects.

Would you be able to provide the data for our currently owned land parcels? Ideally, we’d like to receive this data by the end of this week (June 2nd); would that be possible? I’m also happy to meet with you and provide more context on the project, and have included a bit of background on the report we’re developing the reason for the request.

Background

In September 2022, our Board directed staff to analyze drought management and water sustainability practices and to address our region’s reliance on water resources. The effort is binational and regional in scale and includes a comprehensive regional assessment of San Diego County, as well as interviews with Imperial County and water agencies in Tijuana to identify recommendations (projects) to support addressing the drought equitably. Proposed recommendations are to be aligned with California’s Water Supply Strategy, which includes creating new storage for water to capitalize on big storms, recycle/reuse water to enable safter use of wastewater that we currently discharge to the ocean, improve efficient water use and conservation and creating “new water” through stormwater capture/reuse, desalination, and diversification of supplies.

The OSEJ is leading this multi-county/binational effort, and DPW WPP is helping to collect data, among other tasks. We’re currently at the end of our data collection process and conducting stakeholder interviews with support of our consulting team. Data collection examples include identifying opportunities on county-owned land/facilities where stormwater capture/use and storage can be implemented, as well as opportunities for water diversion.

Best,

subject: RE: Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water - Addendum 2 RWER
body:
Hi Megan,

I'm so glad you're staying on top of this! Let this email serve as NTP on Task 6C, as well as provide an extended scope/cost for Task 1, Project Management, accordingly.

Christine is back in the office next week, so I'll be more available then to discuss tasks and budget, if needed, then issue the amended NTP.

Best,

Stephanie Gaines

PM, DPW WPP

619-964-8337

From: Megan Otto <MMOtto@Geosyntec.com>
Sent: Friday, June 23, 2023 11:48 AM
To: Gaines, Stephanie <Stephanie.Gaines@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Subject: [External] RE: Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water - Addendum 2 RWER

Hi Stephanie,

Our financial support staff are working on formal edits to the Task 6C scope of work. In general, the scope will include:

*	Budget estimate is $72,500
*	The deliverable would be approximately 10-30 more pages, in addition to the document provided by Jacob, for an up-to-50 page report to include as a chapter in the larger context

Does that seem in line with expectations? Given the timeline, they will need to start on Monday, so would it be possible to receive NTP via email for just Task 6C?  I will still plan to send the redline scope of work and corresponding budget for Tasks 6C, 6D, and 7E early next week, but would like to get this task going ASAP if at all possible.

Lastly, since the timeline is being extended from December to March, would I be possible to also increase the Task 1 (PM) budget to cover that coordination? If that sounds ok, I will also include that in the revised amendment.

Thanks,

Megan

Megan M. Otto, PE (CA)

Direct: 619.810.4043

Subject: RE: Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water

Hi Stephanie,

Below are my notes on the proposed regulations for Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water.

Regulatory Objective

To establish risk-based log reduction targets for the removal of pathogens such as enteric viruses, parasitic protozoa, and enteric bacteria for non-potable water sources (graywater, rainwater, stormwater, and blackwater), and non-potable end uses (toilet and urinal flushing, clothes washing, irrigation, and dust suppression).

Non-potable water sources

Non-potable end uses

*	Graywater
*	Rainwater
*	Stormwater
*	Blackwater

*	Toilet Flushing
*	Clothes Washing
*	Irrigation
*	Dust Suppression

Exclusions

Regulations do not apply to:

*	Untreated graywater systems that are used exclusively for subsurface irrigation
*	Untreated rainwater systems that are used exclusively for surface, subsurface, or drip irrigation
*	Municipal stormwater capture and use systems

What systems are subject to the new regulations?

An onsite treatment system is subject to the new regulations if:

*	It treats one or more of the following water sources, in whole or in part:

	*	Rainwater
	*	Stormwater
	*	Graywater, or
	*	Blackwater

*	The water sources are collected, treated, and used onsite
*	The treated water is used for non-potable purpose
*	It is connected to community sewer system as its only mean for disposal (blackwater system)

The regulations are intended for building-scale or district-scale (multiple buildings or campus) systems onsite reuse.

Risk-based Water Quality Standard

The goal is to achieve a (microbial) risk level of health protection from pathogens in onsite treated water of 1 in 10,000 infections per person per year. This is consistent with acceptable risk for EPA drinking water regulations and State of CA potable reuse regulations.

There will be two sets of log reduction targets for 1) indoor uses (toilet flushing, clothes washing) and 2) outdoor uses (irrigation, dust control, fire suppression, and car washing).

Schedule

The State Water Board is required to adopt the regulations by December 1, 2022. The Department of Housing and Community Development is required to develop and propose for adoption any necessary corresponding building standards to support the regulations adopted by the State Water Board by December 1, 2023.

The State Water Board's website <https://www.waterboards.ca.gov/drinking_water/certlic/drinkingwater/onsite_nonpotable_reuse_regulations.html>  for the program offers no evidence that the regulation have been finalized. All procedural dates are listed as TBD.

Let me know if you have any questions you'd like me to look into.

Thanks,

Chris

12. Will the proposed regulations apply to municipal stormwater capture and use systems? Subject: RE: Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water

Hi Stephanie,

Below are my notes on the proposed regulations for Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water.

Regulatory Objective

To establish risk-based log reduction targets for the removal of pathogens such as enteric viruses, parasitic protozoa, and enteric bacteria for non-potable water sources (graywater, rainwater, stormwater, and blackwater), and non-potable end uses (toilet and urinal flushing, clothes washing, irrigation, and dust suppression).

Non-potable water sources

Non-potable end uses

*	Graywater
*	Rainwater
*	Stormwater
*	Blackwater

*	Toilet Flushing
*	Clothes Washing
*	Irrigation
*	Dust Suppression

Exclusions

Regulations do not apply to:

*	Untreated graywater systems that are used exclusively for subsurface irrigation
*	Untreated rainwater systems that are used exclusively for surface, subsurface, or drip irrigation
*	Municipal stormwater capture and use systems

What systems are subject to the new regulations?

An onsite treatment system is subject to the new regulations if:

*	It treats one or more of the following water sources, in whole or in part:

	*	Rainwater
	*	Stormwater
	*	Graywater, or
	*	Blackwater

*	The water sources are collected, treated, and used onsite
*	The treated water is used for non-potable purpose
*	It is connected to community sewer system as its only mean for disposal (blackwater system)

The regulations are intended for building-scale or district-scale (multiple buildings or campus) systems onsite reuse.

Risk-based Water Quality Standard

The goal is to achieve a (microbial) risk level of health protection from pathogens in onsite treated water of 1 in 10,000 infections per person per year. This is consistent with acceptable risk for EPA drinking water regulations and State of CA potable reuse regulations.

There will be two sets of log reduction targets for 1) indoor uses (toilet flushing, clothes washing) and 2) outdoor uses (irrigation, dust control, fire suppression, and car washing).

Schedule

The State Water Board is required to adopt the regulations by December 1, 2022. The Department of Housing and Community Development is required to develop and propose for adoption any necessary corresponding building standards to support the regulations adopted by the State Water Board by December 1, 2023.

The State Water Board's website <https://www.waterboards.ca.gov/drinking_water/certlic/drinkingwater/onsite_nonpotable_reuse_regulations.html>  for the program offers no evidence that the regulation have been finalized. All procedural dates are listed as TBD.

Let me know if you have any questions you'd like me to look into.

Thanks,

Chris

Subject: [External] Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water

Kacen, Stephanie,

Here is some follow-up information from the Policy and Permitting Subcommittee call. The Division of Drinking Water is developing regulations for the Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water. This is a legislative mandate. California Water Code section 13558 requires the State Water Board to adopt regulations on or before December 1, 2022. I just checked the website, and the schedule is still listed as TBD.

There was a workshop earlier this year and several stormwater representatives participated asking a lot of questions about whether this will affect our capture and use projects. The outcome was including the following statement in the FAQ, which is somewhat reassuring, however this might be something to track as the underlying language in the legislation and the draft information shared remains confusing.

12. Will the proposed regulations apply to municipal stormwater capture and use systems? No. The regulations are intended for building-scale or district-scale (multiple buildings or campus) systems onsite reuse. Watershed-scale stormwater capture projects designed to collect and store watershed-wide runoff during dry or wet weather conditions would not fit into the definition of OTNWS since the collection of the source water (stormwater) and in many cases, the use, are not onsite.

See more info here:  https://www.waterboards.ca.gov/drinking_water/certlic/drinkingwater/onsite_nonpotable_reuse_regulations.html

Sandy

Cc: Stephanie Zinn <Stephanie.Zinn@Geosyntec.com <mailto:Stephanie.Zinn@Geosyntec.com> >; Megan Otto <mmotto@geosyntec.com <mailto:mmotto@geosyntec.com> >; Ruiz, Elise <Elise.Ruiz@sdcounty.ca.gov <mailto:Elise.Ruiz@sdcounty.ca.gov> >
Subject: Regional Water Equity Project - Flood Control follow up
Importance: High

Dear Flood Control Team,

Thank you again for participating in the Water Equity Project interview several months ago.  We are just about done wrapping up the other interviews and throughout the process have established a set of common follow-up questions to help with our analysis.  Would your team be able to provide feedback on the three questions below?  This is intended to take less than 10-15 minutes.  Please let us know if you have any questions.

1.	What do you see as the biggest risk(s) to the San Diego region’s water supply portfolio with respect to long-term resilience?

2.	Can you identify the top three water management projects types/solutions that you’d recommend the San Diego region allocate more funding/effort towards?

	a.	Regional Water Recycling
	b.	Localized On-Site Reuse (Graywater)
	c.	Stormwater Capture and Reuse/Recycling
	d.	Desalination
	e.	Storage Management - Increase Dam Capacity
	f.	Storage Management - Manage Groundwater Recharge
	g.	Conservation

3.	Which of the following water supply solutions do you view at the “most at risk” in terms of being a reliable, long term source of water for the region? Which is “least at risk”?  Write “most risk” and “least risk” after two of the options below, and elaborate in 1-2 sentences on why.

	a.	Regional Water Recycling
	b.	Localized On-Site Reuse (Graywater)
	c.	Stormwater Capture and Reuse/Recycling

Subject: RE: Research/Response on Stormwater Capture/Use

Hi Stephanie,

I am not very familiar with this subject matter but here's my attempt at an answer. I put in more language than is probably necessary thinking you could take out whatever you don't want.

1.                   What are the County water quality (i.e., treatment) requirements for using rainwater outdoors / indoors? We're unable to locate standards in either the County or City of San Diego codes.

Answer - In general, onsite collection of rainwater from roof runoff is permissible when the collected water is to be used onsite for an outdoor non-potable end use. Existing regulations for untreated rainwater systems that are used exclusively for surface, sub-surface, or drip irrigation are in Chapter 16 of the California Plumbing Code.

All recycled water in California, including stormwater captured for beneficial use, is subject to Title 22 of California's Water Recycling Criteria (California Code of Regulations, Title 22, Division 4, Chapter 3). Under this regulation, the San Diego Regional Water Quality Control Board has developed treatment standards for different beneficial uses through consultation with the California Department of Public Health. The regulation sets out required treatment levels (e.g. tertiary or secondary) required for different uses, such as park irrigation or industrial use (22 CCR 60301-60355).

The State Water Board is currently developing regulations for onsite treatment and reuse of non-potable water (SBDDW-22-001). These regulations will be applicable to onsite treatment and reuse of non-potable water for non-potable end uses in multifamily residential, commercial, and mixed used buildings.

Hopefully this is helpful.let me know if you need anything else.

Thanks,

Chris

From: Gaines, Stephanie <Stephanie.Gaines@sdcounty.ca.gov <mailto:Stephanie.Gaines@sdcounty.ca.gov> >

One more nugget of info, from the study:

"Title 22 of California's Water Recycling Criteria refers to California state guidelines for how treated and recycled water is discharged and used. The standards also require the state's Department of Health Services to develop and enforce water and bacteriological treatment standards for water recycling and reuse. However, whether or not Title 22 would apply to irrigation projects is unclear at this time."

Subject: RWER Data Collection Support: Data for County-owned Land

Hi Krista,

I hope you’re doing well!  I’m working with the Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice (OSEJ) to develop the Regional Water Equity Report (RWER); our team is collecting data to support development of the report. We recently had a meeting with Fali Field, as well, to request GIS location data on County-owned facilities  (not leased). We’ll be receiving an excel data table with locations of owned facilities & CPNs, and she recommend I reach out to you to see if we could receive similar location and CPN data for county owned land. The purpose of this data collection is to identify sites that may be good candidates for stormwater capture, storage and reuse, and diversion projects.

Would you be able to provide the data for our currently owned land parcels? Ideally, we’d like to receive this data by the end of this week (June 2nd); would that be possible? I’m also happy to meet with you and provide more context on the project, and have included a bit of background on the report we’re developing the reason for the request.

Background

In September 2022, our Board directed staff to analyze drought management and water sustainability practices and to address our region’s reliance on water resources. The effort is binational and regional in scale and includes a comprehensive regional assessment of San Diego County, as well as interviews with Imperial County and water agencies in Tijuana to identify recommendations (projects) to support addressing the drought equitably. Proposed recommendations are to be aligned with California’s Water Supply Strategy, which includes creating new storage for water to capitalize on big storms, recycle/reuse water to enable safter use of wastewater that we currently discharge to the ocean, improve efficient water use and conservation and creating “new water” through stormwater capture/reuse, desalination, and diversification of supplies.

The OSEJ is leading this multi-county/binational effort, and DPW WPP is helping to collect data, among other tasks. We’re currently at the end of our data collection process and conducting stakeholder interviews with support of our consulting team. Data collection examples include identifying opportunities on county-owned land/facilities where stormwater capture/use and storage can be implemented, as well as opportunities for water diversion.

Best,

Subject: RWER Data Collection Support: Data for County-owned Land

Hi Krista,

I hope you’re doing well!  I’m working with the Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice (OSEJ) to develop the Regional Water Equity Report (RWER); our team is collecting data to support development of the report. We recently had a meeting with Fali Field, as well, to request GIS location data on County-owned facilities  (not leased). We’ll be receiving an excel data table with locations of owned facilities & CPNs, and she recommend I reach out to you to see if we could receive similar location and CPN data for county owned land. The purpose of this data collection is to identify sites that may be good candidates for stormwater capture, storage and reuse, and diversion projects.

Would you be able to provide the data for our currently owned land parcels? Ideally, we’d like to receive this data by the end of this week (June 2nd); would that be possible? I’m also happy to meet with you and provide more context on the project, and have included a bit of background on the report we’re developing the reason for the request.

Background

In September 2022, our Board directed staff to analyze drought management and water sustainability practices and to address our region’s reliance on water resources. The effort is binational and regional in scale and includes a comprehensive regional assessment of San Diego County, as well as interviews with Imperial County and water agencies in Tijuana to identify recommendations (projects) to support addressing the drought equitably. Proposed recommendations are to be aligned with California’s Water Supply Strategy, which includes creating new storage for water to capitalize on big storms, recycle/reuse water to enable safter use of wastewater that we currently discharge to the ocean, improve efficient water use and conservation and creating “new water” through stormwater capture/reuse, desalination, and diversification of supplies.

The OSEJ is leading this multi-county/binational effort, and DPW WPP is helping to collect data, among other tasks. We’re currently at the end of our data collection process and conducting stakeholder interviews with support of our consulting team. Data collection examples include identifying opportunities on county-owned land/facilities where stormwater capture/use and storage can be implemented, as well as opportunities for water diversion.

Best,

title: Research_Response on Stormwater Capture_Use.msg
subject: Research/Response on Stormwater Capture/Use
body:
Hi Chris - I have another request, which I hope will be a quick one.

Another consulting firm is gathering data for the Regional Water Equity Report (RWER), this time the Affordable Housing component. One question is related to regulations and requirements around capturing and using stormwater "indoors and outdoors". Our rain barrel, and onsite collection efforts from roof runoff (think cisterns, or larger scale capture from onsite runoff and rooftops for landscapes) are legally allowed; large scale offsite harvesting for larger scale use, are not always. some are subject to Title 22 regulations, or the new SB966 regs you've been watching the state's website for. Additionally, we (County and City, and likely other jurisdictions) don't have regulations related to stormwater (that I'm aware of!) Can you respond to their question below and develop a response that focuses on local stormwater capture/use by tomorrow morning?

Just a note; our SWCFS tech memos do have some language on regulations, primarily related to "regulatory ambiguity", meaning we don't' have clear or specific requirements for stormwater use. We know treatment for larger scale (think parks, golf courses) above ground irrigation use must meet Title 22 requirements.

1.	What are the County water quality (i.e., treatment) requirements for using rainwater outdoors / indoors? We're unable to locate standards in either the County or City of San Diego codes.

Best,

title: RWER Data Collection Support_ Data for County-owned Land.msg
subject: RWER Data Collection Support: Data for County-owned Land
body:
Hi Krista,

I hope you're doing well!  I'm working with the Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice (OSEJ) to develop the Regional Water Equity Report (RWER); our team is collecting data to support development of the report. We recently had a meeting with Fali Field, as well, to request GIS location data on County-owned facilities  (not leased). We'll be receiving an excel data table with locations of owned facilities & CPNs, and she recommend I reach out to you to see if we could receive similar location and CPN data for county owned land. The purpose of this data collection is to identify sites that may be good candidates for stormwater capture, storage and reuse, and diversion projects.

Would you be able to provide the data for our currently owned land parcels? Ideally, we'd like to receive this data by the end of this week (June 2nd); would that be possible? I'm also happy to meet with you and provide more context on the project, and have included a bit of background on the report we're developing the reason for the request.

Background

In September 2022, our Board directed staff to analyze drought management and water sustainability practices and to address our region's reliance on water resources. The effort is binational and regional in scale and includes a comprehensive regional assessment of San Diego County, as well as interviews with Imperial County and water agencies in Tijuana to identify recommendations (projects) to support addressing the drought equitably. Proposed recommendations are to be aligned with California's Water Supply Strategy, which includes creating new storage for water to capitalize on big storms, recycle/reuse water to enable safter use of wastewater that we currently discharge to the ocean, improve efficient water use and conservation and creating "new water" through stormwater capture/reuse, desalination, and diversification of supplies.

The OSEJ is leading this multi-county/binational effort, and DPW WPP is helping to collect data, among other tasks. We're currently at the end of our data collection process and conducting stakeholder interviews with support of our consulting team. Data collection examples include identifying opportunities on county-owned land/facilities where stormwater capture/use and storage can be implemented, as well as opportunities for water diversion.

Best,

Good afternoon everyone,

We hope you are as excited as we are for the workshop on Monday. Below are some logistical pieces of information for Monday.

Date: Monday, November 7
Time: 8:15-9 Arrival, registration. Begins at 9:00 (Agenda with detailed times on the attached)
Attire: Casual
Refreshments: Refreshments and lunch is provided
Parking: Taking the trolley, rideshare, or carpooling is strongly encouraged.  UCSD has been adjusting parking rates, availability, and incentives for transit to discourage driving - which is part of their overall climate plan!
Directions to 6th College – From North Torrey Pines Road turn right on Muir College Drive. You will see some excited UCSD students that will show you which lot to park in holding signs for the SD County RDF Workshop. They will guide you to 1 of 4 options where you will park in an "A" space.

Cc: Aghassi, Sarah <Sarah.Aghassi@sdcounty.ca.gov>; Lawson, Jennifer <Jennifer.Lawson@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Subject: Agenda and Goals for Nov 7 workshop at UCSD

We began the journey on the Regional Decarbonization Framework (RDF) last year in January when our Board of Supervisors directed us to work with UCSD on bringing the best available science to address a challenge that none of us can address in silos on our own – that of decarbonizing every major emitting sector in the region no matter where the emissions originate, for emissions know no boundaries.

As we are now transitioning from study to implementation, we are asking what can we do collectively in partnership with universities, business, labor and community, that will give us greater efficiencies in scale and speed to address climate change in the most effective and humane way possible. All of us from the County have sustainability embedded within the strategic direction of each of our departments. The goals of this workshop are to think about what more can we do? How do we implement sustainability within our core functions? How do we add value to our existing programs so that they also meet the goals of decarbonization? What new programs can achieve a better outcome?

We are meeting offsite at the Public Engagement Building at UCSD to visualize that greener future.

This workshop begins a new chapter in our relationship with UCSD as an academic partner to help us figure out how to implement this framework. This will be the first in a series of three workshops over our 3-year partnership. The UCSD team will focus on the implementation of the RDF for this workshop.  While of course there are many intersecting issues, the exercises will focus on land-based implications of RDF as well as simply getting everyone more proficient in the vocabulary and implications of the RDF itself. We will also walk through specific scenarios so that we leave the day with a practical understanding of how this framework can inform the work we do on a day-to-day basis in all our departments.

Thank you and looking forward to seeing you on Monday,

Murtaza and Sarah

-----Original Appointment-----
From: Lawson, Jennifer <Jennifer.Lawson@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:Jennifer.Lawson@sdcounty.ca.gov>>
Sent: Tuesday, October 18, 2022 5:12 PM
To: Lawson, Jennifer; Lawson, Jennifer; Cooper, Garrett; Dang, Ha; Alfaro, Suedy; Lintvedt, Inga; Sjoblom, Randall; Beaumont, Anne; Abbott, Jamie; Buonomo, Heather; Glueck, John-Ross; Harbert, Amy; Appel, Rebeca; Baxamusa, Murtaza; De La Rosa, Michael; Demorest, Erin; Hanson, Elise A; Acosta, Migell; Albright, Brian; Oakes, Chelsea; Salomon, Johanna; Trojanowska, Kasia; Bray, Kelly; Farmer, Tyler; Slovick, Mark; Talleh, Rami; Benham, Crystal; James, Kamilah; Gade, Derek; Morgan, William; Pasumarthi, Murali; Pirouzian, Ali; Whipple, Richard; Agahi, Sara; Tubongbanua, Peejay; Rasoulzadeh, Yasamin; Aghassi, Sarah; Boghossian Ambrose, Nicole; Isicson, Robin
Cc: Marchesano, Charles
Subject: All Day Offsite Workshop at UCSD
When: Monday, November 7, 2022 9:00 AM-4:00 PM (UTC-08:00) Pacific Time (US & Canada).
Where: UCSD Social Sciences Public Engagement Building, 7th Floor Terrace

Please join us for an exciting new workshop led by our UCSD collaborators. This workshop would provide an initial convening of County of San Diego leadership and departments engaged in the implementation of decarbonization across municipal functions:  (1) Departmental Sustainability Planning, led by LUEG; (2) the Land Acquisition Roundtable, led by Parks & Recreation; and (3) the renewable energy siting framework in the RDF.  This workshop would focus on the County departments’ short/mid/long term goals towards sustainability; geospatial and policy relationships, conflicts, and potential synergies among and between land acquisition for park, conservation, and recreation purposes; and the extent of land area for new solar and wind energy required by alternative strategies in the RDF.  This approach would help build a common understanding of the policy levers and constraints for the departments in relationship to GHG reduction, and the distribution and extent of each set of land use needs, supporting the goal of identifying potential synergies including opportunities for multi-benefit uses of land for agriculture, water and watershed sustainability, recreation, and regional habitat linkage.

LOCATION: UCSD Social Sciences Public Engagement Building, 7th Floor Conference Room, in the new 6th College at UCSD, 9am - 4pm.
Location: https://goo.gl/maps/WzYiL8WjLEesmtyj8

Specific Parking Instructions will come soon.

body:
Greetings Inga and Kelsey,

OSEJ staff have been invited through the Climate Action Campaign (CAC - a CBO partner) to present next week to the Imperial Beach Democratic Club about the Regional Water Equity effort.

Our current inclination is to decline the invitation and instead suggest that their members participate in one of our upcoming workshops and Closing Assembly. It also might be possible for CAC to offer direct outreach with one of CAC's related programs. They are contracted by OSEJ to elevate awareness and active participation from their communities in support of the RDF - and the regional water equity work falls under this umbrella.

Would appreciate your guidance on this type of engagement with the IBDC or other political group.

Thanks for any insights you can share~

smiles,

eden

Sorry for the late response, as I've been in meetings and in route from LA to SD.

We are very well-versed in handling hecklers and disrupters during these types of meetings. While we don't have a specific drafted response, as it really is a case-by-case basis, please be assured that we are prepared to interrupt this type of behavior. Please let me know if you have any questions or concerns.

title: DRAFT FOR REVIEW_ Fallbrook Planning Group meeting (5_15) summary.msg
subject: DRAFT FOR REVIEW: Fallbrook Planning Group meeting (5/15) summary
body:
Greetings,

Any suggested modifications?

e

Greetings Sarah,

Though I was able to share with you briefly a few highlights from Monday evening's 30-minute RDF overview and discussion with the Fallbrook Planning Group meeting, below is a summary with more detail.

-          Rimga presented and Murtaza attended to provide additional support as needed. Participants included Planning Commissioners and a few members of the public.

-          The group was well-informed about climate policies. They were respectful of and appreciated our work to coordinate efforts as well as its potential to create jobs and attract outside funding. They were skeptical that government agencies are considering all consequences.

Priority concerns included:

-          Unintended negative economic consequences (e.g., electricity and PV/EV charging installation costs, especially as we decarbonize household appliances);

-          Energy reliability (e.g., risk of wildfire from transmission lines; black-outs related to grid capacity)

-          Upstream/downstream readiness (e.g., adequate technology for decarbonization of pick-up trucks and emergency vehicles; locations for end-of-life disposal of batteries, especially if these will be aggregated in rural areas)

-          Land use decisions (e.g., policies to build affordable housing appears in conflict with climate policies to acquire and preserve natural/working lands)

-          Realistic solutions (e.g., "riding a bike" likely unreasonable for travel distances to amenities; association of "incentives" with "more taxes to pay for incentives.")

We're happy to share more if there are blanks to fill in~

Thanks,

eden

May 15, 2023 @ 6:30 PM

In-Person Participation

30-Minute RDF Status Overview with Questions

Invited by Fallbrook Planning Chair Eileen Delaney

Additional coordination with RDF Study Group Chair Stephani Baxter.

Approximately 10-12 attendees (9 Planning Commissioners, 1 member of the public in person, and 2-3 intermittently joining online).

Overall Impression:  The group was well-informed about climate policies, and they were skeptical that government agencies were considering all the consequences of those policies.

Comments reflected deep concern about unintended negative economic consequences; energy reliability; and land use decisions as the region pursues NetZero goals.

*	Concerned about the price of electricity now and more so if they must electrify everything.
*	Concerned about wildfire from transmission lines that might need to be added or upgraded.
*	Concerned about how expensive energy upgrades are (costs of solar; appliances; vehicle chargers and other).
*	Worry about increased blackouts as the grid becomes strained and they no longer have non-electric options.
*	Don't believe the technology of electric pick-up trucks and emergency vehicles are adequate to meet their needs.
*	Concerned about how the region will dispose of lithium-ion batteries when they reach end of life; worry that they'll be dumped in the rural areas and be another source of ignition for wildfires.
*	Resent being presented with solutions like "riding a bike" that might work for coastal areas, but not for the distances in Fallbrook.
*	Associate "incentives" with "more taxes to pay for incentives."
*	Feel that County housing policies to build more affordable housing conflict with County climate policies to acquire and preserve natural and working lands.

They expressed the following positive feedback:

*	They appreciated that RDF was an attempt to coordinate climate efforts across the County.
*	They appreciated that the RDF could help attract federal and state dollars to fund infrastructure and other projects.
*	Seemed receptive about the potential for high quality jobs.
*	They would welcome opportunities to provide more input and feedback.

Rimga Viskanta (She/her/hers <https://www.mypronouns.org/> )

Group Program Manager

Land Use and Environment Group | County of San Diego

1600 Pacific Highway, Room 212, MS: A-6

San Diego, CA 92101

Hope your presentation went great yesterday and that you are enjoying your conference!

  *   Tablecloths - were you able to secure tablecloths? Please let me know at your earliest convenience so that if not, I can bring paper ones

Hi Mohsen and Carl,

Great seeing you today, thanks for coming.  Please see attached for the City of SD PUD agenda that went very smoothly timing wise.  You can use this as a go-by for IBWC (and other future binational entities, e.g. ConAgua and potentially the other retailer).

title: _External_ Feedback on current RDF Proposal.msg
subject: [External] Feedback on current RDF Proposal
body:
Good afternoon,
My name is Yvonne Elkin and I live in Board of Supervisors District 3. I attended the District 3 convening on Feb. 21 and listened to your presentation. I have also been doing a bit of research on my own. As a result of what I have heard and read, I am concerned about the validity of the economic data you have used to come to your recommendation that favors large remote solar and wind farms rather than condensed rooftop and parking lot solar. I urge you and the Board of Supervisors to table this discussion for the short term and ask you to go back and recheck you comparative cost estimates and benefits.
It is my understanding that the Regional Decarbonization Framework identifies remote solar and wind in San Diego County, and/or San Diego County backcountry and Imperial County, as the least-cost pathway to decarbonization. That appears to prioritize building large wind and solar farms in areas some distance from the population centers.
While carefully located wind and solar farms should be considered as part of the overall strategy, they should not be the central pillar of that strategy.
Building energy sources at distance from population centers perpetuates the ability of SDG&E to continue to price gouge its customers for the cost of building and maintaining transmission lines across miles to reach the largest population of users. Long transmission lines also continue to create wildfire risk.
We have seen already that communities in the back country do not want large solar and wind farms in their back yards and in many cases building these facilities in wilderness areas is likely to create environmental damage, especially to habitat.
Alternately, investing in more roof top solar and other metropolitan solar installations like on the top of office buildings and as parking lot shade cover keeps the energy generation local and significantly reduces the need to transmit electricity long distances. It also significantly helps the solar customer with the ever-growing cost of electricity.
I recently read that the grid will likely not be ready to handle the amount of electricity needed to support CA’s goal of transitioning to all electric vehicles by 2035. Again, the quickest way to ensure we are able to support all electric vehicles is to build roof top solar on every home and provide incentives for homeowners to install batteries. We, personally own 2 EVs and roof top solar. Most years we break even or generate more electricity that we use.
I question the term “least cost” and who will benefit from this so called least cost. The current proposal may be less costly to build, but it will allow the ownership of the energy generation to remain in the hands of our local for-profit utility company, it will maintain long transmission lines and it will likely end up being more costly over the long run for the consumer. That should not be the future our county Supervisors support. Divert the money that would be spent on building these large “farms” and all the transmission lines and use it to help San Diego homeowners put solar on their roof top.
Regards,
Yvonne Elkin (she/her)

Good afternoon Thomas,

My name is Elise Ruiz, and I am a Group Program Manager with the County of San Diego’s Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice (OSEJ). I am reaching out to you today to inform you about the Regional Water Equity project that OSEJ is currently leading.

In September 2022<https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/bosagenda.sandiegocounty.gov/cob/cosd/cob/doc?id=0901127e80f0faf8__;!!OBed2aHXvKmHymw!wsnlYOkY8-f2n8F07pTBm6V3BuhEKdeYcZHg1ENBhi1zPFdkHWJbe0s1n-Cr57HpW3wx9h-xhC4qy67qQj8YkQfTE610OMoC$>, the County of San Diego Board of Supervisors directed staff to take a proactive, regional approach to address the drought crisis through drought management and water sustainability practices, and to align with how California legislatively recognizes the human right to water, as stated in Assembly Bill (AB) 685. Due to continuous climate change impacts, the strain on water resources will increase and affect all communities, especially those who are disproportionately impacted by water scarcity across the San Diego region.

County staff is partnering with water solution experts Geosyntec, and a supporting team including the University of California, San Diego and Re:Focus, to study these issues and provide recommendations for future Board direction. The regional drought management and water sustainability practices will be driven by three guiding principles:

•         Regional Collaboration - Consider the whole region, including local municipalities, Imperial County, and binational cities.

•         Adapt to a Hotter, Drier Future - Align with California's Water Supply Strategy<https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/resources.ca.gov/-/media/CNRA-Website/Files/Initiatives/Water-Resilience/CA-Water-Supply-Strategy.pdf__;!!OBed2aHXvKmHymw!wsnlYOkY8-f2n8F07pTBm6V3BuhEKdeYcZHg1ENBhi1zPFdkHWJbe0s1n-Cr57HpW3wx9h-xhC4qy67qQj8YkQfTE1juh4_K$>, focusing on potable and non-potable water reuse in the short-, mid-, and long-term.

•         Community, Environmental, and Industry Engagement – Learn from and partner with communities, tribes, and industries throughout various sectors impacted by issues related to water equity, and barriers to water sustainability.

We are currently in the phase of project development and beginning to collect data through one-on-one interviews, which will be used to support the Regional Water Equity Report to disseminate results at the end of this year before the Board hearing. We would greatly appreciate if your organization would consider being an interviewee for this process to better understand how we can identify opportunities for water sustainability practices. If you are interested, please reply to me directly with some of your availability and I can coordinate scheduling a Teams Meeting with our technical consultant, Geosyntec.

Additionally, I’ve included a Fact Sheet for further information about the project and Board direction. Feel free to share with your organization and use this as a reference. I am happy to answer any questions you may have, and I look forward to connecting with you.

All the best,

Elise Ruiz

Hi Tina,

I am following up on Henry’s email below.  We are working to wrap up interview analysis for this effort over the next week.  Would it be possible to get IID’s perspective on the following three questions (these are not meant to take more than 10-15 minutes of your time):

1.	What do you see as the biggest risk(s) to the region’s water supply portfolio with respect to long-term resilience? Lack of long-term water supply planning with regard to growth and development – I don’t see any significant coordination between land use authorities and water supply agencies to ensure growth is managed or limited based on the resource.  I was surprise, and heartened, last week to see Arizona acknowledge they could no longer permit new development projects and then go find the water supply (see https://www.nytimes.com/2023/06/01/climate/arizona-phoenix-permits-housing-water.html <https://www.nytimes.com/2023/06/01/climate/arizona-phoenix-permits-housing-water.html> )  and instead move to invert that process so that new project entitlements will be restricted until such time that supplies are developed or made available.  This is how is should be done, to create those water supply partnerships in advance to allow for that growth to occur or push the growth to the areas with the resources.  The current climate change realities are putting those with senior water rights at risk because the junior priority water users don’t know how to deal with potential cutbacks in a future with less water, and those areas are now pressing for human health and safety water supplies to be prioritized if their supplies become inadequate.
2.	Can you identify the top three water management projects types/solutions that you’d recommend the region allocate more funding/effort towards?

a.       Regional Water Recycling

b.       Localized On-Site Reuse (e.g. Graywater)

c.       Stormwater Capture and Reuse/Recycling

d.       Desalination

e.       Storage Management - Reservoir Storage and Dam Management

f.        Storage Management - Manage Groundwater Recharge

g.       Conservation

3.	Which of the following water supply solutions do you view at the “most at risk” in terms of being a reliable, long term source of water for the region? Which is “least at risk”?  Write “most risk” and “least risk” after two of the options below, and elaborate in 1-2 sentences on why.

a.       Regional Water Recycling least at risk (although potential declines as water availability and/or use declines)

b.       Localized On-Site Reuse (Graywater) least at risk (although potential declines as water availability and/or use declines)

c.       Stormwater Capture and Reuse/Recycling most at risk (due to cyclic nature of storms and climate change – but the potential for large gains when there are strong weather patterns that we need to take advantage of)

d.       Desalination least at risk (augmentation project -the biggest challenge here is cost/affordability)

e.       Storage Management – Reservoir Storage and Dam Management least at risk (once built – but that’s the tricky part these days)

f.        Storage Management - Managed Groundwater Recharge most at risk (again, dependent on “extra supplies”, plus regulatory constraints due to the need for more replenishment due to years of overdrafting)

I am happy to hop on a call anytime to provide more context if you’d like.  I’m attaching the project fact sheet for reference.

Thanks in advance for your time,

Stephanie

body:
2023 Intertribal Earth Day Event a Success!

Another year, another great Intertribal Earth Day event! Every year, eight Southern California Tribes (La Jolla, Los Coyotes, Pala, Pauma, Pechanga, Rincon, San Pasqual, and Santa Ynez) come together to plan and host the annual Intertribal Earth Day. On Saturday, June 24, 2023, 39 participating groups hosted booths to share environmental information with the 458 people attending. The theme this year was Water Is Life and many of the participating tribes and groups shared information around this theme as well as other important information for the community. The event was a zero-waste event and 71% of the waste produced was diverted from the landfill and was recycled or composted. While this is not zero waste sent to the landfill, diverting 71% is a very positive environmental benefit.

The event was opened with a traditional prayer and song by former Pauma Chairman Chris Devers. La Jolla Chairwoman Wendy Schlater, joined by Vice-Chairman Jack Musick and Councilman John Paipa, welcomed everyone to La Jolla and spoke about how Water is Life. If you were there you enjoyed an excellent lunch with pit BBQ provided by the Rodriguez family from La Jolla, grilled veggies and veggie chili by Gary Murrey from La Jolla, green beans and pasta salad by Dorothy Willis from Los Coyotes, and mac & cheese with green salad and rolls provided by Pauma Casino. Thank you all!

The emcees, Jimmy Trujillo and Eric Ortega, did a wonderful job of running the event. La Jolla’s own Tishmal Herrera and Alexis (Cakes) Weeks were in attendance as Pow Wow Princesses from UCR and UCSD. We had four amazing cultural presenters: Wayne Nelson sang birds, the Mikksu Mountain Lion group came from Utah, Blue Water Dancers came from Pauma, and the Kupa Song and Dance Group came from Pala. People were also able to win many different raffle prizes donated by: Morongo Band of Mission Indians, Pala Casino Spa & Resort, Sky Sailing, Inc., Tractor Supply, La Jolla Campground, La Jolla 76 Grill, La Jolla Zipline, La Jolla Adventure Park, Los Coyotes, and NAEPC. We also want to thank our event financial sponsors for their generous donations: La Jolla, Viejas, Rincon, Augustine, Pauma, San Pasqual, Morongo, Los Coyotes, Soboba, Agua Caliente, and Pechanga Band of Indians.

body:
Hi Elise,

Passing this along – the County achieved 4 of 15 points under “water efficiency”, but it’s unclear which specific criteria were fulfilled. We are inquiring to see if we can get more detail on the score breakdown, which could help us to identify areas for enhancement.

Talk to you this afternoon,
Megan

Direct: 619.810.4043

To: Megan Otto <MMOtto@Geosyntec.com>
Subject: FW: LEED Certification for County

CAUTION: This email originated from outside of the organization. Do not click links or open attachments unless you recognize the sender and know the content is safe. If you have any suspicion, please confirm with the sender verbally that this email is authentic. If you suspect fraud, click "Phish Alert Report."

Hi Megan,

Charley just sent me the LEED scoring criteria for the County’s Platinum Certification – water is worth 15 points, but it appears we only were awarded 4 of those… I’ve followed up with Charley to see if there is anything we could have implemented at the time of our rating that would have scored us higher, such as implementing stormwater capture/reuse or other water recycling practices (grey water, purple pipe). Those are practices we’re currently implementing, so my thought is that we may be able to score higher if we were rated today.

Let me know if you think we need anything more?

title: _External_ Meeting Agenda Items.msg
subject: [External] Meeting Agenda Items
body:
Hi Elise and Jacob,

I have gone through the Task 2 comments and would like to discuss the following items with you tomorrow.  All other comments will be addressed in the RWER, and do not require additional discussion.  Blue items are tribal specific which we can perhaps save for our meeting with Roberta on Friday. If I missed anything that you think should be discussed, let me know.

                                              i.     RWEP versus RWEE

                                             ii.     Tribal usage of recycled water – how should this be described in existing condition? (not implemented – medium – high?)

                                           iii.     Shasta from Pala recommended the “tribal position on water” – we like this, let’s discuss how to do this.

                                           iv.     “Unique” border challenges – let’s discuss

                                             v.     New Culture of Water... management? (direct quote from CESPT)

                                           vi.     Expand on tribal background – 17 federally recognized tribes, 18 in total.  Is this just in SD?

                                          vii.     Larger tribal community” versus individual versus “tribal land held in common” – how to incorporate this background? “Held in common” good for recycling?

                                         viii.     Work with academic community to study 7 water supply solutions ... 3 out of 5 focus areas discussion

Looking forward to our meeting tomorrow!

Stephanie

body:
Hi Elise,

I wanted to follow up on the Phase 1 group interview outreach.  I have updated the Sharepoint spreadsheet online with some contacts, but thought I would share them here as well (this also helps me keep this organized a bit and understand next steps in terms of outreach and our roles/responsibilities).  The highlighted ones are in progress, and I think we can come up with these internally as noted below:

1 Contacts we collectively have (or will have soon) include:

  *   Dr. Amy Kerner with UCSD (Task 5, Agriculture Focus) – do you have her contact info?  If so, please send and I will add it to spreadsheet.
  *   Green Building Council  (Task 2A, Developer Focus) – Stephanie Gaines is currently working on finding the correct contact; we should have this soon.

  *   Cara Nager, Environmental Affairs Manager – San Diego County Regional Airport Authority (Task 2A, Business/Development focus)

title: _External_ Public Comments_ County's RDF Draft Playbook (By PCF).msg
subject: [External] Public Comments: County's RDF Draft Playbook (By PCF)
to: "Baxamusa; Murtaza" <Murtaza.Baxamusa@sdcounty.ca.gov>; 	"De La Rosa; Michael" <Michael.DeLaRosa@sdcounty.ca.gov>; elise.ruiz@sdcounty.ca.gov; 	Rebeca.Appel@sdcounty.ca.gov
attachments: 25-jan-23_B Powers_REV FINAL3_problems w RDF treatment of rooftop-parking lot solar.pdf
body:
Greetings Murtaza, Michael, Elise, and Rebecca;

I appreciate the work and effort that you all have contributed related to our County's decarbonization efforts. As mentioned, The Protect Our Communities Foundation, from Bill Powers has identified some key significant errors in the data related to our clean renewable energy source.

There is a concern as you all may be briefed on the protection of our conservation landscape in the backcountry. I do recall hearing this from the panel at the County's RDF. This presentation also highlights this concern as well. I would also like to inquire on section 4.3.1 of the Energy section of the County's Implementation Playbook that suggests waiving permits for utility scale solar projects. PCF would like to be on record in opposing any waiver to utility scale solar projects. If anything, PCF would like to underscore the need for a more rigorous permitting process in the backcountry, and eliminating permitting could be problematic to the communities and nature that live and habitat there. As we consider the impacts of our backcountry with our neighbors, our sensitive conservation land, and possible CEQA impacts; PCF would like to reinforce the need for permitting for remote solar projects. Our permitting process that includes surveying and assessing the area for projects should remain a priority with the County for accountability and protection for nature and those that reside there.

Also, it doesn't appear that the rates used are the most recent from (NREL).

If you have any questions, or comments about these public comments submitted for the County's RDF, please feel free to contact Bill Powers. He is cc'd  on this email.

Would you please notify me that these comments in this email and the presentation attached have been received and will be included in the public comments for the County's draft RDF Playbook? Also please advise if there's another process for submitting these public comments.

Thank you,
Sonja Robinson
The Protect Our Communities Foundation

Thanks Rebeca! I just took another review and this is great. All three presentations have a similar cadence of identifying the purpose and need for action, followed by details on the process you took to figure out what to do, and some of the initial outcomes on the last slide. Any additional actions that are on the near-term horizon that you think is reasonable to share would help folks understand how to move decarbonization forward with low hanging fruit (that may not have been obvious before doing the RDF, such as telecommute policies) while preparing for the next harder steps.

Matt

Have a great evening!

Elise

JB has told me great things about you. I technically am on this project, so not sure if I can be interviewed since I am one of the people responsible at UCSD? Let me know what you think. I'll be helping JB facilitate the April workshop, and my name is actually on the contract with Geosyntec.

On Mon, Mar 6, 2023 at 3:34?PM Ruiz, Elise <Elise.Ruiz@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:Elise.Ruiz@sdcounty.ca.gov>> wrote:

Good afternoon Dr. Lerner,

My name is Elise Ruiz, and I am a Group Program Manager with the County of San Diego’s Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice (OSEJ). I am reaching out to you today to inform you about the Regional Water Equity project that OSEJ is currently leading. We are working with JB with UCSD and she may have informed you about this effort:

In September 2022<https://urldefense.com/v3/__https://bosagenda.sandiegocounty.gov/cob/cosd/cob/doc?id=0901127e80f0faf8__;!!Mih3wA!GvtYTK-e8lpPHszG7mlnkW71Kcqm_x9TcdKpr4T7Pc8gGjpB3m8S7leKpGzUfoDdLvFxExHJzq_A4fwlNSk__jmIyGI$>, the County of San Diego Board of Supervisors directed staff to take a proactive, regional approach to address the drought crisis through drought management and water sustainability practices, and to align with how California legislatively recognizes the human right to water, as stated in Assembly Bill (AB) 685. Due to continuous climate change impacts, the strain on water resources will increase and affect all communities, especially those who are disproportionately impacted by water scarcity across the San Diego region.

County staff is partnering with water solution experts Geosyntec, and a supporting team including the University of California, San Diego and Re:Focus, to study these issues and provide recommendations for future Board direction. The regional drought management and water sustainability practices will be driven by three guiding principles:

•         Regional Collaboration - Consider the whole region, including local municipalities, Imperial County, and binational cities.

•         Adapt to a Hotter, Drier Future - Align with California's Water Supply Strategy<https://urldefense.com/v3/__https://resources.ca.gov/-/media/CNRA-Website/Files/Initiatives/Water-Resilience/CA-Water-Supply-Strategy.pdf__;!!Mih3wA!GvtYTK-e8lpPHszG7mlnkW71Kcqm_x9TcdKpr4T7Pc8gGjpB3m8S7leKpGzUfoDdLvFxExHJzq_A4fwlNSk_2S9irm8$>, focusing on potable and non-potable water reuse in the short-, mid-, and long-term.

•         Community, Environmental, and Industry Engagement – Learn from and partner with communities, tribes, and industries throughout various sectors impacted by issues related to water equity, and barriers to water sustainability.

We are currently in the phase of project development and beginning to collect data through one-on-one interviews, which will be used to support the Regional Water Equity Report to disseminate results at the end of this year before the Board hearing. We would greatly appreciate if you would consider being an interviewee for this process to better understand how we can identify opportunities for water sustainability practices. If you are interested, please reply to me directly with some of your availability and I can coordinate scheduling a Teams Meeting with our technical consultant, Geosyntec.

Additionally, I’ve included a Fact Sheet for further information about the project and Board direction. Feel free to share with your organization and use this as a reference. I am happy to answer any questions you may have, and I look forward to connecting with you.

All the best,

Elise Ruiz

In September 2022<https://bosagenda.sandiegocounty.gov/cob/cosd/cob/doc?id=0901127e80f0faf8>, the County of San Diego Board of Supervisors directed staff to take a proactive, regional approach to address the drought crisis through drought management and water sustainability practices, and to align with how California legislatively recognizes the human right to water, as stated in Assembly Bill (AB) 685. If you have any suspicion, please confirm with the sender verbally that this email is authentic. If you suspect fraud, click "Phish Alert Report."

Hi Megan and Stephanie,

Please find attached the draft Board memo we are circulating through our Executive team to review. As I mentioned on our call, this is an update to the Board since they provided the direction in September where we are sharing the outreach done, future outreach planned, and what the report will entail. We pulled a lot of information from the SOW to inform how we were talking about the report. We’re finalizing this memo by Monday morning, so I know it’s a quick turnaround, but please let us know if you have any concerns, questions, and/or suggestions by Friday afternoon.

Also, as we were working on this, some things came up that we are hoping to discuss with you all as we get closer to the draft report to make sure we are aligned in how we are defining these:

  *   Best practices (page 4, in terms of graywater, however, curious on if there is a phrase we could use for what we mean by this – such as is it industry best practices, or based on outcomes-achieved, etc.)
  *   Short- term and long-term (page 3, in terms of the recommendations for investments in infrastructure. What does short term mean, is that 1-2 years or less than that. Is long -term 10 years, or what timeframe, etc.)
  *   Some additional terms for us to connect on and see how we can align how we are defining: resilience, drought, water sources (there are others and we can continue the conversations as we put together the draft report)

Thank you! Please don’t hesitate to reach out if you have any questions.

Rebeca Appel

subject: [External] Re: Murakawa & OSEJ Water - Weekly Check-In
body:
Hi Elise,

Sorry for the late response, had a crazy day! Sure no worries, whenever there isn't a lot to discuss I'm happy to defer to the following week. I'll be on the lookout early next week for any email updates, as well as look forward to our meeting next week.

Since we didn't meet today, I've recapped our meeting from last week:

RWER Meeting Summary 5/26/23:

Upcoming virtual "Deep Dives" meetings:

*	Duration: Virtual meetings will all be one-hour events
*	Dates/times:  Dates for meetings have been provided, times will be forthcoming (since last week's meeting, times have now been provided)
*	Scheduling: Scheduling is being worked out to confirm appropriate speakers and content, including content aligns with scope of project; lots of interest in Ag, an Ag speaker will be key to specific meetings and as such schedule is still being determined; MC recommends setting schedule including meeting times as soon as possible
*	Format: More conversational, less formal, more engagement with break-out rooms
*	MC day-of role(s): County will be ready to get more in depth on the day-of details in the first two weeks of June, including MC roles; Danielle noted that the sooner we confirm this, the better so that MC can ensure appropriate staffing. MC day-of roles to include Zoom administration including recording; coordinating interpretation; note taking; supporting data collection and keeping conversations moving forward. MC day-of roles may also include monitoring chat/Q & A;  assisting in break-out rooms; previously was noted that MC roles would include co-facilitation/co-management of meetings. Additional roles to be determined
*	MC prep roles: Setting up links and platforms for meetings; monitoring and sharing registration information; email blasts; updating landing page information as needed; coordinating interpretation; translation of collateral
*	Rehearsal: MC recommends a full rehearsal/dry run a week prior to each event with all presenters and appropriate staff, which allows time for tweaks and edits

Deliverables:

*	Meeting summaries: Elise advised that the County requests meeting summaries include responses to questions, responses can be documented as a general summary of the response, verbatim documentation is not required; Danielle noted that this is not typically included, as the responses given are known by the County

For consideration/planning:

*	Satellite locations: Elise noted there may be satellite locations for the virtual meetings, TBD and to be discussed at a future planning meeting
*	Translation of slide decks - timeline: Ideally MC would have them two weeks in advance of when County wants them to be translated, MC needs these a minimum one week in advance
*	Slide deck, including any videos etc. that need to be integrated:  MC needs these one week in advance to prepare for Zoom presentation

*	Interpretation for day-of, including timeline: Spanish will be a standing request and available for all virtual meetings, interpretation of Spanish and any other requested languages will occur even if no one is in the interpretation room and will be recorded; other languages require a one-week advance notice to ensure an interpreter is available, we will make every effort to accommodate requests made later

I hope this is helpful for our next meeting and on-going planning. Please let me know if I missed anything or if you have any comments/revisions to what I captured.

Thank you, have a great weekend!
--Danielle

title: _External_ Re_ RDF's Water Equity Effort Connection.msg
subject: [External] Re: RDF's Water Equity Effort Connection
body:
Thanks for this, Elise! Will update our survey and looking forward to the talking points for our newsletter (going out early next week).

Carmina Paz (she/her)

Program Coordinator

Urban Collaborative Project CDC

San Diego, CA 92114

C: (619) 786-6890

www.ucproject.org <http://www.ucproject.org>

From: "Ruiz, Elise" <Elise.Ruiz@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Date: Friday, July 21, 2023 at 5:59 PM
To: "Facendini, Bethany (She/Her/Ella)" <Bethany.Facendini@sdcounty.ca.gov>, Carmina Paz <c.paz@ucproject.org>
Cc: "Boerboom, Jacob" <Jacob.Boerboom@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Subject: RE: RDF's Water Equity Effort Connection

Hi Carmina,

Thank you so much for your time and helpful insight during our meeting yesterday. It is very exciting to learn more about all the incredible work UCP is doing with our communities!

As discussed, I wanted to provide the questions that could be added to the existing survey. Thank you so much for incorporating these water focused questions so we can understand our community needs:

*	What does water equity mean to you?
*	What are the biggest challenges you and your community face with water or drought impacts?
*	What are some ways you currently conserve water or plan to conserve water?
*	[Provide space for additional responses]

Additionally, I wanted to make sure you had our most recent version of the Deep Dive flyer and Fact Sheet, which includes English and Spanish on each side. I will print these so you have hard copies before the August 26 event.

I will follow up early next week with more points for the newsletter and additional social media graphics for the Deep Dive events, and I’ll coordinate with you to prepare for the August 10 opportunity to present about the Water Equity effort.

I hope you have a wonderful weekend!

Elise

From: Facendini, Bethany (She/Her/Ella) <Bethany.Facendini@sdcounty.ca.gov>

To: Carmina Paz <c.paz@ucproject.org>
Cc: Boerboom, Jacob <Jacob.Boerboom@sdcounty.ca.gov>; Ruiz, Elise <Elise.Ruiz@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Subject: RDF's Water Equity Effort Connection

Hello Carmina,

We are looking forward to meeting with you on Thursday! Thank you for creating the time.

Please see the attached meeting agenda and supplemental documents for your review. We are hoping to get to know you and the team better, discuss the project with you further, and hearing more about the great efforts you have underway to engage the community. Please let us know if you have any questions.

Warm regards,

Subject: Regional Decarbonization Framework Implementation Playbook (Draft for Review)

CAUTION: This email originated from outside of SANDAG. Do not click links or open attachments unless you are expecting the content.
Dear Allison,

Thank you for serving on the Technical Working Group for the County of San Diego’s Regional Decarbonization Framework (RDF). We would like to share with the RDF Implementation Playbook. It was prepared by the University of San Diego’s Energy Policy Initiatives Center at the direction of our Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice. It is intended to be a user-friendly tool that can provide different long-term strategies to get us to our common goals - getting to zero carbon emissions in the region with consideration to time and cost of implementation.?

The textual content of the draft playbook is organized by user type: individuals, organizations/businesses, communities, and regional. For each type of user, there are several pathways for decarbonization: transportation, electric supply, buildings, land use and natural climate solutions, as well as food systems and the circular economy. This draft playbook was prepared through extensive input from working groups for each of these pathways. The video recordings and slides from the working group meetings are available on our website: Outreach-and-Engagement (sandiegocounty.gov)<https://gcc02.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.sandiegocounty.gov%2Fcontent%2Fsdc%2Fsustainability%2Fregional-decarbonization%2Foutreach-and-engagement.html&data=05%7C01%7CSusan.Freedman%40sandag.org%7C35b860abbd7d45326d7308db0a1c048e%7C2bbb5689d9d5406b8d02cf1002b473e7%7C0%7C0%7C638114887703340733%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJWIjoiMC4wLjAwMDAiLCJQIjoiV2luMzIiLCJBTiI6Ik1haWwiLCJXVCI6Mn0%3D%7C3000%7C%7C%7C&sdata=aETR9wnqagpTzaybdyE4pnhNqbmw4Ex0YMtz9XT%2F%2B2c%3D&reserved=0>
We are also building an online “Ideas Bank” of presentations from the community: Ideas Bank (sandiegocounty.gov)<https://gcc02.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.sandiegocounty.gov%2Fcontent%2Fsdc%2Fsustainability%2Fregional-decarbonization%2Fideasbank.html&data=05%7C01%7CSusan.Freedman%40sandag.org%7C35b860abbd7d45326d7308db0a1c048e%7C2bbb5689d9d5406b8d02cf1002b473e7%7C0%7C0%7C638114887703340733%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJWIjoiMC4wLjAwMDAiLCJQIjoiV2luMzIiLCJBTiI6Ik1haWwiLCJXVCI6Mn0%3D%7C3000%7C%7C%7C&sdata=1z8cxXaiqaxEeYaePjxL1TEwFsZV5xS%2FNodrbV0X%2FQM%3D&reserved=0>

We would like your review/feedback on this attached document by February 2. After this date, we will finalize the playbook and produce web and print versions with graphical interfaces to make them broadly accessible once adopted by our Board of Supervisors.

Murtaza

Hi Elise,
Thanks for your email and for providing this info – we can discuss more on Thursday.  ARUP will be joining us during Thursday’s meeting to discuss initial best practices research.

In terms of the 9/27/23 hearing, my understanding is that you don’t need us at that hearing but that you might just ping us about our work leading up to that September hearing, right?

In terms of the January hearing, we can definitely work within the 2-3 min timeframe – no prob at all.  We are flexible and will work within whatever timeframe is requested.  I’ll go ahead and send an invite for the January hearing to my team just to lock down that date.

Thx!
Danny

Hi there JB,

Hope this email finds you well, me and my team are looking forward to Wednesday's meeting!

Re: name tags - we'll be bringing regular paper "I'm ___________"  name tags for attendees as well as for my own MC staff.

The UCSD team is welcome to use these as well. As to whether or not that is preferred over your own UCSD lanyard name tags would be more a question for Elise, who I'm copying here as well as Jacob who is supporting her, so that they can respond.

We appreciate that UCSD students will be there to support the event. As per conversations in our planning meeting, they will be helping with the Poll Everywhere, and it would be great if they can also assist in the following, depending on staff needs that day:

  *   Registration
  *   Refreshments table (monitoring, refreshing)
  *   Stationed outside to help guide folks to the correct location

I'll have five of my own staff, including myself, so some of us will be taking care of these tasks but we'll also have other set-up tasks so extra hands if needed will be greatly appreciated. Please let me know if you have any questions/concerns.

Thank you!
--Danielle

Hi Marcus,

Thanks again for volunteering to participate in a one-hour (virtual) interview with LDC staff, LDC’s sub-consultant (ARUP), and County staff.  Below is a list of meeting times for your consideration.  Our goal is to meet asap with your organization.  Please identify all times that may work for you. I’ve cc’d the folks you listed in your email below.  If necessary, I will send additional dates/times if none of these options work for your team.  I will circulate an agenda and send out a Teams meeting invite as soon as a meeting time has been identified.

*	Friday, June 9th at 4 PM
*	Tuesday, June 13th at 11 AM
*	Tuesday, June 13th at 4 PM
*	Tuesday, June 13th at 3 PM [Please note: this time is not preferred as there is currently a schedule conflict with County of San Diego staff]

Below is a preliminary list of questions that we are anticipating to ask during the interview.  These questions will help to guide our meeting.

*	We are exploring several water conservation, greywater reuse and stormwater reuse strategies for new and rehabilitation affordable housing projects in San Diego County. Have you implemented any of these strategies before?

	*	If so, what did you implement and how did you pay for it/them (e.g., programs, incentives, loans, tax credits etc.)?

	*	How effective were the measures (e.g., water savings, payback, operational performance successes/challenges)?

	*	What would you implement again? If not, why not?

	*	Is there more (efficiency / reuse measures) you would have done if more funding was available?

	*	Please describe, if applicable, how your organization has utilized LEED certification for different development types to help achieve water conservation, greywater reuse, and/or stormwater strategies for affordable housing projects. Do you have LEED accredited staff?

	*	Do you have year over year data on the projects’ water/sewer expenses before and after water conservation measures were implemented (if applicable)? If so, could you please share that data with us?

	*	Would you be willing to share any project proformas that include these water/stormwater strategies that you’ve implemented?

*	If you haven’t implemented any of these strategies before, please describe why.

	*	What were the major barriers (e.g., cost, technical expertise, regulatory hurdles etc.)? What would you need to implement these strategies?

	*	Do you think that it would be more feasible to implement these strategies in new construction or a substantial rehabilitation/retrofit project? Why?

Sincerely,

Hi Marcus,

I hope you are well.  I’m working as a consultant with LeSar Development Consultants for the County of San Diego to identify ways in which to incentivize affordable housing to utilize sustainable use/reuse of water and stormwater.  This research is part of the County’s anticipated Regional Water Equity Report (the attached fact sheet provides additional context) that will help to inform the County’s larger drought management and water sustainability practices to proactively address the challenges of our region’s reliance on water sources.

We’d like to invite you and others from MAAC (e.g., Christopher Ramirez/Director of Real Estate Development) to participate in a one-hour (virtual) interview with LDC’s project team and County staff (Elise Ruiz/Group Program Manager with the County’s Land Use and Environment Group).  Our goal is to learn from your experiences in the affordable housing and stormwater capture and reuse fields which will help us to identify ways in which to incentivize affordable housing to utilize stormwater capture and reuse.  The interview would focus on stormwater infrastructure and affordable housing development process, the financial and regulatory barriers to implementing water and stormwater projects in housing, and potential opportunities to leverage better outcomes in both sectors.  Key themes from the interviews will be summarized in a brief memorandum to County staff.

Please let us know if you and Christopher (and others from your team) would be willing to join us for a one-hour virtual interview.

Thank you for your time and consideration.
