Dear Michael Choi,

I hope you are well.  I’m working as a consultant with LeSar Development Consultants for the County of San Diego to identify ways in which to incentivize affordable housing to utilize sustainable use/reuse of water and stormwater.  This research is part of the County’s anticipated Regional Water Equity Report (the attached fact sheet provides additional context) that will help to inform the County’s larger drought management and water sustainability practices to proactively address the challenges of our region’s reliance on water sources.

We’d like to invite you as well as local KHA staff in the San Diego area to participate in a one-hour (virtual) interview with LDC’s project team and County staff (Elise Ruiz/Group Program Manager with the County’s Land Use and Environment Group).  Our goal is to learn from your experiences in the affordable housing and water conservation/stormwater capture and reuse fields which will help us to identify ways in which to incentivize affordable housing to utilize water conservation/stormwater capture and reuse.  The interview would focus on stormwater infrastructure and affordable housing development process, the financial and regulatory barriers to implementing water and stormwater projects in housing, and potential opportunities to leverage better outcomes in both sectors.  Key themes from the interviews will be summarized in a brief memorandum to County staff.

Please let us know if you (and others from your team) would be willing to join us for a one-hour virtual interview.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely,

The interview would focus on stormwater infrastructure and affordable housing development process, the financial and regulatory barriers to implementing water and stormwater projects in housing, and potential opportunities to leverage better outcomes in both sectors.  Key themes from the interviews will be summarized in a brief memorandum to County staff.

Please let us know if you (and others from your team) would be willing to join us for a one-hour virtual interview.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely,

Hi Michael (and Jessie),

Thanks for your email, and I hope you are enjoying your vacation!

And thanks again for volunteering to participate in a one-hour (virtual) interview with LDC staff, LDC’s sub-consultant (ARUP), and County staff.  Below is a list of meeting times for your consideration.  Our goal is to meet asap with your organization.  Please identify all times that may work for you.  If necessary, I will send additional dates/times if none of these options work for your team.  I will circulate an agenda and send out a Teams meeting invite as soon as a meeting time has been identified.

*	Weds., June 14th at 10 AM
*	Weds., June 14th at 2 PM
*	Weds., June 14th at 3 PM
*	Weds., June 14th at 11 AM [please note: this time is not preferred as there is currently a schedule conflict with County of San Diego staff]

Also - I’m happy to connect with you to further discuss expectations ahead of the interview.  Essentially, we are exploring several water conservation, greywater reuse and stormwater reuse strategies for new and rehabilitation affordable housing projects in San Diego County.  Below is a preliminary list of questions that we are anticipating to ask you (and other KHA folks as appropriate/available) during the interview.  These questions will help to guide our meeting and provide you a better sense as to what we hope to learn from KHA.

*	Describe your typical development scope (e.g., new build vs. significant rehab).
*	Describe the types of water efficiency and stormwater / water reuse measures you are being asked to design in the San Diego area.
*	Where do you see the greatest water saving potential in San Diego for affordable housing (for new build vs. significant rehab)? For example, what’s feasible now and what are the emerging technologies?
*	What are the biggest barriers to implementation (e.g., long-term maintenance, contractor familiarity/expertise, low-tech vs. high-tech solutions etc.)?  How was the permitting process experience (e.g., delays, unforeseen costs/permits)?
*	Please describe, if applicable, how your organization has utilized LEED certification for different development types to help achieve water conservation, greywater reuse, and/or stormwater strategies for affordable housing projects.

Sincerely,

Danny Serrano, AICP

Hi Joel,

We met at the San Diego Water Assembly last week (4/26) and I wanted to follow up with you.  Our team is working with the County of San Diego’s Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice (OSEJ) on identifying drought resilience approaches for San Diego and Imperial Counties as well as border communities in Mexico.  We would like to request a 1-hour virtual interview which will include questions around sustainable and equitable drought management practices and solutions throughout this region.  If you are open to this, please let us know and Chrissie (cc’d) will follow up with you on scheduling.

For some additional background, in September 2022, the County of San Diego Board of Supervisors directed staff to take a proactive, regional approach to address the drought crisis through drought management and water sustainability practices. Our team is leading up the research and recommendations related to various solutions including water recycling, desalination, conservation, storage systems and stormwater capture through the lens of equity. We are currently working with local partners to identify promising ideas and key needs.

Hope to speak with you soon.

Thank you,

Stephanie

Hi Joel,

Thanks again for your participation in the interview for this project.  We do have a couple follow up questions we’d like your input on below.  These are not meant to take more than 10-15 minutes of your time and it would greatly benefit our analysis.  Also, when able, we’d definitely be interested in viewing the maps you mentioned showing historic and current extents of agriculture, as well as ideal lands to increase agriculture throughout the region.

	1.	What do you see as the biggest risk(s) to the San Diego and Imperial region’s water supply portfolio with respect to long-term resilience?

Cost - heavy regional infrastructure investment creates a burden on consumers that they may not be able to support for uses that do not benefit them. Solutions need to be localized to individual communities to ensure resident buy-in and ability to pay. Communities need to be engaged to create community-specific drought resilience plans to prepare for reduced allocations at a neighborhood-level during drought conditions. To ease this burden, non-essential irrigation and consumptions should be eliminated and/or disincentivized with a heavily graduated pay scale based on per-capita volume for residential and commercial customers. This will incentivize further conservation, allowing for existing water supplies to be allocated more equitably. As an essential service for local residents, agricultural allocations should receive priority up to 1/3 of the regional allocation at special rates, so long as these farms contribute to the local food supply. We must prioritize use of precious water resources for urban greening in low-income neighborhoods and for agricultural production for local consumption in order to ensure regional resilience during drought conditions.

	1.	Can you identify the top three water management projects types/solutions that you’d recommend the San Diego and Imperial region allocate more funding/effort towards?

                                                         i.      Regional Water Recycling

                                                       ii.      Localized On-Site Reuse (Graywater) - First, see below.

                                                     iii.      Stormwater Capture and Reuse/Recycling

                                                     iv.      Desalination - Third; costly but reliable source during drought conditions depending on energy availability

                                                       v.      Storage Management - Increase Dam Capacity

                                                     vi.      Storage Management - Manage Groundwater Recharge

                                                   vii.      Conservation - Second; eliminate non-essential consumption to alleviate water budget.

	1.	Which of the following water supply solutions do you view at the “most at risk” in terms of being a reliable, long term source of water for the region? Which is “least at risk”?  Write “most risk” and “least risk” after two of the options below, and elaborate in 1-2 sentences on why.

                                                         i.      Regional Water Recycling

                                                       ii.      Localized On-Site Reuse (Graywater) - Least Risk

                                                     iii.      Stormwater Capture and Reuse/Recycling

                                                     iv.      Desalination

                                                       v.      Storage Management - Increase Dam Capacity

                                                     vi.      Storage Management - Manage Groundwater Recharge - Most Risk

                                                   vii.      Conservation

Least risk - Graywater use effectively eliminates the need for landscape irrigation, which is responsible for roughly half of urban water consumption. This is one of the most effective forms of conservation with the most co-benefits. In terms of resilience, localized systems such as graywater application are more effective at using water with less maintenance costs than largescale regional infrastructure.

Greatest risk - extraction from groundwater basins must be monitored and regulated based on recharge rates in order to avoid depletion. For this reason, groundwater basins are not currently relied upon for urban areas. However, aquifer levels should be monitored and managed in areas which are adding new residential developments, ex: San Pasqual Valley.

Thank you,

Stephanie

Hi Joel,

We met at the San Diego Water Assembly last week (4/26) and I wanted to follow up with you.  Our team is working with the County of San Diego’s Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice (OSEJ) on identifying drought resilience approaches for San Diego and Imperial Counties as well as border communities in Mexico.  We would like to request a 1-hour virtual interview which will include questions around sustainable and equitable drought management practices and solutions throughout this region.  If you are open to this, please let us know and Chrissie (cc’d) will follow up with you on scheduling.

For some additional background, in September 2022, the County of San Diego Board of Supervisors directed staff to take a proactive, regional approach to address the drought crisis through drought management and water sustainability practices. Our team is leading up the research and recommendations related to various solutions including water recycling, desalination, conservation, storage systems and stormwater capture through the lens of equity. We are currently working with local partners to identify promising ideas and key needs.

Hope to speak with you soon.

Thank you,

Stephanie

Hi Joel,

Thanks again for your participation in the interview for this project.  We do have a couple follow up questions we’d like your input on below.  These are not meant to take more than 10-15 minutes of your time and it would greatly benefit our analysis.  Also, when able, we’d definitely be interested in viewing the maps you mentioned showing historic and current extents of agriculture, as well as ideal lands to increase agriculture throughout the region.

	a.	What do you see as the biggest risk(s) to the San Diego and Imperial region’s water supply portfolio with respect to long-term resilience?

Cost - heavy regional infrastructure investment creates a burden on consumers that they may not be able to support for uses that do not benefit them. Solutions need to be localized to individual communities to ensure resident buy-in and ability to pay. Communities need to be engaged to create community-specific drought resilience plans to prepare for reduced allocations at a neighborhood-level during drought conditions. To ease this burden, non-essential irrigation and consumptions should be eliminated and/or disincentivized with a heavily graduated pay scale based on per-capita volume for residential and commercial customers. This will incentivize further conservation, allowing for existing water supplies to be allocated more equitably. As an essential service for local residents, agricultural allocations should receive priority up to 1/3 of the regional allocation at special rates, so long as these farms contribute to the local food supply. We must prioritize use of precious water resources for urban greening in low-income neighborhoods and for agricultural production for local consumption in order to ensure regional resilience during drought conditions.

	a.	Can you identify the top three water management projects types/solutions that you’d recommend the San Diego and Imperial region allocate more funding/effort towards?

                                                         i.      Regional Water Recycling

                                                       ii.      Localized On-Site Reuse (Graywater) - First, see below.

                                                     iii.      Stormwater Capture and Reuse/Recycling

                                                     iv.      Desalination - Third; costly but reliable source during drought conditions depending on energy availability

                                                       v.      Storage Management - Increase Dam Capacity

                                                     vi.      Storage Management - Manage Groundwater Recharge

                                                   vii.      Conservation - Second; eliminate non-essential consumption to alleviate water budget.

	a.	Which of the following water supply solutions do you view at the “most at risk” in terms of being a reliable, long term source of water for the region? Which is “least at risk”?  Write “most risk” and “least risk” after two of the options below, and elaborate in 1-2 sentences on why.

                                                         i.      Regional Water Recycling

                                                       ii.      Localized On-Site Reuse (Graywater) - Least Risk

                                                     iii.      Stormwater Capture and Reuse/Recycling

                                                     iv.      Desalination

                                                       v.      Storage Management - Increase Dam Capacity

                                                     vi.      Storage Management - Manage Groundwater Recharge - Most Risk

                                                   vii.      Conservation

Least risk - Graywater use effectively eliminates the need for landscape irrigation, which is responsible for roughly half of urban water consumption. This is one of the most effective forms of conservation with the most co-benefits. In terms of resilience, localized systems such as graywater application are more effective at using water with less maintenance costs than largescale regional infrastructure.

Greatest risk - extraction from groundwater basins must be monitored and regulated based on recharge rates in order to avoid depletion. For this reason, groundwater basins are not currently relied upon for urban areas. However, aquifer levels should be monitored and managed in areas which are adding new residential developments, ex: San Pasqual Valley.

Thank you,

Stephanie

Hi Joel,

We met at the San Diego Water Assembly last week (4/26) and I wanted to follow up with you.  Our team is working with the County of San Diego’s Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice (OSEJ) on identifying drought resilience approaches for San Diego and Imperial Counties as well as border communities in Mexico.  We would like to request a 1-hour virtual interview which will include questions around sustainable and equitable drought management practices and solutions throughout this region.  If you are open to this, please let us know and Chrissie (cc’d) will follow up with you on scheduling.

For some additional background, in September 2022, the County of San Diego Board of Supervisors directed staff to take a proactive, regional approach to address the drought crisis through drought management and water sustainability practices. Our team is leading up the research and recommendations related to various solutions including water recycling, desalination, conservation, storage systems and stormwater capture through the lens of equity. We are currently working with local partners to identify promising ideas and key needs.

Hope to speak with you soon.

Thank you,

Stephanie

Hi Megan and Stephanie,

Thanks for all the hard work and effort that has gone into this deliverable! Our team was very impressed and we all agreed that it sets a great tone for the overall report. The glossary upfront was very helpful, and the data indicators in the tables made the information easy to follow.

Elise

To: Rob Roy <rob.roy@lajolla-nsn.gov>
Cc: Ruiz, Elise <Elise.Ruiz@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Subject: San Diego County Regional Water Equity Report (RWER)

Good afternoon Mr. Roy,

Thank you for your time this morning. I am following up with information about the Regional Water Equity Assessment/Report. As I mentioned to you over the phone, we are at the tail end of stakeholder interviews and would love to get your interview included in our report by the 31st of May. I have attached a fact sheet on the project and the interview questions that we would like to ask you with our GeoSyntec consultants if you are able to participate. I have cc’d Elise Ruiz who is the lead of this project in the Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice.

Essentially, this process of assessing what communities are/are not able to do to reach water equity in terms of sustainability through stormwater capturing, wastewater systems, and greywater strategies will provide a report to the County Board of Supervisors this September. Subject: [EXTERNAL] San Diego Regional Water Equity Report Follow-up

**This email came from an external source. Be cautious about clicking on any links in this email or opening attachments.**
________________________________

Hi Julie,

Thank you for your participation in the San Diego Regional Water Equity Project interview.  We greatly appreciate your time and all the helpful input you provided.  As discussed, we do have a couple follow up items we’d like to request from you below.  If we could get responses within the next 2 weeks, it would be much appreciated. (Keli – we hope you feel better soon!)

  1.  CIP Equity Scoring Sheets – you mentioned a “scoring sheet” that is now a component of prioritizing and selecting CIP projects.  If public, can you share an example with us?  If not public, we’d be interested to understand how you incorporate equity into your project selection.  We will be doing a similar exercise on a larger scale as part of this project, so are very interested in your methodology.  If not public, perhaps a 30 minute phone call over the next month or two would be very much appreciated.

The scoring sheets themselves are not public (and likely not entirely useful), but here is the link to the council policy that guided the new approach to include equity as a condition for prioritization (https://docs.sandiego.gov/councilpolicies/cpd_800-14.pdf). PUD further defined a couple factors to inform our scoring that considers project location, economic development in structurally excluded communities, economic growth in communities of concern, and public impact. Happy to participate in a phone call if you’d like to discuss methodology more.

  1.  Reservoir Storage Capacities - Are the reservoir storage capacities provided under this link Reservoir Lakes | City of San Diego Official Website<https://www.sandiego.gov/reservoirs-lakes> considering current dam restrictions? If not, could you provide the maximum height storage capacities instead?

They do not and yes I can. The reservoirs with height restrictions include El Capitan, Hodges, and Morena (self-imposed restriction). The allowable storage capacity with height restrictions are ~50,000 AF, 5,999 AF, and 16,742 AF, respectively.

  1.  Pure Water Clarification - For Pure Water Phase 1, we understand the North City Water Reclamation Plant (52 MGD recycled water) is being expanded to provide flow to the North City Pure Water Facility (30 MGD of purified water). What portion of the recycled water flow (if any) is being provided to existing recycled water customers once Pure Water is online?

The City will be honoring existing agreements with recycled water customers. The City is in the process of reviewing our recycled water policy to ensure it aligns with Pure Water needs.

  1.  Recycled Water Sewersheds and Service Areas – As we assess potential regional diversion and capture and use opportunities, we would like to map the sewersheds and service areas to/from the City’s recycled water facilities, including Pure Water. Would it be possible to put us in touch with someone to help with that request? Ideally, we are looking for GIS shapefiles beyond those available on SANGIS.

 Huy Nguyen (HTNguyen@sandiego.gov<mailto:HTNguyen@sandiego.gov>), Senior Engineer. Some data may be considered protected for security reasons. Specific requests will be evaluated once received.

  1.  Interview Follow-up Questions – as discussed, we would also like your input on the questions below.  Please let me know if you need clarification on any of them:

     *   What do you see as the biggest risk(s) to the region’s water supply portfolio with respect to long-term resilience?

While we are excited that Pure Water San Diego will be supplying nearly half of our water supply, we must not get complacent about our continued reliance on imported water. There is always risk associated with imported supplies that include influence by drought/disaster. We are partnering with San Diego County Water Authority on their Master Plan and will continue our own strategic Long Range Water Resource Planning that goes beyond Pure Water SD.

     *   How would you recommend that the San Diego Region allocate future efforts/resources toward the following water supply solutions, by percentage:

                                                               i.      Regional Water Recycling

                                                             ii.      Localized On-Site Reuse (e.g. Graywater)

                                                           iii.      Stormwater Capture and Reuse/Recycling

                                                           iv.      Desalination

                                                             v.      Storage Management - Reservoir Storage and Dam Management

                                                           vi.      Storage Management - Manage Groundwater Recharge

                                                          vii.      Conservation

Not sure I could put a percentage to any of these strategies, they all play such a critical role. I would say that while conservation is still valuable and our education must continue, I’ll echo statements made by Governor Newsom that we cannot conserve our way out of drought. The low-hanging fruit for conservation has mostly been achieved. Our indoor use rates are already practically aligned with very aggressive State targets and will not likely get much lower (and as we discussed during our meeting, lower indoor use could reduce the flows needed to operate Pure Water SD). We still must target outdoor water use, but the best way forward to address issues of supply is to get more creative about our storage solutions and investigate feasibility of other supply sources. I’ll also note that localized on-site reuse, while supported by the City with a permitting process, is not something the City actively promotes because of our regional water recycling program. Localized on-site reuse is better suited for communities that do not have a regional program.

     *   Which of the following water supply solutions do you view at the “most at risk” in terms of being a reliable, long term source of water for the region? Which is “least at risk”?  Write “most risk” and “least risk” after two of the options below, and elaborate in 1-2 sentences on why.

                                                               i.      Regional Water Recycling

                                                             ii.      Localized On-Site Reuse (Graywater)

                                                           iii.      Stormwater Capture and Reuse/Recycling – Most Risk

                                                           iv.      Desalination

                                                             v.      Storage Management – Reservoir Storage and Dam Management – Least Risk

                                                           vi.      Storage Management - Managed Groundwater Recharge

Any strategy that relies on rainwater will be considered “most risky” due to the fact that we know we will be seeing longer dry periods punctuated by heavy storms, and those dry periods would create burdens to water suppliers needing to provide a consistent year-round supply. The better way to make use of those heavy storms, and the option with “least risk”, is leaning into our storage management, particularly in the realm of reservoir storage and dam management.

Thanks again for all your assistance in support of this project.

Stephanie

body:
Hi all,

We’ve been making progress on getting interviews scheduled and conducting them in support of this project.  We’re anticipating on having a busy May and get the majority of the interviews completed.  We’re happy to share some updates from the County team that will allow you to initiate some outreach to additional stakeholders following the protocols from the previous email below:

  *   DMAX:  We’ve received the OK for you to coordinate getting the SF PUC and City of Tucson graywater focused interviews on the calendar.
  *   Re-focus: We’ve received the OK for you to coordinate San Diego Food System Alliance interview (looping in Rebeca Appel with the County who should be included on all future agricultural focused interviews).  FYI, Elise and team are also working to introduce Geosyntec/re-focus to the SD Farm Bureau so we can make progress on interviewing Mary Matava as well as the individual farmers she would like to include and can coordinate on the best way to go about this.  Stay tuned for that.
  *   3i Strategies/Nettleton Strategies: Carl, as discussed today, please let us know if you/Mohsen have any potential labor/workforce contacts that could provide that perspective via an interview (as noted below, we originally identified Labor Council, San Diego Building and Construction Trades Council, and LiUna as being groups of interest.  Open to other suggestions as well!).  Please also keep us posted on your progress with scheduling the IID interview.

Thanks, please let us know if you have any questions.
Stephanie

Stephanie Castle Zinn
Geosyntec Consultants
Mobile: 949-436-0730

From: Stephanie Zinn
Sent: Monday, April 10, 2023 8:12 PM
To: Mohsen Mortada <Mmortada@3istrategies.org>; Carl Nettleton <carl@nettstrategies.com>; shalini@refocuspartners.com; ben@refocuspartners.com; John Quenzer <jquenzer@dmaxinc.com>
Cc: Megan Otto <MMOtto@Geosyntec.com>; Maxwell Dugan <MDugan@Geosyntec.com>; Alyssa Yu <AYu@Geosyntec.com>; Ruiz, Elise <Elise.Ruiz@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Subject: FW: Stakeholder Interviews - Communication Protocol Update

3i Strategies, re-focus and Dmax teams:

In order to continue moving forward with interviews, San Diego County has given us permission to reach out and communicate directly with the various stakeholders, with the exception of the Water Utilities/Agencies whom the County will continue coordinate with (see email below).

Based on this direction, we have preliminarily identified groups that you may have relationships or connection with, and would like you to initiate outreach requesting an interview if this the case.  See below (Dmax, the County is still finalizing the final graywater focus groups, stay tuned):
3i Strategies

  *   Imperial Irrigation District (GM, Henry Martinez)
  *   ConAgua
  *   IBWC
  *   CESPT

Re-focus

  *   NRCS National Office

As a first step, we would like you to prepare a draft email to introduce the RWER and request an interview with your assigned stakeholders. An example .docx template has been provided for your use, and this can be modified based on the contact/relationship. The attached pdf documents (Fact Sheet and Minute Order) should be included in the request to provide additional background. If asked, please note that the “Fact Sheet” is being translated into the eight Threshold Languages<https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/dam/sdc/clerb/docs/2022-documents/10-2022/LanguageServicesTipSheet.pdf> and will be available soon.  The internal briefing sheet has also been provided for you to paraphrase for correspondence/written requests; however, this document should not be shared externally.

The draft email should be sent to me and Megan Otto for initial review. Once the email request has been approved, you may send the email with us cc’d along with Elise Ruiz (Elise.Ruiz@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:Elise.Ruiz@sdcounty.ca.gov>).

In addition, please also provide any other groups/stakeholders where you may have connections that you think may bring value.  Specifically, the County is looking for support identifying the right labor/workforce groups to interview.  We initially identified Labor Council, San Diego Building and Construction Trades Council, and LiUna.  If you have any relationships/contacts at these organizations, please let us know.  You can respond to this email with any suggestions.

Let us know if you have any questions.

Thank you,
Stephanie

Stephanie Castle Zinn
Geosyntec Consultants
Mobile: 949-436-0730

Hi Elise,

Just checking in on our inquiry below regarding Northern Baja regions to focus on?

Also, please see attached for a revised Stakeholder Interview List that has three phases described below.  I’d like to provide a short summary of our thinking behind this.  The graywater focus interviews are more technical in nature, so we feel like we can get those going sooner than later.  For the Task 2A longer list of stakeholders (15 to be interviewed), we didn’t want to start with too many as there are some decisions that still need to be made regarding the 15 to be interviewed.  Therefore, we only proposed 4 stakeholders on this list where we feel they would provide good input and would take less strategy to establish the interviews.  Most agricultural stakeholders are split between Phase 2 and Phase 3, we think the Phase 2 list could likely be reviewed by your team fairly quickly and would take less messaging strategy (e.g. for the national agriculture stakeholders that were proposed by re-focus).  We anticipate that the local agricultural stakeholders will take more strategy and are therefore listed under Phase 3.

  1.  Phase 1 – these stakeholders would require less strategy on messaging during the interview where Geosyntec/subs could be ready for interview scheduling now.
  2.  Phase 2 – these stakeholders require some strategy, and a meeting between Geosyntec/County is necessary to finalize messaging.
  3.  Phase 3 – these stakeholders require a lot of coordination between Geosyntec/County and require strategic messaging during the interviews.

Let’s plan to discuss this at our standing meeting on Wednesday and any questions you may have.  If possible, I think a good goal would be to get some of these Phase 1 stakeholder interviews going in a week from now to stay on schedule.  I’ll also plan to update the Sharepoint site with this revised matrix.

Thank you,
Stephanie

For the Task 2A longer list of stakeholders (15 to be interviewed), we didn’t want to start with too many as there are some decisions that still need to be made regarding the 15 to be interviewed. Most agricultural stakeholders are split between Phase 2 and Phase 3, we think the Phase 2 list could likely be reviewed by your team fairly quickly and would take less messaging strategy (e.g. for the national agriculture stakeholders that were proposed by re-focus).  We anticipate that the local agricultural stakeholders will take more strategy and are therefore listed under Phase 3.

  1.  Phase 1 – these stakeholders would require less strategy on messaging during the interview where Geosyntec/subs could be ready for interview scheduling now.
  2.  Phase 2 – these stakeholders require some strategy, and a meeting between Geosyntec/County is necessary to finalize messaging.
  3.  Phase 3 – these stakeholders require a lot of coordination between Geosyntec/County and require strategic messaging during the interviews.

Let’s plan to discuss this at our standing meeting on Wednesday and any questions you may have.  If possible, I think a good goal would be to get some of these Phase 1 stakeholder interviews going in a week from now to stay on schedule.  I’ll also plan to update the Sharepoint site with this revised matrix.

Thank you,
Stephanie

Hi Elise,

Just checking in on our inquiry below regarding Northern Baja regions to focus on?

Also, please see attached for a revised Stakeholder Interview List that has three phases described below.  I’d like to provide a short summary of our thinking behind this.  The graywater focus interviews are more technical in nature, so we feel like we can get those going sooner than later.  For the Task 2A longer list of stakeholders (15 to be interviewed), we didn’t want to start with too many as there are some decisions that still need to be made regarding the 15 to be interviewed.  Therefore, we only proposed 4 stakeholders on this list where we feel they would provide good input and would take less strategy to establish the interviews.  Most agricultural stakeholders are split between Phase 2 and Phase 3, we think the Phase 2 list could likely be reviewed by your team fairly quickly and would take less messaging strategy (e.g. for the national agriculture stakeholders that were proposed by re-focus).  We anticipate that the local agricultural stakeholders will take more strategy and are therefore listed under Phase 3.

  1.  Phase 1 – these stakeholders would require less strategy on messaging during the interview where Geosyntec/subs could be ready for interview scheduling now.
  2.  Phase 2 – these stakeholders require some strategy, and a meeting between Geosyntec/County is necessary to finalize messaging.
  3.  Phase 3 – these stakeholders require a lot of coordination between Geosyntec/County and require strategic messaging during the interviews.

Let’s plan to discuss this at our standing meeting on Wednesday and any questions you may have.  If possible, I think a good goal would be to get some of these Phase 1 stakeholder interviews going in a week from now to stay on schedule.  I’ll also plan to update the Sharepoint site with this revised matrix.

Thank you,

Stephanie

Also, please see attached for a revised Stakeholder Interview List that has three phases described below.  I’d like to provide a short summary of our thinking behind this.  The graywater focus interviews are more technical in nature, so we feel like we can get those going sooner than later.  For the Task 2A longer list of stakeholders (15 to be interviewed), we didn’t want to start with too many as there are some decisions that still need to be made regarding the 15 to be interviewed.  Therefore, we only proposed 4 stakeholders on this list where we feel they would provide good input and would take less strategy to establish the interviews.  Most agricultural stakeholders are split between Phase 2 and Phase 3, we think the Phase 2 list could likely be reviewed by your team fairly quickly and would take less messaging strategy (e.g. for the national agriculture stakeholders that were proposed by re-focus).  We anticipate that the local agricultural stakeholders will take more strategy and are therefore listed under Phase 3.

  1.  Phase 1 – these stakeholders would require less strategy on messaging during the interview where Geosyntec/subs could be ready for interview scheduling now.
  2.  Phase 2 – these stakeholders require some strategy, and a meeting between Geosyntec/County is necessary to finalize messaging.
  3.  Phase 3 – these stakeholders require a lot of coordination between Geosyntec/County and require strategic messaging during the interviews.

Let’s plan to discuss this at our standing meeting on Wednesday and any questions you may have.  If possible, I think a good goal would be to get some of these Phase 1 stakeholder interviews going in a week from now to stay on schedule.  I’ll also plan to update the Sharepoint site with this revised matrix.

Thank you,

Stephanie

Hello Water Equity Team!

Apologies for my delay in getting these to you - I was PTO for the later half of last week.

Below is a list of our upcoming gatherings as well as a few follow up questions from our team.

Upcoming RDF Gatherings:

*	7/24 - Mira Mesa Community Planning Group (D3)

*	9/2 - RDF tabling at Orgullo Gay Escondido (D5)
*	09/23 - RDF tabling at Oceanside Zine Fair (D5)
*	9/? (date TBD) - RDF presentation/listening session with Solana Center for Environmental Innovation
*	Early Fall (Date TBD) - tabling at the Southwestern Community College
*	10/12 Read aloud; discussion, lesson; hands on activity on RDF at VAPA (elementary school with Mrs. Spinks) (D5)
*	10/22 (tentative) - Youth Climate Event - RDF presentation, hands-on activities, speakers, breakout sessions at MiraMar College (D3 & D2)

Questions from the CAC Team:

*	At your earliest convenience, can you send us that specific language and talking points to use at our gatherings and newsletter communications?
*	If you have a 2-3 sentence blurb describing the project, that would be great as well!
*	Do you mind if we change the wording of the water equity question from "What does water equity mean to you?" to "How are you connected and/or impacted by water accessibility, supply, quality, etc.?"  or something along those lines?

You can see our survey here <https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLScVn3Pm1N5dDb0EThfghb7stMNWC1xIDWSgEkl58Od5Dps_aw/viewform?usp=sf_link> . I already added the questions, but we may modify that first question with your permission. We ask for zip codes, County District (with reference to a map), and email addresses. We have already integrated the questions into our surveys and gatherings (including a recent tabling event in Imperial Beach and at the Lakeside Library), and we will continue to do so going forward!

Excited to work in collaboration on this project going forward.

In Gratitude,

Ali

title: FW_ 4_26 Regional Water Convening - UCSD Coordination.msg
subject: FW: 4/26 Regional Water Convening - UCSD Coordination
body:
-----Original Appointment-----
From: Megan Otto <MMOtto@Geosyntec.com>
Sent: Wednesday, February 22, 2023 2:09 PM
To: Megan Otto; Ruiz, Elise; Baxamusa, Murtaza; Juli Beth Hinds
Cc: Stephanie Zinn
Subject: 4/26 Regional Water Convening - UCSD Coordination
When: Friday, February 24, 2023 9:00 AM-10:00 AM (UTC-08:00) Pacific Time (US & Canada).
Where: Microsoft Teams Meeting

Good afternoon,

We are looking forward to connecting with OSEJ and UCSD on next steps for the upcoming Regional Water Convening. For reference, UCSD’s scope of work includes the following tasks (abbreviated):

  1.  Literature review of existing and emerging water equity considerations, including:
     *   Physical impacts of drought conditions (which may include exposure to heat and pollutants as landscapes are affected);
     *   Equity, affordability, and water access in the face of necessary expenditures to ensure utility and supply resilience;
     *   Impacts on San Diego utilities of re-negotiation and re-structuring within the Colorado River Compact, especially for small and ‘downstream’ utilities;
     *   Implications for housing conditions, availability, and costs as measures are needed to adapt to drought, fire hazards, and shortage; and
     *   Implications for food access and security, given water costs and tradeoffs among uses.
  2.  Short summary report and graphics rich presentation document on the above critical area topics
  3.  Identification of key subject matter experts; appropriate attendees; pertinent data, documents, and research; and questions and exercises that can be used to elicit the most important contributions from participants.
  4.  Prepare workshop materials including agenda
  5.  Following the meeting (collaboratively with the County and Geosyntec), provide a meeting summary identifying specific actions to be taken to inform the report. Particular attention to defining which actors, with which authorities, would be responsible for focus areas or strategies in each of the critical issue areas.

Thanks,
Megan

Good afternoon Stephanie,
Pursuant to our conversation this afternoon UCSD would like to formalize a request for a minor scope amendment to reflect the change in focus and technical content of the Regional Water Equity Report convening slated for Wednesday, April 26th.  As the focus of the meeting will no longer be based on the contents of the drought impact literature review being conducted by UCSD, and as the need for and focus of presentation content and public information has changed, we would like to request approval of the following:

1. UCSD will focus on completion of a technical presentation highlighting preliminary findings of the literature review, submitted in powerpoint format by Friday, April 14th for editing and translation.  It is our understanding that the length of the presentation may be anywhere from ten minutes to roughly one hour, depending on the County’s selection of additional presenters with technical content.

2.  UCSD will complete a summary of the technical presentation for the public meeting.  This will be a graphic-rich handout in print and web-compatible format (likely powerpoint) by Friday, April 14th, offering key information and links in a form suitable for the general public and with links for further information to technical sources.

3.  For the meeting itself, UCSD will NOT be responsible for agendas, printing, name tags, etc.  as it is our understanding that Murakawa Communications has been contracted to supply these materials.  UCSD will have roughly ten (10) students present to assist with sign-in, logistics, polling, and collecting public comments.  UCSD’s students will have (10) iPads with them, with connectivity suitable for use for PollEverywhere questions for those without devices.

3.  UCSD will resume work on the literature review after the meeting, adding a review of available water rate information for San Diego and Imperial Counties and the bi-national region.  The meeting summary likewise will be completed.

Thank you Stephanie for your support and leadership!
Sincerely,
JB

Subject: Announcement: Welcome Bethany Facendini, OSEJ GPM Community Engagement

Greetings All,

I am thrilled to introduce Bethany Facendini, our new Community Engagement and Outreach Manager for the Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice (OSEJ). Bethany is an experienced community organizer and sustainability advocate, and she will lead our efforts to engage and empower diverse communities throughout our region for climate action.

Bethany will develop and implement strategies to foster community connections and participation in environmental justice and sustainability initiatives. She will work closely with community benefit organizations, leaders, practitioners, and residents to create opportunities for collaboration and partnership.

Bethany brings a wealth of experience and expertise to OSEJ, including numerous community engagement roles in the San Francisco Bay Area and beyond, most recently with Sonoma County Regional Parks as the Community Engagement Division Manager. There, she directed marketing, communications, and cross-sector partnerships, as well as created sustainability and equity-based programs for diverse audiences, community needs assessments, and evaluation systems. In addition, Bethany helped increase the number of culturally relevant programs for under-represented populations (BIPOC, youth impacted by systems, people with disabilities, and families with low incomes). She also served as Sonoma County Human Services’ Community Engagement Manager where she led community programs to increase awareness of services and community outreach events; cultivated relationships between private, governmental, and non-profit organizations to improve partnerships; and built community networks to connect marginalized groups to programs and services. From 2013 – 2015 as the Community Engagement Coordinator for the Sonoma County Department of Health Services, Bethany worked on community engagement and outreach to advance health equity systems change initiatives. She has a Master of Arts in Environmental and Social Justice and a Bachelor of Arts degree in English and LGBTQ Studies. She also has an Urban Environmental Education Certification from Cornell University.

Bethany has world travel and living abroad experience in 46 countries, mostly economically developing nations, and recently returned from a year-long sabbatical traveling solo around the world.

We are excited to have Bethany on board and look forward to her leadership in advancing our environmental justice and sustainability goals. Please join me in welcoming Bethany to our team.

Enjoy the day,

eden

Eden Brukman, Chief Sustainability Officer

Subject: Delegation from Saudi Arabia - OSEJ and PDS

Hi Nicole,

As we briefly discussed, the County has been invited to meet with a delegation from Saudi Arabia on this coming Wednesday, June 21 from 1-3:30pm. This is through the International Visitors Leadership Program <https://eca.state.gov/ivlp>  (IVLP) which is the U.S. State Department flagship professional exchange program. This invitation was offered by the San Diego Diplomacy Council yesterday (originally received by Dahvia, who sent to myself and Caroline Smith).

Tyler and I just met with the coordinator at the San Diego Diplomacy Council and it appears to be similar to when we welcomed the Japanese delegation, just on very short notice. Here are some details:

*	The topic of delegation trip is "Approaches to Climate Change Challenges"
*	The 11 individuals span government, private, and entrepreneurship and are traveling with 3 interpreters
*	The delegation is most interested in exploring and hearing stories from us around:

	*	Current policy frameworks of environmental laws, protections and conservation efforts
	*	Strategies for reducing carbon emissions
	*	Integrated approaches to develop climate resilient solutions which support vulnerable populations and maintain biodiversity

*	The delegation is currently in D.C. Once in San Diego, they will meet with Scott and Nilmini from USD-EPIC, and then they head to Imperial Valley for solar panels and lithium.

Some logistic and proposed approach:

*	They have asked us to host, and therefore, we could reserve a room at the CAC
*	They have asked for presentations and discussions to fill the 90 minute slot. Therefore, we propose:

	*	OSEJ Overview (Rebeca) & RDF presentation (Rimga) (same as the Japanese delegation)
	*	Discussion
	*	CAP Presentation (Tyler) (and potentially: Other Sustainability Programs)
	*	Discussion

Questions for you:

*	How should we brief this up to Sarah? Based on our experience with the Japanese delegation, would Sarah want to participate?
*	Could I have some assistance with logistics? With our recent experience with the Japanese delegation, it would be great if Yasamin would be able to help.

	*	Such as room reservations, reaching out to Board offices (if we want), coordinating refreshments and gifts (if needed/desired)

Thank you!

Rebeca Appel, Group Program Manager

Cc: Brukman, Eden <Eden.Brukman@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Subject: RE: Email Distribution Lists & Enewsletter

Hello Bethany. Happy Tuesday.

  *   I am wondering if there are any concerns about having email distribution lists in addition to the database for .gov delivery center functions? For example, can we collect RDF convening participants’ information to send them follow-up information via email or invite them to additional meetings? I can see how the .gov system is useful and effective, and I can also see how that may not be the only tool for email outreach for some groups. I am thinking about the feedback loop and opportunities for further involvement. You can develop additional email list of RDF or OSEJ stakeholders. In fact I would say that the goal is to increase out stakeholder list and become knowledgeable about how folks prefer to be communicate. I will say we must be aware that if we are taking the public information for one purpose, we must declare that we can use it for other projects or if its going to be used for an OSEJ master stakeholder list. I have separate email and communicate to folks separate through my email because I recognize that folks often either ignore the County emails or I do it to make sure they see its directly from our office and they know it’s information I want to be sure that they get.

  *   I am also curious if we have a LUEG enewsletter for our stakeholders/partners that would benefit from having a more concentrated effort to gather contact information from folks outside of the existing stakeholder lists?   Can you clarify if you are looking for another way to communicate to stakeholders? If tha the case, I would stay that if OSEJ can form a newsletter but it woud take a further conversation so we can ensure that it something we have the resources for outline the guidelines to which would guide the types of article and stories that get inserted. Our CAP team created a stakeholder newsletter/commincation piece that was intended to update their stakeholder so we can discuss that effort to see if its what you are inquiring about. Donna will need to opine on this one as well.

  *   I am thinking more about the unofficial community-based leaders and residents, perhaps that may not respond to official government communications, and the ways we can stay connected. I previously used texting for different groups since that was their preferred method of communication. Do we have a way of sending texts to folks for engagement and outreach purposes? An separate list of focus stakeholders is something we use as we get to know our stakeholders and try and communicate to those we know are deeply engaged. I don’t believe we have a mass text system but happy to explore. I have been doing it the hard way in terms of I text folks directly when I need a fast response or need to highlight an issue for them. I do want provide a reminder that all communication, whether text or otherwise can be requested as part of a Public Records Request.

I hope these responses help. Again, thse are the issues that I hope we can discuss in depth in our OSEJ biweekly outreach. If the biweekly are two far apart a you are getting started, then I would be happy to set up a weekly meeting to walk through some of this matters if that is helpful to you.

Thanks
MDLR

Subject: Pala EPA and County Water Equity Project

Good afternoon, Shasta,

I am the new and first official County-Wide Tribal Liaison in the County of San Diego. I met with Pala Tribal Council this past Wednesday and they provided me with your contact information to coordinate potential partnerships with your EPA Department. My colleague Elise and I would really like to connect with you to share what we have going on in the County and to learn more about what Pala is working on.

One of our current projects is a region-wide Water Equity Assessment that we just kicked off at the end of April and will continue through the summer through a series of 6 virtual workshops. We would love to have Pala and other tribes’ participation. Essentially, the outcome of this assessment is a report that identifies areas of concern for Water Equity in the region and that report will be in front of our Board of Supervisors and will likely be used as a reference tool for future policy and funding. I’ve attached a quick fact sheet for your review because it’s important to note that the project surrounds topics of drought conditions and water sustainability through greywater, wastewater, and stormwater capturing.

If you have time in the next week or two, can we set up a time to share more information? Our workshops start near the end of June.

Thank you and have a joyful weekend,

Sent: Friday, July 28, 2023 12:37 PM
To: Viskanta, Rimga <Rimga.Viskanta@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Subject: [External] RDF Clarity and New Direction

Hi Rimga!

Thanks again for being the moderator for Nexus! It's going to be great to have you there!

Regarding the RDF, after our last meeting, we've done some internal discussions and clarified our scope a bit. With the new direction around focusing on identifying specific climate action projects, I wanted to quickly confirm that we are on the right track.

*	Instead of focusing on engaging as many individuals as possible from Communities of Concerns, we will focus now on reaching organizations who are actively working on climate action projects that would benefit from the County's support or would help inform the Regional CAP and other future climate policies. These organizations will continue to be within and uplift Communities of Concern.
*	We will also highlight and focus on reaching local council offices and policy makers who are actively working on or identifying capital improvement projects that may benefit from the RDF as a reference or that may become part of future CAPs.
*	We are communicating that the RDF is a guide for implementing climate action throughout the region and can be used to inform climate policies on local and regional levels. While the County cannot lead the projects themselves, the County may be able to help provide resources in the form of grants, the RDF guidebook, etc.
*	After speaking with the Water Equity Team, we are incorporating water questions into our community gatherings and surveys.

Going forward, we do have a few followup questions as well!

*	When will the Convenings be? After speaking with the Water Equity team, it sounds like they will be in November afterall. Can we schedule a meeting ASAP to discuss programming, roles, and next steps? We are running out of time to book places and we should start promoting those soon for effective turnout.
*	If we are to focus on gathering feedback from organizations about specific projects, do you still need demographic data? If so, do you want that data coupled in a full survey like it currently is, or should we create a smaller demographic data only survey that accompanies the feedback that we receive in other ways (discussion, posters, notes, testimonies, etc.)
*	What do your project portfolios look like? How can we best compile project information to match and add to your existing portfolios?

Thank you!! I super appreciate your time and collaboration on this!

In Gratitude,

ali

November 28 – December 6: County to provide comments on draft

From: Baxamusa, Murtaza <Murtaza.Baxamusa@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Sent: Thursday, February 16, 2023 10:57 AM
To: Mikey Knab <mikey@climateactioncampaign.org>; Brian Pollard <bpollard@ucproject.org>; Carmina Paz <urbancollaborativeprojectcdc@gmail.com>; Ali Mariko Dressel <ali@climateactioncampaign.org>
Cc: Appel, Rebeca <Rebeca.Appel@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Subject: RDF Update: New Board hearing date and extended comment period

Hi,
I am sure you have already seen this notice below, but I wanted to send directly to you. Based on requests for more time for public comment on the initial draft of the playbook, the Board meeting has been moved to April 5. We want this to e an inclusive process and bring everyone along this long journey to decarbonize our region, together.

Thank you for all your comments and feedback on Monday, we are taking it all in and want to apply these lessons learned to our next convenings and our partnership with you all moving forward. You are key to our success and we know we are just at the beginning. Please call me if you have any questions.

Murtaza

________________________________________
Murtaza H. Baxamusa, PhD, AICP
Program Manager for Regional Sustainability
Land Use and Environment Group
Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice
County of San Diego

[cid:image001.png@01D941F5.6F1D3B80]

[San Diego County]

Status Update - Regional Decarbonization Framework

The Regional Decarbonization Framework presentation has been rescheduled to the April 5 Board of Supervisors meeting.

Accordingly, the comment period for the Regional Decarbonization Framework draft Implementation Playbook (Playbook) has been extended until March 31. The draft framework is available for review and comment on the Engage San Diego County<https://lnks.gd/l/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJidWxsZXRpbl9saW5rX2lkIjoxMDAsInVyaSI6ImJwMjpjbGljayIsImJ1bGxldGluX2lkIjoiMjAyMzAyMTYuNzE2NTYyNTEiLCJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL2VuZ2FnZS5zYW5kaWVnb2NvdW50eS5nb3YvcmRmIn0.4sIlQXaVzF4g862slMFsCo7krXqON_-N-Qj5MoL4LLM/s/1798050183/br/154586481607-l> website.

title: FW_ Regional Decarbonization Framework (Proposed CBO Approach) (23).msg
subject: FW: Regional Decarbonization Framework (Proposed CBO Approach)
body:
Hi Eden,

Earlier this week Murtaza sent an email to our CBO contracted partners to set up an introductory call with Rimga for RDF. However, based on our conversation on Tuesday with Michael about engaging with our CBOs for the Water Equity effort, we wanted to provide a suggested approach to see if you have any feedback before we move forward with proposing days/times to meet.

Proposed Approach:

*	Messaging: Ask CBOs to share out flyers on RWER Deep Dives

	*	If there are any questions about how this relates to their contract, Rebeca can have a conversation with contract point of contact on how this is part of our larger RDF foundational work.

*	Relationship Building with our CBOs:

	*	OSEJ team to meet with Bethany week of June 12 to provide historical context of our CBO partnership, efforts to date, and proposed future work
	*	OSEJ team (with Murtaza and Michael for the warm hand off) to meet with Urban Collaborative and Climate Action Campaign week of June 20th with the following agenda:

		*	Team introductions
		*	Where RDF is now
		*	Next Steps for RDF (this will inform direction of 2nd regional convenings maybe in November)
		*	Intersection of Water Equity with RDF

*	As you will be out of office the week of June 20th, we could provide dot points next week on each agenda item and what we plan to discuss. Alternatively, we could schedule this meeting the week of June 26th, once you are back (early in the week, as Rimga will be out starting the 28th).

We met as a team to discuss the overall CBO strategy and think this would be a good first step. We look forward to your feedback!

Thank you,

Rebeca

Subject: Regional Decarbonization Framework - update

Dear community partners,

We wanted to let you know that we are working on a revise to the RDF Playbook that will be posted soon. We know that many of you have been waiting to use this tool in identifying community-driven climate action, and we are grateful for the interest.

Whilst we are on this topic, I wanted to e-introduce you to Rimga Viskanta (copied), who will be leading the RDF in the future. Rimga is systems thinker and super-smart problem-solver that was working on energy codes, climate plan and a zillion other things for Solana Beach. Rimga will be leading the RDF project in the future and supported by a growing & talented OSEJ team with a wide range of expertise.

We would like to schedule a call with Rimga so that you all can get to know her.

Murtaza

________________________________________

Murtaza H. Baxamusa, PhD, AICP

Program Manager for Regional Sustainability

Land Use and Environment Group

County of San Diego

 [cid:image002.jpg@01D94218.62B6DD60]            [cid:image003.png@01D94218.62B6DD60]

From: Baxamusa, Murtaza <Murtaza.Baxamusa@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:Murtaza.Baxamusa@sdcounty.ca.gov>>
Sent: Thursday, February 16, 2023 3:01 PM
To: Boghossian Ambrose, Nicole <Nicole.Ambrose@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:Nicole.Ambrose@sdcounty.ca.gov>>
Subject: FW: Response to Concerns (County RDF): NAACP North San Diego County

From: Baxamusa, Murtaza
Sent: Thursday, February 16, 2023 3:01 PM
To: austinsatia@gmail.com<mailto:austinsatia@gmail.com>; Sonja NAACP ECJ <sonja.naacpecj@gmail.com<mailto:sonja.naacpecj@gmail.com>>
Cc: Wooten, Wilma <Wilma.Wooten@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:Wilma.Wooten@sdcounty.ca.gov>>
Subject: RE: Response to Concerns (County RDF): NAACP North San Diego County

Dear Satia and Sonia,
On behalf of the Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice (Office), we would like to congratulate Satia on your recent award for community service in the city of Oceanside, in the honor Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. We applaud your long-time efforts to engage the youth and in the furtherance of racial justice.
We have received your letter on behalf of NAACP North San Diego County (NSDC).  Thank you for applauding the County’s efforts with the Regional Decarbonization Framework. I appreciate the attention NAACP NSDC is bringing to important equity considerations and look forward to being able to address your concerns.
By way of background, our Office was created by Board direction to have a regional lens on both sustainability as well as environmental justice. The founding principle of our Office is to address past and present injustices, and to ensure that these injustices do not occur in the future. We are in the process of establishing the programs of this Office and would truly appreciate working with you on this. You can find more information about us at: Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice (sandiegocounty.gov)<https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/sdc/lueg/Office-of-Environmental-and-Climate-Justice/>
Our flagship project - the Regional Decarbonization Framework (RDF) - supports our visionary goal of reaching zero carbon emissions by 2045 or sooner in the San Diego region, and it is based on the guiding principles of science-based pathways, regional collaboration and community engagement centered on equity. The work on this framework began with Board direction in January 2021, and with Board direction in April, will continue until we no longer have a climate crisis in the region. We sincerely appreciate the participation of NAACP NSDC leadership in this project, some of whom I have known and admired for their heroic advocacy for many years.
The County’s strategic initiatives span across the entire organization, break down silos and set measurable goals on sustainability, community, equity, empowerment, and justice. Our Board of Supervisors has broken down historical barriers to inclusivity and participation through strong leadership in policies and programs.  This is my own calling to be part of this transformation. I strongly believe that equity is the key to sustainability<http://web.mit.edu/dusp/dusp_extension_unsec/projections/issue_8/issue_8_baxamusa.pdf>, and that we cannot address climate change without meaningful participation of all communities. Our RDF team’s innovative work on community outreach through new forums, venues and tools of community engagement, new forms of partnerships with community-based organizations, and the new ways of access to experts and technical material, demonstrate our commitment to the founding principles of our Office.
However, we recognize that more can and should be done and are grateful for the points raised in your letter to the County Board of Supervisors. Here are some of our initial thoughts on the questions that you raise:
Engagement for the Technical Study:
The technical study authored by a team of experts led by UC San Diego School of Global Policy & Strategy began their work in July 2021 and have updated the Board of Supervisors and the public five times over this period. Three drafts of the Regional Decarbonization Framework Technical Report were prepared followed by public comment and review periods, focus groups, as well as concurrent reviews by a Technical Work Group on each draft. We had workshops on every topic last year, and the authors discussed their findings with a variety of stakeholders. A summary of this report has been available online on the RDF website<https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/sdc/sustainability/regional-decarbonization/projects.html>, in eight languages since the very beginning. The RDF team appreciates the participation of NAACP NSDC leaders in the development of the technical study.
Engagement for the Implementation Playbook:
The Playbook is the first-ever user-friendly compilation of best practices that resulted from an inventory of climate action measures/activities in all Climate Action Plan (CAP) in the region. It is being supplemented by stakeholder and community feedback on activities that need to be included, as well as case studies locally or from other regions. By making this resource available to the public, we hope that it will guide future CAP updates for all jurisdictions in the San Diego region and serve as a living resource informed by the learned experiences of individuals, communities, businesses, and agencies. Work to shape the Playbook began in August last year starting with a co-design process by working groups tailored to the five sectors that were studied. We organized regional convenings by each Supervisorial District to provide a basic understanding of the impacts of climate change on public health in the region and how we can get communities to be engaged in the implementation activities for climate mitigation and resiliency.
Public comment has always been welcome on the RDF throughout our process. We receive comments through our website, Engage platform<https://engage.sandiegocounty.gov/rdf>, emails, phone calls and meetings, and will continue to receive input and comments throughout the development and implementation of the RDF. The meeting presentation for the regional convenings were posted in advance on our website on January 15, translated in all 8 threshold languages. District 3 residents could view the publicly posted materials in an accessible format, as well as participate in any of the regional convenings, both in person or virtually. The intent of having a convening physically located within a Supervisorial District was to increase access to residents throughout our vast region that want to attend a meeting in person. We also received written comments from Sonja on February 1, to whom we are appreciative for participating in person at the District 5 regional convening. We understand the hardship of the cancelled event in District 3 beyond our control and worked to reschedule it at the earliest date that the speakers were available.
The County released a partial draft on the Framework’s Implementation Playbook in January, and our team is currently incorporating some recommended information and public comments on the initial draft. The public comment period for that partial initial draft has been extended to March 31 to reflect community input that will serve as a basis for a newly scheduled Board meeting discussion on April 5. Public comment will continue throughout the implementation process and to help the region reach its goals our efforts will continue evolve and reflect best practices available in current regulatory and technical environments. Following the April Board discussion on the Playbook, we will take it back out into area neighborhoods to explore possibilities, get reactions and suggestions from the community.  This fall, we are planning a second series of regional convenings by supervisorial district as well as in tribal lands. This series of convenings will be focused on community-driven implementation activities. To bolster participation, please send us recommendations of people you would like included.
It is important to note that the County is not recommending or mandating any particular activity in the Playbook. This is a collective knowledge base that needs to be continually informed by some of the climate-related activities that are already occurring in frontline communities. The work to date is just the beginning of our journey to decarbonize the region, and the success of this effort depends on active participation by all stakeholders and communities. We would like to know how we can work together to implement decarbonization activities at a scale and in the pathways that interest you and members of your community. Please continue to be engaged and participate in RDF implementation.
Representation Terminology
We are sensitive to the concerns raised regarding representation terminology and use of the term “disadvantaged community”. We agree that the region needs to come together on terms and definitions in order to meet our goals of inclusivity and justice, and we would like to invite you to a regional discussion on this nomenclature. We have had many internal discussions of this topic so far, and the various terms that are used across agencies and agree conversations must continue. This is an important topic that needs consultation with frontline communities throughout San Diego county who would self-determine this regional approach. Our RDF technical study also shows that the integration of social equity in Climate Action Plans in the region is limited, inconsistent, and lacks specificity. We will have a preface statement clarifying the use of “disadvantaged community” in the Implementation Playbook that will recognize the need to have a regional conversation around representation terminology. We would welcome your input and comments on the development of guidance on terminology in the near future as part of an upcoming regional social equity working group that will be hosted by our Office.
We do however, want to note that with the intent to align regional climate-related activities across local jurisdictions, particularly to attract State and federal funds that are needed to support community-level involvement and work on future implementation projects, the term “disadvantaged community” is used consistently for both funding applications and processes. For example, the Justice40 Initiative in President Biden’s Executive Order 14008<https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2021/01/27/executive-order-on-tackling-the-climate-crisis-at-home-and-abroad/> (Section 223), State statutes such as Clean Energy and Pollution Act of 2015, and State laws for greenhouse gas reduction funds. We hope that we can continue to work together to ensure our frontline communities benefit from these investments in the future.
Stakeholder Inclusivity:
We recognize that improvements can always be made to be inclusive, and we welcome your thoughts on what actions could be taken, from a contracting standpoint or otherwise, to be more inclusive and better serve the community. Our County is committed to working with the community to co-create transformative, enduring structural, and systematic change in San Diego County government. We appreciate your attention to this and look forward to working with NAACP NSDC to refining our approach to date, to include groups that have not been reached by our efforts so far. Working together, we can build upon what we’ve been able to achieve, for example, through the Partners for Places grant. This grant supports BIPOC-led frontline organizations such as the Partnership for Advancement of New Americans, Majdal Center, YouthWill and the Global Action Research Center. Their reach is regional in nature, so that it covers District 3 as well as other districts. In addition, our Office recently co-partnered in a National Institute for Health grant application with UCSD School of Public Health and the Multicultural Health Foundation that serves mostly African Americans in Southeast San Diego. Although this grant application was not successful, we will continue to look for opportunities to fund similar partnerships with frontline communities. Our contractors on community engagement for the RDF regional convenings, Climate Action Campaign and The Urban Collaborative Project, were selected through a competitive solicitation process with criteria that emphasized community engagement of all the different demographics within each district. They have therefore put together a network of different community-based organizations to reach the unique communities of each district. This is just the starting point of what we can do as a region, and we welcome your input in this area.
Our community engagement to date, over a two-year period covering different stages of RDF studies, has included 32 public meetings with over 2,000 participants. In case anyone missed the meetings, they are posted on our website<https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/sdc/sustainability/regional-decarbonization/outreach-and-engagement.html> and we welcome participation through our Engage website<https://engage.sandiegocounty.gov/rdf>. We have had over 200 meetings with business, labor, community, environmental advocates, cities, tribes, regional agencies, etc. since our goal is to tailor the conversation to each group and meet them where they are. We will continue to reach out with more individuals and groups that have not yet been engaged in developing implementation options for this visionary framework.
We would like to work with NAACP NSDC to help us identify the organizations and community members for involvement and explore potential forms of partnership to help us reach zero carbon emissions in the region, together.
In closing, we appreciate the interest of NAACP NSDC executive leadership in participating in the RDF. We hope we have addressed your comments regarding the RDF timeline, representation terminology, and stakeholder inclusivity. We look forward to ongoing collaboration to strengthen all we have done to this point to engage the community, please feel free to reach me directly if you have any follow up questions or would like to set up a meeting.
Thank you,
Murtaza
________________________________________
Murtaza H. Baxamusa, PhD, AICP

Subject: [External] Response to Concerns (County RDF): NAACP North San Diego County

Greetings Chairwoman Vargas, Vice-Chair Lawson-Remer, and Board of Supervisors;

Please find attached a letter from the NAACP North San Diego County of significant issues that exist/ed in the County's Regional Decarbonization Framework. I will share some details of the sequence of events that prompted this letter with issues to be addressed. In general, we want to applaud the County for taking bold steps to address the climate crisis and environmental injustices. There are a lot of great things listed in the RDF. We also appreciate that the County is actively addressing the issues listed in the attached letter. As a public government body, it's important that these sequences of events are on record and noted to be addressed. This in itself helps to increase constituents' faith in our public officials. I want to say thank you, and we appreciate that our voices are being heard.

Public Sign of Bravery
I would like to share that many throughout the County felt it was commendable for Vice-Chair Lawson-Remer to stand with the janitorial union members on January 23, 2023, yet felt like the constituents in County District 3 were penalized for the RDF rescheduling when the public comments closed on February 2, 2023. As a member of our great County, I did address the RDF program management about this immediately.

Highlighted Issues
This letter highlights the inequitable process of the RDF project timeline, as well as other inequities to address that includes the following;

Extend the public comments section for the draft Implementation Playbook phase of the RDF to accommodate County District 3 constituents and residents.

Replace the terminology of "disadvantaged communities" that is meant to address the Black, Indigenous, People of Color communities with language that is acceptable from that community.

Adopt equitable contracting practice with Black frontline organizations throughout the RDF process. Include frontline communities as major stakeholders throughout the process.

Sequence of Events (How Did We Get Here)
I would like to share a brief list of sequence of events on the need to address the observation of inequities in the process of the County's Regional Decarbonization Framework.

Wednesday, February 1, 2023: I emailed Murtaza Baxamusa asking if the public comments were going to be extended until County District 3 has their convening.

As a member of the project team, this letter was emailed to Dr. Wooten and her team on Monday, February 13, 2023.

February 14, 2023, I had a discussion with Chairwoman Vargas senior staff, David Flores and he shared that Chairwoman Vargas agrees with the issues that are raised in this letter and that these matters are being addressed.

February 15, 2023, I had a discussion with Vice-chair Lawson-Remer’s staff, Rebecca Smith and she shared similar sentiments from my conversation with Chairwomen Vargas’s office. We also discussed perception from the public’s perspective of the timeline and public engagement in the process. She offered an open communication with Vice-chair Lawson-Remer’s office in sharing information that could be helpful from the community. Also, that the public feels like the March 15, 2023 Board vote is rushed.

This letter is being sent by the NAACP North San Diego County Branch. Many organizations, individuals, and groups share and support the positions listed in the letter. An example of some of the support includes:

Affinity clubs/groups, ADEMS, CEC, Women led workspace organizations, community based health professions, community members, environmental justice coalitions, Indivisible Groups, SURJ, Clean Earth 4Kids, San Diego Urban Sustainability Coalition, Interfaith Collaborations, Faith churches (North County, and the City of San Diego), Youth Focus Organizations, list of previous candidates for public office, etc.

Please feel free to contact us with any inquiries, comments, and questions.

Best regards and Environmentally yours,
Sonja Robinson
