Subject: UCSD workshops

Dear UCSD team,

The approach on the following workshops has been approved. The next steps for the UCSD team are:

Workshop #1: Please place a hold on November 7 on all your calendars and reserve the PEB space. It would be helpful to begin drafting an agenda/program that we would be discuss with Sarah on September 2.
Workshop #2: We will be coordinating with the Planning and Development Services Department and get back to you.
Workshop #3: It would be helpful if we can develop a timeline. We will be coordinating with our Vice Chair Nora Vargas.

Thank you!
Murtaza
____________________________

  1.  Enterprise-wide Alignment of RDF
Date: November 7, 2022 (back-up would be November 4, 2022)
Participants:  County of San Diego internal department leadership, internal stakeholders
Duration: Full-day 2-part workshop
Location: 7th floor terrace at the Public Engagement Building

This workshop would provide an initial convening of County of San Diego leadership and departments engaged in the implementation of decarbonization across municipal functions:  (1) Departmental Sustainability Planning, led by LUEG; (2) the Land Acquisition Roundtable, led by Parks & Recreation; and (3) the renewable energy siting framework in the RDF.  This workshop would focus on the County departments’ short/mid/long term goals towards sustainability; geospatial and policy relationships, conflicts, and potential synergies among and between land acquisition for park, conservation, and recreation purposes; and the extent of land area for new solar and wind energy required by alternative strategies in the RDF.  This approach would help build a common understanding of the policy levers and constraints for the departments in relationship to GHG reduction, and the distribution and extent of each set of land use needs, supporting the goal of identifying potential synergies including opportunities for multi-benefit uses of land for agriculture, water and watershed sustainability, recreation, and regional habitat linkage.

***This workshop would be in tandem with the preparation of document defining the scope of work regarding the team’s advisory role for LUEG and the RDF. [Ref: Tasks 2.1 & 2.2]

  2.  Sustainable Land Use Framework (SLUF)
Timeline: Early 2023
Participants: County’s Planning & Development Services Department, external stakeholders
Location: First floor lab on the ground floor of the Public Engagement Building

This workshop will focus on the themes adopted by the Board in September 2022 in the context of the General Plan for the unincorporated area of the County. It would not be framed as RDF implementation but would examine the potential alignments of SLUF with decarbonization pathways. These themes could include: (1) decarbonization of buildings, communities, and transportation through policies and land use; (2) increase opportunities for sustainable and resilient development and housing for all; (3) support green economies, innovative infrastructure, agriculture, and sustainable best practices; (4) conserve and protect existing natural habitats and resources, and increase access to open and green spaces; and (5) prioritize social equity and environmental justice in sustainable land use policies, programs, and plans.

  3.  Binational Regional Climate Action Plan
Timeframe:  Last quarter 2023/first quarter 2024
Participants:  Jurisdictions in San Diego County with CAPs (municipalities; SANDAG; Unified Port of San Diego; US Department of Defense); California Office of Policy & Research
Invited Guests:  Governments of Baja California Norte; City of Tijuana; UABC

The third workshop would engage stakeholders across the county and San Diego-Tijuana region in evaluating the consistency and commonality of purpose and strategies among and between the individual Climate Action Plans (CAPs) adopted pursuant to State directives and local initiative.  UCSD students would prepare assessments of each plan in a unified framework illustrating the baselines, policies, action steps, and reporting metrics across the region.  The workshop will focus on building common awareness and purpose; exchanging strategies and ideas; identifying areas of potential re-alignment; and building a binational baseline for emissions and measures. This workshop would explore the possibility of a Binational Regional Climate Action Plan.

**UCSD also could extend some of the mapping into Baja California to illustrate trans-border issues, notably for transportation, housing, watersheds, and habitat.

_____________________________________
Murtaza H. Baxamusa, PhD, AICP
Program Manager for Regional Sustainability
Land Use and Environment Group
County of San Diego

***This workshop would be in tandem with the preparation of document defining the scope of work regarding the team’s advisory role for LUEG and the RDF. [Ref: Tasks 2.1 & 2.2]

  2.  Sustainable Land Use Framework (SLUF)
Timeline: Early 2023
Participants: County’s Planning & Development Services Department, external stakeholders
Location: First floor lab on the ground floor of the Public Engagement Building

This workshop will focus on the themes adopted by the Board in September 2022 in the context of the General Plan for the unincorporated area of the County. It would not be framed as RDF implementation but would examine the potential alignments of SLUF with decarbonization pathways. These themes could include: (1) decarbonization of buildings, communities, and transportation through policies and land use; (2) increase opportunities for sustainable and resilient development and housing for all; (3) support green economies, innovative infrastructure, agriculture, and sustainable best practices; (4) conserve and protect existing natural habitats and resources, and increase access to open and green spaces; and (5) prioritize social equity and environmental justice in sustainable land use policies, programs, and plans.

  3.  Binational Regional Climate Action Plan
Timeframe:  Last quarter 2023/first quarter 2024
Participants:  Jurisdictions in San Diego County with CAPs (municipalities; SANDAG; Unified Port of San Diego; US Department of Defense); California Office of Policy & Research
Invited Guests:  Governments of Baja California Norte; City of Tijuana; UABC

The third workshop would engage stakeholders across the county and San Diego-Tijuana region in evaluating the consistency and commonality of purpose and strategies among and between the individual Climate Action Plans (CAPs) adopted pursuant to State directives and local initiative.  UCSD students would prepare assessments of each plan in a unified framework illustrating the baselines, policies, action steps, and reporting metrics across the region.  The workshop will focus on building common awareness and purpose; exchanging strategies and ideas; identifying areas of potential re-alignment; and building a binational baseline for emissions and measures. This workshop would explore the possibility of a Binational Regional Climate Action Plan.

**UCSD also could extend some of the mapping into Baja California to illustrate trans-border issues, notably for transportation, housing, watersheds, and habitat.

_____________________________________
Murtaza H. Baxamusa, PhD, AICP
Program Manager for Regional Sustainability
Land Use and Environment Group
County of San Diego

subject: [External] Re: Accepted: RDF Leadership/SDSU Smart Grid Lab
body:
Dear Rimga,

Thank you for your follow up and reaching out and considering my input for the upcoming Energy Study. I appreciate your dedication towards decarbonizing our electrical grid and exploring solar potential in our region.

I believe it's important to highlight the current limitations of rooftop solar due to voltage constraints. As we've previously discussed in county meetings, a substantial portion of residential rooftop solar is being curtailed, preventing power from being effectively injected into the grid. Therefore, understanding how much of rooftop solar generation actually contributes to the grid could be a significant aspect of the study.

In terms of efficiency, we might want to compare the rooftop solar potential to the benefits of utility-scale solar investments, a topic I have found intriguing and significant from a grid perspective.

I agree that knowing the distribution of solar power across the county is crucial. Moreover, studying solar social equity could be another fascinating aspect - exploring who is injecting solar power and how much they're generating would give us a better understanding of solar adoption and utilization within our county.

The recent rate hikes have been quite concerning for residents across all income levels. Therefore, another potential research question could be to estimate how much of these hikes could have been avoided with smarter planning and better utilization of renewable energy sources.

I’m currently traveling to Europe for a related sustainability project and my availability is limited. However, I understand the importance of this project and would be happy to discuss these points with you in a meeting next week. Please let me know a suitable time for you and I will do my best to accommodate it in my schedule.

Best,

Saeed

body:
Hi Rimga,

It is a pleasure to help.

Rooftop solar is limited to the hosting capacity of the the feeder. If voltage is out of range, the solar generation will be waist. Therefore, as a rule of thumb, after 30-50% (depending on location in the feeder and a dozen other technical details) penetration level, adding more rooftop is not a good idea unless there is local storage.

Let me tell you what is wrong with the current setup which will unfortunately be the case for future rate hikes: NEM is treating the grid as an storage which you inject to and get back later. In reality, there is no such storage exists but a live market is there. The wholesale price is on average MUCH cheaper than the rate utilities are enforced to buy from customers. Once get back from the utilities though the wholesale (most of the time) is still MUCH MUCH cheaper with a couple of days a year being WAY more expensive than average. Here is my point: the problem is a rigid and non-transparent regulated rates which belongs to a different era in the history. I’m in full support for regulations but the current practice in place is just socializing a loss to Californians each year. What is my exit plan? A smarter and more transparent way to regulate. I would be happy to discuss this with you in more detail upon my return next week.

Best,
Saeed

title: _External_ Re_ Energy study question.msg
subject: [External] Re: Energy study question
body:
Hi Rimga,

I’d be happy to chat with you about this. I’ll also ask my team tomorrow about this— we have a micro grid team that supports communities interested in developing micro grids and the CPUC has two programs (including the microgrid incentive program) that you might want to look into.

My primary question though is what problem you’re trying to solve. Micro grids are a solution— and can be very costly— so I’ll be interested in hearing more about the issue you’re trying to tackle.

Cheers,
Heather

Sent from my iPhone

On Apr 18, 2023, at 8:05 PM, Viskanta, Rimga <Rimga.Viskanta@sdcounty.ca.gov> wrote:

?
Heather,

Thanks in advance for your time! I’m hoping you might have some feedback or advice, but of course let me know whether you don’t have enough information or time to provide input.

The quick summary is that I’m trying to develop a scope of work for a regional energy study to supplement the technical information that’s already been included in the County’s Regional Decarbonization Framework (RDF).

The RDF included a focus on utility-scale renewable energy and mentioned some generalized information about the potential for power generation from rooftop solar.  We are exploring whether an energy study could provide useful data to the region at a more community and localized level and want to be sure we are asking the right questions of the study.

Some general themes or current ideas for the study include cost/benefit analyses for when rooftop solar and battery storage might be a better option for a community (like Solana Beach, for example) versus just hooking into utility-scale energy providers for renewable energy (like the CCA’s or SDGE renewable energy options).  When does a microgrid makes sense for a community to try to implement?

Honestly, right now the topic for the study is wide open and none of us has a strong enough technical background in energy matters to understand whether are we even asking the right questions in an energy study.  One goal of the study would be to support community projects around the region by helping to secure some of the federal funding coming to the area.  If the projects could be part of a bigger regional picture, perhaps their chances of getting funding would be stronger.

Here was a study we saw that we were considering using as a reference to develop our own scope of work: Chapter 4. Customer-Adopted Rooftop Solar and Storage (nrel.gov)<https://www.nrel.gov/docs/fy21osti/79444-4.pdf>

I am open to any input you might have on this topic.

Thank you for your time!

body:
Viskanta, Rimga has shared a OneDrive for Business file with you. To view it, click the link below.

[icon]
20230721 OSEJ REN Briefing.pptx<https://sdcountycagov.sharepoint.com/sites/LUEG-OSEJ/Shared%20Documents/General/Initiatives/RDF-Regional%20Focus/3_Pathways-Regional%20Project%20Initiatives/Energy/2_Regional%20Energy%20Network%20(REN)/20230721%20OSEJ%20REN%20Briefing.pptx?web=1>

As discussed here is a draft email.

***

Dear Sarah,

We met with SDCP again on Monday 7/17 to discuss the County’s potential role in development of a San Diego Regional Energy Network (SD-REN). SDCP previously confirmed that they have 100% capacity in-house to complete all the work, administrative and logistical, to stand up the REN allowing us to define the County’s role, and therefore the resources we would like to assign to the task, to ensure the REN aligns with priorities identified throughout the RDF process and forthcoming Energy Supply Study.  SDCP confirmed there is no fiscal or legal commitment required from the County other than resources we choose to assign to the task.

We recommend the County serve as the second government agency in partnership with SDCP in an advisory role capacity (“thought leadership”). This would offer the County the ability to ensure what SD-REN proposes is aligned with the County’s other programmatic initiatives.

To meet SDCP’s desired deadline to submit a completed application to the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) for approval by December, we recommend the County submit a letter of support (draft attached) to SDCP by October 1, 2023.

  *   If you agree with this approach what should our next steps be to inform the Board Offices?
The letter of support can come from administrative staff.  There is no CPUC requirement for it to come from the Board of Supervisors, but it is an option as well.  If the CPUC accepts the application, then the Board of Supervisors will need to formally approve an MOU sometime in 2024 depending upon when CPUC approval of the application is received.

Here are some dates of which to be aware:

  *   8/9/23 – SDCP will present draft programs at San Diego Regional Climate Collaborative (SDRCC) Working Group meeting for initial feedback. While they will be presenting the full draft program portfolio, they will specifically be looking for feedback on the draft public sector programs. There is other engagement planned for draft residential, commercial and workforce development programs.
  *   9/11/23 – Deadline for stakeholders to provide initial feedback on draft programs to SDCP.
  *   9/28/23 – Update on REN will be provided at the SDCP Board of Directors Meeting (Supervisor Terra Lawson-Remer serves on the SDCP Board).
We have also attached a revised REN presentation that could be used to inform the Board Offices about the initiative.

Rimga Viskanta, Group Program Manager

title: Energy Study BL Question.msg
subject: Energy Study BL Question
to: Hernandez, Stephanie <Stephanie.Hernandez@sdcounty.ca.gov>; Brukman, Eden <Eden.Brukman@sdcounty.ca.gov>; Baxamusa, Murtaza <Murtaza.Baxamusa@sdcounty.ca.gov>
body:
Here is our proposed language and we are wondering whether we should call out NREL directly as a possible vendor to do the study, because what if they do not want to?  Do we need to have a specific vendor identified at this point?

We propose a scope of work for an expanded regional renewable energy supply study that incorporates local context and geographic conditions to better inform policy decisions at the jurisdictional level.

The energy section in the Regional Decarbonization Framework (RDF) examined the financial costs of producing renewable energy from a societal macro perspective. It did not examine other potentially negative externalities created by utility scale power, such as increased financial costs for new or expanded transmission lines; effects on flora and fauna; or view impacts to neighboring communities, for example.  Nor did it quantify the benefits of infill renewable energy generation, such as self-sufficiency and resilience when combined with storage; peace-of-mind protection against power outages; grid stability; and lower risks from wildfire due to transmission lines.

An accompanying energy study to the RDF could address the following question: How can all people in the County of San Diego have affordable and reliable access to renewable energy? Using the lens of the regulatory context in California and the existing energy supply ecosystem that impacts this region, the study could review three scales of energy production, distribution, and transmission:

1.       Rooftop Solar (i.e., residential scale);

2.       Community microgrids (i.e., community-scale); and

3.       Utility scale.

Paired with this, the study could include appropriate storage solutions relative to each scale to help inform and quantify capacity for representative land use types that roughly translate to characteristics of the County’s diverse geographies. It could also integrate “Triple Bottom Line” analyses to account for lifecycle financial, social, and environmental co-impacts.

Suggested Board Direction (Option 2):

1. Find that the proposed actions are not a project pursuant to the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) pursuant to Section 15378(b)(5) of the CEQA Guidelines.

2. Pursuant to Board Policy B-66, authorize the Director, Department of Purchasing and Contracting, upon successful negotiations and determination of fair and reasonable price, to award a contract with the National Renewable Energy Laboratory to do a study of the renewable energy generation and storage capacity of the region that considers resiliency from power outages, economic benefits and costs including transmission and distribution, and local community context.

3. Direct the Chief Administrative Officer to include the study in future reports and updates of the Integrated Regional Decarbonization Framework.

Rimga Viskanta (She/her/hers<https://www.mypronouns.org/>)
Group Program Manager
Land Use and Environment Group | County of San Diego
1600 Pacific Highway, Room 212, MS: A-6
San Diego, CA 92101

title: FW_  Re_ measuring emissions in the RDF.msg
subject: FW:  Re: measuring emissions in the RDF
body:
Just FYI.  Seems like it could have limited use for rooftop solar data, but the fact that the tool cannot differentiate whether emissions are from federal, state or local sources doesn’t make it useful for measuring emissions resulting from the local activities we’d seek to monitor.

Rimga Viskanta, Group Program Manager

(she/her/hers)

Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice <https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/osej/>

Regional Decarbonization Framework <https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/sdc/sustainability/regional-decarbonization.html>

C: 619-929-9891

From: Nilmini Silva-Send <silvasend@sandiego.edu>
Sent: Sunday, July 23, 2023 3:02 PM
To: Viskanta, Rimga <Rimga.Viskanta@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Cc: YichaoGu@sandiego.edu; Cory Downs <cdowns@chulavistaca.gov>; Xiaodan Chen <xiaodanchen@sandiego.edu>
Subject: [External] Re: measuring emissions in the RDF

Hi Rimga,

We are familiar with some of the team members contributing to this story  (specifically I have spoken on panels with the HESTIA and the Vulcan group) but we have not used this group’s tools. It provides near real-time emissions data, also partly modeled using AI, and uses remote sensing and satellite data.

You are right that it is different from the way we do inventories. Specifically for rooftop solar, we rely on California DG Stats, which provides actual installed distributed solar data from which we can estimate the GHGs avoided due to that. So it would complement our work in monitoring some things. Similar to this link you sent, we recently used Google’s Project Sunroof data (it is what Cory referred to a while back) - although it is now fairly dated, to estimate and identify the gap between the potential rooftop solar as determined by Google’s Sunroof project (which also uses AI) and low income areas in the county. This was merely to identify areas which could have rooftop solar installed, (as estimated by Google’s method based on roof space and orientation) in particular in LI areas.

For emissions analysis, it uses different boundaries, and allocates/attributes emissions differently to cities, from the standard way that cities in California do (which use the US Communities Protocol developed by ICLEI which is similar to the Global Protocols). It would be unable to distinguish federal/state/local emissions sources, . For electricity for example we estimate the emissions based on electricity end-use, whereas this  method would only “see" emissions from wherever fossil fuels are combusted, so at the electricity-generation plant, and natural gas combustion in buildings.

Happy to chat more! I’ve also copied Xiaodan Chen, our other staff member who is familiar with the Google Project Sunroof data.

Nilmini

	On Jul 20, 2023, at 9:28 AM, Viskanta, Rimga <Rimga.Viskanta@sdcounty.ca.gov <mailto:Rimga.Viskanta@sdcounty.ca.gov> > wrote:

	Nilmini & Yichao,

	Are you familiar with this tool?  Seems the San Diego region could potentially use this tool for no cost if we apply and I’m wondering whether it would augment our current GHG inventory efforts?  Or will it move us away from our existing methodology too much?

	Here is a sample of how the tool is being used in Los Angeles:

	CCI Case Study: Targeting Residential Rooftop Solar (arcgis.com) <https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/1073581020eb46d5b16c0b03f6d9e2ed>

	I’m cc’ing Cory from Chula Vista, because I remember a regional CAP meeting many moons ago where he had shared some info about various GHG quantification methods he looked into.  I believe that was a Google tool at the time, but can’t really remember the details now.

	Rimga Viskanta, Group Program Manager

	(she/her/hers)

	Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice <https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/osej/>

	Regional Decarbonization Framework <https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/sdc/sustainability/regional-decarbonization.html>

	C: 619-929-9891

	<image001.png>

	From: Joe Houde <joe@ecinstitute.com <mailto:joe@ecinstitute.com> >
	Sent: Wednesday, May 24, 2023 10:29 AM
	To: Baxamusa, Murtaza <Murtaza.Baxamusa@sdcounty.ca.gov <mailto:Murtaza.Baxamusa@sdcounty.ca.gov> >; Viskanta, Rimga <Rimga.Viskanta@sdcounty.ca.gov <mailto:Rimga.Viskanta@sdcounty.ca.gov> >
	Subject: [External] measuring emissions in the RDF

	Hi,

	Attached is a description of a new tool for measuring emissions.  I recommend the County evaluate it and suggest it would be a great addition to the RDF process. If you can’t measure it, you can’t manage it.

	The tools is offered in conjunction with the World Meteorological Organization, and other world-class groups at NO cost, as you’ll see.

	One of the key players, Kevin Gurney from NAU, architect of Project Hestia,  has done presentations for NCCCA and we’ve had multiple rewarding discussions.  He shared one presentation with Ralph Keeling from UCSD and Nilmini Silva-Send from USD. I know USD has contracts for bottom-up emissions measurement for several organizations in the County.

	At the end of the document, there is an option to reach out to be included in the next round of cities covered by Tier 2 and Tier 3 emissions analysis.  I’d love to have all of San Diego included (LA is already complete). Would the RDF team be interested in joining NCCCA and hopefully other climate-focused groups in submitting a request to RMI for inclusion? USD is certainly welcome to participate. The County would be a great lead organization for this project.

	Best,

	Joe

	<city_climate_intelligence_addressing_the_urban_greenhouse_gas_emissions_information.pdf>

Subject: 5/25 Governor Press Conference - Building Clean Energy Projects

Points from today's Governor Newsom press conference on building clean energy projects are below. Here is link to UT article: California governor seeks to speed up water, clean energy projects delayed by lawsuits, permits (msn.com) <https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/politics/california-governor-seeks-to-speed-up-water-clean-energy-projects-delayed-by-lawsuits-permits/ar-AA1bqp2s>

The Governor's Clean Energy Energy Plan includes:

*	Cut project timelines by more than three years
*	Save businesses and state and local governments hundreds of millions of dollars
*	Reduce paperwork by hundreds of thousands pages

The legislative package and executive order (attached) will:

*	Speed Up Construction: Current construction procurement processes drive delays and increase project costs. The Governor's proposals include methods to offer a streamlined process for project delivery to reduce project timeframes and costs.
*	Expedite Court Review: Legal challenges often tie up projects even after they've successfully gone through environmental review. These proposals would authorize expedited judicial review to avoid long delays on the back end and advance projects without reducing the environmental and government transparency benefits of CEQA.
*	Streamline Permitting: Makes various changes to California law to accelerate permitting for certain projects, reducing delays and project costs.
*	Address cumbersome CEQA processes across the board: Streamlines procedures around document retention and review.
*	Maximize Federal Dollars: Establish a Green Bank Financing Program within the Climate Catalyst Fund so that the state can leverage federal dollars for climate projects that cut pollution, with an emphasis on projects that benefit low-income and disadvantaged communities.

This is great news for speeding up clean energy projects, battery storage projects and other work and all of the RDF work.

David Flores

Office of Chairwoman Nora Vargas | County Supervisor, First District

Subject: FW: measuring emissions in the RDF

Tyler,

Are you familiar with this tool?  Seems the San Diego region could potentially use this tool for no cost if we apply and I'm wondering whether it would augment our current GHG inventory efforts?  Or will it move us away from our existing methodology too much?  I'm reaching out to Nilmini as well for her take since it seems they presented to her as well.

Here is a sample of how the tool is being used in Los Angeles:

CCI Case Study: Targeting Residential Rooftop Solar (arcgis.com) <https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/1073581020eb46d5b16c0b03f6d9e2ed>

Rimga Viskanta, Group Program Manager

From: Joe Houde <joe@ecinstitute.com <mailto:joe@ecinstitute.com> >
Sent: Wednesday, May 24, 2023 10:29 AM
To: Baxamusa, Murtaza <Murtaza.Baxamusa@sdcounty.ca.gov <mailto:Murtaza.Baxamusa@sdcounty.ca.gov> >; Viskanta, Rimga <Rimga.Viskanta@sdcounty.ca.gov <mailto:Rimga.Viskanta@sdcounty.ca.gov> >
Subject: [External] measuring emissions in the RDF

Hi,

Attached is a description of a new tool for measuring emissions.  I recommend the County evaluate it and suggest it would be a great addition to the RDF process. If you can't measure it, you can't manage it.

The tools is offered in conjunction with the World Meteorological Organization, and other world-class groups at NO cost, as you'll see.

One of the key players, Kevin Gurney from NAU, architect of Project Hestia,  has done presentations for NCCCA and we've had multiple rewarding discussions.  He shared one presentation with Ralph Keeling from UCSD and Nilmini Silva-Send from USD. I know USD has contracts for bottom-up emissions measurement for several organizations in the County.

At the end of the document, there is an option to reach out to be included in the next round of cities covered by Tier 2 and Tier 3 emissions analysis.  I'd love to have all of San Diego included (LA is already complete). Would the RDF team be interested in joining NCCCA and hopefully other climate-focused groups in submitting a request to RMI for inclusion? USD is certainly welcome to participate. The County would be a great lead organization for this project.

Best,

Joe

Subject: Regional Water Equity - Comprehensive Report

Good afternoon all,

I hope all is well and that you've been enjoying the start to summer! My name is Elise Ruiz, and I am a group Program Manager with the Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice.

You may be aware of the Regional Water Equity effort <https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/osej/waterequity/> , which was directed by the Board in September 2022. OSEJ and DPW have been working with our technical consulting team Geosyntec on this effort to develop a region-wide assessment to analyze water sustainability best practices, and produce a comprehensive report with recommendations and opportunities. The report will identify strategies to address drought impacts, and we are now finalizing the next steps to prepare for the review of the first draft comprehensive report in early August.

I wanted to connect with the PDS team to notify you all for awareness that this report is coming down the pipeline, and provide review dates in case your team is interested in contributing technical reviews. The report will go through first draft reviews from August 11 and through August 16, before going to Deputy Chief Administrative Officer, Sarah Aghassi for review. It will then go to public comment, before return to the Board in winter 2024. I've summarized these milestones below:

Comprehensive Report Review

*         Review first draft August 11 - August 16

*         Review before DCAO review August 29 - September 5

*         Review after public comment October 15 - October 20

I've attached the project fact sheet as well for your reference. Please let me know if you would like more information on these efforts, I'm happy to answer any questions you may have or set up a call to talk through this more.

Have a great weekend,

Elise Ruiz, Group Program Manager

Cc: Aghassi, Sarah <Sarah.Aghassi@sdcounty.ca.gov>; Lawson, Jennifer <Jennifer.Lawson@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Subject: Agenda and Goals for Nov 7 workshop at UCSD

We began the journey on the Regional Decarbonization Framework (RDF) last year in January when our Board of Supervisors directed us to work with UCSD on bringing the best available science to address a challenge that none of us can address in silos on our own – that of decarbonizing every major emitting sector in the region no matter where the emissions originate, for emissions know no boundaries.

As we are now transitioning from study to implementation, we are asking what can we do collectively in partnership with universities, business, labor and community, that will give us greater efficiencies in scale and speed to address climate change in the most effective and humane way possible. All of us from the County have sustainability embedded within the strategic direction of each of our departments. The goals of this workshop are to think about what more can we do? How do we implement sustainability within our core functions? How do we add value to our existing programs so that they also meet the goals of decarbonization? What new programs can achieve a better outcome?

We are meeting offsite at the Public Engagement Building at UCSD to visualize that greener future.

This workshop begins a new chapter in our relationship with UCSD as an academic partner to help us figure out how to implement this framework. This will be the first in a series of three workshops over our 3-year partnership. The UCSD team will focus on the implementation of the RDF for this workshop.  While of course there are many intersecting issues, the exercises will focus on land-based implications of RDF as well as simply getting everyone more proficient in the vocabulary and implications of the RDF itself. We will also walk through specific scenarios so that we leave the day with a practical understanding of how this framework can inform the work we do on a day-to-day basis in all our departments.

Thank you and looking forward to seeing you on Monday,

Murtaza and Sarah

Subject: All Day Offsite Workshop at UCSD
When: Monday, November 7, 2022 9:00 AM-4:00 PM (UTC-08:00) Pacific Time (US & Canada).
Where: UCSD Social Sciences Public Engagement Building, 7th Floor Terrace

Please join us for an exciting new workshop led by our UCSD collaborators. This workshop would provide an initial convening of County of San Diego leadership and departments engaged in the implementation of decarbonization across municipal functions:  (1) Departmental Sustainability Planning, led by LUEG; (2) the Land Acquisition Roundtable, led by Parks & Recreation; and (3) the renewable energy siting framework in the RDF.  This workshop would focus on the County departments’ short/mid/long term goals towards sustainability; geospatial and policy relationships, conflicts, and potential synergies among and between land acquisition for park, conservation, and recreation purposes; and the extent of land area for new solar and wind energy required by alternative strategies in the RDF.  This approach would help build a common understanding of the policy levers and constraints for the departments in relationship to GHG reduction, and the distribution and extent of each set of land use needs, supporting the goal of identifying potential synergies including opportunities for multi-benefit uses of land for agriculture, water and watershed sustainability, recreation, and regional habitat linkage.

LOCATION: UCSD Social Sciences Public Engagement Building, 7th Floor Conference Room, in the new 6th College at UCSD, 9am - 4pm.
Location: https://goo.gl/maps/WzYiL8WjLEesmtyj8

Specific Parking Instructions will come soon.

The EPA announced the first phase of the $5B Climate Pollution Reduction Grants Program. Counties are eligible entities. Is PDS reviewing this opportunity? Do you see any potential for DPW commitments in the CAP to be threaded into a PDS application?

Climate Pollution Reduction Grants | US EPA<https://www.epa.gov/inflation-reduction-act/climate-pollution-reduction-grants#CPRGProgramGuidance>

CPRG planning grant funds are restricted to projects that are directly related to the development, updating, or evaluation of state, local, tribal or territorial plans to reduce climate pollution (i.e., to reduce GHG emissions and/or enhance carbon sinks). In general, funds may be used for:

   *   Staffing and contractual costs necessary to develop the deliverables identified in this document;
   *   Planning and implementing meetings, workshops, and convenings to foster collaboration among and between levels of government, the public, and key stakeholders;
   *   Outreach and education for stakeholders and members of the public
   *   Subawards to municipalities, air pollution control agencies, regional planning organizations, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), academic institutions, etc.;
   *   Modeling and analytical costs, including purchase or licensing of software, data, or tools;
   *   Studies, assessments, data collection, etc., needed to develop the required deliverables;
   *   Evaluation and metrics-tracking activities;
   *   Training and staff capacity-building costs;
   *   Supplies (e.g., office supplies, software;, printing, etc.);
   *   Incidental costs related to the above activities, including but not limited to travel, membership fees, and indirect costs; and/or,
   *   Other allowable activities as necessary to complete the required deliverables.

title: RDF Follow Up.msg
subject: RDF Follow Up
body:
Morning Tyler,

I wanted to follow up on our Monday check in with some more about our existing contracts, as well as a recap of our public meeting last night for your awareness.

Contracts
   *   UCSD – overall policy and implementation support, sustainable agriculture/food systems (screenshot of task below). Contract is through April 2025.

   *   USD EPIC – implementation playbook, implementation playbook with specific/tailored actions for the unincorporated county, supplemental report on other agencies/large companies CAPs and other emissions (Task 3), social equity guidelines (Task 6), and climate equity indicators (Task 7). Contract is through June 2025.
        *   As discussed – we are working with EPIC on timeframes and can follow up with you.

7/26 Public Meeting
   *   Playbook – a lot of questions on why no metrics or targets in this. We explained that this is our first step to work towards implementation, and as this is a visionary framework we want to work collaboratively and with local governments and organization to bring them into this effort to collectively work towards our goal.
        *   Also emphasized that the Playbook actions will be shaped by our working groups, EPIC will provide some places to start based on the Local Policy Opportunity (chapter 8), but we want this shaped and guided by our working groups.
   *   Overall folks were pretty happy with the inclusion of our new sector – food systems & circular economy – many comments around how waste diversion is often not included and overlooked.
   *   Based on feedback we received from Sarah, we included the link to the PDS site with the actions going before the Board on 8/31 and we received a question on whether the climate farming pilot would fall under land use & natural climate solutions or food systems & circular economy – my response was that these sectors intersect and are closely related as carbon farming improves soil health, as well as in agricultural production specific to food. So we kept it general to show that there will be overlap.
        *   Another example is in electricity when we talk about rooftop and infill solar – it starts in electricity (generation), but can intersect with buildings as those will need to connect.

I’ve also attached our PPT from last night. The slides specific to the Playbook will be the base for future stakeholder presentations. Please let me know if you have any questions – I know this is a lot of info, so happy to chat about it to.

Rebeca Appel

Hi Nicole,

As we briefly discussed, the County has been invited to meet with a delegation from Saudi Arabia on this coming Wednesday, June 21 from 1-3:30pm. This is through the International Visitors Leadership Program <https://eca.state.gov/ivlp>  (IVLP) which is the U.S. State Department flagship professional exchange program. This invitation was offered by the San Diego Diplomacy Council yesterday (originally received by Dahvia, who sent to myself and Caroline Smith).

Tyler and I just met with the coordinator at the San Diego Diplomacy Council and it appears to be similar to when we welcomed the Japanese delegation, just on very short notice. Here are some details:

*	The topic of delegation trip is “Approaches to Climate Change Challenges”
*	The 11 individuals span government, private, and entrepreneurship and are traveling with 3 interpreters
*	The delegation is most interested in exploring and hearing stories from us around:

	*	Current policy frameworks of environmental laws, protections and conservation efforts
	*	Strategies for reducing carbon emissions
	*	Integrated approaches to develop climate resilient solutions which support vulnerable populations and maintain biodiversity

*	The delegation is currently in D.C. Once in San Diego, they will meet with Scott and Nilmini from USD-EPIC, and then they head to Imperial Valley for solar panels and lithium.

Some logistic and proposed approach:

*	They have asked us to host, and therefore, we could reserve a room at the CAC
*	They have asked for presentations and discussions to fill the 90 minute slot. Therefore, we propose:

	*	OSEJ Overview (Rebeca) & RDF presentation (Rimga) (same as the Japanese delegation)
	*	Discussion
	*	CAP Presentation (Tyler) (and potentially: Other Sustainability Programs)
	*	Discussion

Questions for you:

*	How should we brief this up to Sarah? Based on our experience with the Japanese delegation, would Sarah want to participate?
*	Could I have some assistance with logistics? With our recent experience with the Japanese delegation, it would be great if Yasamin would be able to help.

	*	Such as room reservations, reaching out to Board offices (if we want), coordinating refreshments and gifts (if needed/desired)

Thank you!

On May 12, 2023, at 3:19 PM, Stephani Baxter <stephani.fallbrook@gmail.com<mailto:stephani.fallbrook@gmail.com>> wrote:

Thanks Rimga for your time on the phone this afternoon! Looking forward to meeting you Monday. If you come up for dinner before, Village Roots or Coal Bunker are a couple great restaurants on Main Ave.

Below are a few general questions/concerns the Fallbrook Planning Group would like to discuss on Monday. If you want to send me a presentation before Monday early afternoon, that’d be great!

ENERGY RELIABILITY/VULNERABILITY.

                1. GRID STRAIN. How will the increased electrification of everything without back-up infrastructure (wind, solar, natural gas, etc) expose us to security vulnerability and energy reliability?
                2. EMS COST/RELIABILITY. Costs to replace EMS vehicles and retrofit buildings will be on the backs of taxpayers. If grid is strained, how can EMS vehicles and buildings serve to protect and save lives?

RECYCLING.

  1.  RECYCLING. What is the plan for recycling lithium ion batteries when they reach their end of life, which will begin 10-15 years FROM NOW?
  2.  CIRCULAR ECONOMY - Can you help explain this concept?
  3.  How can we protect unincorporated and high fire areas from becoming dumping grounds for these hazardous materials which have an inconvenient tendency to explode if disassembled incorrectly? Once a lithium ion battery ignites, it cannot be extinguished with conventional fire fighting methods. This is exceptionally concerning for high-fire areas such as Fallbrook.
WATER RELIABILITY and AFFORDABILITY.

  1.  What efforts are RDF and BOS collaborating on with MET, Co River and more locally, SDCWA to help lift the burden of rising water costs?
  2.  North County is home to a variety of precious agriculture which is sadly on the decline due to the some of the highest water rates in the country. CA’s food contribution to the nation and world is of great importance. San Diego County ranks as the 19th largest FARM ECONOMY in the nation (of 3000 Counties).
EQUITY.

  1.  HVAC/APPLIANCES. If conversion to electric appliances is mandated or even incentivized for existing structures, low-income and middle-class households are hit the hardest. A large percentage of already underserved Fallbrook residents would be negatively affected.

  1.  TRANSPORTATION. North County workers will be disproportionally affected.  any workers in North County drive to work. Those who rely on their cars/trucks will be hit hard. Fleet industries will suffer. Mass transit and bicycling incentives have little benefit to North County residents. For example, contractors; from appliance repair to the roofer, cannot unitize transit options for their vocation, and will be forced to use “managed lanes” to be time efficient. These costs are passed on to the consumer.
  2.  HOUSING. Retrofitting homes and businesses. Tenant costs will skyrocket (residential and commercial). Home prices will increase. Taxes and “fees” will increase.
The unintended consequences as they relate to economics, energy reliability and Land-Use for a NetZero by 2035 or even 2045 goal, are of great concern.
Thanks Rimga and have a wonderful weekend,

-Stephani Baxter

This sounds like a great opportunity for OSEJ!  I was thinking this would be a wonderful event for Eden to join if she were interested, but I see that she's out through the 23rd.

I'd be happy to have one of our Sustainability staff join, but also wanted to reach out to you and LUEG.

We do provide solar fee waivers and previously provided green building fee waivers (that program has concluded). We are currently working on an affordable green building study that may lead to additional incentives.  I can provide more details and also reach out to Lulu on the key topics.

Question for you is if you'd like to join or have any representation from OSEJ?

Caroline, copying you here from the intergovernmental lens, as the IVLP is tied to the U.S. State Department.  We haven't worked with them much and wasn't sure if the County had a relationship with this entity.

Thank you.

Dahvia

Subject: [External] Meeting Opportunity: Climate Action Delegation from Saudi Arabia

Good afternoon Dahvia,

I hope you are having a great week.

I am reaching out from the San Diego Diplomacy Council to see if you or another County representative is interested and available to meet with an incoming International Visitors Leadership Program <https://eca.state.gov/ivlp>  (IVLP) delegation we are hosting.

Through IVLP, the U.S. State Department's flagship professional exchange program, we will be hosting a delegation exploring "Approaches to Climate Change Challenges" later this month. Featuring 11 subject matter experts from Saudi Arabia, this delegation will be exploring:

*	Current policy frameworks of environmental laws, protections and conservation efforts
*	Strategies for reducing carbon emissions
*	Integrated approaches to develop climate resilient solutions which support vulnerable populations and maintain biodiversity

Please see bios attached for the visitors.

Would you be interested and available to meet with this delegation from 1:30 - 3:00pm on Wednesday, June 21?

During this meeting, we hope to discuss incentives provided by San Diego County to encourage sustainable building practices throughout the region, with a particular focus on remodels and renovations, and developer relations.

Let me know if you or one of your colleagues is available to meet with this delegation

Thank you very much - I look forward to hearing from you soon.

Warm regards,

Lulu Bonning

Dahvia,
This is an Esri ArcGIS Portal tool called “Experience Builder”. We have the same tool in our Portal(s) in the event you or the team are interested in this kind of dashboard building feature.
If the USDOT data is more interesting than the specific website wrapper, we can get it from them and host it locally or recreate the methodology if necessary.

As data it is largely the information from American Community Survey being filtered with specific thresholds (e.g., poverty) and then value added with Health, Environmental, and Economic cost burdens by community or tract. The value to the tool is that it allows you to drill down to specific communities. The unfortunate element is that it does not consider the unincorporated county as a separate community area (just the cities). We could download and extract this unique area of the unincorporated if needed.
Just FYI – no action needed.

Department of Transportation Equitable Transportation Community Explorer Tool

The Department of Transportation (DOT) has released its Equitable Transportation Community (ETC) Explorer<https://experience.arcgis.com/experience/0920984aa80a4362b8778d779b090723/page/Homepage/> to support the agency’s implementation of the Justice40 initiative. The Justice40 initiative, created by the Biden Administration through Executive Order, is a key component in DOT’s efforts to confront and address decades of underinvestment in transportation.

The ETC Explorer is an interactive web application that uses 2020 Census Tracts and data to explore the cumulative burden communities experience caused by underinvestment in transportation. Its purpose is to provide a deeper understanding into how communities experience transportation disadvantage to help ensure the benefits of investments address the transportation-related causes of disadvantage. The ETC explorer assesses transportation disadvantage in five components:  Transportation Insecurity, Climate and Disaster Risk Burden, Environmental Burden, Health Vulnerability, and Social Vulnerability.  It is designed to complement Council for Environmental Quality’s Climate & Economic Justice Screening Tool (CEJST).

DOT’s Justice40 website<https://www.transportation.gov/equity-Justice40> also includes information on how stakeholders can address the “Three Major Components of DOT’s Justice40 Initiative” and provides links to more than sixty Technical Assistance resources offered by USDOT.

title: REQUEST_ Building Decarbonization Workshop Input.msg
subject: REQUEST: Building Decarbonization Workshop Input
body:
Hello County Colleagues,

OSEJ, in partnership with the Department of Urban Studies and Planning at UC San Diego, will conduct a workshop for local governments and agencies in the region to further discussions in areas of focus identified in the Regional Decarbonization Framework (RDF) documents, with an emphasis on building decarbonization. We hope that you will attend; we are currently holding time on the calendar for the morning of December 11.

To help frame the conversation, we welcome your input to inform the content and design of the workshop so that it might support the work you are doing or would like to do to decarbonize buildings in the unincorporated areas or more broadly across the county.

If you could answer any or all of the following questions by October 15th, it will help us create a workshop more tailored to your needs:

1.                  What is your jurisdiction doing already (or planning to do) in terms of building decarbonization (lowering carbon emissions of existing or new buildings)?

2.                  What are the building types or sectors (residential, commercial, industrial, rentals, etc.) that pose the great challenge for you in terms of lowering carbon emissions in your jurisdiction?

3.                  What are your biggest concerns and challenges with the implementation of building decarbonization in your jurisdiction? Is there a topic you feel would be beneficial to learn more about or discuss as a region in a workshop format with the County and other local jurisdictions?

4.                  If you feel there is someone else in your organization who would like to provide input or attend this SD County/UCSD-led workshop on building decarbonization with other local jurisdictions, please list their name, job title, and email address(es).

5.                  Are you available to attend a workshop at UCSD on Monday, December 11th from 9 AM to 12:30 PM with lunch included?

We look forward to your input and any other suggestions.

Rimga Viskanta, Group Program Manager

(she/her/hers)

Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice <https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/osej/>

Regional Decarbonization Framework <https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/sdc/sustainability/regional-decarbonization.html>

C: 619-929-9891

title: Request_ County building decarb workshop strategy.msg
subject: Request: County building decarb workshop strategy
to: "Viskanta; Rimga" <Rimga.Viskanta@sdcounty.ca.gov>; "Farmer; Tyler"	<Tyler.Farmer@sdcounty.ca.gov>; "Marchesano; Charles"	<Charles.Marchesano@sdcounty.ca.gov>; Susan Freedman	<Susan.Freedman@sandag.org>; "Buso; Shelby" <SBuso@sandiego.gov>
cc: "Facendini; Bethany (She/Her/Ella)" <Bethany.Facendini@sdcounty.ca.gov>;	"De La Rosa; Michael" <Michael.DeLaRosa@sdcounty.ca.gov>; Amy Lerner	<amlerner@ucsd.edu>
body:
Greetings Folks!

I'm reaching out today because OSEJ is collaborating with UCSD to facilitate several workshops related to the RDF, and we are just starting to think about purpose/content for the second convening this fall - identified as an opportunity to further explore building decarbonization. (My understanding is that the first one, held last November, had a broad decarbonization focus and included County staff). Would appreciate your insights!

For context: There were (at least!) a couple of milestone moments this week that have got my wheels turning about how this workshop can be purposeful for the region:

*	City of San Diego initiated their 3-part workshop "sprint" focusing on existing building decarbonization
*	SANDAG hosted the kick-off meeting for the EPA's Climate Pollutant Reduction Grant Priority Climate Action Plan that reinforced the significance of the existing building sector as a key focus area for the region.

I am curious how our workshop can benefit from the learnings of City of San Diego's sprint and possibly feed into the regional P-CAP process... or other related work.

A few themes have been posed:

*	Municipal portfolios
*	Single family residential (owned/rentals)
*	Multiunit rentals

Of course, open to other ideas/approaches, too! Depending on your feedback, we can plan to include the other jurisdictions (including those representatives participating the in CPRG P-CAP and others) and/or some friends who are central to that aspect of the ecosystem.

Starting this as an email thread to gauge your interest and am happy to arrange a meeting if that forum can better support sharing/brainstorming.

Thanks in advance for your thoughts on how this workshop can bring value to our collective efforts.

smiles,

eden

Eden Brukman, Chief Sustainability Officer

Good afternoon Stephanie,
Pursuant to our conversation this afternoon UCSD would like to formalize a request for a minor scope amendment to reflect the change in focus and technical content of the Regional Water Equity Report convening slated for Wednesday, April 26th.  As the focus of the meeting will no longer be based on the contents of the drought impact literature review being conducted by UCSD, and as the need for and focus of presentation content and public information has changed, we would like to request approval of the following:

1. UCSD will focus on completion of a technical presentation highlighting preliminary findings of the literature review, submitted in powerpoint format by Friday, April 14th for editing and translation.  It is our understanding that the length of the presentation may be anywhere from ten minutes to roughly one hour, depending on the County’s selection of additional presenters with technical content.

2.  UCSD will complete a summary of the technical presentation for the public meeting.  This will be a graphic-rich handout in print and web-compatible format (likely powerpoint) by Friday, April 14th, offering key information and links in a form suitable for the general public and with links for further information to technical sources.

3.  For the meeting itself, UCSD will NOT be responsible for agendas, printing, name tags, etc.  as it is our understanding that Murakawa Communications has been contracted to supply these materials.  UCSD will have roughly ten (10) students present to assist with sign-in, logistics, polling, and collecting public comments.  UCSD’s students will have (10) iPads with them, with connectivity suitable for use for PollEverywhere questions for those without devices.

3.  UCSD will resume work on the literature review after the meeting, adding a review of available water rate information for San Diego and Imperial Counties and the bi-national region.  The meeting summary likewise will be completed.

Thank you Stephanie for your support and leadership!
Sincerely,
JB

Sent: Friday, July 28, 2023 12:37 PM
To: Viskanta, Rimga <Rimga.Viskanta@sdcounty.ca.gov <mailto:Rimga.Viskanta@sdcounty.ca.gov> >
Subject: [External] RDF Clarity and New Direction

Hi Rimga!

Thanks again for being the moderator for Nexus! It's going to be great to have you there!

Regarding the RDF, after our last meeting, we've done some internal discussions and clarified our scope a bit. With the new direction around focusing on identifying specific climate action projects, I wanted to quickly confirm that we are on the right track.

*	Instead of focusing on engaging as many individuals as possible from Communities of Concerns, we will focus now on reaching organizations who are actively working on climate action projects that would benefit from the County's support or would help inform the Regional CAP and other future climate policies. These organizations will continue to be within and uplift Communities of Concern.
*	We will also highlight and focus on reaching local council offices and policy makers who are actively working on or identifying capital improvement projects that may benefit from the RDF as a reference or that may become part of future CAPs.
*	We are communicating that the RDF is a guide for implementing climate action throughout the region and can be used to inform climate policies on local and regional levels. While the County cannot lead the projects themselves, the County may be able to help provide resources in the form of grants, the RDF guidebook, etc.
*	After speaking with the Water Equity Team, we are incorporating water questions into our community gatherings and surveys.

Going forward, we do have a few followup questions as well!

*	When will the Convenings be? After speaking with the Water Equity team, it sounds like they will be in November afterall. Can we schedule a meeting ASAP to discuss programming, roles, and next steps? We are running out of time to book places and we should start promoting those soon for effective turnout.
*	If we are to focus on gathering feedback from organizations about specific projects, do you still need demographic data? If so, do you want that data coupled in a full survey like it currently is, or should we create a smaller demographic data only survey that accompanies the feedback that we receive in other ways (discussion, posters, notes, testimonies, etc.)
*	What do your project portfolios look like? How can we best compile project information to match and add to your existing portfolios?

Thank you!! I super appreciate your time and collaboration on this!

In Gratitude,

ali

subject: [External] FW: County Regional Water Equity Convening - Scope Modification
to: "Benham; Crystal" <Crystal.Benham@sdcounty.ca.gov>; "Gaines; Stephanie"	<stephanie.gaines@sdcounty.ca.gov>; "Baxamusa; Murtaza"	<Murtaza.Baxamusa@sdcounty.ca.gov>; "Ruiz; Elise"	<Elise.Ruiz@sdcounty.ca.gov>; Rebeca Appel <Rebeca.Appel@sdcounty.ca.gov>
cc: Megan Otto <MMOtto@Geosyntec.com>; Maxwell Dugan <MDugan@Geosyntec.com>;	Ken Susilo <KSusilo@Geosyntec.com>
body:
Good afternoon,

I wanted to share this scope modification request from UCSD regarding the literature review and the content of the April 26 Water Assembly.  The original scope referenced that the main content for the Water Assembly will be based around UCSD’s literature review.  Due to some ongoing changes associated with the Water Assembly from the original scope, and a primary goal to execute meaningful resources to be provided at the Water Assembly, Geosyntec believes this request is reasonable.

We can plan to discuss this at our standing biweekly meeting tomorrow.  We’d also like to discuss Murakawa’s role and make sure everyone’s on the same page with their scope and contract vehicle.

Ultimately, if the County is in agreement with this revised approach below, we will just want to have this documented via email from your team.

Thank you,
Stephanie

Stephanie Castle Zinn
Geosyntec Consultants
Mobile: 949-436-0730

From: Juli Beth Hinds <jhinds@ucsd.edu>
Sent: Monday, April 3, 2023 4:03 PM
To: Stephanie Zinn <Stephanie.Zinn@Geosyntec.com>
Cc: Amy Lerner <amlerner@ucsd.edu>
Subject: County Regional Water Equity Convening - Scope Modification

CAUTION: This email originated from outside of the organization. Do not click links or open attachments unless you recognize the sender and know the content is safe. If you have any suspicion, please confirm with the sender verbally that this email is authentic. If you suspect fraud, click "Phish Alert Report."

Good afternoon Stephanie,
Pursuant to our conversation this afternoon UCSD would like to formalize a request for a minor scope amendment to reflect the change in focus and technical content of the Regional Water Equity Report convening slated for Wednesday, April 26th.  As the focus of the meeting will no longer be based on the contents of the drought impact literature review being conducted by UCSD, and as the need for and focus of presentation content and public information has changed, we would like to request approval of the following:

1. UCSD will focus on completion of a technical presentation highlighting preliminary findings of the literature review, submitted in powerpoint format by Friday, April 14th for editing and translation.  It is our understanding that the length of the presentation may be anywhere from ten minutes to roughly one hour, depending on the County’s selection of additional presenters with technical content.

2.  UCSD will complete a summary of the technical presentation for the public meeting.  This will be a graphic-rich handout in print and web-compatible format (likely powerpoint) by Friday, April 14th, offering key information and links in a form suitable for the general public and with links for further information to technical sources.

3.  For the meeting itself, UCSD will NOT be responsible for agendas, printing, name tags, etc.  as it is our understanding that Murakawa Communications has been contracted to supply these materials.  UCSD will have roughly ten (10) students present to assist with sign-in, logistics, polling, and collecting public comments.  UCSD’s students will have (10) iPads with them, with connectivity suitable for use for PollEverywhere questions for those without devices.

3.  UCSD will resume work on the literature review after the meeting, adding a review of available water rate information for San Diego and Imperial Counties and the bi-national region.  The meeting summary likewise will be completed.

Thank you Stephanie for your support and leadership!
Sincerely,
JB

Juli Beth Hinds, AICP
Staff Research Associate & Instructor
Department of Urban Studies & Planning
UC San Diego
802.324.5760
jhinds@ucsd.edu<mailto:jhinds@ucsd.edu>

title: UCSD workshops.msg
subject: UCSD workshops
to: Amy Lerner <amlerner@ucsd.edu>; Juli Beth Hinds <jhinds@ucsd.edu>; "Gordon McCord" <gmccord@ucsd.edu>
body:
Dear UCSD team,

The approach on the following workshops has been approved. The next steps for the UCSD team are:

Workshop #1: Please place a hold on November 7 on all your calendars and reserve the PEB space. It would be helpful to begin drafting an agenda/program that we would be discuss with Sarah on September 2.

Workshop #2: We will be coordinating with the Planning and Development Services Department and get back to you.

Workshop #3: It would be helpful if we can develop a timeline. We will be coordinating with our Vice Chair Nora Vargas.

Thank you!

Murtaza

____________________________

1.	Enterprise-wide Alignment of RDF

Date: November 7, 2022 (back-up would be November 4, 2022)
Participants:  County of San Diego internal department leadership, internal stakeholders
Duration: Full-day 2-part workshop

Location: 7th floor terrace at the Public Engagement Building

This workshop would provide an initial convening of County of San Diego leadership and departments engaged in the implementation of decarbonization across municipal functions:  (1) Departmental Sustainability Planning, led by LUEG; (2) the Land Acquisition Roundtable, led by Parks & Recreation; and (3) the renewable energy siting framework in the RDF.  This workshop would focus on the County departments’ short/mid/long term goals towards sustainability; geospatial and policy relationships, conflicts, and potential synergies among and between land acquisition for park, conservation, and recreation purposes; and the extent of land area for new solar and wind energy required by alternative strategies in the RDF.  This approach would help build a common understanding of the policy levers and constraints for the departments in relationship to GHG reduction, and the distribution and extent of each set of land use needs, supporting the goal of identifying potential synergies including opportunities for multi-benefit uses of land for agriculture, water and watershed sustainability, recreation, and regional habitat linkage.

***This workshop would be in tandem with the preparation of document defining the scope of work regarding the team’s advisory role for LUEG and the RDF. [Ref: Tasks 2.1 & 2.2]

2.	Sustainable Land Use Framework (SLUF)

Timeline: Early 2023

Participants: County’s Planning & Development Services Department, external stakeholders

Location: First floor lab on the ground floor of the Public Engagement Building

This workshop will focus on the themes adopted by the Board in September 2022 in the context of the General Plan for the unincorporated area of the County. It would not be framed as RDF implementation but would examine the potential alignments of SLUF with decarbonization pathways. These themes could include: (1) decarbonization of buildings, communities, and transportation through policies and land use; (2) increase opportunities for sustainable and resilient development and housing for all; (3) support green economies, innovative infrastructure, agriculture, and sustainable best practices; (4) conserve and protect existing natural habitats and resources, and increase access to open and green spaces; and (5) prioritize social equity and environmental justice in sustainable land use policies, programs, and plans.

3.	Binational Regional Climate Action Plan

Timeframe:  Last quarter 2023/first quarter 2024

Participants:  Jurisdictions in San Diego County with CAPs (municipalities; SANDAG; Unified Port of San Diego; US Department of Defense); California Office of Policy & Research

Invited Guests:  Governments of Baja California Norte; City of Tijuana; UABC

The third workshop would engage stakeholders across the county and San Diego-Tijuana region in evaluating the consistency and commonality of purpose and strategies among and between the individual Climate Action Plans (CAPs) adopted pursuant to State directives and local initiative.  UCSD students would prepare assessments of each plan in a unified framework illustrating the baselines, policies, action steps, and reporting metrics across the region.  The workshop will focus on building common awareness and purpose; exchanging strategies and ideas; identifying areas of potential re-alignment; and building a binational baseline for emissions and measures. This workshop would explore the possibility of a Binational Regional Climate Action Plan.

**UCSD also could extend some of the mapping into Baja California to illustrate trans-border issues, notably for transportation, housing, watersheds, and habitat.

_____________________________________

Murtaza H. Baxamusa, PhD, AICP

Program Manager for Regional Sustainability

Land Use and Environment Group

County of San Diego

Subject: Invitation to Food Services Leadership Committee Meeting on September 20th re. County Food Procurement Policy

Good Morning Eden,

I wanted to introduce myself.  My name is Elizabeth Hernandez, and I am the Director of Public Health Services (PHS).  On behalf of PHS, I’m writing to let you know about an ARPA funded program we lead that has some relevant touch points with your office and to invite you to an upcoming meeting.

The Sustainable, Equitable, and Local Food Sourcing Program and Policy focuses on County food procurement to direct public dollars through food purchasing towards value categories that reflect broader County of San Diego goals. Specifically, the Program and Policy prioritize Board directed value categories to ensure that County of San Diego food service operation purchases positively impact a sustainable, equitable, and local food system. Values-based food sourcing prioritizes principles that go beyond just price when deciding which food items to purchase. The values include: local sourcing, equity-informed sourcing, elevated labor standards, organic or regenerative certification, low-carbon intensity, and nutritional co-benefit. As you can see, there are several value categories that overlap with the Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice.

We have contracted with nationally recognized organizations in the field of values-based food procurement (Karen Karp & Partners and the Center for Good Food Purchasing) to provide technical assistance to our County’s food service operations and program managers. We are wrapping up our first year of implementation of the program which has included assessing purchasing data and collaboratively developing action plans. Our team is also working on developing a policy for the Sustainable, Equitable, and Local Food Sourcing Program with a return to the Board date of 12/5. This will include an Environmental and Economic Assessment.

We would like to invite you to the next Food Services Leadership Committee meeting on September 20th, where the TA providers will provide an overview of program progress so far. We’ll also have time set aside during the meeting to receive input and review from the food service operators and program leads on the draft policy. The Food Services Leadership Committee is made up of all County of San Diego food service operations and is also attended by Rebeca Appel, who is a part of the Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice.

I’m attaching relevant Board Letters to this email for additional context. Before the September 20th meeting, you will be hearing from our Project Lead, Meghan Murphy (copied), who will schedule a time to further brief you on the Program and Policy as well as answer any questions you may have.  We are looking forward to connecting with you on this exciting program!

Thank you,

Elizabeth A. Hernandez, Ph.D.

From: Adam Aron <adamaron@ucsd.edu>
Sent: Wednesday, March 1, 2023 10:04 PM
To: Lawson-Remer, Terra <Terra.Lawson-Remer@sdcounty.ca.gov>; BOS, District1Community <District1Community@sdcounty.ca.gov>; Fletcher, Nathan (BOS) <Nathan.Fletcher@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Cc: Smith, Rebecca (BOS) <Rebecca.Smith2@sdcounty.ca.gov>; Flores, David <David.Flores@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Subject: [External] My comment on the RDF - observing the science-based reality and paying attention to the conflict of interest

Dear Supervisors Lawson-Remer, Nora Vargas and Nathan Fletcher,

I am concerned that you guide our county to take the fastest possible route to cutting our local emissions. My comment focuses on the 20% of regional emissions from electricity production, as this forms the backbone for much else, including how electricity needs for EVs (private and public) will need to be massively scaled up in the future, as will electricity needs for buildings when they are not burning gas.

First, we need much faster cuts in emissions than 2045, and we also need to ditch the “net zero” language which is an accounting trick that should not seduce us. For this I refer you to the expert testimony of Prof Kevin Anderson on our remaining carbon budget. He points out that: IPCC projections are always conservative, Net Zero is an accounting farce, and accepting that, and using the IPCC’s own data, that cuts of greenhouse emissions must now proceed at 5% per annum to have an 83% chance of staying beneath < 2 C above pre-industrial levels, see https://climateuncensored.com/how-alive-is-1-5part-one-a-small-budget-shrinking-fast/ for a summary. Let’s be clear. 5% per annum. To have a decent chance of 2 C. A level of heating not experienced in 3 million years on Earth. And without these cuts, we will broach 2 C in the 2040 to 2060 time frame (IPCC 2021 report) - not a safe world for us our our children, the plants and animals, where Tipping Points and mass catastrophe beckons (Professor Rockstrom, Potsdam Center, Germany), and see Science magazine: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.abn7950.

There is thus a need for great haste. And this has important implications for how our implementation pathway for decarbonization of electricity is chosen from the RDF scenarios. We must consider not only cost, but also speed, and also the level of local conflict that might occur over land rights. The summary for policymakers of the RDF includes Table 3.1 which refers to Scenarios 1 and 2 (utility scale solar in the backcountry) as “low cost”, relative to other scenarios such as 7 and 9 which are rooftop solar. But the "low cost" of 1 and 2 uses the wrong numbers for transmission lines, 89m instead of 4 billion, the wrong numbers for rooftop solar, and doesn't factor in land conflict. These erroneous conclusions permeate the technical report and arrive in the summary to policymakers even if some language looks good. The errors have been documented carefully by Bill Powers, a California-wide expert on energy policy, see here: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_MOYILFDg8JrMKbFEcaWaqdqN4P4TSoE/view?usp=sharing

If we want to stop climate change fast, we need to go with the fastest and cheapest and least conflictual approach. Approval of the RDF as is will allow powerful forces to seize on the erroneous conclusions to create implementation lock-in for a vision under corporate control (SDG&E) that I also expect will be very slow in ultimate implementation. Indeed Table 7.1 of the technical report refers to build of transmission lines taking decades and it’s clear already there will be court cases around land conflict even if “permitting is waived". I recommend you pause the approval process until you can get independent eyes on this - and I believe that when you do so the errors will be highlighted and the fast, not especially costly, least conflictual and immediately implementable pathway of 20 GW of local rooftop and parking lot solar installation will become clear.

Please pause the approval process temporarily and get some independent expert eyes on this issue. This is all the more important since the consultants for this technical part are from UC San Diego GPS which is well-established to have taken funds from SDG&E, parent company Sempra and the EPRI (a lobbying arm for the investor owned utilities) which is an apparent conflict of interest that was called out in a lawsuit, see yesterday’s SD Tribune: https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/news/watchdog/story/2023-02-28/decarbonization-utility-solar-lawsuit-ucsd-david-victor

Please pause RDF approval, get new and independent eyes on the technical part concerning electricity and then proceed with haste.

Thank you
-Adam Aron

---------------------------------------------
Prof. Adam Aron
University of California San Diego
aronlab.org | ucsdgreennewdeal.net

On Mon, May 17, 2021 at 3:12 PM Rotto, Gary <Gary.Rotto@sdcounty.ca.gov <mailto:Gary.Rotto@sdcounty.ca.gov> > wrote:

	Hi Elly - This looking promising!  Here is how we have phrased what the Supervisor is working towards:

	Food Assistance: Sustainability, Equity and Local-Sourcing Procurement Guidelines

	Justification: Procurement criteria for County Food Assistance services should maximize both the health benefits to the recipients and the regional co-benefits of purchases, and align with our County’s commitment to equity, environmental sustainability, environmental justice, good jobs for working families, and ending climate change.   We have an obligation to ensure that the supply chain impacts on our community and our world advance our County’s mission and purpose.

	Program Design: All ARPA funds directed towards Food Assistance will be governed by a new Sustainability and Equity Procurement Guidelines, that replaces current procurement criteria with criteria designed to maximize regional co-benefits, including but not limited to: 1) best-value rather than lowest-cost, 2) local sourcing, 3) equity-informed sourcing, 4) elevated labor standards, 5) organic or regenerative certification, 6) low carbon-intensity, and/or 7) other comparable forms of nutritional or regional co-benefit.  Any and every kind or type of food assistance would be permitted, so long as these procurement standards are met. For example, assistance to a Food Bank would be allowed, but the funds would need to be used to obtain food that meets theses procurement criteria. Assistance to start and support Community Gardens would be a good candidate under these criteria.  Likewise, food vouchers that can be used exclusively at local farmers markets would be an excellent candidate for funding under these criterial.  There are many other programs that could meet these Procurement Criteria, so long as the program is properly designed.

	Procurement Criteria Development Process: Staff will develop draft Sustainability and Equity Procurement Guidelines and report back to the Fiscal Subcommittee for additional input and guidance within 30 days.  Staff will bring Sustainability and Equity Procurement Criteria to the full Board for approval within 60 days.  Staff will develop criteria relying on internal expertise and input from stakeholder consultations, and will develop rigorous metrics to facilitate assessment of benefit, cost-effectiveness, and scalability.

	Do you feel that the program you've identified would line up with this description? - Gary
