	Hi Emily and Ruth/ Rosa,

	I hope you are doing well.

	Thank you so much for all our partnership on San Diego County Food Vision 2030 <http://sdfoodvision2030.org/> . We are looking forward to Supervisor Fletcher and Supervisor Vargas's video at Project New Village to be used for the launch event mid-June!

	While we plan to work on a policy agenda along with our Food Vision 2030 network partners immediately after the launch, we wanted to bring forward a specific policy opportunity that we have been promoting for the last few years, along with a diverse coalition.

	The Good Food Purchasing Policy (GFPP) is a comprehensive procurement policy that encourages large institutions to direct their food buying power toward five core values: local economies, environmental sustainability, valued workforce, animal welfare and nutrition. It provides a metric-based, flexible framework to assess the progress of public institutions as they work to become a recognized Good Food Provider. This procurement framework, managed by the Center for Good Food Purchasing, has been successfully adopted by over 28 institutions in 14 major cities across the nation. Most recently, the County of Alameda has adopted GFPP (see article here <https://www.spur.org/news/2021-02-18/alameda-county-joins-growing-movement-buy-better-food> ). I have attached a flyer regarding GFPP for more information.

	In San Diego, we have a diverse coalition under San Diego Food System Alliance's GFPP WG, representing diverse value interests including Community Health Improvement Partners, UCSD Center for Community Health, Farm Forward, Teamsters, Friends of the Earth, San Diego 350, and others. We also have the County HHSA team participating in our WG meetings as they have been working on nutrition standards within County operations and with institution partners. The GFPP WG recently worked on the adoption of GFPP at 2 school districts, Escondido Union School District and Oceanside Unified School District.

Our coalition is happy to work on policy language recommendations, drawing from best practices nationally.

There is thus a need for great haste. And this has important implications for how our implementation pathway for decarbonization of electricity is chosen from the RDF scenarios. We must consider not only cost, but also speed, and also the level of local conflict that might occur over land rights. The summary for policymakers of the RDF includes Table 3.1 which refers to Scenarios 1 and 2 (utility scale solar in the backcountry) as “low cost”, relative to other scenarios such as 7 and 9 which are rooftop solar. But the "low cost" of 1 and 2 uses the wrong numbers for transmission lines, 89m instead of 4 billion, the wrong numbers for rooftop solar, and doesn't factor in land conflict. These erroneous conclusions permeate the technical report and arrive in the summary to policymakers even if some language looks good. The errors have been documented carefully by Bill Powers, a California-wide expert on energy policy, see here: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_MOYILFDg8JrMKbFEcaWaqdqN4P4TSoE/view?usp=sharing <https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_MOYILFDg8JrMKbFEcaWaqdqN4P4TSoE/view?usp=sharing>

If we want to stop climate change fast, we need to go with the fastest and cheapest and least conflictual approach. Approval of the RDF as is will allow powerful forces to seize on the erroneous conclusions to create implementation lock-in for a vision under corporate control (SDG&E) that I also expect will be very slow in ultimate implementation. Indeed Table 7.1 of the technical report refers to build of transmission lines taking decades and it’s clear already there will be court cases around land conflict even if “permitting is waived". I recommend you pause the approval process until you can get independent eyes on this - and I believe that when you do so the errors will be highlighted and the fast, not especially costly and immediately implementable pathway of 20 GW of local rooftop and parking solar installation will become clear.

Please pause the approval process temporarily and get some independent expert eyes on this issue. This is all the more important since the consultants for this technical part are from UC San Diego GPS which is well-established to have taken funds from SDG&E, parent company Sempra and the EPRI (a lobbying arm for the investor owned utilities) which is a conflict of interest that should draw your attention and motivate you to check the conclusions more carefully.

Thank you

-Adam Aron

---------------------------------------------
Prof. Adam Aron

University of California San Diego

aronlab.org <http://aronlab.org>  | ucsdgreennewdeal.net <http://ucsdgreennewdeal.net>

Subject: RE: [External] Dept Sustainability Plans Information

Dear Murtaza, Rebeca and Nicole,

Thanks for the very useful conversation today.  As follow-up, I’ve drafted the attached concept note on what benchmarking the County’s efforts against the SDGs could look like.  I stress that this is meant to be complementary to the existing sustainability framework used by the county, but the benefit is that it benchmarks the county’s progress against internationally-recognized goals for environmental sustainability and social inclusion.

I’d be eager to hear your feedback and incorporate your advice.  I’m excited about a data-driven, integrated strategic planning process to meet the SDGs, using the common framework they provide and the quantitative 2030 as an useful organizing principle for some of our conversations (again, as a complement to existing county vision and goals around sustainability).  The SDGs also open the door to strategic collaborations with other jurisdictions in the region to meet the SDGs (including the City of San Diego, which has announced it wants to do a VLR but has not yet started).

Regards,

Gordon

PS Copying Jeff Myers who supports me on SDGPI work.

From: Ali Mariko Dressel <ali@climateactioncampaign.org>
Sent: Friday, July 28, 2023 12:37 PM
To: Viskanta, Rimga <Rimga.Viskanta@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Subject: [External] RDF Clarity and New Direction

Hi Rimga!

Thanks again for being the moderator for Nexus! It's going to be great to have you there!

Regarding the RDF, after our last meeting, we've done some internal discussions and clarified our scope a bit. With the new direction around focusing on identifying specific climate action projects, I wanted to quickly confirm that we are on the right track.

*	Instead of focusing on engaging as many individuals as possible from Communities of Concerns, we will focus now on reaching organizations who are actively working on climate action projects that would benefit from the County's support or would help inform the Regional CAP and other future climate policies. These organizations will continue to be within and uplift Communities of Concern.
*	We will also highlight and focus on reaching local council offices and policy makers who are actively working on or identifying capital improvement projects that may benefit from the RDF as a reference or that may become part of future CAPs.
*	We are communicating that the RDF is a guide for implementing climate action throughout the region and can be used to inform climate policies on local and regional levels. While the County cannot lead the projects themselves, the County may be able to help provide resources in the form of grants, the RDF guidebook, etc.
*	After speaking with the Water Equity Team, we are incorporating water questions into our community gatherings and surveys.

Going forward, we do have a few followup questions as well!

*	When will the Convenings be? After speaking with the Water Equity team, it sounds like they will be in November afterall. Can we schedule a meeting ASAP to discuss programming, roles, and next steps? We are running out of time to book places and we should start promoting those soon for effective turnout.
*	If we are to focus on gathering feedback from organizations about specific projects, do you still need demographic data? If so, do you want that data coupled in a full survey like it currently is, or should we create a smaller demographic data only survey that accompanies the feedback that we receive in other ways (discussion, posters, notes, testimonies, etc.)
*	What do your project portfolios look like? How can we best compile project information to match and add to your existing portfolios?

Thank you!! I super appreciate your time and collaboration on this!

In Gratitude,

ali

Subject: CONFIDENTIAL ATTORNEY-CLIENT COMMUNICATION: POC Forum Summary

*CONFIDENTIAL ATTORNEY-CLIENT COMMUNICATION*

"Competing Visions of San Diego County's Energy Future" Zoom Forum Summary

June 12, 2023 | 6:00-8:00 PM

Organized by: Protect Our Communities Foundation <https://www.protectourcommunities.org/>

Highlights

*	Approximately 100 in attendance on Zoom
*	Presentation (slide image below) included the following assertion: The RDF concluded that utility scale solar is the “low cost option” for solar energy in San Diego which in effect implies County endorsement of utility scale solar and construction of new transmission lines.

*	Proposed an alternative to utility scale renewables that eliminates the need for new transmission lines and solar or wind farms in rural areas.
*	Argued that there is enough capacity for rooftop and parking lot solar arrays coupled with battery storage to fulfill the region’s future energy needs (specific study not cited).
*	Not happy with SDGE high rates and purported transition to a business model that profits through the addition of infrastructure; believe that this incentive creates a bias for utility scale options.

o   One comment in the chat implied connection between SDGE and authors of RDF study.

*	Criticized RDF for not accounting for transmission costs.
*	Called for creation of a non-profit utility provider to replace SDGE and the CCA’s.

o   Modeled after Pine Tree Power <https://ourpowermaine.org/>  in Maine

*	Call to Action: Join POC <https://www.protectourcommunities.org/>  Mailing List and create an “army” to advocate for infill solar at public meetings or through outreach to neighbors.

Observations

The dialogue had environmental undertones which could serve as common ground for decarbonization initiatives:

	*	Protect open space and designated wilderness.
	*	Clean energy workforce development opportunities with rooftop and parking lot solar.
	*	Air quality and human health concerns with new transmission lines.
	*	Biodiversity and carbon sequestration lost when new transmission lines built.
	*	Desire for lower utility rates.

Description of Event from Organizers

“The Protect Our Communities Foundation presents "Competing Visions of San Diego County's Energy Future". This forum will compare different clean energy approaches for our County to reach zero-carbon by 2045. The discussion will focus on impacts, implications, and trade-offs to ratepayers in the form of economic impacts, transmission projects, and the pros/cons of rooftop solar vs. utility-scale remote solar. The panelists will highlight voices from our Backcountry communities (Anza Borrego Springs, Valley Center, Jacumba, and Boulevard). Come out to hear local voices addressing local solutions for the least cost and least impact as we work collectively for our clean renewable future”

Presenters

Bill Powers, P.E.                                 Board Member, Protect Our Communities Foundation

Bri Fordem                                          Executive Director, Anza-Borrego Foundation

Jeff Osborne                                       Jacumba Hot Springs

Mark Ostrander                                  Jacumba-Boulevard Revitalization Alliance

J. David Garmon, M.D.                       Tubb Canyon Desert Conservancy

Moderated by Dianne Jacob              Former 2nd District Supervisor, San Diego County

Rimga Viskanta, Group Program Manager

*CONFIDENTIAL ATTORNEY-CLIENT COMMUNICATION*

"Competing Visions of San Diego County's Energy Future" Zoom Forum Summary

June 12, 2023 | 6:00-8:00 PM

Organized by: Protect Our Communities Foundation <https://www.protectourcommunities.org/>

Highlights

*	Approximately 100 in attendance on Zoom
*	Presentation (slide image below) included the following assertion: The RDF concluded that utility scale solar is the “low cost option” for solar energy in San Diego which in effect implies County endorsement of utility scale solar and construction of new transmission lines.

*	Proposed an alternative to utility scale renewables that eliminates the need for new transmission lines and solar or wind farms in rural areas.
*	Argued that there is enough capacity for rooftop and parking lot solar arrays coupled with battery storage to fulfill the region’s future energy needs (specific study not cited).
*	Not happy with SDGE high rates and purported transition to a business model that profits through the addition of infrastructure; believe that this incentive creates a bias for utility scale options.

o   One comment in the chat implied connection between SDGE and authors of RDF study.

*	Criticized RDF for not accounting for transmission costs.
*	Called for creation of a non-profit utility provider to replace SDGE and the CCA’s.

o   Modeled after Pine Tree Power <https://ourpowermaine.org/>  in Maine

*	Call to Action: Join POC <https://www.protectourcommunities.org/>  Mailing List and create an “army” to advocate for infill solar at public meetings or through outreach to neighbors.

Observations

The dialogue had environmental undertones which could serve as common ground for decarbonization initiatives:

	*	Protect open space and designated wilderness.
	*	Clean energy workforce development opportunities with rooftop and parking lot solar.
	*	Air quality and human health concerns with new transmission lines.
	*	Biodiversity and carbon sequestration lost when new transmission lines built.
	*	Desire for lower utility rates.

Description of Event from Organizers

“The Protect Our Communities Foundation presents "Competing Visions of San Diego County's Energy Future". This forum will compare different clean energy approaches for our County to reach zero-carbon by 2045. The discussion will focus on impacts, implications, and trade-offs to ratepayers in the form of economic impacts, transmission projects, and the pros/cons of rooftop solar vs. utility-scale remote solar. The panelists will highlight voices from our Backcountry communities (Anza Borrego Springs, Valley Center, Jacumba, and Boulevard). Come out to hear local voices addressing local solutions for the least cost and least impact as we work collectively for our clean renewable future”

Sarah-

My team met with the group described below on Friday (UCSD, SANDAG, Climate Action Campaign was added & UCSD spoke with the City of SD earlier so they did not join).  UCSD is looking for us to sign onto a Letter of Intent by COB today including providing bios and resumes of key staff.  The LOI is a precursor to be able to apply for the grant.   In short, there is much to be flushed out with this research effort before committing to join a grant application.  We don't think there is application to the CAP but there may be for the Sustainable Land Use Framework, possibly RDF and other data analyses that the PODS could lead.  It is not clear if the ROI would be there for us.  This type of thing can easily balloon into a substantial work effort, which we would not be able to commit to with our current project responsibilities.  However, the City plans to join (I believe SANDAG does, too, but confirming) and we think it would be better to sign on than miss the opportunity, recognizing that the LOI is an initial formality and we can drop off prior to grant application if we determine the ROI doesn't pencil.  We were very transparent with the group that it sounds like there are exciting possibilities here but we cannot commit until we know more.

Question by COB: Are you ok with us moving forward at this preliminary stage, recognizing we will need to flush out more details and reassess prior to joining on any formal application? (We can also give the BOS offices a heads up asap, if so.)

More detail about the grant project

*	Goal: Create a tool that uses existing data to help support decision-making

	*	Scenario planning tool
	*	Performance based approach
	*	Seeks to fill existing gaps in data analysis and layering (looking at the intersection of various existing data, etc.)
	*	To be designed based on what our needs are (i.e., parking policies, SB-9, relationship between built and natural environment to things like ghg, health and other impacts)
	*	(Not applicable to CAP because there are prescribed or highly vetted methodologies for the CAP work and new tools are not needed)

*	2 years up to $10M (likely 2-5M more than enough)
*	Outcomes- critical that the tool is used and the outcomes are the crux of the project

Ask/ County Obligation:

*	In-kind match- UCSD indicated this would not be a monetary match from us- no funding; some resources may even pass through UCSD and support our activities
*	Help shape proposal- collect data we have, participate in interactive working groups (outreach, other agencies)
*	Commit to ongoing use of research
*	Looking for suburban land use authority (other jurisdiction)

UCSD is requesting bios and resume for the County's representatives by COB today.  We propose myself, Rami (for now- possibly swap with new PODs Deputy in the future), Murtaza, Don Chase (LRP Planning Manager).

Thank you.

Dahvia

Subject: [External] Climate Action Research Grant - Letter of Intent (LOI) Due Jan 17th
Importance: High

Hi Everyone:

I hope you are all doing well and had a wonderful holiday season!  I am writing to provide an overview of the Climate Action Research Grant Program and the formation of a San Diego based team, and next steps.

Climate Action Research Grant Program

Just before the holidays in December, the state of California finally released the long awaited call for research (and action) proposals for projects that can demonstrate the ability to hit the ground running and sustain lasting practical and GHG mitigation, reduction and  impacts.  These will be 2 year projects ranging from around 500k up to $10 Million.  A letter of intent (LOI)  is due January 17th which is very soon for projects both with or without matching funds.

We are fortunate to have received a great deal of enthusiasm from all of the partners needed to generate a very competitive application.  The City of San Diego, San Diego County, SANDAG, the Climate Action Campaign, UCSD and other research partners have the ability to form a very strong team with complementary roles and skills that meet the requirements of this RFP.  Each organization has expressed an interest in working together to leverage our collective strengths, expertise, resources, and interests to create a strong and competitive LOI.  It is also possible that we may have the ability to show a significant matching funds by directly supporting other synergistic efforts underway in our region.  Foremost, I will soon be introducing the researchers who will be part of this effort - drawn from several research institutions.

We all share a collective interest and vision for reducing travel and place-based GHG emissions, providing affordable housing, and promoting public health, social justice, and safety through transit and active transportation investments combined with sustainable land use practices.  The policy and regulatory environment is rapidly changing with significant advancements at the state, regional, and local level taking place.  The immediate goal is to craft a compelling LOI that is sufficiently focused and targeted while also being general enough to be something we can all agree to quickly to get the green light from the state to move on to the proposal development stage where we will truly craft our work plan and what we want to accomplish.  There is a tremendous amount of work underway within each of our member organizations to generate a very unique and compelling project.

Next Steps

1.	Confirming who is on our team
2.	Getting your input - convening to discuss focus for LOI - stay tuned
3.	Drafting the AIMS, objectives, approach, and products
4.	Creating budget, timeline, and confirming match
5.	Completing letters of support
6.	Meeting all LOI requirements (see below)
7.	Filing LOI by the 17th

RFP Overview

The RFP can be found at this link: 2023 Request for Proposals (RFP) for the California Climate Action Research Initiative <https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/ucop.us12.list-manage.com/track/click?u=2ae4678f6e94927e764ad58e5&id=2b1d6c9087&e=bdebfa5d99__;!!Mih3wA!C1EvLsrcFiLia4KrfJdlY70QxN39F1ZYvogi7XN4zYQMjSavP3C5PmbMvgHyowNMdVAe1s49NEnRFlYxhkb3QKU$> .  "The CA Climate Action Research Grants are intended to spur innovative applied research that addresses California's climate goals, ensures that local communities are prepared and resilient, and prevents future disasters. This Request for Proposals (RFP) outlines two grant categories: CA Climate Action Seed Grants and CA Climate Action Matching Grants. Proposals for both grant categories must be synergistic with the State of California's climate action priority or priorities. The California Climate Adaptation Strategy, in particular, presents a holistic vision for the state with the following outcome- based priorities:

1.	Strengthen protections for climate vulnerable communities
2.	Bolster public health and safety to protect against increasing climate risks
3.	Build a climate resilient economy
4.	Accelerate nature-based climate solutions and strengthen climate resilience of natural systems
5.	Make decisions based on the best available climate science
6.	Partner and collaborate to leverage resources

There are several goals and actions under each priority area. Together, this set of priorities requires the participation of multiple disciplines and different types of partners. There are also many other state resources and strategic plans that highlight agency-specific priorities. Appendix A provides a partial list of these resources.  An important emphasis of both grant programs is near-term outcome-based solutions for public impact. (See Sec. 2.4.) To that end, proposal teams must consider thoughtful partnerships, broadly defined based on the proposed project, that will lead to high-impact solutions informed by collective insights and experiences.

Letter of Intent

A letter of intent (LOI) is required for both grant categories. The Applicant PI must specify whether they are applying for a Seed Grant or Matching Grant. Then they must complete the appropriate application materials in the RGPO SmartSimple portal.

Letter of Intent Content. LOI submissions must include the following information:

*	Proposal title (100 characters or less)
*	Identification of Applicant PI and three-page biosketch/CV upload

Good afternoon Stephanie,

Pursuant to our conversation this afternoon UCSD would like to formalize a request for a minor scope amendment to reflect the change in focus and technical content of the Regional Water Equity Report convening slated for Wednesday, April 26th.  As the focus of the meeting will no longer be based on the contents of the drought impact literature review being conducted by UCSD, and as the need for and focus of presentation content and public information has changed, we would like to request approval of the following:

1. UCSD will focus on completion of a technical presentation highlighting preliminary findings of the literature review, submitted in powerpoint format by Friday, April 14th for editing and translation.  It is our understanding that the length of the presentation may be anywhere from ten minutes to roughly one hour, depending on the County’s selection of additional presenters with technical content.

2.  UCSD will complete a summary of the technical presentation for the public meeting.  This will be a graphic-rich handout in print and web-compatible format (likely powerpoint) by Friday, April 14th, offering key information and links in a form suitable for the general public and with links for further information to technical sources.

3.  For the meeting itself, UCSD will NOT be responsible for agendas, printing, name tags, etc.  as it is our understanding that Murakawa Communications has been contracted to supply these materials.  UCSD will have roughly ten (10) students present to assist with sign-in, logistics, polling, and collecting public comments.  UCSD’s students will have (10) iPads with them, with connectivity suitable for use for PollEverywhere questions for those without devices.

3.  UCSD will resume work on the literature review after the meeting, adding a review of available water rate information for San Diego and Imperial Counties and the bi-national region.  The meeting summary likewise will be completed.

Subject: Climate Action Research Grant - Letter of Intent (LOI) Due Jan 17th

Hi Everyone:

I hope you are all doing well and had a wonderful holiday season!  I am writing to provide an overview of the Climate Action Research Grant Program and the formation of a San Diego based team, and next steps.

Climate Action Research Grant Program

Just before the holidays in December, the state of California finally released the long awaited call for research (and action) proposals for projects that can demonstrate the ability to hit the ground running and sustain lasting practical and GHG mitigation, reduction and  impacts.  These will be 2 year projects ranging from around 500k up to $10 Million.  A letter of intent (LOI)  is due January 17th which is very soon for projects both with or without matching funds.

We are fortunate to have received a great deal of enthusiasm from all of the partners needed to generate a very competitive application.  The City of San Diego, San Diego County, SANDAG, the Climate Action Campaign, UCSD and other research partners have the ability to form a very strong team with complementary roles and skills that meet the requirements of this RFP.  Each organization has expressed an interest in working together to leverage our collective strengths, expertise, resources, and interests to create a strong and competitive LOI.  It is also possible that we may have the ability to show a significant matching funds by directly supporting other synergistic efforts underway in our region.  Foremost, I will soon be introducing the researchers who will be part of this effort – drawn from several research institutions.

We all share a collective interest and vision for reducing travel and place-based GHG emissions, providing affordable housing, and promoting public health, social justice, and safety through transit and active transportation investments combined with sustainable land use practices.  The policy and regulatory environment is rapidly changing with significant advancements at the state, regional, and local level taking place.  The immediate goal is to craft a compelling LOI that is sufficiently focused and targeted while also being general enough to be something we can all agree to quickly to get the green light from the state to move on to the proposal development stage where we will truly craft our work plan and what we want to accomplish.  There is a tremendous amount of work underway within each of our member organizations to generate a very unique and compelling project.

Next Steps

1.	Confirming who is on our team
2.	Getting your input - convening to discuss focus for LOI – stay tuned
3.	Drafting the AIMS, objectives, approach, and products
4.	Creating budget, timeline, and confirming match
5.	Completing letters of support
6.	Meeting all LOI requirements (see below)
7.	Filing LOI by the 17th

RFP Overview

The RFP can be found at this link: 2023 Request for Proposals (RFP) for the California Climate Action Research Initiative <https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/ucop.us12.list-manage.com/track/click?u=2ae4678f6e94927e764ad58e5&id=2b1d6c9087&e=bdebfa5d99__;!!Mih3wA!C1EvLsrcFiLia4KrfJdlY70QxN39F1ZYvogi7XN4zYQMjSavP3C5PmbMvgHyowNMdVAe1s49NEnRFlYxhkb3QKU$> .  “The CA Climate Action Research Grants are intended to spur innovative applied research that addresses California’s climate goals, ensures that local communities are prepared and resilient, and prevents future disasters. This Request for Proposals (RFP) outlines two grant categories: CA Climate Action Seed Grants and CA Climate Action Matching Grants. Proposals for both grant categories must be synergistic with the State of California’s climate action priority or priorities. The California Climate Adaptation Strategy, in particular, presents a holistic vision for the state with the following outcome- based priorities:

1.	Strengthen protections for climate vulnerable communities
2.	Bolster public health and safety to protect against increasing climate risks
3.	Build a climate resilient economy
4.	Accelerate nature-based climate solutions and strengthen climate resilience of natural systems
5.	Make decisions based on the best available climate science
6.	Partner and collaborate to leverage resources

There are several goals and actions under each priority area. Together, this set of priorities requires the participation of multiple disciplines and different types of partners. There are also many other state resources and strategic plans that highlight agency-specific priorities. Appendix A provides a partial list of these resources.  An important emphasis of both grant programs is near-term outcome-based solutions for public impact. (See Sec. 2.4.) To that end, proposal teams must consider thoughtful partnerships, broadly defined based on the proposed project, that will lead to high-impact solutions informed by collective insights and experiences.

Letter of Intent

A letter of intent (LOI) is required for both grant categories. The Applicant PI must specify whether they are applying for a Seed Grant or Matching Grant. Then they must complete the appropriate application materials in the RGPO SmartSimple portal.

Letter of Intent Content. LOI submissions must include the following information:

*	Proposal title (100 characters or less)
*	Identification of Applicant PI and three-page biosketch/CV upload
*	Identification of Co-PIs, Co-Investigators/senior personnel, and other participating personnel

and/or organizations, institutions, or agencies, and a three-page biosketch/CV for each
o IdentifyatleastoneotherCaliforniaacademic/researchinstitutioncollaborator(requiredfor

Matching Grant; encouraged for Seed Grant).
o Identify at least one community/end-user partner (required for Matching Grant; encouraged for

Seed Grant). See Appendix B.

*	Specific California climate priority or priorities the research will address, with links to supporting

agency documents or reports (required). See Appendix A.

*	Actionable outcome(s) expected from the project
*	Abstract/Project Summary addressing the proposed scope of research and activities, rationale, and

potential impact and expected outcomes (2400 characters max)

*	Brief plans for required programmatic components, including collaboration plan, plan for engaging

communities and other end-users, and approach to leveraging available climate related resources,

or infrastructure.

*	Keywords: Research Categories and Identifiers to be selected from a drop-down menu.
*	Seed Grants only: Specific plan for leveraging the Seed Grant during or immediately after grant

period (specific grant or other funding source or opportunity)

*	Matching Grants only: Anticipated contributions for matching commitments (cash and/or in-kind).

See Appendix C.

Subject: [External] H3SD Summit Updated Planning Documents, Some Resources, and Beginning to Collage Ideas for Breakout Sessions

Good morning everyone!

I went out last night to calm my mind and picked up a bag of trash. Litter-picking as many of you know and likely have experienced, is really interesting. It makes one reflect on our society and the stuff that has resulted from modern life, and it makes my mind slow down and very grateful.  A flock of parakeets that are now part of PB shot by, which is really weird if you think they are native to South America and now have happy populations living in our palm trees. I was grateful for the evidence of family dinners, as I was kind of hungry and delicious smells of non-vegan meals wafting toward me.  We personally had Costco chicken bakes with salad last night, and my kids were okay with it. the PB community center now has repurposed surfboards adorning the building and it's really beautiful.  And when I came home, our tomato plants are going crazy! For those that have been to what we call the Fun Yun House in PB - you know what a green thumb my mother-in-law has. We expect a bumper crop of sweet cherry tomatoes and would love to share with each of you when our family sees you. I thought of each one of you as I was walking, and grateful in these wandering adventures that I met you trying to address climate change but also trying to have fun with purposeful work.  And that is my truth, and I think we are so lucky to be together in this moment in time - to try to put H3SD together.

With that, I had never been a litter-picker before four years ago and now I am. We've never tried to put on H3SD (and indeed no one has) and now we are going to do it! As my husband says, never let perfect get in the way of good. He's really smart, student of literature and Shakespeare masked as a musculoskeletal radiologist.

So just wanted to share since I've been in the center of this beautiful whirlwind of emails and references and articles that folks have sent me.  I'm reading and digesting too. But essentially everyone who is mostly blind cc'ed is in the major planning group and/or heading a breakout session.  I only included Isabel one of the epidemiologist from county and Murtaza who we had hoped would have a question and answer section.  Mary Lou is the liason for the cooling centers breakout and I don't want to scare County off with my emails. I know I can be a bit much for folks sometimes, because I move at Vi-speed. I talk fast.

Attached is the most recent H3SD planning document and the eventbrite registration

 https://www.eventbrite.com/e/h3-sd-san-diegos-heat-and-human-health-summit-tickets-630537242867

I'll send emails out this evening e-introducing folks who don't know each other, who are working on sessions together.

The UCSD team (Luis, Wayne, and Valita) are helpiing/guiding some decisions on the plenary speakers and hopefully will have that settled this week or next.  Luis and I will discuss later which sessions will go into what rooms, and possibly recording the sessions.  I need to get out to UCSD SOM and sit with him, which is my most favorite thing - getting to hang out at UCSD!

Kaiser , we have begun the CME process and although we are waiting to hear about funding from other sources - I am grateful to have received news from Seema Wadha the head of Kaiser Environmental Stewardship for all the kaisers in the country , that they are supportive and will make it happen financially no matter what. But I want to be cost effective which is the kaiser way!

Plugging the Summit: Dave Neison, Rachel Abbot and I submitted under the advice of our AAMD Will Tseng (mostly thanks to Dave's writing) an article in the San Diego County Medical Magazine that will drop soon.  I was interviewed for two segments in Contemporary Pediatrics last week, and plugged it twice in two interviews. Mary Lou Lindegren and Kristin Hampshire will be working on a joint op-ed to drop in the SD-UT hopefully that will have also at least Will Tseng's signature to plug a hopeful message on us doing something on planning for heat.  And I'll talk it up when I go to an award ceremony this week. I'm grateful to be receiving Top San Diego Asian Pacific Islander Leaders of Influence.

Okay. And thank you to Kenneth Bush and Mary Lou for helping me with more planning.  Okay. Tell me where to go and I'll go there, so we can get to August 12 together. It is going to be such a beautiful day and I'll looking forward to finally meeting many of you!

Vi

Text me 6194587561 anytime. Seriously.  You know all I do is climate stuff.

Vi

	Hi Amy & JB: Thank you for your patience. It is my privilege to introduce you to our County’s first/new Chief Sustainability Office (CSO), Eden Brukman. Eden has an extensive background on building decarbonization and nationally recognized expertise on green buildings & embodied carbon. I have been eagerly waiting for her to take the helm of our Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice. She would provide guidance on how we approach this workshop.

	Hi Eden: Dr. Amy Lerner and BJ Hinds are faculty from UC San Diego’s School of Urban Studies and Planning that are helping us on high-tech multi-stakeholder workshops at their campus. The first one was on energy, and it was quite successful (and exciting!) in getting all our departments to get a basic understanding of the RDF and to be part of this work from their fabulous classroom overlooking the pacific ocean. So with this next one, we plan to open it up to selected stakeholders on specific topic.

			Hi Murtaza,

			Here is what we have so far:

			The Regional Development Framework for San Diego County provides pathways for getting to zero emissions in the county, including energy generation, transportation, natural climate solutions, and buildings. Decarbonization of buildings is especially important because the County and local jurisdictions must work together to provide similar incentives and building codes for consistency across the San Diego region. Workshop 2 will bring together key staff and leadership in the incorporated cities, County, and key external stakeholders to: (1) develop a common understanding of the RDF’s building decarbonization goals and strategies; (2) outline roles of local ordinances, state codes, and utility policies in decarbonization actions; and (3) build consensus on common, cross-jurisdiction strategies as well as individual approaches.  Participants also will be asked to identify where state legislation, investment, or regulatory change is needed to support building decarbonization.

			Prior to the workshop, UCSD will prepare summaries of existing building energy regulations and incentives in each of San Diego County’s 16 jurisdictions, establishing a framework for identifying commonalities, differences, and options among and across jurisdictions.  Existing and planned utility programs and incentives also will be compiled so participants can see where and how these support or conflict with local needs.  Case studies with cost information (where applicable) will be identified for presentation during the workshop to highlight how decarbonization takes place in practice.

			Let us know what you think.

Hi Everyone:

Please Refer to this slightly revised Agenda for the Meeting This morning:

1.  Overview of Meeting Purpose and Focus

2.  Meeting Participants – Introductions and Core Aspirations

3.  Planning Activities Underway (many are shared across agencies):
*   County
                                                               i.      Regional Decarbonization Framework
*   City
                                                               i.      Climate Action Plan
                                                             ii.      Mobility and Land Use Measures and Actions
*   SANDAG
                                                               i.      Regional Plan / RTP
                                                             ii.       Accelerate to Zero

4.  Goals
*   Quantifying Impacts of Land Use and Transportation Investments
                                                               i.      Meeting GHG Reduction Targets
                                                             ii.      Reducing Chronic Disease Burden
                                                           iii.      Near and Longer Term Economic Benefits
*   Building New Tools to Inform Decision Making
                                                               i.      Decision Support / Scenario Planning Tool – Testing options at a range of scales
                                                             ii.      Cost Benefit – Internalizing GHG and Health Costs
*   Impacting Public Awareness and Discourse
                                                               i.      Mechanisms and Points of Contact
                                                             ii.      Quantifying Impact
*   Demonstrating Lasting Effects

5.  Measure of Success

On Mon, Mar 27, 2023 at 12:20 PM Brukman, Eden <Eden.Brukman@sdcounty.ca.gov <mailto:Eden.Brukman@sdcounty.ca.gov> > wrote:

	Greetings All,

	It was a treat to virtually meet you all on Friday. I am excited about how this upcoming workshop can help cultivate building decarbonization literacy and confidence for meaningful action.

	As we were talking, a few resources immediately came to mind that might be of interest for you (apologies if these are already on your radar!) I have direct contacts with all the folks noted below and am happy to make introductions if you like. I will also include a contact if you prefer to reach out directly – of course, no pressure to pursue ??.

	*	Autocase has two software, one that offers a triple-bottom line analysis <mailto:https://autocase.com/software/>  for building design/construction decisions (addresses some ‘intangibles’ together with lifecycle carbon footprints); and another recently launched free tool that aggregates EJ issues/impacts to guide development decisions <mailto:https://www.ejtoolkit.com/> . Simon Fowell is their Principal Economist (simon.fowell@autocase.com <mailto:simon.fowell@autocase.com> ).
	*	Building Decarbonization Coalition is a nonprofit that started just over 5 years ago as a think and do tank for all things building decarbonization <mailto:https://buildingdecarb.org/> . They offer collaborative approaches to education and policy development for electrification. Panama Bartholomy (panama@buildingdecarb.org <mailto:panama@buildingdecarb.org> ) is the organization’s ED. Local agencies liaison is Lawrence Garber (lawrence@buildingdecarb.org <mailto:lawrence@buildingdecarb.org> ).
	*	Carbon Block Challenge is a design and carbon emissions game codeveloped by StopWaste (Alameda County) and Arup in 2019 to help people understand the delicate balance between operational carbon, embodied carbon, affordable housing/development, sense of place/cultural history, and political will for progressive policies. It is super fun and eye-opening to play. I couldn’t locate a webpage for it; here’s a link to a panel we did at Greenbuild <mailto:https://www.usgbc.org/education/sessions/carbon-block-challenge-design-and-carbon-emissions-game-12847084> . Miya Kitahara was the StopWaste POC for the game’s development (miya@stopwaste.org <mailto:miya@stopwaste.org> )
	*	CALGreen Carbon Reduction Collaborative is the core group working on embodied carbon requirements for statewide policy adoption <mailto:https://www.dgs.ca.gov/BSC/Rulemaking/2022-Intervening-Cycle/2022-PreCycle> . To date, the State Architect’s office has been driving this process with leadership from New Buildings Institute (Webly Bowles, webly@newbuildings.org <mailto:webly@newbuildings.org> ), Rocky Mountain Institute (Anish Tilak, atilak@rmi.org <mailto:atilak@rmi.org> ), and AIA California (Mike Malinowski, mfm@appliedarts.net <mailto:mfm@appliedarts.net> ).
	*	Carbon Leadership Forum is an organization that operates under the wing of University of Washington in Seattle. Founded by professor Kate Simonen (ksimonen@uw.edu <mailto:ksimonen@uw.edu> )  they have become a preeminent force for embodied carbon reductions <mailto:https://carbonleadershipforum.org/> . POC for policy matters is Meghan Lewis (meghancl@uw.edu <mailto:meghancl@uw.edu> ). Full disclosure: I recently transitioned off the CLF Advisory Board, after completing a 3-year term.

	Plenty more connecting-the-dots opportunities when the time is right!

	Enjoy the day,

	eden

body:
Erin, Marvin and Murtaza-  fyi

SANDAG reached out last week to connect us with Lawrence (Larry) Frank and Isaac Martin from UCSD (attached email).  They are putting together a research grant proposal for the California Climate Action Research program. This grant is through the UC system and requires institutional partners. Proposals must address California climate action priorities and result in actionable outcomes within 1-3 years. Awards will be from $2-10 million per proposal. Subject: [External] Climate Action Research Grant - Letter of Intent (LOI) Due Jan 17th
Importance: High

Hi Everyone:

I hope you are all doing well and had a wonderful holiday season!  I am writing to provide an overview of the Climate Action Research Grant Program and the formation of a San Diego based team, and next steps.

Climate Action Research Grant Program

Just before the holidays in December, the state of California finally released the long awaited call for research (and action) proposals for projects that can demonstrate the ability to hit the ground running and sustain lasting practical and GHG mitigation, reduction and  impacts.  These will be 2 year projects ranging from around 500k up to $10 Million.  A letter of intent (LOI)  is due January 17th which is very soon for projects both with or without matching funds.

We are fortunate to have received a great deal of enthusiasm from all of the partners needed to generate a very competitive application.  The City of San Diego, San Diego County, SANDAG, the Climate Action Campaign, UCSD and other research partners have the ability to form a very strong team with complementary roles and skills that meet the requirements of this RFP.  Each organization has expressed an interest in working together to leverage our collective strengths, expertise, resources, and interests to create a strong and competitive LOI.  It is also possible that we may have the ability to show a significant matching funds by directly supporting other synergistic efforts underway in our region.  Foremost, I will soon be introducing the researchers who will be part of this effort - drawn from several research institutions.

We all share a collective interest and vision for reducing travel and place-based GHG emissions, providing affordable housing, and promoting public health, social justice, and safety through transit and active transportation investments combined with sustainable land use practices.  The policy and regulatory environment is rapidly changing with significant advancements at the state, regional, and local level taking place.  The immediate goal is to craft a compelling LOI that is sufficiently focused and targeted while also being general enough to be something we can all agree to quickly to get the green light from the state to move on to the proposal development stage where we will truly craft our work plan and what we want to accomplish.  There is a tremendous amount of work underway within each of our member organizations to generate a very unique and compelling project.

Next Steps

1.	Confirming who is on our team
2.	Getting your input - convening to discuss focus for LOI - stay tuned
3.	Drafting the AIMS, objectives, approach, and products
4.	Creating budget, timeline, and confirming match
5.	Completing letters of support
6.	Meeting all LOI requirements (see below)
7.	Filing LOI by the 17th

RFP Overview

The RFP can be found at this link: 2023 Request for Proposals (RFP) for the California Climate Action Research Initiative <https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/ucop.us12.list-manage.com/track/click?u=2ae4678f6e94927e764ad58e5&id=2b1d6c9087&e=bdebfa5d99__;!!Mih3wA!C1EvLsrcFiLia4KrfJdlY70QxN39F1ZYvogi7XN4zYQMjSavP3C5PmbMvgHyowNMdVAe1s49NEnRFlYxhkb3QKU$> .  "The CA Climate Action Research Grants are intended to spur innovative applied research that addresses California's climate goals, ensures that local communities are prepared and resilient, and prevents future disasters. This Request for Proposals (RFP) outlines two grant categories: CA Climate Action Seed Grants and CA Climate Action Matching Grants. Proposals for both grant categories must be synergistic with the State of California's climate action priority or priorities. The California Climate Adaptation Strategy, in particular, presents a holistic vision for the state with the following outcome- based priorities:

1.	Strengthen protections for climate vulnerable communities
2.	Bolster public health and safety to protect against increasing climate risks
3.	Build a climate resilient economy
4.	Accelerate nature-based climate solutions and strengthen climate resilience of natural systems
5.	Make decisions based on the best available climate science
6.	Partner and collaborate to leverage resources

There are several goals and actions under each priority area. Together, this set of priorities requires the participation of multiple disciplines and different types of partners. There are also many other state resources and strategic plans that highlight agency-specific priorities. Appendix A provides a partial list of these resources.  An important emphasis of both grant programs is near-term outcome-based solutions for public impact. (See Sec. 2.4.) To that end, proposal teams must consider thoughtful partnerships, broadly defined based on the proposed project, that will lead to high-impact solutions informed by collective insights and experiences.

Letter of Intent

A letter of intent (LOI) is required for both grant categories. The Applicant PI must specify whether they are applying for a Seed Grant or Matching Grant. Then they must complete the appropriate application materials in the RGPO SmartSimple portal.

Letter of Intent Content. LOI submissions must include the following information:

*	Proposal title (100 characters or less)
*	Identification of Applicant PI and three-page biosketch/CV upload
*	Identification of Co-PIs, Co-Investigators/senior personnel, and other participating personnel

and/or organizations, institutions, or agencies, and a three-page biosketch/CV for each
o IdentifyatleastoneotherCaliforniaacademic/researchinstitutioncollaborator(requiredfor

Matching Grant; encouraged for Seed Grant).
o Identify at least one community/end-user partner (required for Matching Grant; encouraged for

Seed Grant). See Appendix B.

*	Specific California climate priority or priorities the research will address, with links to supporting

agency documents or reports (required). See Appendix A.

*	Actionable outcome(s) expected from the project
*	Abstract/Project Summary addressing the proposed scope of research and activities, rationale, and

potential impact and expected outcomes (2400 characters max)

*	Brief plans for required programmatic components, including collaboration plan, plan for engaging

communities and other end-users, and approach to leveraging available climate related resources,

or infrastructure.

*	Keywords: Research Categories and Identifiers to be selected from a drop-down menu.
*	Seed Grants only: Specific plan for leveraging the Seed Grant during or immediately after grant

period (specific grant or other funding source or opportunity)

*	Matching Grants only: Anticipated contributions for matching commitments (cash and/or in-kind).

See Appendix C.

Subject: [External] H3SD Summit Updated Planning Documents, Some Resources, and Beginning to Collage Ideas for Breakout Sessions

Good morning everyone!

I went out last night to calm my mind and picked up a bag of trash. Litter-picking as many of you know and likely have experienced, is really interesting. It makes one reflect on our society and the stuff that has resulted from modern life, and it makes my mind slow down and very grateful.  A flock of parakeets that are now part of PB shot by, which is really weird if you think they are native to South America and now have happy populations living in our palm trees. I was grateful for the evidence of family dinners, as I was kind of hungry and delicious smells of non-vegan meals wafting toward me.  We personally had Costco chicken bakes with salad last night, and my kids were okay with it. the PB community center now has repurposed surfboards adorning the building and it's really beautiful.  And when I came home, our tomato plants are going crazy! For those that have been to what we call the Fun Yun House in PB - you know what a green thumb my mother-in-law has. We expect a bumper crop of sweet cherry tomatoes and would love to share with each of you when our family sees you. I thought of each one of you as I was walking, and grateful in these wandering adventures that I met you trying to address climate change but also trying to have fun with purposeful work.  And that is my truth, and I think we are so lucky to be together in this moment in time - to try to put H3SD together.

With that, I had never been a litter-picker before four years ago and now I am. We've never tried to put on H3SD (and indeed no one has) and now we are going to do it! As my husband says, never let perfect get in the way of good. He's really smart, student of literature and Shakespeare masked as a musculoskeletal radiologist.

So just wanted to share since I've been in the center of this beautiful whirlwind of emails and references and articles that folks have sent me.  I'm reading and digesting too. But essentially everyone who is mostly blind cc'ed is in the major planning group and/or heading a breakout session.  I only included Isabel one of the epidemiologist from county and Murtaza who we had hoped would have a question and answer section.  Mary Lou is the liason for the cooling centers breakout and I don't want to scare County off with my emails. I know I can be a bit much for folks sometimes, because I move at Vi-speed. I talk fast.

Attached is the most recent H3SD planning document and the eventbrite registration

 https://www.eventbrite.com/e/h3-sd-san-diegos-heat-and-human-health-summit-tickets-630537242867

I'll send emails out this evening e-introducing folks who don't know each other, who are working on sessions together.

The UCSD team (Luis, Wayne, and Valita) are helpiing/guiding some decisions on the plenary speakers and hopefully will have that settled this week or next.  Luis and I will discuss later which sessions will go into what rooms, and possibly recording the sessions.  I need to get out to UCSD SOM and sit with him, which is my most favorite thing - getting to hang out at UCSD!

Kaiser , we have begun the CME process and although we are waiting to hear about funding from other sources - I am grateful to have received news from Seema Wadha the head of Kaiser Environmental Stewardship for all the kaisers in the country , that they are supportive and will make it happen financially no matter what. But I want to be cost effective which is the kaiser way!

Plugging the Summit: Dave Neison, Rachel Abbot and I submitted under the advice of our AAMD Will Tseng (mostly thanks to Dave's writing) an article in the San Diego County Medical Magazine that will drop soon.  I was interviewed for two segments in Contemporary Pediatrics last week, and plugged it twice in two interviews. Mary Lou Lindegren and Kristin Hampshire will be working on a joint op-ed to drop in the SD-UT hopefully that will have also at least Will Tseng's signature to plug a hopeful message on us doing something on planning for heat.  And I'll talk it up when I go to an award ceremony this week. I'm grateful to be receiving Top San Diego Asian Pacific Islander Leaders of Influence.

Okay. And thank you to Kenneth Bush and Mary Lou for helping me with more planning.  Okay. Tell me where to go and I'll go there, so we can get to August 12 together. It is going to be such a beautiful day and I'll looking forward to finally meeting many of you!

Vi

Text me 6194587561 anytime. Seriously.  You know all I do is climate stuff.

Vi

					Hi Murtaza,

					Here is what we have so far:
					The Regional Development Framework for San Diego County provides pathways for getting to zero emissions in the county, including energy generation, transportation, natural climate solutions, and buildings. Decarbonization of buildings is especially important because the County and local jurisdictions must work together to provide similar incentives and building codes for consistency across the San Diego region. Workshop 2 will bring together key staff and leadership in the incorporated cities, County, and key external stakeholders to: (1) develop a common understanding of the RDF’s building decarbonization goals and strategies; (2) outline roles of local ordinances, state codes, and utility policies in decarbonization actions; and (3) build consensus on common, cross-jurisdiction strategies as well as individual approaches.  Participants also will be asked to identify where state legislation, investment, or regulatory change is needed to support building decarbonization.

					Prior to the workshop, UCSD will prepare summaries of existing building energy regulations and incentives in each of San Diego County’s 16 jurisdictions, establishing a framework for identifying commonalities, differences, and options among and across jurisdictions.  Existing and planned utility programs and incentives also will be compiled so participants can see where and how these support or conflict with local needs.  Case studies with cost information (where applicable) will be identified for presentation during the workshop to highlight how decarbonization takes place in practice.

subject: OSEJ Management Fellows
body:
Hi Murtaza and Elise,

I have kept you both up to date on our progress in our OSEJ Management Fellows and now looking for your input/perspective. The interview panel has recommended four top candidates, and we have two positions available. Please find attached the candidates resumes and applications, and note the last page on the application questions #5 and #6 where we asked them to write about their experience and interest to join OSEJ efforts.

These positions will be reporting to me so that I can develop work plans, manage their workload, and provide guidance as needed - however, I do anticipate them working on RDF, water, and overall OSEJ items, etc. Therefore, could you please review the attached and be prepared to share your thoughts on the candidates on our Monday OSEJ check in?

Thank you!

Rebeca Appel

She/her/hers <https://www.mypronouns.org/>

San Diego, CA 92101

Subject: [External] H3SD Summit Updated Planning Documents, Some Resources, and Beginning to Collage Ideas for Breakout Sessions

Good morning everyone!

I went out last night to calm my mind and picked up a bag of trash. Litter-picking as many of you know and likely have experienced, is really interesting. It makes one reflect on our society and the stuff that has resulted from modern life, and it makes my mind slow down and very grateful.  A flock of parakeets that are now part of PB shot by, which is really weird if you think they are native to South America and now have happy populations living in our palm trees. I was grateful for the evidence of family dinners, as I was kind of hungry and delicious smells of non-vegan meals wafting toward me.  We personally had Costco chicken bakes with salad last night, and my kids were okay with it. the PB community center now has repurposed surfboards adorning the building and it's really beautiful.  And when I came home, our tomato plants are going crazy! For those that have been to what we call the Fun Yun House in PB - you know what a green thumb my mother-in-law has. We expect a bumper crop of sweet cherry tomatoes and would love to share with each of you when our family sees you. I thought of each one of you as I was walking, and grateful in these wandering adventures that I met you trying to address climate change but also trying to have fun with purposeful work.  And that is my truth, and I think we are so lucky to be together in this moment in time - to try to put H3SD together.

With that, I had never been a litter-picker before four years ago and now I am. We've never tried to put on H3SD (and indeed no one has) and now we are going to do it! As my husband says, never let perfect get in the way of good. He's really smart, student of literature and Shakespeare masked as a musculoskeletal radiologist.

So just wanted to share since I've been in the center of this beautiful whirlwind of emails and references and articles that folks have sent me.  I'm reading and digesting too. But essentially everyone who is mostly blind cc'ed is in the major planning group and/or heading a breakout session.  I only included Isabel one of the epidemiologist from county and Murtaza who we had hoped would have a question and answer section.  Mary Lou is the liason for the cooling centers breakout and I don't want to scare County off with my emails. I know I can be a bit much for folks sometimes, because I move at Vi-speed. I talk fast.

Attached is the most recent H3SD planning document and the eventbrite registration

 https://www.eventbrite.com/e/h3-sd-san-diegos-heat-and-human-health-summit-tickets-630537242867

I'll send emails out this evening e-introducing folks who don't know each other, who are working on sessions together.

The UCSD team (Luis, Wayne, and Valita) are helpiing/guiding some decisions on the plenary speakers and hopefully will have that settled this week or next.  Luis and I will discuss later which sessions will go into what rooms, and possibly recording the sessions.  I need to get out to UCSD SOM and sit with him, which is my most favorite thing - getting to hang out at UCSD!

Kaiser , we have begun the CME process and although we are waiting to hear about funding from other sources - I am grateful to have received news from Seema Wadha the head of Kaiser Environmental Stewardship for all the kaisers in the country , that they are supportive and will make it happen financially no matter what. But I want to be cost effective which is the kaiser way!

Plugging the Summit: Dave Neison, Rachel Abbot and I submitted under the advice of our AAMD Will Tseng (mostly thanks to Dave's writing) an article in the San Diego County Medical Magazine that will drop soon.  I was interviewed for two segments in Contemporary Pediatrics last week, and plugged it twice in two interviews. Mary Lou Lindegren and Kristin Hampshire will be working on a joint op-ed to drop in the SD-UT hopefully that will have also at least Will Tseng's signature to plug a hopeful message on us doing something on planning for heat.  And I'll talk it up when I go to an award ceremony this week. I'm grateful to be receiving Top San Diego Asian Pacific Islander Leaders of Influence.

Okay. And thank you to Kenneth Bush and Mary Lou for helping me with more planning.  Okay. Tell me where to go and I'll go there, so we can get to August 12 together. It is going to be such a beautiful day and I'll looking forward to finally meeting many of you!

Vi

Text me 6194587561 anytime. Seriously.  You know all I do is climate stuff.

Vi

body:
Thank you Murtaza! I reached out to Angie and she's excited to be the facilitator, and hang out with you. This will make the Sharp people happy.  She and her husband Dave are kind of this amazing climate and health couple, but they have two young boys - so she is happy doing an easier job facilitating rather than leading session. I swapped people around a bit. You'll make a good friend, and I've eaten at their place at North Park several times and if you like good plant-based foods - they are great friends to have! Not sure how they whip up these salads that are so filling, really quick.  They are really cool people. Not that I'm not cool, but their coolness is evident really quick.  But I feel like I have to take care of them, because they give so much to climate work and sometimes don't speak up for themselves when too much is asked of them. So I didn't realize that Angie really needed to do a session like yours and is looking forward to getting to know you.

This is how it's listed if that is okay? Thank you for being so welcoming to the UCSD Urban Studies students!

Thank you! Yes, I think you are right. I don't think there is any additional meeting with you or Rigma which is good for me too! Just looking forward to August 12.  I'll just circle back closer when I need to give you more information about room stuff.  We are going to record some of the sessions and apply for CME credit for some, but since yours is not medical and I think it will be more comfortable if things are not recorded.

Have a wonderful rest of the week in our shared beautiful city!

Vi

PS here are just some funny and actually really sweet and delicious carrots my mother-in-law planted in planters in our garden.  I just think they are really interesting.  We at the tops too in a stir-fry.  The outside was really sweet and the inside was kind of like a potato? Just really interesting. I like to send pictures to friends.

Vi

				Hi Murtaza,

				Here is what we have so far:

				The Regional Development Framework for San Diego County provides pathways for getting to zero emissions in the county, including energy generation, transportation, natural climate solutions, and buildings. Decarbonization of buildings is especially important because the County and local jurisdictions must work together to provide similar incentives and building codes for consistency across the San Diego region. Workshop 2 will bring together key staff and leadership in the incorporated cities, County, and key external stakeholders to: (1) develop a common understanding of the RDF’s building decarbonization goals and strategies; (2) outline roles of local ordinances, state codes, and utility policies in decarbonization actions; and (3) build consensus on common, cross-jurisdiction strategies as well as individual approaches.  Participants also will be asked to identify where state legislation, investment, or regulatory change is needed to support building decarbonization.

				Prior to the workshop, UCSD will prepare summaries of existing building energy regulations and incentives in each of San Diego County’s 16 jurisdictions, establishing a framework for identifying commonalities, differences, and options among and across jurisdictions.  Existing and planned utility programs and incentives also will be compiled so participants can see where and how these support or conflict with local needs.  Case studies with cost information (where applicable) will be identified for presentation during the workshop to highlight how decarbonization takes place in practice.

				Let us know what you think.

			Hi Murtaza,

			Here is what we have so far:

			The Regional Development Framework for San Diego County provides pathways for getting to zero emissions in the county, including energy generation, transportation, natural climate solutions, and buildings. Decarbonization of buildings is especially important because the County and local jurisdictions must work together to provide similar incentives and building codes for consistency across the San Diego region. Workshop 2 will bring together key staff and leadership in the incorporated cities, County, and key external stakeholders to: (1) develop a common understanding of the RDF’s building decarbonization goals and strategies; (2) outline roles of local ordinances, state codes, and utility policies in decarbonization actions; and (3) build consensus on common, cross-jurisdiction strategies as well as individual approaches.  Participants also will be asked to identify where state legislation, investment, or regulatory change is needed to support building decarbonization.

			Prior to the workshop, UCSD will prepare summaries of existing building energy regulations and incentives in each of San Diego County’s 16 jurisdictions, establishing a framework for identifying commonalities, differences, and options among and across jurisdictions.  Existing and planned utility programs and incentives also will be compiled so participants can see where and how these support or conflict with local needs.  Case studies with cost information (where applicable) will be identified for presentation during the workshop to highlight how decarbonization takes place in practice.

			Let us know what you think.

			Take care,

					Hi Murtaza,

					Here is what we have so far:

					The Regional Development Framework for San Diego County provides pathways for getting to zero emissions in the county, including energy generation, transportation, natural climate solutions, and buildings. Decarbonization of buildings is especially important because the County and local jurisdictions must work together to provide similar incentives and building codes for consistency across the San Diego region. Hi Murtaza,

Here is what we have so far:
The Regional Development Framework for San Diego County provides pathways for getting to zero emissions in the county, including energy generation, transportation, natural climate solutions, and buildings. Decarbonization of buildings is especially important because the County and local jurisdictions must work together to provide similar incentives and building codes for consistency across the San Diego region. Workshop 2 will bring together key staff and leadership in the incorporated cities, County, and key external stakeholders to: (1) develop a common understanding of the RDF’s building decarbonization goals and strategies; (2) outline roles of local ordinances, state codes, and utility policies in decarbonization actions; and (3) build consensus on common, cross-jurisdiction strategies as well as individual approaches.  Participants also will be asked to identify where state legislation, investment, or regulatory change is needed to support building decarbonization.

Prior to the workshop, UCSD will prepare summaries of existing building energy regulations and incentives in each of San Diego County’s 16 jurisdictions, establishing a framework for identifying commonalities, differences, and options among and across jurisdictions.  Existing and planned utility programs and incentives also will be compiled so participants can see where and how these support or conflict with local needs.  Case studies with cost information (where applicable) will be identified for presentation during the workshop to highlight how decarbonization takes place in practice.

Let us know what you think.
Take care,
-Amy

body:
Hi Murtaza,

1) We can of course use the PEB at UCSD again.  Regardless of where we meet, I do think that 40-50 people is a good maximum for a workshop to be able to discuss in groups.
2) For participants - this is really called by you all in the county, but it seems that county staff relevant for the topic, as well as representation from jurisdictions (not sure if you are already working with all of them on this or some are more relevant than others), and potentially some key external stakeholders. I know you already had working groups for the RDF, right? So perhaps you already have lists of relevant stakeholders and govt' staff on decarbonization of buildings?

Cheers,
-Amy

Subject: FW: Climate Action Research Grant - Letter of Intent (LOI) Due Jan 17th

Sarah-

My team met with the group described below on Friday (UCSD, SANDAG, Climate Action Campaign was added & UCSD spoke with the City of SD earlier so they did not join).  UCSD is looking for us to sign onto a Letter of Intent by COB today including providing bios and resumes of key staff.  The LOI is a precursor to be able to apply for the grant.   In short, there is much to be flushed out with this research effort before committing to join a grant application.  We don’t think there is application to the CAP but there may be for the Sustainable Land Use Framework, possibly RDF and other data analyses that the PODS could lead.  It is not clear if the ROI would be there for us.  This type of thing can easily balloon into a substantial work effort, which we would not be able to commit to with our current project responsibilities.  However, the City plans to join (I believe SANDAG does, too, but confirming) and we think it would be better to sign on than miss the opportunity, recognizing that the LOI is an initial formality and we can drop off prior to grant application if we determine the ROI doesn’t pencil.  We were very transparent with the group that it sounds like there are exciting possibilities here but we cannot commit until we know more.

Question by COB: Are you ok with us moving forward at this preliminary stage, recognizing we will need to flush out more details and reassess prior to joining on any formal application? (We can also give the BOS offices a heads up asap, if so.)

More detail about the grant project

*	Goal: Create a tool that uses existing data to help support decision-making

	*	Scenario planning tool
	*	Performance based approach
	*	Seeks to fill existing gaps in data analysis and layering (looking at the intersection of various existing data, etc.)
	*	To be designed based on what our needs are (i.e., parking policies, SB-9, relationship between built and natural environment to things like ghg, health and other impacts)
	*	(Not applicable to CAP because there are prescribed or highly vetted methodologies for the CAP work and new tools are not needed)

*	2 years up to $10M (likely 2-5M more than enough)
*	Outcomes- critical that the tool is used and the outcomes are the crux of the project

Ask/ County Obligation:

*	In-kind match- UCSD indicated this would not be a monetary match from us- no funding; some resources may even pass through UCSD and support our activities
*	Help shape proposal- collect data we have, participate in interactive working groups (outreach, other agencies)
*	Commit to ongoing use of research
*	Looking for suburban land use authority (other jurisdiction)

UCSD is requesting bios and resume for the County’s representatives by COB today.  We propose myself, Rami (for now- possibly swap with new PODs Deputy in the future), Murtaza, Don Chase (LRP Planning Manager).

Thank you.

Dahvia

Dahvia Lynch, AICP, Director

Subject: [External] Climate Action Research Grant - Letter of Intent (LOI) Due Jan 17th
Importance: High

Hi Everyone:

I hope you are all doing well and had a wonderful holiday season!  I am writing to provide an overview of the Climate Action Research Grant Program and the formation of a San Diego based team, and next steps.

Climate Action Research Grant Program

Just before the holidays in December, the state of California finally released the long awaited call for research (and action) proposals for projects that can demonstrate the ability to hit the ground running and sustain lasting practical and GHG mitigation, reduction and  impacts.  These will be 2 year projects ranging from around 500k up to $10 Million.  A letter of intent (LOI)  is due January 17th which is very soon for projects both with or without matching funds.

We are fortunate to have received a great deal of enthusiasm from all of the partners needed to generate a very competitive application.  The City of San Diego, San Diego County, SANDAG, the Climate Action Campaign, UCSD and other research partners have the ability to form a very strong team with complementary roles and skills that meet the requirements of this RFP.  Each organization has expressed an interest in working together to leverage our collective strengths, expertise, resources, and interests to create a strong and competitive LOI.  It is also possible that we may have the ability to show a significant matching funds by directly supporting other synergistic efforts underway in our region.  Foremost, I will soon be introducing the researchers who will be part of this effort – drawn from several research institutions.

We all share a collective interest and vision for reducing travel and place-based GHG emissions, providing affordable housing, and promoting public health, social justice, and safety through transit and active transportation investments combined with sustainable land use practices.  The policy and regulatory environment is rapidly changing with significant advancements at the state, regional, and local level taking place.  The immediate goal is to craft a compelling LOI that is sufficiently focused and targeted while also being general enough to be something we can all agree to quickly to get the green light from the state to move on to the proposal development stage where we will truly craft our work plan and what we want to accomplish.  There is a tremendous amount of work underway within each of our member organizations to generate a very unique and compelling project.

Next Steps

1.	Confirming who is on our team
2.	Getting your input - convening to discuss focus for LOI – stay tuned
3.	Drafting the AIMS, objectives, approach, and products
4.	Creating budget, timeline, and confirming match
5.	Completing letters of support
6.	Meeting all LOI requirements (see below)
7.	Filing LOI by the 17th

RFP Overview

The RFP can be found at this link: 2023 Request for Proposals (RFP) for the California Climate Action Research Initiative <https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/ucop.us12.list-manage.com/track/click?u=2ae4678f6e94927e764ad58e5&id=2b1d6c9087&e=bdebfa5d99__;!!Mih3wA!C1EvLsrcFiLia4KrfJdlY70QxN39F1ZYvogi7XN4zYQMjSavP3C5PmbMvgHyowNMdVAe1s49NEnRFlYxhkb3QKU$> .  “The CA Climate Action Research Grants are intended to spur innovative applied research that addresses California’s climate goals, ensures that local communities are prepared and resilient, and prevents future disasters. This Request for Proposals (RFP) outlines two grant categories: CA Climate Action Seed Grants and CA Climate Action Matching Grants. Proposals for both grant categories must be synergistic with the State of California’s climate action priority or priorities. The California Climate Adaptation Strategy, in particular, presents a holistic vision for the state with the following outcome- based priorities:

1.	Strengthen protections for climate vulnerable communities
2.	Bolster public health and safety to protect against increasing climate risks
3.	Build a climate resilient economy
4.	Accelerate nature-based climate solutions and strengthen climate resilience of natural systems
5.	Make decisions based on the best available climate science
6.	Partner and collaborate to leverage resources

There are several goals and actions under each priority area. Together, this set of priorities requires the participation of multiple disciplines and different types of partners. There are also many other state resources and strategic plans that highlight agency-specific priorities. Appendix A provides a partial list of these resources.  An important emphasis of both grant programs is near-term outcome-based solutions for public impact. (See Sec. 2.4.) To that end, proposal teams must consider thoughtful partnerships, broadly defined based on the proposed project, that will lead to high-impact solutions informed by collective insights and experiences.

Letter of Intent
