Sarah-

My team met with the group described below on Friday (UCSD, SANDAG, Climate Action Campaign was added & UCSD spoke with the City of SD earlier so they did not join).  UCSD is looking for us to sign onto a Letter of Intent by COB today including providing bios and resumes of key staff.  The LOI is a precursor to be able to apply for the grant.   In short, there is much to be flushed out with this research effort before committing to join a grant application.  We don't think there is application to the CAP but there may be for the Sustainable Land Use Framework, possibly RDF and other data analyses that the PODS could lead.  It is not clear if the ROI would be there for us.  This type of thing can easily balloon into a substantial work effort, which we would not be able to commit to with our current project responsibilities.  However, the City plans to join (I believe SANDAG does, too, but confirming) and we think it would be better to sign on than miss the opportunity, recognizing that the LOI is an initial formality and we can drop off prior to grant application if we determine the ROI doesn't pencil.  We were very transparent with the group that it sounds like there are exciting possibilities here but we cannot commit until we know more.

Question by COB: Are you ok with us moving forward at this preliminary stage, recognizing we will need to flush out more details and reassess prior to joining on any formal application? (We can also give the BOS offices a heads up asap, if so.)

More detail about the grant project

*	Goal: Create a tool that uses existing data to help support decision-making

	*	Scenario planning tool
	*	Performance based approach
	*	Seeks to fill existing gaps in data analysis and layering (looking at the intersection of various existing data, etc.)
	*	To be designed based on what our needs are (i.e., parking policies, SB-9, relationship between built and natural environment to things like ghg, health and other impacts)
	*	(Not applicable to CAP because there are prescribed or highly vetted methodologies for the CAP work and new tools are not needed)

*	2 years up to $10M (likely 2-5M more than enough)
*	Outcomes- critical that the tool is used and the outcomes are the crux of the project

Ask/ County Obligation:

*	In-kind match- UCSD indicated this would not be a monetary match from us- no funding; some resources may even pass through UCSD and support our activities
*	Help shape proposal- collect data we have, participate in interactive working groups (outreach, other agencies)
*	Commit to ongoing use of research
*	Looking for suburban land use authority (other jurisdiction)

UCSD is requesting bios and resume for the County's representatives by COB today.  We propose myself, Rami (for now- possibly swap with new PODs Deputy in the future), Murtaza, Don Chase (LRP Planning Manager).

Thank you.

Dahvia

Hi Everyone:

I hope you are all doing well and had a wonderful holiday season!  I am writing to provide an overview of the Climate Action Research Grant Program and the formation of a San Diego based team, and next steps.

Climate Action Research Grant Program

Just before the holidays in December, the state of California finally released the long awaited call for research (and action) proposals for projects that can demonstrate the ability to hit the ground running and sustain lasting practical and GHG mitigation, reduction and  impacts.  These will be 2 year projects ranging from around 500k up to $10 Million.  A letter of intent (LOI)  is due January 17th which is very soon for projects both with or without matching funds.

We are fortunate to have received a great deal of enthusiasm from all of the partners needed to generate a very competitive application.  The City of San Diego, San Diego County, SANDAG, the Climate Action Campaign, UCSD and other research partners have the ability to form a very strong team with complementary roles and skills that meet the requirements of this RFP.  Each organization has expressed an interest in working together to leverage our collective strengths, expertise, resources, and interests to create a strong and competitive LOI.  It is also possible that we may have the ability to show a significant matching funds by directly supporting other synergistic efforts underway in our region.  Foremost, I will soon be introducing the researchers who will be part of this effort - drawn from several research institutions.

We all share a collective interest and vision for reducing travel and place-based GHG emissions, providing affordable housing, and promoting public health, social justice, and safety through transit and active transportation investments combined with sustainable land use practices.  The policy and regulatory environment is rapidly changing with significant advancements at the state, regional, and local level taking place.  The immediate goal is to craft a compelling LOI that is sufficiently focused and targeted while also being general enough to be something we can all agree to quickly to get the green light from the state to move on to the proposal development stage where we will truly craft our work plan and what we want to accomplish.  There is a tremendous amount of work underway within each of our member organizations to generate a very unique and compelling project.

Next Steps

1.	Confirming who is on our team
2.	Getting your input - convening to discuss focus for LOI - stay tuned
3.	Drafting the AIMS, objectives, approach, and products
4.	Creating budget, timeline, and confirming match
5.	Completing letters of support
6.	Meeting all LOI requirements (see below)
7.	Filing LOI by the 17th

RFP Overview

The RFP can be found at this link: 2023 Request for Proposals (RFP) for the California Climate Action Research Initiative <https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/ucop.us12.list-manage.com/track/click?u=2ae4678f6e94927e764ad58e5&id=2b1d6c9087&e=bdebfa5d99__;!!Mih3wA!C1EvLsrcFiLia4KrfJdlY70QxN39F1ZYvogi7XN4zYQMjSavP3C5PmbMvgHyowNMdVAe1s49NEnRFlYxhkb3QKU$> .  "The CA Climate Action Research Grants are intended to spur innovative applied research that addresses California's climate goals, ensures that local communities are prepared and resilient, and prevents future disasters. This Request for Proposals (RFP) outlines two grant categories: CA Climate Action Seed Grants and CA Climate Action Matching Grants. Proposals for both grant categories must be synergistic with the State of California's climate action priority or priorities. The California Climate Adaptation Strategy, in particular, presents a holistic vision for the state with the following outcome- based priorities:

1.	Strengthen protections for climate vulnerable communities
2.	Bolster public health and safety to protect against increasing climate risks
3.	Build a climate resilient economy
4.	Accelerate nature-based climate solutions and strengthen climate resilience of natural systems
5.	Make decisions based on the best available climate science
6.	Partner and collaborate to leverage resources

There are several goals and actions under each priority area. Together, this set of priorities requires the participation of multiple disciplines and different types of partners. There are also many other state resources and strategic plans that highlight agency-specific priorities. Appendix A provides a partial list of these resources.  An important emphasis of both grant programs is near-term outcome-based solutions for public impact. (See Sec. 2.4.) To that end, proposal teams must consider thoughtful partnerships, broadly defined based on the proposed project, that will lead to high-impact solutions informed by collective insights and experiences.

Letter of Intent

A letter of intent (LOI) is required for both grant categories. The Applicant PI must specify whether they are applying for a Seed Grant or Matching Grant. Then they must complete the appropriate application materials in the RGPO SmartSimple portal.

		Hi Murtaza,

		Here is what we have so far:

		The Regional Development Framework for San Diego County provides pathways for getting to zero emissions in the county, including energy generation, transportation, natural climate solutions, and buildings. Decarbonization of buildings is especially important because the County and local jurisdictions must work together to provide similar incentives and building codes for consistency across the San Diego region. Workshop 2 will bring together key staff and leadership in the incorporated cities, County, and key external stakeholders to: (1) develop a common understanding of the RDF’s building decarbonization goals and strategies; (2) outline roles of local ordinances, state codes, and utility policies in decarbonization actions; and (3) build consensus on common, cross-jurisdiction strategies as well as individual approaches.  Participants also will be asked to identify where state legislation, investment, or regulatory change is needed to support building decarbonization.

		Prior to the workshop, UCSD will prepare summaries of existing building energy regulations and incentives in each of San Diego County’s 16 jurisdictions, establishing a framework for identifying commonalities, differences, and options among and across jurisdictions.  Existing and planned utility programs and incentives also will be compiled so participants can see where and how these support or conflict with local needs.  Case studies with cost information (where applicable) will be identified for presentation during the workshop to highlight how decarbonization takes place in practice.

		Let us know what you think.

Hi.Murtaza, do we know if this UCSD team is working with Gordon and the rest of the UCSD team working with us on RDF?  How are these teams aligning and not duplicating efforts?  thx

Sarah E. Aghassi | She-Her-Hers

Deputy Chief Administrative Officer | Land Use and Environment Group

County of San Diego

From: Lynch, Dahvia <Dahvia.Lynch@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Sent: Tuesday, January 17, 2023 2:27 PM
To: Aghassi, Sarah <Sarah.Aghassi@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Cc: Demorest, Erin <Erin.Demorest@sdcounty.ca.gov>; Baxamusa, Murtaza <Murtaza.Baxamusa@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Subject: FW: Climate Action Research Grant - Letter of Intent (LOI) Due Jan 17th

Sarah-

My team met with the group described below on Friday (UCSD, SANDAG, Climate Action Campaign was added & UCSD spoke with the City of SD earlier so they did not join).  UCSD is looking for us to sign onto a Letter of Intent by COB today including providing bios and resumes of key staff.  The LOI is a precursor to be able to apply for the grant.   In short, there is much to be flushed out with this research effort before committing to join a grant application.  We don't think there is application to the CAP but there may be for the Sustainable Land Use Framework, possibly RDF and other data analyses that the PODS could lead.  It is not clear if the ROI would be there for us.  This type of thing can easily balloon into a substantial work effort, which we would not be able to commit to with our current project responsibilities.  However, the City plans to join (I believe SANDAG does, too, but confirming) and we think it would be better to sign on than miss the opportunity, recognizing that the LOI is an initial formality and we can drop off prior to grant application if we determine the ROI doesn't pencil.  We were very transparent with the group that it sounds like there are exciting possibilities here but we cannot commit until we know more.

Question by COB: Are you ok with us moving forward at this preliminary stage, recognizing we will need to flush out more details and reassess prior to joining on any formal application? (We can also give the BOS offices a heads up asap, if so.)

More detail about the grant project

*	Goal: Create a tool that uses existing data to help support decision-making

	*	Scenario planning tool
	*	Performance based approach
	*	Seeks to fill existing gaps in data analysis and layering (looking at the intersection of various existing data, etc.)
	*	To be designed based on what our needs are (i.e., parking policies, SB-9, relationship between built and natural environment to things like ghg, health and other impacts)
	*	(Not applicable to CAP because there are prescribed or highly vetted methodologies for the CAP work and new tools are not needed)

*	2 years up to $10M (likely 2-5M more than enough)
*	Outcomes- critical that the tool is used and the outcomes are the crux of the project

Ask/ County Obligation:

*	In-kind match- UCSD indicated this would not be a monetary match from us- no funding; some resources may even pass through UCSD and support our activities
*	Help shape proposal- collect data we have, participate in interactive working groups (outreach, other agencies)
*	Commit to ongoing use of research
*	Looking for suburban land use authority (other jurisdiction)

UCSD is requesting bios and resume for the County's representatives by COB today.  We propose myself, Rami (for now- possibly swap with new PODs Deputy in the future), Murtaza, Don Chase (LRP Planning Manager).

Thank you.

Dahvia

Dahvia Lynch, AICP, Director

Subject: [External] Climate Action Research Grant - Letter of Intent (LOI) Due Jan 17th
Importance: High

Hi Everyone:

I hope you are all doing well and had a wonderful holiday season!  I am writing to provide an overview of the Climate Action Research Grant Program and the formation of a San Diego based team, and next steps.

Climate Action Research Grant Program

Just before the holidays in December, the state of California finally released the long awaited call for research (and action) proposals for projects that can demonstrate the ability to hit the ground running and sustain lasting practical and GHG mitigation, reduction and  impacts.  These will be 2 year projects ranging from around 500k up to $10 Million.  A letter of intent (LOI)  is due January 17th which is very soon for projects both with or without matching funds.

We are fortunate to have received a great deal of enthusiasm from all of the partners needed to generate a very competitive application.  The City of San Diego, San Diego County, SANDAG, the Climate Action Campaign, UCSD and other research partners have the ability to form a very strong team with complementary roles and skills that meet the requirements of this RFP.  Each organization has expressed an interest in working together to leverage our collective strengths, expertise, resources, and interests to create a strong and competitive LOI.  It is also possible that we may have the ability to show a significant matching funds by directly supporting other synergistic efforts underway in our region.  Foremost, I will soon be introducing the researchers who will be part of this effort - drawn from several research institutions.

We all share a collective interest and vision for reducing travel and place-based GHG emissions, providing affordable housing, and promoting public health, social justice, and safety through transit and active transportation investments combined with sustainable land use practices.  The policy and regulatory environment is rapidly changing with significant advancements at the state, regional, and local level taking place.  The immediate goal is to craft a compelling LOI that is sufficiently focused and targeted while also being general enough to be something we can all agree to quickly to get the green light from the state to move on to the proposal development stage where we will truly craft our work plan and what we want to accomplish.  There is a tremendous amount of work underway within each of our member organizations to generate a very unique and compelling project.

Next Steps

1.	Confirming who is on our team
2.	Getting your input - convening to discuss focus for LOI - stay tuned
3.	Drafting the AIMS, objectives, approach, and products
4.	Creating budget, timeline, and confirming match
5.	Completing letters of support
6.	Meeting all LOI requirements (see below)
7.	Filing LOI by the 17th

RFP Overview

The RFP can be found at this link: 2023 Request for Proposals (RFP) for the California Climate Action Research Initiative <https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/ucop.us12.list-manage.com/track/click?u=2ae4678f6e94927e764ad58e5&id=2b1d6c9087&e=bdebfa5d99__;!!Mih3wA!C1EvLsrcFiLia4KrfJdlY70QxN39F1ZYvogi7XN4zYQMjSavP3C5PmbMvgHyowNMdVAe1s49NEnRFlYxhkb3QKU$> .  "The CA Climate Action Research Grants are intended to spur innovative applied research that addresses California's climate goals, ensures that local communities are prepared and resilient, and prevents future disasters. This Request for Proposals (RFP) outlines two grant categories: CA Climate Action Seed Grants and CA Climate Action Matching Grants. Proposals for both grant categories must be synergistic with the State of California's climate action priority or priorities. The California Climate Adaptation Strategy, in particular, presents a holistic vision for the state with the following outcome- based priorities:

1.	Strengthen protections for climate vulnerable communities
2.	Bolster public health and safety to protect against increasing climate risks
3.	Build a climate resilient economy
4.	Accelerate nature-based climate solutions and strengthen climate resilience of natural systems
5.	Make decisions based on the best available climate science
6.	Partner and collaborate to leverage resources

There are several goals and actions under each priority area. Together, this set of priorities requires the participation of multiple disciplines and different types of partners. There are also many other state resources and strategic plans that highlight agency-specific priorities. Appendix A provides a partial list of these resources.  An important emphasis of both grant programs is near-term outcome-based solutions for public impact. (See Sec. 2.4.) To that end, proposal teams must consider thoughtful partnerships, broadly defined based on the proposed project, that will lead to high-impact solutions informed by collective insights and experiences.

Letter of Intent

A letter of intent (LOI) is required for both grant categories. The Applicant PI must specify whether they are applying for a Seed Grant or Matching Grant. Then they must complete the appropriate application materials in the RGPO SmartSimple portal.

Letter of Intent Content. LOI submissions must include the following information:

*	Proposal title (100 characters or less)
*	Identification of Applicant PI and three-page biosketch/CV upload
*	Identification of Co-PIs, Co-Investigators/senior personnel, and other participating personnel

and/or organizations, institutions, or agencies, and a three-page biosketch/CV for each
o IdentifyatleastoneotherCaliforniaacademic/researchinstitutioncollaborator(requiredfor

Matching Grant; encouraged for Seed Grant).
o Identify at least one community/end-user partner (required for Matching Grant; encouraged for

Seed Grant). See Appendix B.

*	Specific California climate priority or priorities the research will address, with links to supporting

agency documents or reports (required). See Appendix A.

*	Actionable outcome(s) expected from the project
*	Abstract/Project Summary addressing the proposed scope of research and activities, rationale, and

potential impact and expected outcomes (2400 characters max)

*	Brief plans for required programmatic components, including collaboration plan, plan for engaging

communities and other end-users, and approach to leveraging available climate related resources,

or infrastructure.

*	Keywords: Research Categories and Identifiers to be selected from a drop-down menu.
*	Seed Grants only: Specific plan for leveraging the Seed Grant during or immediately after grant

period (specific grant or other funding source or opportunity)

*	Matching Grants only: Anticipated contributions for matching commitments (cash and/or in-kind).

See Appendix C.

Dr. Lawrence Frank, Professor

UC San Diego - Dept of Urban Studies and Planning

Social Sciences Public Engagement Building (PEB)

9625 Scholars Drive North MC 0517, PEB La Jolla, CA 92093

UCSD is looking for us to sign onto a Letter of Intent by COB today including providing bios and resumes of key staff.  The LOI is a precursor to be able to apply for the grant.   In short, there is much to be flushed out with this research effort before committing to join a grant application.  We don't think there is application to the CAP but there may be for the Sustainable Land Use Framework, possibly RDF and other data analyses that the PODS could lead.  It is not clear if the ROI would be there for us.  This type of thing can easily balloon into a substantial work effort, which we would not be able to commit to with our current project responsibilities.  However, the City plans to join (I believe SANDAG does, too, but confirming) and we think it would be better to sign on than miss the opportunity, recognizing that the LOI is an initial formality and we can drop off prior to grant application if we determine the ROI doesn't pencil.  We were very transparent with the group that it sounds like there are exciting possibilities here but we cannot commit until we know more.

Question by COB: Are you ok with us moving forward at this preliminary stage, recognizing we will need to flush out more details and reassess prior to joining on any formal application? (We can also give the BOS offices a heads up asap, if so.)

More detail about the grant project

*	Goal: Create a tool that uses existing data to help support decision-making

	*	Scenario planning tool
	*	Performance based approach
	*	Seeks to fill existing gaps in data analysis and layering (looking at the intersection of various existing data, etc.)
	*	To be designed based on what our needs are (i.e., parking policies, SB-9, relationship between built and natural environment to things like ghg, health and other impacts)
	*	(Not applicable to CAP because there are prescribed or highly vetted methodologies for the CAP work and new tools are not needed)

*	2 years up to $10M (likely 2-5M more than enough)
*	Outcomes- critical that the tool is used and the outcomes are the crux of the project

Ask/ County Obligation:

*	In-kind match- UCSD indicated this would not be a monetary match from us- no funding; some resources may even pass through UCSD and support our activities
*	Help shape proposal- collect data we have, participate in interactive working groups (outreach, other agencies)
*	Commit to ongoing use of research
*	Looking for suburban land use authority (other jurisdiction)

UCSD is requesting bios and resume for the County's representatives by COB today.  We propose myself, Rami (for now- possibly swap with new PODs Deputy in the future), Murtaza, Don Chase (LRP Planning Manager).

Thank you.

Dahvia

Subject: [External] Climate Action Research Grant - Letter of Intent (LOI) Due Jan 17th
Importance: High

Hi Everyone:

I hope you are all doing well and had a wonderful holiday season!  I am writing to provide an overview of the Climate Action Research Grant Program and the formation of a San Diego based team, and next steps.

Climate Action Research Grant Program

Just before the holidays in December, the state of California finally released the long awaited call for research (and action) proposals for projects that can demonstrate the ability to hit the ground running and sustain lasting practical and GHG mitigation, reduction and  impacts.  These will be 2 year projects ranging from around 500k up to $10 Million.  A letter of intent (LOI)  is due January 17th which is very soon for projects both with or without matching funds.

We are fortunate to have received a great deal of enthusiasm from all of the partners needed to generate a very competitive application.  The City of San Diego, San Diego County, SANDAG, the Climate Action Campaign, UCSD and other research partners have the ability to form a very strong team with complementary roles and skills that meet the requirements of this RFP.  Each organization has expressed an interest in working together to leverage our collective strengths, expertise, resources, and interests to create a strong and competitive LOI.  It is also possible that we may have the ability to show a significant matching funds by directly supporting other synergistic efforts underway in our region.  Foremost, I will soon be introducing the researchers who will be part of this effort - drawn from several research institutions.

We all share a collective interest and vision for reducing travel and place-based GHG emissions, providing affordable housing, and promoting public health, social justice, and safety through transit and active transportation investments combined with sustainable land use practices.  The policy and regulatory environment is rapidly changing with significant advancements at the state, regional, and local level taking place.  The immediate goal is to craft a compelling LOI that is sufficiently focused and targeted while also being general enough to be something we can all agree to quickly to get the green light from the state to move on to the proposal development stage where we will truly craft our work plan and what we want to accomplish.  There is a tremendous amount of work underway within each of our member organizations to generate a very unique and compelling project.

Next Steps

1.	Confirming who is on our team
2.	Getting your input - convening to discuss focus for LOI - stay tuned
3.	Drafting the AIMS, objectives, approach, and products
4.	Creating budget, timeline, and confirming match
5.	Completing letters of support
6.	Meeting all LOI requirements (see below)
7.	Filing LOI by the 17th

RFP Overview

The RFP can be found at this link: 2023 Request for Proposals (RFP) for the California Climate Action Research Initiative <https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/ucop.us12.list-manage.com/track/click?u=2ae4678f6e94927e764ad58e5&id=2b1d6c9087&e=bdebfa5d99__;!!Mih3wA!C1EvLsrcFiLia4KrfJdlY70QxN39F1ZYvogi7XN4zYQMjSavP3C5PmbMvgHyowNMdVAe1s49NEnRFlYxhkb3QKU$> .  "The CA Climate Action Research Grants are intended to spur innovative applied research that addresses California's climate goals, ensures that local communities are prepared and resilient, and prevents future disasters. This Request for Proposals (RFP) outlines two grant categories: CA Climate Action Seed Grants and CA Climate Action Matching Grants. Proposals for both grant categories must be synergistic with the State of California's climate action priority or priorities. The California Climate Adaptation Strategy, in particular, presents a holistic vision for the state with the following outcome- based priorities:

1.	Strengthen protections for climate vulnerable communities
2.	Bolster public health and safety to protect against increasing climate risks
3.	Build a climate resilient economy
4.	Accelerate nature-based climate solutions and strengthen climate resilience of natural systems
5.	Make decisions based on the best available climate science
6.	Partner and collaborate to leverage resources

There are several goals and actions under each priority area. Together, this set of priorities requires the participation of multiple disciplines and different types of partners. There are also many other state resources and strategic plans that highlight agency-specific priorities. Appendix A provides a partial list of these resources.  An important emphasis of both grant programs is near-term outcome-based solutions for public impact. (See Sec. 2.4.) To that end, proposal teams must consider thoughtful partnerships, broadly defined based on the proposed project, that will lead to high-impact solutions informed by collective insights and experiences.

Letter of Intent

A letter of intent (LOI) is required for both grant categories. The Applicant PI must specify whether they are applying for a Seed Grant or Matching Grant. Then they must complete the appropriate application materials in the RGPO SmartSimple portal.

Letter of Intent Content. LOI submissions must include the following information:

*	Proposal title (100 characters or less)
*	Identification of Applicant PI and three-page biosketch/CV upload
*	Identification of Co-PIs, Co-Investigators/senior personnel, and other participating personnel

and/or organizations, institutions, or agencies, and a three-page biosketch/CV for each
o IdentifyatleastoneotherCaliforniaacademic/researchinstitutioncollaborator(requiredfor

Matching Grant; encouraged for Seed Grant).
o Identify at least one community/end-user partner (required for Matching Grant; encouraged for

Seed Grant). See Appendix B.

*	Specific California climate priority or priorities the research will address, with links to supporting

agency documents or reports (required). See Appendix A.

*	Actionable outcome(s) expected from the project
*	Abstract/Project Summary addressing the proposed scope of research and activities, rationale, and

potential impact and expected outcomes (2400 characters max)

*	Brief plans for required programmatic components, including collaboration plan, plan for engaging

communities and other end-users, and approach to leveraging available climate related resources,

or infrastructure.

*	Keywords: Research Categories and Identifiers to be selected from a drop-down menu.
*	Seed Grants only: Specific plan for leveraging the Seed Grant during or immediately after grant

period (specific grant or other funding source or opportunity)

*	Matching Grants only: Anticipated contributions for matching commitments (cash and/or in-kind).

See Appendix C.

Subject: Climate Action Research Grant - Letter of Intent (LOI) Due Jan 17th

Hi Everyone:

I hope you are all doing well and had a wonderful holiday season!  I am writing to provide an overview of the Climate Action Research Grant Program and the formation of a San Diego based team, and next steps.

Climate Action Research Grant Program

Just before the holidays in December, the state of California finally released the long awaited call for research (and action) proposals for projects that can demonstrate the ability to hit the ground running and sustain lasting practical and GHG mitigation, reduction and  impacts.  These will be 2 year projects ranging from around 500k up to $10 Million.  A letter of intent (LOI)  is due January 17th which is very soon for projects both with or without matching funds.

We are fortunate to have received a great deal of enthusiasm from all of the partners needed to generate a very competitive application.  The City of San Diego, San Diego County, SANDAG, the Climate Action Campaign, UCSD and other research partners have the ability to form a very strong team with complementary roles and skills that meet the requirements of this RFP.  Each organization has expressed an interest in working together to leverage our collective strengths, expertise, resources, and interests to create a strong and competitive LOI.  It is also possible that we may have the ability to show a significant matching funds by directly supporting other synergistic efforts underway in our region.  Foremost, I will soon be introducing the researchers who will be part of this effort – drawn from several research institutions.

We all share a collective interest and vision for reducing travel and place-based GHG emissions, providing affordable housing, and promoting public health, social justice, and safety through transit and active transportation investments combined with sustainable land use practices.  The policy and regulatory environment is rapidly changing with significant advancements at the state, regional, and local level taking place.  The immediate goal is to craft a compelling LOI that is sufficiently focused and targeted while also being general enough to be something we can all agree to quickly to get the green light from the state to move on to the proposal development stage where we will truly craft our work plan and what we want to accomplish.  There is a tremendous amount of work underway within each of our member organizations to generate a very unique and compelling project.

Next Steps

1.  Confirming who is on our team
2.  Getting your input - convening to discuss focus for LOI – stay tuned
3.  Drafting the AIMS, objectives, approach, and products
4.  Creating budget, timeline, and confirming match
5.  Completing letters of support
6.  Meeting all LOI requirements (see below)
7.  Filing LOI by the 17th
RFP Overview
The RFP can be found at this link: 2023 Request for Proposals (RFP) for the California Climate Action Research Initiative.  “The CA Climate Action Research Grants are intended to spur innovative applied research that addresses California’s climate goals, ensures that local communities are prepared and resilient, and prevents future disasters. This Request for Proposals (RFP) outlines two grant categories: CA Climate Action Seed Grants and CA Climate Action Matching Grants. Proposals for both grant categories must be synergistic with the State of California’s climate action priority or priorities. The California Climate Adaptation Strategy, in particular, presents a holistic vision for the state with the following outcome- based priorities:
1.  Strengthen protections for climate vulnerable communities
2.  Bolster public health and safety to protect against increasing climate risks
3.  Build a climate resilient economy
4.  Accelerate nature-based climate solutions and strengthen climate resilience of natural systems
5.  Make decisions based on the best available climate science
6.  Partner and collaborate to leverage resources
There are several goals and actions under each priority area. Together, this set of priorities requires the participation of multiple disciplines and different types of partners. There are also many other state resources and strategic plans that highlight agency-specific priorities. Appendix A provides a partial list of these resources.  An important emphasis of both grant programs is near-term outcome-based solutions for public impact. (See Sec. 2.4.) To that end, proposal teams must consider thoughtful partnerships, broadly defined based on the proposed project, that will lead to high-impact solutions informed by collective insights and experiences.
Letter of Intent
A letter of intent (LOI) is required for both grant categories. The Applicant PI must specify whether they are applying for a Seed Grant or Matching Grant. Then they must complete the appropriate application materials in the RGPO SmartSimple portal.
Letter of Intent Content. LOI submissions must include the following information:
*   Proposal title (100 characters or less)
*   Identification of Applicant PI and three-page biosketch/CV upload
*   Identification of Co-PIs, Co-Investigators/senior personnel, and other participating personnel
and/or organizations, institutions, or agencies, and a three-page biosketch/CV for each
o IdentifyatleastoneotherCaliforniaacademic/researchinstitutioncollaborator(requiredfor
Matching Grant; encouraged for Seed Grant).
o Identify at least one community/end-user partner (required for Matching Grant; encouraged for
Seed Grant). See Appendix B.
*   Specific California climate priority or priorities the research will address, with links to supporting
agency documents or reports (required). See Appendix A.
*   Actionable outcome(s) expected from the project
*   Abstract/Project Summary addressing the proposed scope of research and activities, rationale, and
potential impact and expected outcomes (2400 characters max)
*   Brief plans for required programmatic components, including collaboration plan, plan for engaging
communities and other end-users, and approach to leveraging available climate related resources,
or infrastructure.
*   Keywords: Research Categories and Identifiers to be selected from a drop-down menu.
*   Seed Grants only: Specific plan for leveraging the Seed Grant during or immediately after grant
period (specific grant or other funding source or opportunity)
*   Matching Grants only: Anticipated contributions for matching commitments (cash and/or in-kind).
See Appendix C.

title: UCSD & County of San Diego_ Climate Action Grant Opportunity.msg
subject: UCSD & County of San Diego: Climate Action Grant Opportunity
body:
Good morning, everyone.

Thank you for participating in the meeting with UCSD this morning. I wanted to provide some initial information, so everyone knows what to expect heading into this discussion.

UCSD has would like to pursue a grant to develop a tool to assist in decision making and/or scenario planning. They are interested in evaluating transportation, GHG emissions reductions, land use, and equity-based outcomes. UCSD is looking for an application of this tool and would like to learn more about the County’s needs. In the meeting, it would be helpful to describe efforts that you may have related to these topics and, if applicable, describe how such a tool may be beneficial to your work program.

We are not committed to joining the grant or offering a need for such a tool. This grant does present an opportunity and I wanted to connect those working in this space with the UCSD team.

Thanks again and please let me know if you have any questions.

body:
Dear Board Staff,

Our RDF team wanted to provide the Board of Supervisors with a written update. Attached is a Board Memo providing an update on the RDF with the Draft Implementation Playbook, which is also separately attached to this email. We intend to shortly release the document for public review and seek comments on this Draft Implementation Playbook through February 2, in order to finalize it for the Board meeting tentatively on March 15. The event details and sign-ins for these hybrid meetings are posted here: Outreach-and-Engagement (sandiegocounty.gov) <https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/sdc/sustainability/regional-decarbonization/outreach-and-engagement.html>

Cc: Aghassi, Sarah <Sarah.Aghassi@sdcounty.ca.gov>; Demorest, Erin <Erin.Demorest@sdcounty.ca.gov>; De La Rosa, Michael <Michael.DeLaRosa@sdcounty.ca.gov>; Durckel, Donna <Donna.Durckel@sdcounty.ca.gov>; Appel, Rebeca <Rebeca.Appel@sdcounty.ca.gov>; Hanson, Elise A <EliseA.Hanson@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Subject: Updates on Regional Decarbonization Framework (RDF)

Dear Board Staff,

Since the Board update on August 31, our RDF team has completed 10 workshops that cover all 5 topics in Special Topics Working Groups. These working groups are intended to provide community and stakeholder input into the drafting of the Implementation Playbook that will be presented to the Board in Spring 2023. The working groups used an innovative Engage platform <https://engage.sandiegocounty.gov/>  that allows users to directly comment on documents and see or respond to others' comments. We also tried out a new format with curated stakeholder presentations on specific decarbonization topics that we intend to provide as an "Ideas Bank". The video recordings of these workshops and presentations are now available on the RDF website: Regional Decarbonization Framework (sandiegocounty.gov) <https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/sdc/sustainability/regional-decarbonization.html>

In addition, our team wanted to highlight the following activities:

*	There are two virtual public meetings scheduled for December evenings, that we would appreciate if you can help us get the word out:

	*	December 6 <https://us06web.zoom.us/meeting/register/tZwrdO-vqzksHNDuW7GN9aiIXGa4L9WTeTmB>  (Spanish-language community meeting)
	*	December 13 <https://us06web.zoom.us/meeting/register/tZAkc-6gqT8tHNAOUAiw5iW8C3675rYRCQxM>  (Public workshop on Draft Implementation Playbook)

We will be sending out notices in the coming weeks.

*	RDF is being presented as an information item at SANDAG's Sustainable Communities Working Group next Thursday, November 17 (Item 5). Location, agenda and Zoom information here: SWCG | 11.17.22 (sandag.org) <https://www.sandag.org/uploads/meetingid/meetingid_6175_33093.pdf>
*	Some notable past events from our RDF team since our last update to the Board:

	*	Moderated a panel on Natural Climate Solutions at the Lesly K. McAllister Symposium on Climate and Energy Law <https://www.sandiego.edu/epic/symposium/>  at the University of San Diego School of Law on November 4.
	*	Presented at the Global Conference on Sustainability in Higher Education <https://www.aashe.org/conference/>  on November 3.
	*	Participated in the Marquee Panel at NEXUS Climate Conference <https://www.climateactioncampaign.org/post/nexus-recap>  on October 21.
	*	Organized panel at the California Climate and Energy Forum <https://eecoordinator.info/forum-program-2/>  on September 21.
	*	City Council informational presentations at National City <https://www.nationalcityca.gov/Home/Components/Calendar/Event/13184/786?curm=9&cury=2022>  (Item 6.1 September 20), Carlsbad <https://www.carlsbadca.gov/home/showpublisheddocument/11504/638006528101870000>  (Item #12, October 11)

*	For your awareness, the Air Pollution Control District released a "Draft 2022 Regional Air Quality Strategy <https://www.sdapcd.org/content/dam/sdapcd/documents/grants/planning/2022RAQS_Final_10242022.pdf> " (RAQS). The draft RAQS discusses collaboration with the County RDF on programs, policies and strategies to reduce emissions, and APCD highlighted the alignment on the RAQS with RDF in their public workshop yesterday.
*	As we had informed you in summer, the County's Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice, in partnership with the San Diego Foundation, was selected for the Partners for Places grant award <https://www.fundersnetwork.org/partners-for-places-eight-u-s-communities-receive-nearly-1-3-million-in-grants-for-community-led-sustainability-projects/>  from The Funders Network. This award is for outreach to refugees, asylees and immigrant communities as part of our community engagement efforts on decarbonization. With the assistance of The Global Action Research Center, the San Diego Foundation and us have selected Youth Will, Majdal Community Center and Partnership for Advancement of New Americans as our community partners for the Partners for Places grant award.

And finally, we are working on RDF Regional Convenings for each Supervisorial District in the latter half of January. We appreciate each of you for confirming the dates on the Supervisors' calendars for each District! We are now working on finalizing the facilities, program, community/CBO partners and facilitation/marketing contracts to support these events. We are also excited to partner with the Public Health Services for our speakers. We will keep you posted and looking forward to coordinating with your respective offices for these convenings.

Thank you!

Murtaza

________________________________________

Murtaza H. Baxamusa, PhD, AICP

Program Manager for Regional Sustainability

Land Use and Environment Group

Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice

County of San Diego

title: Year Seven (FY 23-24) Road Resurfacing Update.eml
subject: Year Seven (FY 23-24) Road Resurfacing Update
body:
Dear Chairperson,

Back in June 2023, the Department of Public Works (DPW) shared the Year Seven (FY 2023-24) Road Resurfacing List with you and provided a resurfacing update. Since then, DPW has been working hard to prepare the designs for the Year Seven Road Resurfacing Program and we are almost ready to begin the contracting process for our projects. We are planning to go to the Board of Supervisors on January 24th to request authority to advertise and award several resurfacing projects with a total of approximately 100 miles of roads valued at more than $44M.  DPW anticipates that construction of the Year Seven Road Resurfacing Program will begin in Summer 2024 and finish around Summer 2025.

DPW has seen increases in construction costs this past year and the total number of miles of roads able to be resurfaced as part of the Year Seven Road Resurfacing Program will depend on the bid prices we receive from contractors, but we anticipate that it will be less than the 100 miles originally identified. As is the case each year, any road not awarded in the current year will move to a subsequent year for resurfacing.

For more information on DPW's resurfacing program visit DPW's Annual Roadway Resurfacing Program website at: http://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/sdc/dpw/roads/Resurfacing_Program.html.  The website also provides the status of individual road segments (i.e., "Completed", "In-Construction", and "Programmed") and a construction estimate for contracts currently in construction (Year six) which will be updated with Year Seven roads once projects are awarded and construction schedules are received.

We appreciate your interest in supporting road improvements in your community.  If you have any questions about DPW's Annual Roadway Resurfacing Program website or the road selection process, please contact Frank Arebalo at frank.arebalo@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:frank.arebalo@sdcounty.ca.gov>. For any other questions please contact me.

title: Virtual Meeting Options.eml
subject: Virtual Meeting Options
body:
Good Afternoon Community Planning and Sponsor Group Chairs-

Hope that your week is going well.

I wanted to provide an update on the issue regarding the County-managed Zoom account. As you are all aware, access to this account was recently restricted to County personnel by the County Technology Office for security purposes. However, recognizing the importance of providing a virtual meeting option for our CPSG's, we have conducted a thorough review of County Policy I-1 and consulted with County Counsel to find a solution.

PDS can provide reimbursement to CPSG's for the purchase of virtual meeting solutions.

Some potential options, all of which include a dial-in feature:

  *   Zoom Pro<https://zoom.us/pricing>:
     *   Cost:
        *   $15.99 per month (annual cost of $191.88), up to 9 users
     *   Features:
        *   Up to 100 participants per meeting

  *   Google Meet - Business Starter<https://workspace.google.com/pricing.html>:
     *   Cost:
        *   $6 per month per user (1-year commitment; annual cost would be a minimum of $72, increasing if additional users are added)
     *   Features:
        *   Up to 100 participants per meeting

  *   Microsoft Teams Essentials<https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-teams/essentials?activetab=pivot:overviewtab>:
     *   Cost:
        *   $4 per month per user (1-year commitment; annual cost would be a minimum of $48, increasing if additional users are added)
     *   Features:
        *   Up to 300 participants per meeting

Reimbursement for this can be submitted to our pds.cor@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:pds.cor@sdcounty.ca.gov> directly (please cc: communitygroups.LUEG@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:communitygroups.LUEG@sdcounty.ca.gov> when submitting).  If you have any questions about this or would like to discuss any aspect of virtual meetings further, please feel free to contact either myself or Dawn Noble.

We appreciate your commitment to our CPSG's and look forward to supporting you as we deal with this change together.

Best regards,

[cid:image001.png@01DAD868.65705530]
Samuel Murray | Chief | Support Services

body:
Dear Interested Stakeholder,

We want to update you on our progress to implement the Board of Supervisors (Board) direction related to a Vehicle Miles Traveled (VMT) mitigation program.

On March 1, 2023, the Board received a report on VMT mitigation program options and provided direction to continue coordination with outside agencies and jurisdictions, to estimate costs to project applicants, to solicit stakeholder input, and to receive additional Board direction before the VMT mitigation program is fully developed.

A VMT mitigation program will play a role in determining where development efforts are focused in the unincorporated area, such as near jobs and transit to reduce travel and greenhouse gas emissions, consistent with the intent of Senate Bill (SB) 743, balanced with considerations regarding development feasibility.

On May 22, 2024, staff will provide an update to the Board on the development of the VMT mitigation program and options that staff are evaluating as part of the program.

Two public meetings options are available to learn about the development of a VMT mitigation program.

Public Meeting 1 (Virtual)

When: April 18, 2024 at 5:30pm

Link to Join: https://us06web.zoom.us/j/85959265420
                       Meeting ID: 859 5926 5420

Public Meeting 2 (In-Person)

When: April 23, 2024 at 6:30 pm

Where: County Operations Center Chambers
               5520 Overland Avenue

               San Diego, CA 92123

Disability-related accommodations necessary to facilitate meeting participation, language interpretation, including American Sign Language, and/or written materials in alternative languages and formats are available upon request. Please submit your request at least 72 hours in advance of the event to Damon Davis at damon.davis@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:damon.davis@sdcounty.ca.gov>.

We are also reaching out specifically to your individual groups as you have previously requested meetings or expressed interest in the County's ongoing implementation of VMT policies, as well as identifying your group as an area of interest related to our current efforts associated with potential VMT mitigation programs.  In addition to the announced Public Meetings, if you group would like to request an individual meeting with County staff, please contact Damon Davis at damon.davis@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:damon.davis@sdcounty.ca.gov>, and we will coordinate an in-person or virtual meeting at your convenience.

Thank you,

A notice announcing the availability of a draft Habitat Conservation Plan and Environmental Assessment for the Alpine Park in San Diego County, California, is on public view today at the Federal Register<https://public-inspection.federalregister.gov/2025-01341.pdf> and will officially publish on January 21, 2025.

The proposed incidental take permit would allow for the incidental take of Quino Checkerspot Butterfly and Western Spadefoot resulting from establishment of an approximately 25-acre local active park, complete with active recreational uses (Alpine Park) and 67.5-acre preserve (Alpine Park Preserve) on a 96.6-acre site.

The application, application supporting materials, and any comments and other materials that we receive will be available for public viewing at https://www.regulations.gov<http://www.regulations.gov> in Docket No. FWS–R8–ES–2024–0133.

DeMaio Exposes Gavin Newsom’s 5 Biggest Failures on State Budget

DeMaio Slams Newsom as “Dishonest and Irresponsible” and Says CA Democrats to Blame for State’s Fiscal Crisis

California State Assemblymember Carl DeMaio is blasting Governor Gavin Newsom for proposing another “dishonest and irresponsible budget plan that cuts services, raises taxes, and leaves our state headed for a fiscal cliff.”
“Gavin Newsom is a liar who is utterly incapable of fixing the fiscal crisis he has created,” DeMaio warns.
“Newsom and California Democrats are desperately trying to blame Donald Trump for the years of their reckless and irresponsible spending decisions – and their job-killing policies that have resulted in significant lost revenues to our state,” DeMaio adds.
Two months ago DeMaio – who is a national government budget reform expert – was removed by CA Democrat politicians from the State Budget Committee after he warned that Newsom was lying to Californians in claiming to have a “modest surplus” in the state budget – and for exposing the true cost to state taxpayers ($9.5 billion) of providing illegal immigrants free healthcare.
As Newsom unveils his latest budget plan today, DeMaio offers a list of Gavin Newsom’s 5 Biggest Failures on the State Budget:

1. NOT JUST A DEFICIT — A FULL-BLOWN FISCAL CRISIS:
DeMaio warns California isn’t facing just a deficit—it's in a full-scale fiscal meltdown. He accuses Gov. Newsom of using accounting tricks to hide the true scope of the crisis, which he says rivals the Great Recession in scale and impact.
2. BLAME RECKLESS SPENDING, NOT TRUMP:
DeMaio says Newsom and Sacramento Democrats are wrongly blaming Trump for a crisis caused by their own overspending. He offers key stats:

  *   Government Bloat: State workforce has grown over 20% since Newsom took office in 2019.
  *   Skyrocketing Pay: Salaries and benefits are up 42%, now averaging $177,000 per employee.
  *   Budget Explosion: State spending has jumped over 60% under Newsom.

3. THE WORST IS YET TO COME:
DeMaio predicts revenues will fall further than projected due to illegal use of federal funds and job-killing policies. He says wealthier residents are fleeing while lower-income households remain due to overly generous welfare programs.
4. WORKING FAMILIES PAY THE PRICE:
DeMaio criticizes Newsom for slashing core services while rewarding political allies. He cites tax breaks for Hollywood and a new payroll tax on small businesses, along with a Gas Tax hike and billions wasted on the High-Speed Rail.
5. PRIORITIES UPSIDE DOWN:
DeMaio slams Newsom for funding welfare for illegal immigrants while neglecting basic services. He highlights failures to implement Prop 36 and underfund wildfire prevention efforts even after destructive fires.

DeMaio has offered a counter-plan to fix the California budget crisis – a plan that avoids tax hikes and fully funds core services by instead reforming waste, fraud and abuse in state government. Assembly Democrats thus far have refused to bring that plan up for hearings.

California State Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (R-San Diego) is a member of the California State Assembly representing District 75 which includes the communities of Fallbrook, Bonsall, Valley Center, Ramona, Poway, Scripps Ranch, Santee, Lakeside, Alpine, Julian, Borrego Springs, Pala, Jamul, Pine Valley, Pauma Valley, and Bonita.

to: Travis Lyon <travislyonacpg@gmail.com>, Maggie Sleeper <maggie.sleeper@sdcounty.ca.gov>, Andrew Hayes <andrew.hayes@sdcounty.ca.gov>, Payton Galvez <payton.galvez@asm.ca.gov>, Brian Jones <brian.jones@sen.ca.gov>, Nicholas Brust <nicholas.brust@sen.ca.gov>, "Scott R. -FS Tangenberg" <scott.tangenberg@usda.gov>, Smith Kyle - FS CA <kyle.smith4@usda.gov>, Carl DeMaio <carl.demaio@sen.ca.gov>, "daryl.hopkins@mail.house.gov" <daryl.hopkins@mail.house.gov>, Christopher Mika <christopher.mika@mail.house.gov>, Kevin May <kjmaymsi@cox.net>, Preston Brown <brown.preston@gmail.com>
cc: "kyle.evans@wildlife.ca.gov" <kyle.evans@wildlife.ca.gov>, Susan Wynn <susan_wynn@fws.gov>, "rob.bonta@doj.ca.gov" <rob.bonta@ca.gov>, OpenJustice <openjustice@doj.ca.gov>, "rob.bonta@doj.ca.gov" <rob.bonta@doj.ca.gov>, PIU <piu.piu@doj.ca.gov>, "piu@doj.ca.gov" <piu@doj.ca.gov>, "michael.lauffer@waterboards.ca.gov" <michael.lauffer@waterboards.ca.gov>, "eric.oppenheimer@waterboards.ca.gov" <eric.oppenheimer@waterboards.ca.gov>, Congressman Darrell Issa <ca50di.outreach@mail.house.gov>, "larry.cohen@mail.house.gov" <larry.cohen@mail.house.gov>, Veronica Wong <veronica.wong@mail.house.gov>, "john.mendez@sen.ca.gov" <john.mendez@sen.ca.gov>
body:
Dear East County Elected Representatives: 

Many of us have asked Sweetwater Authority to be transparent about Loveland's future. Now, not when it is too late for you and your constituents to respond to another socially and ecologically devastating dewatering of the lake. 

Despite the broad spectrum damage inflicted on Loveland and environment downstream recently, no interest, or compassion,  in answering the question has been shown by Sweetwater Authority Management or Directors. Every month the water district shows  that 99 % of the water in Loveland is available to transfer. 

Anyone who cares about Loveland or the people who care about Loveland, as your many letters of support show you do, would be bothered that there is no certainty that Sweetwater won't hit Loveland hard again next year, or perhaps the next.

Sweetwater would normally be low enough for a big transfer by this coming winter. Plenty of water is available by Sweetwater's historical methods of procurement , including a publicly funded desalination plant and local wells that CA taxpayers have paid to drill for Sweetwater Authority.   It is not clear what minimum water level  State Waterboards would enforce at this time. With .the currently known State of California  interpretation of the transfer maximum, 14,300 Acre Feet,  and some evaporation,   Loveland could go down to approximately 2000 Acre feet, or less, in one transfer.Waterboards has committed to respond regarding capture limits from the Loveland Diversion License  that support a good minimum pool and all it provides and protects (please see email pasted below to me from CA Water Board's Chief Counsel Lauffer) .  State Waterboards  Chair, Joaquin Esquivel recently made a similar commitment.  Based on what is currently known and Sweetwater Authority's stated commitment to drain Lovleand , in a single transfer  Loveland's water  would be far outside of the public area again. 
The next excessive dewatering could be followed by years of invasive , flammable weed growth in the lake basin and  drought in our fire prone region. We got lucky with record rains before. 

Some of the regular advocates, and some new ones are talking about a protest at Loveland, or a return to Sweetwater HQ to demand transparency and push sunrise to sunset and fish stocking. Please,  we would like to know first ,if this transparency issue for water levels and a renewed call for sunrise to sunset access and fishery repairs  can be handled by leaders in our community. 

Please let me know if you will follow up on your previous support efforts with a request that Sweetwater leadership  tell you and your constituents its intentions. 

Sincerely, 

Russell 

Russell Walsh 

4639 Montiel Truck Trail

Jamul CA, 91935

619-922-6235

Hello  Karen,

Thank you for your recent complimentary work on the Loveland fishing float platform and other items of concern for Loveland Lake users. 

During the Alpine community planning group meeting last week, a significant issue regarding access to Loveland Reservoir was raised. Your board member, Darlene Cossio,  who is also on the planning group board, attempted to block the group's motion for a letter of support  to Sweetwater Authority and the US Forest Service for sunrise-to-sunset access. title: Stoney Oak Ranch Support.eml
subject: Stoney Oak Ranch Support
body:
I’m writing in support of Stoney Oaks Ranch ahead of the community planning group meeting tomorrow.

Stoney Oaks Ranch has been a little slice of heaven for my two girls. Almost 3 years ago, for my oldest’s 5th birthday we reached out about hosting our party there and she has been hooked ever since.

We have attended their once a week camps, summer camps, and take horse riding lessons as well.

My girls have learned skills they wouldn’t have learned had they not had people like Angie and Krystal leading the way to teach kids from a young age a deep appreciation for being outdoors, working with your hands, and caring for animals. Kids don’t just get to show up and play. They work hard and they learn. They learn about respect, and responsibility, how to work as a team, and even self confidence. And when it’s time to go home, they don’t want to leave because they are where children should be: outside, climbing in a treehouse, getting dirty, and exploring.

We live in a small home with a small yard and what my girls get to experience at Stoney Oaks is unique and something they can’t get by just walking into our own backyard. Certainly not the joy and therapeutic wonder of being around horses and other farm animals!

We’re so grateful for everyone at Stoney Oaks Ranch and our weekly schedule has felt empty without my kids being able to gather with other kids who share the same love of being outside and caring for animals.

We LOVE Stoney Oaks and give our full whole hearted support to everything they do.

Sincerely,
Vittoria Allen

body:
Dear Mr. Lyon,

We were at last weeks (9/26/24) Alpine Planning Group meeting.  We would like you to add our emails to your list for any updates on progression of this very impractical venture.  Living in one of the highest fire zones and living on a street where we only have one way in and one way out, it seems so dangerous and illogical to approve a project like this.  It seemed apparent that after additional information at the meeting, it would not be an “if” there was a fire but “when” there would be a fire.  Additionally, if there was one, the water with the chemicals released would have unknown effects on our ground water, being that we are all on wells.  It’s extremely challenging to get fire insurance, and we can’t fathom how that will be affected.  Our assets are completely tied up in the value of our land and home, and fear this would be greatly compromised.
We know you heard the group loud and clear and hope your responses will reflect our great concern for this permit to be approved.

Thank you for your support on our behalf.

Sincerely,

cc: Smith Kyle - FS CA <kyle.smith4@usda.gov>, "nicholas.brust@sen.ca.gov" <nicholas.brust@sen.ca.gov>, Travis Lyon <travislyonacpg@gmail.com>, Maggie Sleeper <maggie.sleeper@sdcounty.ca.gov>, Carlos Quintero <cquintero@sweetwater.org>, Erick Del Bosque <edelbosque@sweetwater.org>, Preston Brown <brown.preston@gmail.com>, "imarquez@sweetwater.org" <imarquez@sweetwater.org>
body:
Claudia Valenzuela Regional Public Affairs ManagerSDGE

Dear SDGE  Public Affairs Manager and Land Use Professionals, 

There is an opportunity for SDGE leadership and the Land Use Department to step up for shared regional goals of public welfare recreation opportunities and conservation. 

This is a once in a generation style opportunity to better the lives of people in our region through increased access to public land while avoiding negative conservation impacts that normally come with such important improvements. I am sure SDGE is broadly supported by government partners, such as the county of San Diego and Sweetwater Authority in cooperating with this proposal
I am involved in a meetings for a California   recreation program enhancement grant to the Sweetwater Authority that is being lead by Senator Brian Jones's local staff and Sweetwater Authority General Manager, Carlos Quintero. 

One proposal is to use the SDGE Easement in one or more locations to facilitate the ability of  hikers, fishers, and nature watchers to enjoy this beautiful but difficult to access area. The goal is to allow lake users to benefit from the US Forest Service , 5 mile shoreline fishing easement. 

I would like to present reassurance that by working with partners on opening up access throught the Sunrise Powerlink Easement on  Sweewtater managed public property, SDGE would be accomplishing important Livewell partnership goals for the County of San Diego and Region and our diverse friends and neighbors, including income limited and mobility challenged people. 
Furthermore, access around Loveland Resevoir is not a new goal or solely connected to this current opportunity.Maximizing Hiking and Fishing at Loveland Reservoir is a goal stated several times in the Alpine Communtity Plan. 

I am including a google earth image of the area with the SDGE easement and a map of  the Forest Service easement for reference.
Please provide a contact person who I can talk with and introduce to our government partners, Sweetewater Authority and Loveland user group stakeholders as appropriate during this great Loveland  trails and access enhancement effort some of whom I am CC'ing this email. 
Conservation and taxpayer Benefits"
Public money savings and conservation wins:. 
Since the land disturbance is already there this is a huge conservation win. California money from the AB 102 grant can be better utilized elsewhere on the stie. 

Google earth image of SDGE easement on both side of the reservoir. 

Forest Service Public hiking, fishing and bird watching, easment map. 

Please let me know who our contact for the goal of increasing this access is and how I can help with this effort. 
Appreciatively,
Russell Walsh4639 Montiel Truck TrailJamul CA, 91935

body:
Hello All,

Last week I met (zoom) with Staff from SANDAG re their Vision Zero Program. This program is still a work in progress and they estimate that it won’t be completed for at least the next few months.
Vision Zero
sandag.org

Vision Zero is a comprehensive data driven program to identify roads/areas in our region that have the highest concentration of major accidents where law enforcement has been involved and reports have been generated.

With this accident information, these areas have then been analyzed to determine what changes or improvements could be made so that there could potentially be zero future accidents.

This information could then also be used by municipalities and the County to apply for approximately $1 billion dollars in federal grants.

One of the concerns that I have is that this data is 2 years behind, so the numbers are from 2022. It seems to me that after Covid, the public generally appears to be driving a lot faster and in a much more unsafe manner, hence an increase in accidents that these initial studies might not capture.

Below is a link for the SANDAG’s interactive map associated with this program. It shows the areas that have the highest concentration of accidents, amongst other data.
Traffic Safety Dashboard
opendata.sandag.org

While SANDAG’s goal for this program is to provide the data to help with grants, I see this as a great tool to use when we are asking DPW and TAC to reduce speeds and study roads in our area for traffic calming or other ways to reduce accidents.

I’ll keep you posted when I get further updates. If you have any questions, please let me know.
Best regards,

Eileen Delaney
Vice Chair, APG- San Diego County

title: San Diego County Street Lighting District Annual Assessment Rate.eml
subject: San Diego County Street Lighting District Annual Assessment Rate
body:
Hello Community Planning Group Members,

The San Diego County Street Lighting District operates and maintains public streetlights in the unincorporated region and is dedicated to providing quality streetlighting services at a low cost to property owners. Streetlights benefit all communities in the unincorporated area by providing lighting services to ensure safety for all who drive, bike, or walk our County roads. The Department of Public Works (DPW) is proposing no change to the Street Lighting District assessment rate for Fiscal Year 2024-25. Energy cost savings from an LED retrofit project in 2020 have resulted in rate reductions over the last four fiscal years, with the current assessment rate sufficient to fund operation and maintenance of streetlights for next fiscal year.

On June 26, 2024, the Board of Supervisors will hold a Public Hearing to confirm the annual levy for Fiscal Year 2024-25. If approved by the Board of Supervisors, the annual assessment rate will remain unchanged at $2.00, per residential unit annually.  The last rate adjustment was in 2022, which reduced the rate by 71%, from $7.00 to the current rate of $2.00.

For any questions, please contact our program in the Department of Public Works, at 858-694-2691 or SpDist.LUEG@SDCounty.ca.gov<mailto:SpDist.LUEG@SDCounty.ca.gov>.

body:
Hello All: Our planning group has reached out to the BOS to request
that the county promulgate regulations for siting new cemeteries in
groundwater dependent communities. Our letter to the supervisors is
attached. None of them have responded, to date.

Currently, there is not one state or county regulation to defend
groundwater from pollution by large-volume human burial sites. This is
important because graveyards have a long track record of polluting the
water beneath them, and some have even been credited with causing
outbreaks of fatal diseases.
So far, our community is the only one that has been targeted, but we
believe that, as land in town becomes scarcer and more expensive, this
issue will crop up again.
We're asking for support letters from any planning/sponsor groups who
agree -- or even the APG as a whole. Even a simple endorsement of our
letter would help. I would be happy to send our original letter to
staff to anyone who would like to see the many issues we have
identified with the cemetery proposal in our community.
Sincerely,
Billie Jo Jannen, ChairmanCampo Lake Morena Community Planning Group

body:
Hi Travis,

Hope this email finds you well! The County of San Diego's Land Use & Environment Group (LUEG) is conducting a series of public meetings from May 20 - June 4 to gather public feedback and input on an upcoming Notice of Funding Availability (NOFA) on a $9 million ARPA-funded grant program to help address broadband access and affordability in unincorporated communities. title: Request for Input on San Diego CountyΓÇÖs Cannabis Program.eml
subject: Request for Input on San Diego County’s Cannabis Program
body:
Good Afternoon,

I’m reaching out on behalf of Assemblyman Carl DeMaio regarding the County of San Diego’s Socially Equitable Cannabis Program, which proposes significant changes to existing regulations that will allow for new and expanded commercial cannabis businesses in unincorporated areas.

The County is moving forward with a program that includes:

  *   Regulatory Changes – Current policies will be revised to allow new and expanded cannabis businesses in unincorporated areas, impacting zoning and land use regulations.

  *   Licensing & Permitting – A new system will be established to oversee the approval and operation of cannabis businesses.

  *   Environmental Impact Report (EIR) – The County has released a draft report assessing the potential consequences of these regulatory changes. More information on this report can be seen here: Cannabis Program Draft Environmental Impact Report<https://engage.sandiegocounty.gov/cannabis-program-eir>

For full details, the County’s cannabis program information is available here: San Diego County Cannabis Program<https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/sdc/pds/Cannabis.html>.

  *   Public comments on the Cannabis Program Draft EIR and draft ordinances are being accepted through March 31, 2025

Assemblyman DeMaio, along with many residents of the unincorporated areas within our district, strongly opposes proposed changes and some of the alternatives listed for the following reasons:

  *   The growing presence of cannabis businesses near residential areas – Expanding cannabis businesses would place them too close to homes and schools, potentially compromising the safety and well-being of our neighborhoods.

  *   Crime and public safety risks – Cannabis dispensaries and cultivation sites often attract criminal activity, raising concerns about safety in already vulnerable areas.

  *   Loss of local control over zoning and regulatory decisions – These changes would take decision-making power away from local communities, overriding established zoning protections.

  *   Environmental concerns, including water usage and land development impact – Cannabis cultivation requires significant water resources and land use, which could strain local ecosystems and the water supply.

Please let us know if your planning group supports or opposes parts/alternatives of the program, or if your group is still waiting to meet and discuss this issue.

If you have any questions, need additional information, or would like to discuss how we can best support your position, please don’t hesitate to reach out. We are here to assist in any way possible.

Best,

Trinity Hannaway
District Outreach Director
Office of Assemblyman Carl DeMaio, District 75

body:
"California’s open meetings law, the Ralph M. Brown Act, requires that
meetings of a local agency’s governing body be open to the public, except
in specific circumstances. The Brown Act also requires that on request by a
member of the public, the agency must mail that person a copy of the agenda
for a governing body meeting, or a copy of all the documents constituting
the agenda packet.

SB 274 aims to improve accessibility of these materials. It does this by
allowing members of the public to request delivery of agendas and agenda
packets by email. Under SB 274, if a person requests a copy of a local
agency governing body meeting agenda or agenda packet, the agency must
email the person either the requested documents or a link to a website
where the documents can be accessed. If a local agency determines that it
is technologically infeasible to send an entire agenda packet by email or
make it available online, the agency has the option to instead send only
the agenda by email and mail the remainder of the agenda packet."

Please email me a copy of all ACPG agendas until further notice.

Thank you,

Louis Russo

body:
Report to the Association of Planning Groups - San Diego County (APG)
On July 16th the first scheduled evacuation tour for SANDAG and Caltrans
staff was held in the Ramona area. Currently in the planning stages is an
evacuation tour for the SR 94 area.

APG's representative on the SANDAG Board of Directors, Robin Joy Maxson,
extended an invitation to SANDAG and Caltrans staff to participate in a
tour of the expected routes for evacuation in the event of a wildfire or
other emergency. Maxson emphasised the importance of experiencing the
evacuation routes in-person in order to accurately evaluate the routes for
safety and viability in an emergency.

Roadways examined were Wildcat Canyon, SR 67, Highland Valley Road and SR
78.

Issues considered and discussed were:
- Shelter-in-place orders and the likelihood of evacuees choosing to heed
evacuation orders. Visitors will most likely choose to leave the area.
- Physical constraints to safe and effective evacuation,  e.g., present
roadway design, traffic bottlenecks due to changes in the number of lanes
and/or their configuration.
- The presence of deadly chimney effect fires and other geographical
hazards to evacuee safety.
- Residents and visitors vary in familiarity with the roadways.
- Fluctuation in the numbers of evacuees on any given day as the number of
residents is not a static indicator of how many people may need to
evacuate; the number of weekend visitors to the area greatly expands the
number of evacuees.
 - Types of vehicles utilized during an evacuation in rural areas have
historically been large vehicles/trucks and many vehicle/trailer
combinations in order to evacuate livestock.
- The unpredictability of fire during a firestorm created by the combined
conditions of high temperatures, dry fuel and high winds.

Local fire behavior expert, Dan Summers, identified and explained to the
group the behavior of fire as it relates to evacuees safety during an
evacuation event on these four routes. Evacuees are exposed to:
- Oxygen deprivation which also deprives combustion engine vehicles of the
oxygen required to operate.
- Extreme heat which impairs human judgement.
- Chimney effect fires which are corridors in the landscape where heavy
brush and trees combine to create a rapid, deadly, blistering, upward burn
path.

The tour was educational as attendees shared their knowledge of roadway
construction, fire behavior and human behavior during a crisis.
Attendees were:

Robin Joy Maxson, Chair, Association of Planning Groups and Representative
on the SANDAG Board of Directors
Dan Summers, Former County of San Diego Fire Advisory Board and
Fire/Paramedic Technology Instructor
Stephen Welborn, Caltrans
Karina Cantero-Angel, Caltrans
Nicholas Buenviaje, Caltrans
Mimi Morisaki, SANDAG
Michael Terlep, SANDAG
Jose Alvarez, SANDAG

Report Submitted by:
Robin Joy Maxson, Representative to SANDAG
