body:
Randy Moore

US Chief Forester

1400 Independence Ave. 

Washington DC 20250-0003

Dear Chief Moore,
The public in the region of Loveland Reservoir in the Cleveland National Forest are in great need of your  long-standing resolution to public service. 

I am writing to follow up on our recent local non-profit Friends of Loveland Reservoir to Forest Service contact regarding Sunrise to Sunset access and the compatibility of the easement-protected "shoreline"  fishing program with Sweetwater Authority's water licenses and California environmental and water regulations. 

As you will see from this 4 year old email chain, this is something I was pleading for your help with and trying to help the Forest Service understand as far back as September 2020.

It is clear from the easement, land swap origination documents, and past  Forest Service oversight of Loveland Reservoir that volunteers are not a factor in the public's right and need to access the hiking, fishing, and birdwatching program.  I don't agree with the pursuit of such a program of volunteers, or with exposing Loveland recreation users to the risk of failure of it and another lengthy setback on therapeutic recreation and subsistence fishing for lower-income earners in the region.

Sweetwater is simply obligated by the land swap and easement to provide access to the lake until sunset 365 days a year. Supervision during those hours, or lack thereof, is Sweetwater's business, not that of citizens, or the US Forest Service.  This is all 100% legally unambiguous. Please call out your legal department’s claims otherwise and/or have that analysis reviewed by another independent agency.

Fortunately, others in the community are stepping up. Please create a path for remedies to having lost much of Loveland's public benefits since our earlier failed communications and failure to implement the protection and remedies at Loveland that so many of us have petitioned Supervisor Tangenberg to act on for so many years now. 

Sincerely,

Russell Walsh

4639 Montiel Truck Trail

Jamul CA, 91935

619-922-6235

    On Friday, September 18, 2020 at 08:35:44 AM PDT, Russell Walsh <russellwalsh2003@yahoo.com> wrote:

  Mr. Tangenberg,

Thank you for that email. Why would you want to renew the agreement other than to weaken what is already a substantially good easement as far as hours of access if it were respected? Mr. Walsh,
I've been as clear as I can be in my previous communications.  Sweetwater Authority has the jurisdiction on access to Loveland Reservoir.  While a public access easement exists, our partner knows best during these trying times how access can be facilitated.  The Cleveland National Forest (and every National Forest in California) is currently closed to public access given the extreme fire risk and dangerous fire conditions.  The Valley Fire burn area will be closed for some time in the future as well.

All that said, I've cc'd Bob Heiar, our District Ranger for the Descanso Ranger District, and the local manager for this part of the Forest.  He has expressed to me an interest in revisiting the expired agreement with Sweetwater Authority sometime in the future, in order to reaffirm that commitment and establish a good arrangement for continued access and opportunities for the public there.

This has also been our approach. I update my ad template with current
vacancy info, them post it far and wide on electronic and physical
bulletin boards. I also send it out to my agenda email list. The
reason we have a posting on our county page is that I send the ad to
the liaison with a request that he/she post it there. That, IMO,
should be the limit of staff involvement.

I have accidentally stumbled on a county posting for one of my
vacancies, and found that it bypassed me altogether for the initial
stages and I 100 percent reject that approach. It deprives the
applicant of personal guidance and locally-focused experience and
sends the applicant into a chilly, impersonal application process
without even giving him/her an opportunity to ask questions and
receive answers from the humans that know the most about serving on
the group. It's completely inappropriate and puts staff, rather than
us, in initial control of who may be seated.
Billie Jo

body:
Dear Interested Stakeholder,

Reminder regarding our progress to implement the Board of Supervisors (Board) direction related to a Vehicle Miles Traveled (VMT) mitigation program.

On March 1, 2023, the Board received a report on VMT mitigation program options and provided direction to continue coordination with outside agencies and jurisdictions, to estimate costs to project applicants, to solicit stakeholder input, and to receive additional Board direction before the VMT mitigation program is fully developed.

A VMT mitigation program will play a role in determining where development efforts are focused in the unincorporated area, such as near jobs and transit to reduce travel and greenhouse gas emissions, consistent with the intent of Senate Bill (SB) 743, balanced with considerations regarding development feasibility.

On May 22, 2024, staff will provide an update to the Board on the development of the VMT mitigation program and options that staff are evaluating as part of the program.

There is an in-person public meeting tonight to learn about the development of a VMT mitigation program.

Public Meeting 2 (In-Person)

When: April 23, 2024 at 6:30 pm

Where: County Operations Center Chambers
               5520 Overland Avenue

               San Diego, CA 92123

Disability-related accommodations necessary to facilitate meeting participation, language interpretation, including American Sign Language, and/or written materials in alternative languages and formats are available upon request. Please submit your request at least 72 hours in advance of the event to Damon Davis at damon.davis@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:damon.davis@sdcounty.ca.gov>.

We are also reaching out specifically to your individual groups as you have previously requested meetings or expressed interest in the County's ongoing implementation of VMT policies, as well as identifying your group as an area of interest related to our current efforts associated with potential VMT mitigation programs.  In addition to the announced Public Meetings, if you group would like to request an individual meeting with County staff, please contact Damon Davis at damon.davis@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:damon.davis@sdcounty.ca.gov>, and we will coordinate an in-person or virtual meeting at your convenience.

Thank you,
[cid:image001.png@01DA9555.6925E1A0]
Jacob Armstrong, Chief
County of San Diego, Planning & Development Services
Land Development Division
5510 Overland Avenue | Suite 310 | San Diego, CA 92123 | MS: O-377
*619-756-2463 cell | jacob.armstrong@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:jacob.armstrong@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Planning & Development Services Homepage: www.SDCPDS.org<http://www.sdcpds.org/>

The smell of weed is wreaking havoc across California
The state's largest indoor cannabis farm is under fire thanks to the "disgusting" smell of pot
By Lester Black, Cannabis editorMarch 5, 2025

David Bernard, left, the COO of C4 USA, said the company plans to push forward with an expansion even as neighbors complain about cannabis odor.
Courtesy of C4 USA
California is globally synonymous with cannabis, but the plant’s distinctive smell has become a major headache for people across the state.
From Northern California to the desert to the coast, California residents have been complaining for years that the smell of legal cannabis farms is destroying their quality of life. And in some places, local governments are beginning to act.

In Cathedral City, a small enclave near Palm Springs, the city council approved a moratorium last week that will block any new cannabis businesses from opening or expanding after years of complaints over cannabis odors. The moratorium was aimed directly at Cat City Cannabis Co., a massive indoor marijuana cultivation facility that has generated complaints for years from nearby residents who say the facility emits a “disgusting” smell.
Mayor Pro Tem Raymond Gregory said during the meeting that the moratorium would stop the facility from expanding further.

“That won’t affect what we’re going to be continuing to work with on the current issue, but it will stop them building a whole ’nother building,” Gregory said.

David Bernard, the COO of C4 USA, which owns the facility, said in an emailed statement to SFGATE that they are actively working with the city to develop an “effective odor management solution” but that they are also pushing forward with their phase 2 expansion. It will add 168,000 square feet of space to the existing 325,000-square-foot facility, which is already the largest indoor pot farm in the state, according to the company’s website.
“Though the moratorium has impacted our timeline, we view this as an opportunity to work collaboratively with the city and the local community to develop a long-term, effective odor management solution,” Bernard said.

The Cathedral City action comes after the Santa Barbara County Planning Commission unanimously recommended last month that all greenhouse cannabis growers install carbon filters within a year. The area near the coastal town of Carpinteria is a major hub for greenhouse cannabis growers, and residents have been complaining about the “sewer-like” smell of cannabis for years. The recommendation still needs to be approved by the county’s Board of Supervisors before it becomes law.

Some of the greenhouses have already installed the filtration systems, which can cost millions of dollars, while others have installed misting systems that attempt to camouflage the smell of fresh marijuana, although those systems have been panned as making entire neighborhoods smell like laundromats.
Most agricultural companies are protected from neighborhood complaints over nuisances like odor through so-called “Right to Farm” laws, but most local governments, including Santa Barbara’s, have exempted cannabis farms from receiving those protections.

Some California residents are saying the smell of cannabis is more than just a nuisance and that it could actually be causing health problems. The Sonoma Neighborhood Coalition, a group that is critical of cannabis policies, has been pushing for the county to ban outdoor cannabis farms entirely because, according to the group, pot plants release toxic chemicals including beta-myrcene. In December, the group warned against allowing outdoor cannabis farms, saying allowing pot farms would be “assaulting your right to defend your home from businesses that spew carcinogens into your yard and your house.”

Beta-myrcene is a naturally occurring compound found in thousands of plants. Studies have shown it can have carcinogenic effects when exposed at high levels, but SFGATE was not able to independently verify if cannabis farms would ever produce enough of the chemical to meet those toxic levels to nearby residents. Hops also produce the compound, and there do not appear to be problems in Yakima Valley where over 50,000 acres of hops are planted every year.

In Cathedral City, the smell of cannabis has tainted what was originally a genial relationship between the town and the pot industry. Locals were ecstatic when plans for the Cat City Cannabis Co. facility were first announced in 2018, with the planning commission unanimously approving the project and local neighbors telling the Desert Sun that they were happy a long vacant lot was becoming a job creator. The facility, which ballooned in price to $120 million, traded hands before opening under its current ownership.

Now, the mood is decidedly angry. Debbie Price, a local resident, told the council that “we are all flipping trapped” and called for an injunction to cease operations immediately until “there is no smell.”

“Is Cathedral City slated to be another Salton Sea area? You may laugh, but you know what, so did they,” Price said.
Gregory, the mayor pro tem, said that the council would have acted differently in 2020 if they knew about the smell and directed the company to end the odor.

“Stop the odor, and we’ll be done,” Gregory said.

Lester Black
CANNABIS EDITOR
Lester Black is SFGATE's cannabis editor. He was born in Torrance, raised in Seattle, and has written for FiveThirtyEight.com, High Country News, The Guardian, The Albuquerque Journal, The Tennessean, and many other publications. He was previously the cannabis columnist for The Stranger.

--
Kathleen M. Lippitt, MPH
Public Health Practitioner

The smell of weed is wreaking havoc across California
The state's largest indoor cannabis farm is under fire thanks to the "disgusting" smell of pot
By Lester Black, Cannabis editorMarch 5, 2025

David Bernard, left, the COO of C4 USA, said the company plans to push forward with an expansion even as neighbors complain about cannabis odor.
Courtesy of C4 USA
California is globally synonymous with cannabis, but the plant’s distinctive smell has become a major headache for people across the state.
From Northern California to the desert to the coast, California residents have been complaining for years that the smell of legal cannabis farms is destroying their quality of life. And in some places, local governments are beginning to act.

In Cathedral City, a small enclave near Palm Springs, the city council approved a moratorium last week that will block any new cannabis businesses from opening or expanding after years of complaints over cannabis odors. The moratorium was aimed directly at Cat City Cannabis Co., a massive indoor marijuana cultivation facility that has generated complaints for years from nearby residents who say the facility emits a “disgusting” smell.
Mayor Pro Tem Raymond Gregory said during the meeting that the moratorium would stop the facility from expanding further.

“That won’t affect what we’re going to be continuing to work with on the current issue, but it will stop them building a whole ’nother building,” Gregory said.

David Bernard, the COO of C4 USA, which owns the facility, said in an emailed statement to SFGATE that they are actively working with the city to develop an “effective odor management solution” but that they are also pushing forward with their phase 2 expansion. It will add 168,000 square feet of space to the existing 325,000-square-foot facility, which is already the largest indoor pot farm in the state, according to the company’s website.
“Though the moratorium has impacted our timeline, we view this as an opportunity to work collaboratively with the city and the local community to develop a long-term, effective odor management solution,” Bernard said.

The Cathedral City action comes after the Santa Barbara County Planning Commission unanimously recommended last month that all greenhouse cannabis growers install carbon filters within a year. The area near the coastal town of Carpinteria is a major hub for greenhouse cannabis growers, and residents have been complaining about the “sewer-like” smell of cannabis for years. The recommendation still needs to be approved by the county’s Board of Supervisors before it becomes law.

Some of the greenhouses have already installed the filtration systems, which can cost millions of dollars, while others have installed misting systems that attempt to camouflage the smell of fresh marijuana, although those systems have been panned as making entire neighborhoods smell like laundromats.
Most agricultural companies are protected from neighborhood complaints over nuisances like odor through so-called “Right to Farm” laws, but most local governments, including Santa Barbara’s, have exempted cannabis farms from receiving those protections.

Some California residents are saying the smell of cannabis is more than just a nuisance and that it could actually be causing health problems. The Sonoma Neighborhood Coalition, a group that is critical of cannabis policies, has been pushing for the county to ban outdoor cannabis farms entirely because, according to the group, pot plants release toxic chemicals including beta-myrcene. In December, the group warned against allowing outdoor cannabis farms, saying allowing pot farms would be “assaulting your right to defend your home from businesses that spew carcinogens into your yard and your house.”

Beta-myrcene is a naturally occurring compound found in thousands of plants. Studies have shown it can have carcinogenic effects when exposed at high levels, but SFGATE was not able to independently verify if cannabis farms would ever produce enough of the chemical to meet those toxic levels to nearby residents. Hops also produce the compound, and there do not appear to be problems in Yakima Valley where over 50,000 acres of hops are planted every year.

In Cathedral City, the smell of cannabis has tainted what was originally a genial relationship between the town and the pot industry. Locals were ecstatic when plans for the Cat City Cannabis Co. facility were first announced in 2018, with the planning commission unanimously approving the project and local neighbors telling the Desert Sun that they were happy a long vacant lot was becoming a job creator. The facility, which ballooned in price to $120 million, traded hands before opening under its current ownership.

Now, the mood is decidedly angry. Debbie Price, a local resident, told the council that “we are all flipping trapped” and called for an injunction to cease operations immediately until “there is no smell.”

“Is Cathedral City slated to be another Salton Sea area? You may laugh, but you know what, so did they,” Price said.
Gregory, the mayor pro tem, said that the council would have acted differently in 2020 if they knew about the smell and directed the company to end the odor.

“Stop the odor, and we’ll be done,” Gregory said.

Lester Black
CANNABIS EDITOR

body:
Steve HalesDirector Friends of Loveland Reservoir

Hello Steve,

Steve, I want to express my sincere gratitude to you and your board for the commendable actions you've taken in support of Sunrise to Sunset. Your efforts have not gone unnoticed and are greatly appreciated. 

Have you reached out to Congressman Issa? Our easement is primarily a federal issue, and while we need follow-through, and community support everywhere we can get it, Congressman Issa is our strongest ally where the Forest Service is concerned. Please ask your board to promote a quality petition for progress on the restoration of  Sunrise to Sunset access ASAP.  As you said recently, agencies like to work with and respond to groups like Friends of Loveland Reservoir. If you need help, please let me and others know, perhaps via membership and a website.  

Your help at the ACPG is important:The ACPG has been a good base at times for Loveland Advocacy but there have been let downs too. Your board members know that  I went to a half dozen meetings with the Alpine Community Planning group for help with Loveland in the year before it was drained and to many meetings since. In the spring of 2022 a strong vote passed by ACPG to encourage Sweetwater to come to the Alpine Group. There was a least one previous resolution to write letters of support on recreation themes.  However, the chair did not complete these tasks despite the strong votes. The same thing appears to be happening with April's nearly unanimous vote for a letter of support from the ACPG on the Sunrise to Sunset. I believe you are aware through CC'd email on this trajectory. We need to work together so the ACPG honors community work and interests at Loveland and the work of the people on the planning advisory board itself on behalf of Loveland Reservoir so we can have success on Sunrise to Sunset and full defense of future complete dewatering which are here. We all agree that land use organizations are falling short of legal easement adherence and should be advised and strenuously petitioned to do otherwise. 

Please check your emails from me about Sweetwater's goal to float 200 acres of solar panels at Sweetwater Reservoir. 

The minimum water levels to float that industrial-type project will likely come from Loveland Reservoir and create new cyclical dewatering episodes. Sweetwater refuses to remove the threat, which is a factor. The good news is that it is being challenged locally in South Bay and here by us. 

Appreciatively,

Russell

Karen Wood

Executive Director 

Friends of Loveland Reservoir

Alpine CA

  

Hello  Karen,

  

Thank you for your recent complimentary work on the Loveland fishing float platform and other items of concern for Loveland Lake users. 

  

During the Alpine community planning group meeting last week, a significant issue regarding access to Loveland Reservoir was raised. Your board member, Darlene Cossio,  who is also on the planning group board, attempted to block the group's motion for a letter of support  to Sweetwater Authority and the US Forest Service for sunrise-to-sunset access. She claimed that the issue was already being addressed.

  

Would you please clarify what your board members' actions and comments mean for restoring access at Loveland according to the easement? Why does your board member see this being resolved so that she would block a letter of support and make the statements I am asking about?

  

Another spring and summer of afternoon and early evening recreation at Loveland is slipping away from working people and their families. Please support independent advocates in requesting that the ACPG bring the Cleveland National Forest administrators back to the ACPG meeting for a public follow-up on our meeting with them at the ACPG  last October. 

  

Appreciatively,

  

Russell

Russell,

The FOLR board supports sunrise to sunset hours at Loveland.

You are incorrect about what happened at the ACPG meeting.  In Darlene’s position as a member of the ACPG board, she abstained from voting on the motion – but she did not vote “No” or try to “block” it as you say.  And she abstained only after it was obvious the motion would pass anyway.

Regardless, Darlene can vote however she likes as a member of the ACPG board, without FOLR approving or justifying that vote.

I hope this clarifies the misunderstanding.

Steve
FOLR

Steve HalesDirector Friends of LovelandCC Karen Wood Executive Director Friends of Loveland

Steve,
I am following up on your letter from April regarding FOLR support for Sunrise to Sunset at Loveland Reservoir.As we near the point of longest day length in the summer of 2024 I am curious as to progress made, or effort given for our nature viewer and other recreation users on this matter. 
Also, I have advised you about how Sweetwater Authority is a constant applicant and recipient of State and Federal grants, yet is comfortable shortchanging taxpayers and citizens on even the limited sunrise to sunset access to Loveland's shoreline. You told me that FOLR supports that. Thank you for you work for  nature lovers , fishers and hikers who need this recreation and proper voice and action in our communities by our leaders. I have letters of support on Sunrise to Sunset from Supervisor Anderson if you can use that in you advocacy. Regardless, Darlene can vote however she likes as a member of the ACPG board, without FOLR approving or justifying that vote. 

  

I hope this clarifies the misunderstanding.

  

Steve

On Aug 11, 2024, at 9:17 AM, Eileen Delaney <eileen.fallbrook@gmail.com> wrote:

﻿Hello All,

Last week I met (zoom) with Staff from SANDAG re their Vision Zero Program. This program is still a work in progress and they estimate that it won’t be completed for at least the next few months.
Vision Zero
sandag.org

<sandag-favicon-primary.png>

Vision Zero is a comprehensive data driven program to identify roads/areas in our region that have the highest concentration of major accidents where law enforcement has been involved and reports have been generated.

With this accident information, these areas have then been analyzed to determine what changes or improvements could be made so that there could potentially be zero future accidents.

This information could then also be used by municipalities and the County to apply for approximately $1 billion dollars in federal grants.

One of the concerns that I have is that this data is 2 years behind, so the numbers are from 2022. It seems to me that after Covid, the public generally appears to be driving a lot faster and in a much more unsafe manner, hence an increase in accidents that these initial studies might not capture.

Below is a link for the SANDAG’s interactive map associated with this program. It shows the areas that have the highest concentration of accidents, amongst other data.
<open-uri20230922-79-ls0orx.png>
Traffic Safety Dashboard
opendata.sandag.org

While SANDAG’s goal for this program is to provide the data to help with grants, I see this as a great tool to use when we are asking DPW and TAC to reduce speeds and study roads in our area for traffic calming or other ways to reduce accidents.

I’ll keep you posted when I get further updates. If you have any questions, please let me know.
Best regards,

Eileen Delaney
Vice Chair, APG- San Diego County

Fallbrook Planning Group

Eileen,

Thank you for attending this meeting and providing the update.

Did they say what the timeframe for the $1B in federal grants was? And if the grant money is in addition to the normal grant funding pot?

I’m trying to consider if we can tap into it for CIP projects to improve unsafe roads which are listed in the 5-year plan, yet ‘unfunded’ at this point in time. (We have one such in Rainbow called “Dead Man’s Curve”.)  It would be great to be able to have those projects in the County addressed through the additional funding if available using this data (if it is additional to the scheme the County is currently employing to fund projects through grants.)

Thanks again,
Lynne Malinowski

Subject: SANDAG Vision Zero

Hello All,

Last week I met (zoom) with Staff from SANDAG re their Vision Zero Program. This program is still a work in progress and they estimate that it won’t be completed for at least the next few months.
Vision Zero<https://www.sandag.org/projects-and-programs/regional-initiatives/vision-zero>
sandag.org<https://www.sandag.org/projects-and-programs/regional-initiatives/vision-zero>
[cid:image001.png@01DAEDA7.62DC5860]<https://www.sandag.org/projects-and-programs/regional-initiatives/vision-zero>

Vision Zero is a comprehensive data driven program to identify roads/areas in our region that have the highest concentration of major accidents where law enforcement has been involved and reports have been generated.

With this accident information, these areas have then been analyzed to determine what changes or improvements could be made so that there could potentially be zero future accidents.

This information could then also be used by municipalities and the County to apply for approximately $1 billion dollars in federal grants.

One of the concerns that I have is that this data is 2 years behind, so the numbers are from 2022. It seems to me that after Covid, the public generally appears to be driving a lot faster and in a much more unsafe manner, hence an increase in accidents that these initial studies might not capture.

Below is a link for the SANDAG’s interactive map associated with this program. It shows the areas that have the highest concentration of accidents, amongst other data.
[cid:image002.jpg@01DAEDA7.62DC5860]
Traffic Safety Dashboard<https://opendata.sandag.org/stories/s/5f7y-nefe>
opendata.sandag.org<https://opendata.sandag.org/stories/s/5f7y-nefe>

While SANDAG’s goal for this program is to provide the data to help with grants, I see this as a great tool to use when we are asking DPW and TAC to reduce speeds and study roads in our area for traffic calming or other ways to reduce accidents.

I’ll keep you posted when I get further updates. If you have any questions, please let me know.

Best regards,

Eileen Delaney
Vice Chair, APG- San Diego County

Subject: San Diego County Broadband NOFA Public Meetings

Hi Travis,

Hope this email finds you well! The County of San Diego's Land Use & Environment Group (LUEG) is conducting a series of public meetings from May 20 - June 4 to gather public feedback and input on an upcoming Notice of Funding Availability (NOFA) on a $9 million ARPA-funded grant program to help address broadband access and affordability in unincorporated communities. This is a continuation of public engagement activities that helped inform the Comprehensive Broadband Plan<https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/lueg/broadband/> released January 2023. We are inviting Alpine Community Planning Group to participate in this process.

The County is seeking public input on the criteria and scoring for the grant awards that were recently released via a draft Notice of Funding Availability (NOFA)<https://engage.sandiegocounty.gov/broadband>. There are a couple ways your community members can provide their feedback:

  1.  Attending one of the scheduled in-person public meetings (meeting flyer attached) or virtual webinar (details forthcoming)
  2.  Submitting written comments directly through the County's broadband engagement website (https://engage.sandiegocounty.gov/broadband) or by email (broadband.grants@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:broadband.grants@sdcounty.ca.gov>)

We kindly ask you to help circulate this information with your network. All public comments on the draft NOFA are due by June 10th.

The County has contracted Guidehouse, a management consulting firm, to assist in this effort. I have copied the Guidehouse team members; please reach out to Lucy O'Keeffe (lokeeffe@guidehouse.com<mailto:lokeeffe@guidehouse.com>) and Harrison Phelan (hphelan@guidehouse.com<mailto:hphelan@guidehouse.com>) with questions. Also copied on this email are Stephanie Johnson (Stephanie.Johnson@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:Stephanie.Johnson@sdcounty.ca.gov>) and Michael De La Rosa (Michael.DeLaRosa@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:Michael.DeLaRosa@sdcounty.ca.gov>), the County contacts for this engagement.

Thank you for your support of this endeavor, and we hope to see you there.

Best,
Lucy

﻿Report to the Association of Planning Groups - San Diego County (APG)On July 16th the first scheduled evacuation tour for SANDAG and Caltrans staff was held in the Ramona area. Currently in the planning stages is an evacuation tour for the SR 94 area.
APG's representative on the SANDAG Board of Directors, Robin Joy Maxson, extended an invitation to SANDAG and Caltrans staff to participate in a tour of the expected routes for evacuation in the event of a wildfire or other emergency. Maxson emphasised the importance of experiencing the evacuation routes in-person in order to accurately evaluate the routes for safety and viability in an emergency. 
Roadways examined were Wildcat Canyon, SR 67, Highland Valley Road and SR 78. 
Issues considered and discussed were:- Shelter-in-place orders and the likelihood of evacuees choosing to heed evacuation orders. Visitors will most likely choose to leave the area.- Physical constraints to safe and effective evacuation,  e.g., present roadway design, traffic bottlenecks due to changes in the number of lanes and/or their configuration.- The presence of deadly chimney effect fires and other geographical hazards to evacuee safety.
- Residents and visitors vary in familiarity with the roadways.- Fluctuation in the numbers of evacuees on any given day as the number of residents is not a static indicator of how many people may need to evacuate; the number of weekend visitors to the area greatly expands the number of evacuees. - Types of vehicles utilized during an evacuation in rural areas have historically been large vehicles/trucks and many vehicle/trailer combinations in order to evacuate livestock.- The unpredictability of fire during a firestorm created by the combined conditions of high temperatures, dry fuel and high winds.
Local fire behavior expert, Dan Summers, identified and explained to the group the behavior of fire as it relates to evacuees safety during an evacuation event on these four routes. Evacuees are exposed to:- Oxygen deprivation which also deprives combustion engine vehicles of the oxygen required to operate.- Extreme heat which impairs human judgement.- Chimney effect fires which are corridors in the landscape where heavy brush and trees combine to create a rapid, deadly, blistering, upward burn path.
The tour was educational as attendees shared their knowledge of roadway construction, fire behavior and human behavior during a crisis.Attendees were:

﻿Report to the Association of Planning Groups - San Diego County (APG)
On July 16th the first scheduled evacuation tour for SANDAG and Caltrans staff was held in the Ramona area. Currently in the planning stages is an evacuation tour for the SR 94 area.

APG's representative on the SANDAG Board of Directors, Robin Joy Maxson, extended an invitation to SANDAG and Caltrans staff to participate in a tour of the expected routes for evacuation in the event of a wildfire or other emergency. Maxson emphasised the importance of experiencing the evacuation routes in-person in order to accurately evaluate the routes for safety and viability in an emergency.

Roadways examined were Wildcat Canyon, SR 67, Highland Valley Road and SR 78.

Issues considered and discussed were:
- Shelter-in-place orders and the likelihood of evacuees choosing to heed evacuation orders. Visitors will most likely choose to leave the area.

- Physical constraints to safe and effective evacuation,  e.g., present roadway design, traffic bottlenecks due to changes in the number of lanes and/or their configuration.

- The presence of deadly chimney effect fires and other geographical hazards to evacuee safety.

- Residents and visitors vary in familiarity with the roadways.
- Fluctuation in the numbers of evacuees on any given day as the number of residents is not a static indicator of how many people may need to evacuate; the number of weekend visitors to the area greatly expands the number of evacuees.
 - Types of vehicles utilized during an evacuation in rural areas have historically been large vehicles/trucks and many vehicle/trailer combinations in order to evacuate livestock.
- The unpredictability of fire during a firestorm created by the combined conditions of high temperatures, dry fuel and high winds.

Local fire behavior expert, Dan Summers, identified and explained to the group the behavior of fire as it relates to evacuees safety during an evacuation event on these four routes. Evacuees are exposed to:
- Oxygen deprivation which also deprives combustion engine vehicles of the oxygen required to operate.
- Extreme heat which impairs human judgement.
- Chimney effect fires which are corridors in the landscape where heavy brush and trees combine to create a rapid, deadly, blistering, upward burn path.

The tour was educational as attendees shared their knowledge of roadway construction, fire behavior and human behavior during a crisis.
Attendees were:

Robin Joy Maxson, Chair, Association of Planning Groups and Representative on the SANDAG Board of Directors
Dan Summers, Former County of San Diego Fire Advisory Board and Fire/Paramedic Technology Instructor
Stephen Welborn, Caltrans
Karina Cantero-Angel, Caltrans

Nicholas Buenviaje, Caltrans
Mimi Morisaki, SANDAG
Michael Terlep, SANDAG
Jose Alvarez, SANDAG

Report Submitted by:
Robin Joy Maxson, Representative to SANDAG

Subject: Report on SANDAG's September Meetings to the Association of Planning Groups - San Diego County

Good Afternoon APG Members,

September 13th and 27th reports are in two segments below:

September 27th Meeting (Eileen):

Due to a communication error I was not given complete instructions to attend the Sept. SANDAG board meeting remotely and be promoted to a separate screen.

It was difficult to hear the conversations and I was unable to participate. I am attaching the agenda for your review.

On a different subject… As Robin has let you know, Congressman Issa held a meeting with the mayors of most of the cities, along with SANDAG’s new CEO, to discuss their transportation and other needs.  Unfortunately the APGs which represents ALL of the County’s unincorporated residents was not included.

When Robin notified the Congressman’s staff, we were given the impression that this would be rectified and another meeting would be scheduled with us.

Instead, we have been invited to a mixer/open house for their new offices in Santee “for invited guest” with no plans to sit down for a discussion.

This is a concern on many levels.

Attached please find the emails that Robin and I have both sent.  (Included at end of this email.)

We’ll let you know if/when we have any updates.

September 13th Meeting (Robin):

SANDAG's CEO, Mario Orso:

Mario Orso confirmed he had received the request from the APG to attend a joint meeting between Congressman Darrell Issa, APG members and himself.  Hannah Stern of SANDAG will coordinate with the APG and Congressman Issa to ensure attendance at a future meeting.

Background: The Congressional Representative (Darrell Issa), who's district encompasses the vast majority of the unincorporated area, held a meeting during his open house in Escondido. In a private meeting before the event Congressman Issa had invited SANDAG CEO, Mario Orso and staff to discuss transportation and funding. The Congressman had included Mayors from his district. There was no County representation nor unincorporated area through the APG.

This oversight was immediately brought to the attention of the Congressman and his office staff by the APG. The APG sent a letter to the Congressman and copied Mario Orso. See complete letter at end of this email.

SR 125 Investigation Summary:

"The investigation found ETAN's Fastlane financial reporting cannot be relied upon, and the Finance department lacks adequate internal controls, including proper review and supervision, to ensure SR 125 financial information is accurately recorded and reported. The report recommends an independent assessment of the Finance department's policies, procedures, and practices."

Office of the Independent Auditor - FY 2024 Annual Investigations Report:

The Independent Performance Auditor, Courtney Ruby, made a defining statement of the state of SANDAG's contracts invoicing and payment process;

- The system is broken. -

"Most concerning is the finding that invoices totaling $13055,123 or 32.39% of the sample size, did not include sufficient documentation to determine what work was completed by contractors."

This report included 7 recommendations by the auditor.

APG Comment to Board: Thank you for the great report. I have done accounts payable in the past. With a more than 32% failure to follow the process for accounts payable, I am going to assume there is some overpayment of taxpayer dollars. And then, recommendations 1 through 7 - I did not see a plan for recovery or potential recovery of taxpayer dollars. Is there overpayment out there and how we would know if documentation was not done correctly? Is there a plan for this? Thank you. (2:10:30)

SANDAG response (Courtney Ruby): When we evaluated the invoice payments. This would be with the project managers and contracting whether the information was there. Then it was passed on for payment. So we're seeing insufficient documentation and it's being passed on for payment. We would have to drill down further in relation to determine was the work done or not done. This procedure did not go to evaluating whether everything going back to project managers that would have been a different audit. A different audit, this was looking to see based on their procedures. Are they following their procedures? Is the documentation there? So, in order to quantify that, that would take, that would be a different audit.

Public Comment:

Paul The Bold, comment to the Board: Does SANDAG really work for the whole county? You've got Robin Joy Maxson sitting over there. Theoretically, we're sending half the county, yet she doesn't have a vote. Since SANDAG is in the tax business. This is really taxation without representation... (2:26:24)

Questions from APG members:

Question - Is SANDAG informed of freeway projects in the County? Or, are freeway projects strictly a state affair? Does SANDAG have a role in the scheduling and decision making?

Response from Roy Abboud, Caltrans: The answer is it depends. General maintenance projects led by Caltrans are managed and scheduled by Caltans. Projects led by SANDAG, e.g. managed lane conversions, are scheduled by SANDAG. Caltrans gives updates to the SANDAG Board on the work they are doing in the County regardless of the lead agency.

Resources for APG members:

Link to the Traffic Safety Dashboard  <https://www.sandag.org/trafficsafety> https://www.sandag.org/trafficsafety. It is located in SANDAG’s Open Data Portal.

Original SANDAG documents and meeting minutes are available directly from SANDAG's Board of Directors website: https://www.sandag.org/meetings-and-events/board-of-directors

Report Submitted by:

Robin Joy Maxson, Representative to SANDAG

Eileen Delaney, Representative Alternate to SANDAG

Association of Planning Groups - San Diego County

**************************************************************************************

(Response to Congressman Issa - Escondidio Open House)

Complete Letter:

August 3, 2024

Good Afternoon Congressman Issa,

The Association of Planning Groups - San Diego County (APG) was formed to provide unincorporated representation on the SANDAG Board of Directors. The APG represents over 513,00 unincorporated area residents residing in the 48th District - we are the second largest population in the County of San Diego and comprise the majority of the constituents in your district.

At Friday's Escondido District Office Open House event there was a closed meeting with SANDAG CEO Mario Orso, several mayors and yourself discussing the issue of transportation in your district. There was no representation from the unincorporated community on the regional issues of transportation funding and projects. As are the mayors, we are also elected by our communities to represent them. As such, we need to be included in all future discussions and planning sessions. Regional Transportation Plans are a very important subject for the thousands of residents in the area we represent. It's important that our voices are heard. Moving forward, to correct the history of incomplete transportation projects and diverted funding from the traditionally underserved and underrepresented people of the 48th District, the APG must be part of any regional planning discussions.

Since there was a meeting with Mario Orso and city mayors - the  APG requests an equal opportunity to meet for our elected unincorporated community representatives.

The APG looks forward to meeting in-person with you, Mario Orso, and the Association of Planning Group members before the end of summer. Please have your office reach out for available meeting dates and attendee information.

Respectfully,

Robin Joy Maxson

Chair, Association of Planning Groups - San Diego County

Board Member, SANDAG Board of Directors

760-705-7435

Eileen Delaney

Vice-Chair, Association of Planning Groups - San Diego County

Board Member (Alternate), SANDAG Board of Directors

"The 48th District encompasses the central and eastern parts of San Diego County and a portion of Riverside County, including the communities of Fallbrook, Bonsall, Valley Center, Ramona, Escondido, Santee, Poway, Lakeside, Alpine, Temecula, Murrieta and the mountain and desert areas of the San Diego-Imperial County line."

*************************************************************************************************

(Response to Congressman Issa - East County Leadership Open House)

September 28, 2024

Hello,

Thank you for the invitation. I am sorry that I won't be able to attend on behalf of the Association of Planning Groups. I believe our Chair, Robin Joy Maxson will be there.

As you may be aware, members of the  Association of Planning Groups - San Diego County are representatives from every Community Planning Group throughout the unincorporated areas in the County of San Diego. Planning Group members are elected by the Citizens of each planning area. We represent nearly 600,000 residents..

I hope we have the opportunity to meet with the Congressman on another occasion and sit down to discuss the transportation and other needs of these 600,000 residents. (many of whom are also constituents of the Congressman:)

Thank you!

Regards,

Eileen Delaney, Chair

Fallbrook Planning Group

Fallbrook Design Review Board

Vice Chair- Assoc. of Planning Groups, SD County

On Sun, Oct 27, 2024 at 8:08 PM APG <associationofplanninggroups@gmail.com> wrote:

Good Evening APG Members,

Please note our next APG meeting will be in-person on Saturday, January 4th, 2025, from 10:00am to noon at the Lakeside Library.

APG Announcement to SANDAG Board on Oct. 25th:
We have good news. The second wildfire and emergency evacuation tour was held last Friday for SR-94. Organizing the tour were SANDAG's Ariana Galvan and Jamul-Dulzura Community Planning Group member, Paul Dombkowski. In addition to several members from the Planning Group and SANDAG there were participants from Caltrans, San Diego County Sheriff's office, and CalFire, including Battalion Chief, Sam Friedman. The unincorporated communities value the partnership and collaboration these tours create as we work toward a safer travel experience for all. Thank you.

SANDAG CEO, Mario Orso Report on Oct. 11th:
-Mario Orso said that they were cooperating with the Independent Auditor and working to build openness and trust.
-Regarding taking the 125 out of the Regional Plan as a toll road - would we be in compliance with CARB (California Air Resources Board). We would barely be meeting our GHG emissions and VMT measure.

-Otay Mesa East has 65% of the design completed.

APG comment to Board: Mario, this is October, wildfire season in the rural areas. What have we done to alleviate the bottleneck issues with the highways that are used for evacuation heading west? There are bottlenecks that have been there forever and we've highlighted those as being potential fatal zones for evacuees. Where are we with resolving bottleneck issues with lanes that are one lane, two, three, that are continuing to change as people evacuate west? Thank you. (32:00/ Oct. 11)

SANDAG reponse (Mario Orso): What route did you mention?

APG response: This would be specifically 67, but there are bottlenecks on other evacuation routes.

SANDAG response (Mario Orso): Everett, do you want to help me on what's the emergency evacuation plan from Caltrans?

Caltrans response (Everett Townsend): Yeah, so Caltrans has been working with emergency responders, CalFire, CHP and others to reassess on an annual basis, is what we do to reassess our highway system. And, to identify where additional improvements may be made. Over the last few years, Caltrans has completed projects there that create some widening and create opportunities to improve traffic flow through there. Most of those issues that state route 67 project is at some point will be presented here at the Board, but you know, just to be informed that Caltrans is well aware of the concerns of the communities in Ramona and further east. As well as CHP and CalFire. And, we certainly have a plan to address any issues that may come up during this time.

State Route 125 Toll Removal Oct. 11th and 25th:
Oct. 11th, Mario Orso, reported that a pre-environmental analysis and an equity analysis need to be performed and these two actions will take one year.

Vivian Moreno, City of San Diego comment: I continue to be extremely disappointed with how SANDAG is handling the 125. We're the only community (South Bay Area) that gets tripled taxed on this toll. We pay taxes every single year. We pay the toll and we pay Transnet funding. We're the only community that does this. This seems to me like we are slow walking this issue.... How much longer do we have to wait? 2042?

Oct. 25th Courtney Ruby, SANDAG Independent Performance Auditor, reported that the Executive Management Team which included former CEO, Hasan Ikhrata; were aware of and actively working to resolve major issues with the 125 Tolling System, yet failed to notify the Board of this until October of 2023. Fully 18 months passed before the Board was informed of these significant issues impacting residents of the South Bay Region. A single-source contract was presented and approved by the Board in January of 2024 based on the Boards belief that they could rely on the recommendations of Executive Management. As it turned out this contract between SANDAG and Deloitte to manage the 125 Toll Road systems was deficient and absent an exchange of basic system requirements.

Ed Musgrove, City of San Marcos comment: We were lied to by the Executive Team. Until the names of those in charge are revealed I have no confidence.

Wildfire Evacuation Tour SR-94:
On Friday, October 18th members of SANDAG, Caltrans and the Janual Community Planning Group completed an evacuation tour. Please see Paul Dombkowski's report sent in a previous email on October 23rd.

News:
At the October 11th and 25th SANDAG Board meetings we had zero voting representation from anyone living in the Unincorporated Area. Only Nora Vargas was present to vote on behalf of the County. Chair Vargas lives in Chula Vista according to her profile.

Questions from APG members
No questions received this month.

Original SANDAG documents and meeting minutes are available directly from SANDAG's Board of Directors website: https://www.sandag.org/meetings-and-events/board-of-directors

Report Submitted by:
Robin Joy Maxson, Representative to SANDAG
Association of Planning Groups - San Diego County

On Nov 30, 2024, at 9:35 AM, APG <associationofplanninggroups@gmail.com> wrote:

﻿Good Morning APG Members,

Our next APG meeting will be in-person on Saturday, January 4th, 2025, from 10:00am to noon at the Lakeside Library. As always, if you cannot attend, please send another member from your Group.

SANDAG CEO, Mario Orso Report:
-Mario Orso reported that LAFCO would be conducting a review of SANDAG as a Metropolitan Planning Organization for the fiscal years 2024-2025.
-Everett Townsend, current Caltrans Rep at SANDAG, announced that Ann Fox would be returning as the new District 11 Director. She will be the Caltrans Representative at the SANDAG Board of Directors.

Border Environmental Task Force Report:
This is a new task force forming to address regional issues in the geographical zone of the Pacific Ocean to the Arizona border and 10 miles both south and north of the border with Mexico. "The Task force will be comprised of representation from federal, state and local jurisdictions within the border region and sector advisors with interests involved in climate adaptation, environmental health, and environmental justice issues. SANDAG may solicit interest from other entities in participating in the Task
force based on project needs.
Taskforce member agencies are asked to designate an alternate representative when the primary
representative is unable to attend to promote participation in meetings." The task force will be one location for all work occurring in this area. Identification of gaps in serving the area and binational coordination will be strengthened. The meetings will be held remotely (virtually) and the APG has requested membership on this new task force. For any Community Planning/Sponsor Groups in this area who wish to be on the task force, please contact kim.smith@sandag.org

Otay Mesa East and SR 11 Report:
More material will be transported to the US side of the port in order to match the elevation of the facility/road on the Mexican side. There is a plan to open SR 11 to local traffic in the near future. The flow of revenues from the completed project are delineated in this attachment: https://legistarweb-production.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/attachment/pdf/2988061/Item_11__Att._1_-_Memorandum_from_PFM__SANDAG_Financial_Advisor.pdf

Jack Fisher, City of Imperial Beach comment: The third largest port in the world -70 miles south of Ensenada is being constructed. Traffic coming through commercial ports of entry will increase. We need part of the toll to fix problems. We need to fix this now for our kids' future. The Border Region needs to fix the problem.

Transnet Major Corridors Update for North Coast Corridor and SR 78 Corridor:
Victor Mercado, Caltrans - reported $1.06 billion from Federal, State and Transnet funds for the region broken into highway improvements, rail improvements and lagoon, bike, pedestrian improvements. This money funds active transportation improvements for the north coast corridor.

APG comment to Board: Good morning. I won't be as polished as I'd hoped to be. Being in the rural area and seeing these wonderful coastal projects, 78 really does need help at both ends. There's a big need there. But when I see additional bike trails, pedestrian trails; this is a very bedecked out plan and it's beautiful and it's wonderful, but if we're going to truly be regional in how we reach out and spend the tax dollars; we're leaving the unincorporated area in the dirt: literally. It's geographically isolated, car dependent - it continues to be. You cannot walk anywhere, especially on anything other than dirt or on the side of a highway. And, this has been the situation for so long and I would like to see this regional agency truly think about, okay, we have some healthy transportation alternatives in parts of the region, but in the other regions there are none. I mean there's nothing. I cannot walk to my neighbor's house. I must drive. And, this has been the situation for years and Transnet is paid by everyone since 1988. What is the percentage that has been spent by the folks in the unincorporated region? Is that funding amount broken out anywhere? Is that even available? And, if you were to break it out by population, maybe it would be that we have received our fair share of the money. But maybe not. There's a lack of information and it's important that it be transparent, so that people know, gee, you know, this is really wonderful. Let's keep improving the north coast there and give them more because the people out in the unincorporated area have already gotten their share. That would go a long way to developing trust and transparency. But, we don't know that. That's an unknown piece of information. And, so, I'm a glass half-full person and I love seeing these projects. And, I have my mountain bike and I love to walk. But I have to put everything in my car and go find a park to go do this. There is not a kid in the neighborhood who can hop on their bike or walk. That's the life of being out in a rural area. The Youth Opportunity Pass, wonderful program. Nobody can use it. You know very few unincorporated communities have that advantage. We're going to have microtransit. Another great option. Can't use it. So, you know, I want to be here and to be excited and to rah-rah because these are great programs, but we need to spread it out a bit more. To share these programs, make this happen, not just talk about it, but actually have some real programs in place that operate for people that are outside of the coastal and I-5 and I-15 corridors. We need to really move this to the unincorporated area too and include our neighbors. Thank you.

Terry Gaasterland, City of Del Mar comment: ...So, I'm a big biker. My e-bike and I get along really well. And I use it nearly everyday to get to the UCSD campus from Del Mar. And, I take it to Trader Joe's, which is out SR 56 on that new bike trail. And, I go north to Solana Beach and beyond. Because the trails underneath San Elijo Lagoon are just absolutely - under the highway there are fantastic.....And, I will bring one last - the SR 56 bike trail.  There's a new little piece that's just been put in right at the old Carmel Valley Road connecting in....But I'll point out that Sorrento Valley Road is a big part of that bike path. It has the biggest potholes. It's pretty awful. And I don't know who's maintaining it, but it's certainly not being attended to.  So I hope that as this new piece is finished, perhaps Sorrento Valley Road can be improved as well.

John Minto, City of Santee comment: Thank you for the opportunity to speak. I wasn't going to speak on this at all, but I'm listening to a lot of stuff and you know what? All these projects are great. If you live in east county everyone's going to say, no, we need to come out to east county and do ours first. If you live in north county you say, oh no, don't come up to east county - come up to north county. And, vice versa. All the way around the city. Bottom line, all extremely important to get done. And, get it done before sooner than later. I do have to be a little bit flippant, and I apologize ahead of time. Maybe not. About the bicycle lane thing. You know, you talk um, Terry you know you talked about avid bicycling and e-bike and if you know - with the exception of east county at the 52 there is only one protected bicycle lane in all of east county. And, that's so you can make sure to get out of east county. Why they did that? I do not know. And, that goes into Tierra Santa. I average about 30, 40 sometimes 50 miles on my bike, e-bike. And I go through La Mesa, San Diego, Lemon Grove. All the way out to Spring Valley, Dehesa. All the way into Alpine. And you know what? I still haven't seen any protected bike lanes. The only protection I get is when I say my prayer before I get on the bike and say, please don't let a car hit me because they are only a few feet away. Because even where there is a bicycle lane, most of the time they kind of faked a bicycle lane because there wasn't enough room. So where you normally have, I think it's an average four foot bicycle lane, I think we're lucky to get a two foot bicycle lane and many of those are along the seams of the roadway. And just talking to Mayor Jones and you know what? When cities do their slurries or road repairs. They go up to the bike lane and stop. So there's always potholes and there's always breaks along the seams and things of that nature. So nobody really cares in east county if you have a good bike lane. That's just my opinion. And, it goes back to what Robin said earlier about maybe if we're going to talk about equity, equity should be looking at safety more than anything else. Because I don't care who you are and you're riding on a bike lane or a lack of bike lane in those areas; you know what? Where's the equity and safety? And maybe a new term we ought to bring up in safety is not just VMT, but EBMT, electric bike miles traveled. And how safe are you on those EBMT's? That's all I have to say.

Chief Executive Officer Performance Evaluation Process:
On December 6th and 13th all SANDAG Board members are invited to participate in developing performance goals for the CEO position.

APG News:
Congressman Darrell Issa - representing the majority of the unincorporated area in San Diego County - has not set a meeting date with the APG as of this report. Since July, the APG has been working to set up a joint meeting with the Congressman, SANDAG CEO Mario Orso and our APG members without success. SANDAG CEO Mario Orso has stated he will be available and happy to attend our joint meeting. Congressman Issa has not been available and very little communication has come from his office. The APG sent a request to his Chief of Staff, Veronica Smith Wong. She has responded, but not with a set date, yet.
The subject of the meeting will be:
"Transportation funding and safety in the Unincorporated Area; addressing fatality rate on rural highways, safe wildfire evacuation, lack of public transportation resulting in geographic isolation of vulnerable populations and continued diversion of transportation funds from rural highway projects."

Planning/Sponsor Groups that wish to support the establishment of this joint meeting with Congressman Issa may also communicate directly with Veronica Smith Wong: veronica.smith@mail.house.gov

Questions from APG members
No questions received this month.

Original SANDAG documents and meeting minutes are available directly from SANDAG's Board of Directors website: https://www.sandag.org/meetings-and-events/board-of-directors

Report Submitted by:
Robin Joy Maxson, Representative to SANDAG
Association of Planning Groups - San Diego County

With regards to a requested meeting with Congressman Issa, as you may be aware, he invited and hosted a meeting with local officials to discuss transportation, etc. APG was not included.

It has been brought to his staff’s attention that the APG represents thousands of Issa’s constituents in the unincorporated areas and we were not represented /invited to the meeting.

Robin and I have sent multiple communications to his staff requesting a meeting so that the Congressman can hear the concerns and suggestions of those living in the unincorporated areas.

Robin has done an excellent job of continuing to request this meeting. However it still appears to be of little concern to them to rectify the situation. (my opinion)

As Robin suggested in her report, our Planning /Sponsor Groups should all send a letter/email to Veronica Smith Wong (veronica.smith@mail.house.gov ) at Congressman Issa’s office requesting this meeting with him.

It shouldn’t be this difficult for the APG, that/who represents over 500,000 residents to get an audience with our elected Congressman.

Best regards,

Eileen Delaney, Chair

> from 10:00am to noon at the Lakeside Library. As always, if you cannot
> attend, please send another member from your Group.
>
> *SANDAG CEO, Mario Orso Report:*
> -Mario Orso reported that LAFCO would be conducting a review of SANDAG as
> a Metropolitan Planning Organization for the fiscal years 2024-2025.
> -Everett Townsend, current Caltrans Rep at SANDAG, announced that Ann Fox
> would be returning as the new District 11 Director. She will be the
> Caltrans Representative at the SANDAG Board of Directors.
>
> *Border Environmental Task Force Report:*
> This is a new task force forming to address regional issues in the
> geographical zone of the Pacific Ocean to the Arizona border and 10 miles
> both south and north of the border with Mexico. "The Task force will be
> comprised of representation from federal, state and local jurisdictions
> within the border region and sector advisors with interests involved in
> climate adaptation, environmental health, and environmental justice issues.
> SANDAG may solicit interest from other entities in participating in the
> Task force based on project needs. Taskforce member agencies are asked to
> designate an alternate representative when the primary representative is
> unable to attend to promote participation in meetings." The task force will
> be one location for all work occurring in this area. Identification of gaps
> in serving the area and binational coordination will be strengthened. The
> meetings will be held remotely (virtually) and the APG has requested
> membership on this new task force. For any Community Planning/Sponsor
> Groups in this area who wish to be on the task force, please contact
> kim.smith@sandag.org
>
> *Otay Mesa East and SR 11 Report:*
> More material will be transported to the US side of the port in order to
> match the elevation of the facility/road on the Mexican side. There is a
> plan to open SR 11 to local traffic in the near future. The flow of
> revenues from the completed project are delineated in this attachment:
> https://legistarweb-production.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/attachment/pdf/2988061/Item_11__Att._1_-_Memorandum_from_PFM__SANDAG_Financial_Advisor.pdf
>
> Jack Fisher, City of Imperial Beach comment: The third largest port in the
> world -70 miles south of Ensenada is being constructed. Traffic coming
> through commercial ports of entry will increase. We need part of the toll
> to fix problems. We need to fix this now for our kids' future. The Border
> Region needs to fix the problem.
>
> *Transnet Major Corridors Update for North Coast Corridor and SR 78
> Corridor:*
> Victor Mercado, Caltrans - reported $1.06 billion from Federal, State and
> Transnet funds for the region broken into highway improvements, rail
> improvements and lagoon, bike, pedestrian improvements. This money funds
> active transportation improvements for the north coast corridor.
>
> APG comment to Board: Good morning. I won't be as polished as I'd hoped to
> be. Being in the rural area and seeing these wonderful coastal projects, 78
> really does need help at both ends. There's a big need there. But when I
> see additional bike trails, pedestrian trails; this is a very bedecked out
> plan and it's beautiful and it's wonderful, but if we're going to truly be
> regional in how we reach out and spend the tax dollars; we're leaving the
> unincorporated area in the dirt: literally. It's geographically isolated,
> car dependent - it continues to be. You cannot walk anywhere, especially on
> anything other than dirt or on the side of a highway. And, this has been
> the situation for so long and I would like to see this regional agency
> truly think about, okay, we have some healthy transportation alternatives
> in parts of the region, but in the other regions there are none. I mean
> there's nothing. I cannot walk to my neighbor's house. I must drive. And,
> this has been the situation for years and Transnet is paid by everyone
> since 1988. What is the percentage that has been spent by the folks in the
> unincorporated region? Is that funding amount broken out anywhere? Is that
> even available? And, if you were to break it out by population, maybe it
> would be that we have received our fair share of the money. But maybe not.
> There's a lack of information and it's important that it be transparent, so
> that people know, gee, you know, this is really wonderful. Let's keep
> improving the north coast there and give them more because the people out
> in the unincorporated area have already gotten their share. That would go a
> long way to developing trust and transparency. But, we don't know that.
> That's an unknown piece of information. And, so, I'm a glass half-full
> person and I love seeing these projects. And, I have my mountain bike and I
> love to walk. But I have to put everything in my car and go find a park to
> go do this. There is not a kid in the neighborhood who can hop on their
> bike or walk. That's the life of being out in a rural area. The Youth
> Opportunity Pass, wonderful program. Nobody can use it. You know very few
> unincorporated communities have that advantage. We're going to have
> microtransit. Another great option. Can't use it. So, you know, I want to
> be here and to be excited and to rah-rah because these are great programs,
> but we need to spread it out a bit more. To share these programs, make this
> happen, not just talk about it, but actually have some real programs in
> place that operate for people that are outside of the coastal and I-5 and
> I-15 corridors. We need to really move this to the unincorporated area too
> and include our neighbors. Thank you.
>
> Terry Gaasterland, City of Del Mar comment: ...So, I'm a big biker. My
> e-bike and I get along really well. And I use it nearly everyday to get to
> the UCSD campus from Del Mar. And, I take it to Trader Joe's, which is out
> SR 56 on that new bike trail. And, I go north to Solana Beach and beyond.
> Because the trails underneath San Elijo Lagoon are just absolutely - under
> the highway there are fantastic.....And, I will bring one last - the SR 56
> bike trail.  There's a new little piece that's just been put in right at
> the old Carmel Valley Road connecting in....But I'll point out that
> Sorrento Valley Road is a big part of that bike path. It has the biggest
> potholes. It's pretty awful. And I don't know who's maintaining it, but
> it's certainly not being attended to.  So I hope that as this new piece is
> finished, perhaps Sorrento Valley Road can be improved as well.
>
> John Minto, City of Santee comment: Thank you for the opportunity to
> speak. I wasn't going to speak on this at all, but I'm listening to a lot
> of stuff and you know what? All these projects are great. If you live in
> east county everyone's going to say, no, we need to come out to east county
> and do ours first. If you live in north county you say, oh no, don't come
> up to east county - come up to north county. And, vice versa. All the way
> around the city. Bottom line, all extremely important to get done. And, get
> it done before sooner than later. I do have to be a little bit flippant,
> and I apologize ahead of time. Maybe not. About the bicycle lane thing. You
> know, you talk um, Terry you know you talked about avid bicycling and
> e-bike and if you know - with the exception of east county at the 52 there
> is only one protected bicycle lane in all of east county. And, that's so
> you can make sure to get out of east county. Why they did that? I do not
> know. And, that goes into Tierra Santa. I average about 30, 40 sometimes 50
> miles on my bike, e-bike. And I go through La Mesa, San Diego, Lemon Grove.
> All the way out to Spring Valley, Dehesa. All the way into Alpine. And you
> know what? I still haven't seen any protected bike lanes. The only
> protection I get is when I say my prayer before I get on the bike and say,
> please don't let a car hit me because they are only a few feet away.
> Because even where there is a bicycle lane, most of the time they kind
> of faked a bicycle lane because there wasn't enough room. So where you
> normally have, I think it's an average four foot bicycle lane, I think
> we're lucky to get a two foot bicycle lane and many of those are along the
> seams of the roadway. And just talking to Mayor Jones and you know what?
> When cities do their slurries or road repairs. They go up to the bike lane
> and stop. So there's always potholes and there's always breaks along the
> seams and things of that nature. So nobody really cares in east county if
> you have a good bike lane. That's just my opinion. And, it goes back to
> what Robin said earlier about maybe if we're going to talk about equity,
> equity should be looking at safety more than anything else. Because I don't
> care who you are and you're riding on a bike lane or a lack of bike lane in
> those areas; you know what? Where's the equity and safety? And maybe a new
> term we ought to bring up in safety is not just VMT, but EBMT, electric
> bike miles traveled. And how safe are you on those EBMT's? That's all I
> have to say.
>
> *Chief Executive Officer Performance Evaluation Process:*
> On December 6th and 13th all SANDAG Board members are invited to
> participate in developing performance goals for the CEO position.
>
> *APG News:*
> Congressman Darrell Issa - representing the majority of the unincorporated
> area in San Diego County - has not set a meeting date with the APG as of
> this report. Since July, the APG has been working to set up a joint meeting
> with the Congressman, SANDAG CEO Mario Orso and our APG members without
> success. SANDAG CEO Mario Orso has stated he will be available and happy to
> attend our joint meeting. Congressman Issa has not been available and very
> little communication has come from his office. The APG sent a request to
> his Chief of Staff, Veronica Smith Wong. She has responded, but not with a
> set date, yet.
> The subject of the meeting will be:
> "Transportation funding and safety in the Unincorporated Area; addressing
> fatality rate on rural highways, safe wildfire evacuation, lack of public
> transportation resulting in geographic isolation of vulnerable populations
> and continued diversion of transportation funds from rural highway
> projects."
>
> Planning/Sponsor Groups that wish to support the establishment of this
> joint meeting with Congressman Issa may also communicate directly with
> Veronica Smith Wong: veronica.smith@mail.house.gov
>
> *Questions from APG members*
> *No questions received this month.*
>
> Original SANDAG documents and meeting minutes are available directly from
> SANDAG's Board of Directors website:
> https://www.sandag.org/meetings-and-events/board-of-directors
>
> Report Submitted by:
> Robin Joy Maxson, Representative to SANDAG
> Association of Planning Groups - San Diego County
>
