Carl DeMaio Wins Endorsement of Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association PAC

“Carl DeMaio is an outstanding tax fighter and government reformer with a national reputation for getting results for taxpayers.” — Jon Coupal, President of HJTA

The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (HJTA) PAC has officially endorsed Carl DeMaio for State Assembly — highlighting DeMaio’s years of fighting state and local tax hikes and delivering wins for Californian’s’ wallets.

HJTA was formed by tax crusader Howard Jarvis after the passage of California’s landmark Proposition 13 in 1978. With the stated mission to protect Prop 13 and fight for lower taxes in the state, HJTA and DeMaio have frequently teamed up on like-minded tax-fighting efforts — such as the Gas Tax Repeal Initiative in 2018 and the current campaign to pass the California Taxpayer Protection Initiative in 2024.

Jon Coupal, president of HJTA, praised DeMaio for his decades of fiscal responsibility and saving taxpayers money, stating that “Carl DeMaio has been a consistent and powerful voice for California taxpayers as well as a reliable ally of Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. With California on the brink of a fiscal crisis, we’re excited to see Carl DeMaio’s voice coming into the state legislature.”

Carl DeMaio thanked the HJTA PAC for their support.

"I’m very glad to have the endorsement of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association PAC and I look forward to advancing reforms in the State Assembly to eliminate wasteful spending and reduce the burden on taxpayers with their help.”

For more information about the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association PAC, visit HJTA.org<https://cmi.capitolmedia.co/te/cl/eyJ2Ijoie1wiYVwiOjM2ODYyOSxcImxcIjoxMTEyNzM2NzY1NjU5MDczMDQsXCJyXCI6MTExMjczNjc3OTMwMTA0MjMyfSIsInMiOiJkNjAzNzRhMDYxNGY1ZTMyIn0>

title: Carl DeMaio Proposes Contract to Reform CA.eml
subject: Carl DeMaio Proposes Contract to Reform CA
body:
Just wanted you to see that Carl DeMaio is proposing a Contract to Reform California. Would love your feedback on the 10 points being proposed.

[https://storage.mlcdn.com/account_image/368629/msfpMWxCgs3mpXLi6LYLEmyLC3jTdKCJCHIUgU9Z.png]

For Immediate Release

November 25, 2024

Contact: Dylan Martin<mailto:dylan@capitolmedia.co>

760-710-7599

Assemblymember-elect Carl DeMaio Unveils 10-Point “Contract to Reform California”

“The 2024 election shows California voters are hungry for change, but to satisfy that demand, California Republicans must unite and commit to a comprehensive and common-sense reform package to fix the problems causing so many to flee our state.”

Taking a page from the successful “Contract with America” thirty years ago, incoming California State Assemblymember Carl DeMaio today unveiled a Contract to Reform California — a 10-point agenda that offers bold proposals to fix the state’s pressing problems. On December 2, 2024 — his first day in office — DeMaio plans to introduce 10 legislative proposals to advance the agenda.

“Exactly 30 years ago, the Contract with America catapulted Republicans from what was thought to be a permanent minority to a governing majority in the US Congress and ushered in an era of common-sense reform on national issues.

The 2024 election shows California voters are hungry for change, but to satisfy that demand, California Republicans must unite and commit to a comprehensive and common-sense reform package to fix the problems causing so many to flee our state.

The Contract to Reform California is a pledge to enact specific and detailed legislation to address the biggest problems facing our state — including reducing cost of living, reforming schools, balancing the budget, combatting crime, securing the border, reducing homelessness, restoring election integrity, and holding state politicians accountable.

If our Democratic colleagues won’t join us in advancing these reforms over the next two years, then we should be prepared to present our Contract to Reform California directly to the voters in the 2026 election.” – Carl DeMaio

DeMaio is available for further comment and interviews on the Contract to Reform California by phone, zoom or in-person.

ABOUT THE PROPOSAL:

[https://storage.mlcdn.com/account_image/368629/msfpMWxCgs3mpXLi6LYLEmyLC3jTdKCJCHIUgU9Z.png]

CONTRACT TO REFORM CALIFORNIA

ContractToReformCA.org<https://cmi.capitolmedia.co/tb/cl/eyJ2Ijoie1wiYVwiOjM2ODYyOSxcImxcIjoxMzg5OTU3ODI1Nzk2NTI0OTQsXCJyXCI6MTM4OTk1Nzk0NDA3NTg4OTAyfSIsInMiOiJiMzdmZDY4YjcxODgwMWI1In0>

1: Cost-of-Living Reduction Act

California’s cost-of-living crisis was caused by insane regulations and high taxes imposed by our price-gouging politicians. This law would provide each middle-class family with $2,500 in cost-of-living relief rebates annually — as well as suspend all state taxes and fees on gas and utilities until politicians reform state policies that spike costs. Once this model is proven successful in driving down energy and utility costs, it would be expanded to reduce costs in home insurance, housing, and healthcare. If we want politicians to address the cost crisis, we have to force them to pay the price — not our families!

2: Taxpayer Protection Act

This measure limits the ability of politicians to raise taxes — and prohibits them from imposing a new Mileage Tax, Exit Tax, or Wealth Tax — or increasing Gas or Car Taxes. The measure also restores a two-thirds vote requirement on local special tax increases and requires honest ballot titles with a “Tax Increase” warning be placed on any ballot measure that increases taxes.

3: Balanced Budget Accountability Act

We must balance the budget without tax hikes and cuts in important services. This measure would lead to a responsible consensus by requiring a two-thirds vote of both houses of the Legislature to pass the budget — or impose or increase taxes or fees. The measure would also reduce expense by cutting then capping total annual labor costs and imposing competitive sourcing reforms on all state agencies.

4: Education Choice and Parental Empowerment Act

The only way to truly empower parents is to give them financial freedom to choose the best school for their child. This law would provide $13,000 annually in education vouchers for every student — starting with middle-class and low-income families and then expanding the program.

5: Homelessness Reduction Act

This law would end the corrupt and wasteful “Housing First” homeless model currently used and replace it with a “People First” model, which will redirect funds to programs that require mental health and substance abuse treatment to address the root causes of homelessness. The law would also prioritize expansion of shelter beds over permanent supportive housing, impose work requirements on individuals receiving assistance, and require the removal of homeless camps near schools and in public areas. Developers that give campaign contributions would be barred from receiving funds.

6: End Reckless Release of Criminals Act

Passage of Prop 36 was just the first step in combatting the rising crime wave in California — we must also end “reckless release” of criminals across our state. This law would prohibit the early release of violent criminal and repeat offenders by repealing provisions of Prop 57 and prohibiting the placement of Sexually Violent Predators (SVPs) in residential communities. The law would also require mental health evaluations and referrals to proper treatment in any release decisions.

7: California Secure Borders Act

This law combats illegal immigration and helps secure the border by repealing the Sanctuary State law (SB 54 -2017) and ending taxpayer-funded handouts to illegal immigrants for welfare, healthcare, housing, travel, and other services. The law also provides for cross-deputization training of local law enforcement to support federal border security actions and provides standards for deployment of the national guard to the border.

8: Voter ID and Election Integrity Act

The biggest threat to democracy is the loss of confidence in the integrity of our elections. Starting with the 2026 election, this law requires a government-issued ID to vote, strengthens citizenship verification of voter registrations, requires audits of voter lists to ensure they are properly maintained, imposes penalties on counties that fail to count ballots on time, and enhances signature reviews on ballots.

9: Punish Unconstitutional Actions Act

California politicians have developed a bad habit of repeatedly imposing laws and orders that are blatantly unconstitutional — just to score political points while depriving citizens of their rights and forcing them to bear the upfront legal costs to regain them. This law would penalize the Governor who signs and any legislator who votes for a law that is later found to be unconstitutional in federal courts with a 25% cut in their annual state compensation for each offense.

10: Cut the Politicians’ Perks Act

California politicians have granted themselves lavish perks and exemptions from state laws they impose on regular citizens. This law would ban politicians from accepting gifts or trading in individual stocks; impose a lifetime lobbying ban; eliminate exemptions for the Legislature from labor, workplace, and public record laws; and eliminate pensions for local elected officials.

Contract to Reform California - By the Numbers:

  *   $2,500: Annual cost-of-living relief rebates
  *   $13,000: Annual education vouchers for each child
  *   2/3rds: Vote requirement for approving the state budget
  *   5%: Immediate labor cost reduction in state budget
  *   25%: Cut in pay for politicians who impose unconstitutional laws or mandates
  *   $0: A ban on gifts for politicians, and end to handouts to illegal immigrants

ContractToReformCA.org<https://cmi.capitolmedia.co/tb/cl/eyJ2Ijoie1wiYVwiOjM2ODYyOSxcImxcIjoxMzg5OTU3ODI1ODM4NDY4MDAsXCJyXCI6MTM4OTk1Nzk0NDA3NTg4OTAyfSIsInMiOiIyMzU0NTlkNDRjOTkxN2IyIn0>

On December 2, 2024, Carl DeMaio will be sworn in as a new member of the California State Assembly – District 75. DeMaio is also Chairman of Reform California – one of the largest grassroots political organizations in the state. The 75th District includes the communities of Fallbrook, Bonsall, Valley Center, Ramona, Poway, Scripps Ranch, Santee, Lakeside, Alpine, Julian, Borrego Springs, Pala, Jamul, Pine Valley, Pauma Valley, and Bonita.

More information: CarlDeMaio.com<https://cmi.capitolmedia.co/tb/cl/eyJ2Ijoie1wiYVwiOjM2ODYyOSxcImxcIjoxMzg5OTU3ODI1ODY5OTI1MzEsXCJyXCI6MTM4OTk1Nzk0NDA3NTg4OTAyfSIsInMiOiI5NWI2Y2JlOTFiYmI1NTRlIn0> or ReformCalifornia.org<https://cmi.capitolmedia.co/tb/cl/eyJ2Ijoie1wiYVwiOjM2ODYyOSxcImxcIjoxMzg5OTU3ODI1OTIyMzU0MTMsXCJyXCI6MTM4OTk1Nzk0NDA3NTg4OTAyfSIsInMiOiIxNjNiZjQxNmEwZGRhODU0In0>

[County of San Diego]
There is still time to apply for the first phase of the Cannabis Social Equity Program! 

This application period closes on August 23rd at 11:59 pm. There will be opportunities to apply for future application periods. The next one will open in late 2024. 

The application<https://equity.projectcannabis.org/> will help determine if you meet the program’s eligibility requirements. All applicants who meet the requirements will be contacted by the County.

Those who qualify will receive various benefits.  These include expungement assistance, and one-on-one mentoring, training – workshops, webinars, and classes to help program participants prepare for the opportunity to open a cannabis business in the unincorporated area of the county. 

This application cycle also includes a grant lottery.  Ten awardees will be selected on September 18th.  Additional future grant opportunities may be available depending on funding. 

Currently, new cannabis licensing is not permitted in the unincorporated county but is estimated to begin in Winter 2025.

To review the eligibility criteria and apply please visit:
Cannabis Equity Eligibility Application (projectcannabis.org)<https://equity.projectcannabis.org/>

This application period closes on August 23rd at 11:59 pm. There will be opportunities to apply for future application periods. The next one will open in late 2024. 

The application<https://equity.projectcannabis.org/> will help determine if you meet the program’s eligibility requirements. All applicants who meet the requirements will be contacted by the County.

Those who qualify will receive various benefits.  These include expungement assistance, and one-on-one mentoring, training – workshops, webinars, and classes to help program participants prepare for the opportunity to open a cannabis business in the unincorporated area of the county. 

This application cycle also includes a grant lottery.  Ten awardees will be selected on September 18th.  Additional future grant opportunities may be available depending on funding. 

Currently, new cannabis licensing is not permitted in the unincorporated county but is estimated to begin in Winter 2025.

To review the eligibility criteria and apply please visit:
Cannabis Equity Eligibility Application (projectcannabis.org)<https://equity.projectcannabis.org/>

More Program Information
Stay informed by visiting the Engage San Diego Socially Equitable Cannabis Program Hub<https://engage.sandiegocounty.gov/hub-page/cannabis-program>.

Questions
Have questions about the program?
For questions about the Social Equity Program, contact Brandon Lewis, Social Equity Manager, at brandon.lewis@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:brandon.lewis@sdcounty.ca.gov>. 

For questions about the County’s Cannabis Licensing, Enforcement, Ordinances and Environmental Impact Report contact pds.longrangeplanning@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:pds.longrangeplanning@sdcounty.ca.gov>.

Informational Sessions
Future informational sessions for the Cannabis Social Equity Program will be held in-person. Click here for more details, request language services, and let us know if you plan to attend.

  *   August 22nd at Spring Valley Community Center, 8735 Jamacha Blvd, Spring Valley, 91977 - 6pm

  *   October 24th at Jaxx Cannabis (Ramona), 1210 Olive St, Ramona, 92065 - TBD

[County of San Diego]

Cannabis Social Equity Program Notice

Upcoming Board Hearing: Update on Cannabis Social Equity Program, Cannabis Social Equity Eligibility Criteria, Cannabis Social Equity Related Ordinances, Cannabis Oversight Community Collaborative

Dear Interested Stakeholder,

The Board of Supervisors of the County of San Diego will conduct a public hearing on the Cannabis Social Equity Program.

 The hearing information is as follows:

Date:  Tuesday, March 12, 2024

Time: 9:00 a.m.

Location: County Administration Center, 1600 Pacific Highway, Room 310, San Diego, California 92101

Public Participation

Those wishing to participate in the meeting and/or comment should visit the Clerk of the Board website at https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/sdc/cob/bosa.html<https://lnks.gd/l/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJidWxsZXRpbl9saW5rX2lkIjoxMDAsInVyaSI6ImJwMjpjbGljayIsInVybCI6Imh0dHBzOi8vd3d3LnNhbmRpZWdvY291bnR5Lmdvdi9jb250ZW50L3NkYy9jb2IvYm9zYS5odG1sIiwiYnVsbGV0aW5faWQiOiIyMDI0MDExOC44ODc4ODY2MSJ9.YUQ9J8lNHI3XjodiVQV1b7TiEsOnyrQyomHj_jB8r4w/s/2974027410/br/235646667840-l>. If you have any questions, please contact please contact the Board Operations Unit at (619) 531-5434 or via email to publiccomment@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:publiccomment@sdcounty.ca.gov>.

Project Background

On January 27, 2021 (4), the Board of Supervisors (Board) directed staff to implement measures to provide economic access and equity in the cannabis industry. These measures included components of a Social Equity Program (SEP), Zoning Ordinance amendments, and a licensing/permitting system. The Board further directed that grant funding be secured to support implementation of the SEP, which would include numerous elements to prioritize equity, access, and business opportunities to help rectify the injustices caused by the War on Drugs and be in place prior to issuance of the first cannabis business license.

Further, on March 3, 2021 (11), the Board directed the Office of Equity and Racial Justice (OERJ) to lead the development of the framework and strategy, including grant funding options, needed to initiate a SEP and coordinate this with the land use permitting system being developed by Planning & Development Services (PDS).

The goal of the SEP is to ensure that those negatively or adversely impacted by cannabis criminalization are provided with the opportunity to successfully participate in the regulated cannabis market and for people and communities impacted by the War on Drugs to receive assistance and benefits. This assistance and benefits will be vital to the success of these future entrepreneurs and beneficiaries. OERJ will continue to work with PDS on ensuring social equity is a priority for all programming related to cannabis.

These actions provide an update on the coordinated development of the Cannabis Social Equity Program focusing on and development of the SEP components of the Social Equity Entrepreneurs Program and the Social Equity Beneficiaries Program. The recommendations include receiving an update on the program, providing policy direction on the social equity eligibility criteria, and the SEP related ordinance components, as well as approving the structure of the program’s oversight body.

title: Cannabis Social Equity Program Application - County of San Diego.eml
subject: Cannabis Social Equity Program Application - County of San Diego
body:
Dear Stakeholder,

The County of San Diego's Cannabis Social Equity Program application is now live.  Please visit Cannabis Equity Eligibility Application (projectcannabis.org)<https://equity.projectcannabis.org/>.
To be eligible, an equity applicant must be at least 21 years of age at the time of application and meet criteria for Tier A OR criteria for Tier B.
Tier A
Incarcerated for San Diego County arrest or conviction for any crime under the laws of the State of California or United States related to the sale, possession, use, manufacture, or cultivation of Cannabis that occurred prior to November 8, 2016.
Tier B
Deported, Arrested, or Convicted: In San Diego County for any crime under the laws of the State of California or United States related to the sale, possession, use, manufacture, or cultivation of cannabis that occurred prior to November 8, 2016, AND
Low Income- 80% or below of the Area Median Income (San Diego County) determined by US Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD).

Translation services are available on the online application or if you need additional interpretation services, please contact Brandon Lewis in your preferred language at brandon.lewis@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:brandon.lewis@sdcounty.ca.gov>.

More information regarding the Cannabis Social Equity Program and the County's overarching Socially Equitable Cannabis Program can be found on the County's Socially Equitable Cannabis Program website<https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/sdc/pds/Cannabis.html> or on County's Engage San Diego website<https://engage.sandiegocounty.gov/hub-page/cannabis-program>.

If you have any additional questions, please reach out.

Please help us spread the word - share this message with your friends, family, and colleagues!

Thank you,

Brandon Lewis

body:
[County Logo Banner]

Cannabis Licensing Outreach Recap and Draft EIR Guidance Virtual Meetings

Dear Interested Stakeholder,

The County of San Diego Planning & Development Services (PDS) invites you to attend our upcoming virtual public meetings for the Cannabis Program ahead of the release of the Draft Cannabis Environmental Impact Report (EIR). Both meetings will have the same content and format, so you only need to attend one.

At these meetings, staff will:
·       Recap the feedback received during the summer 2024 Licensing and Enforcement outreach meetings
·       Inform stakeholders of the Draft EIR public review timeline and next steps
·       Provide an overview of the Draft EIR public review process
·       Explain how to submit effective comments on the Draft EIR

If you would like interpretation services available at the meeting, please contact Dara Elkurdi in your preferred language at PDS.LongRangePlanning@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:PDS.LongRangePlanning@sdcounty.ca.gov> by October 18, 2024.

title: Building at 2249 Alpine Blvd - Veterinary Clinic.eml
subject: Building at 2249 Alpine Blvd - Veterinary Clinic
body:
Hi Travis.

Hope all is well. I wanted to reach out to you regarding a tenant that we
have that is moving into the space located at 2249 Alpine Blvd (next to the
shell station). Its a veterinary office that submitted plans for a build
out of the vacant space. They submitted their plans to the County, but the
County is saying that the plans need to be reviewed by the Alpine Planning
Group. I wanted to confirm this is correct, since the improvements are only
for the interior of the space (nothign to do with the exterior). Its

body:
﻿Hi All,

This is an urgent request to everyone to review the EIR for the County’s Cannabis Program and send your comments in by the deadline of  March 31, 2025.

Our Planning Group has been delving in to the EIR and Zoning Amendments.  Alternate 2 in the EIR appears to be favored by the County and this is very concerning.

This isn’t about whether we approve or disapprove of Cannabis. This is about what would be the least destructive to our unincorporated towns and about certain parts of the program that if approved by the BOS, could have a very negative impact on our rural way of life.

Our CPG Cannabis Ad-hoc Committee has been in touch with other Cities and Counties throughout the State who have had Cannabis programs for a number of years now. Because the grows, cultivation and other aspects of their Cannabis Programs have had such a negative impact on their residents, they are now amending their programs.  Our County should take a lesson from them.

As mentioned, the County appears to be favoring Alternate 2 in the EIR. This would allow, amongst other things, the outdoor growing of Cannabis. Our Committee’s general opinion is that Alternate 4 would be a better alternative because it only allows indoor grows. If your zoning is like Fallbrook’s, Ag zones (where Cannabis grows would be allowed) are interspersed throughout our town with residential zones. This could conceivably be a nightmare for the enjoyment of the outdoors and our rural way of life.

Alternative 4 also expands what is considered sensitive areas/activities and the distance that any Cannabis business or grows need to be away from.

We also have major concerns about number of grows allowed, lounges, number of retail dispensaries, people that are under the influence driving on our rural roads, etc.

Here is the link to the EIR:
https://engage.sandiegocounty.gov/cannabis-program-eir/guest_bookThe County Cannabis Program Manager, Jessica Norton will be at our CPG meeting this Tuesday February 18.  Our meeting starts at 6:30 pm and is in-person and on Zoom. I invite you to attend either way. You can listen in, ask questions and offer your comments. Then go back to your Group and send in your formal comments as well.

---------- Forwarded message ---------
From: Ron Nehring, Crest Planning Group Chairman <ronnehring@ronnehring.ccsend.com>
Date: Mon, Jan 27, 2025 at 3:26 PM
Subject: PLANNING GROUP: What we have done so far on wildfire
To:  <associationofplanninggroups@gmail.com>

 

Fellow Planning Group Chairs,

Following the interest and feedback I received regarding our new Firewise USA site, I wanted to share additional resources and insights from our work on wildfire preparedness and evacuation in our subregion. I’m also interested in knowing what work your Planning Group has done that perhaps we have not thought of so we can strengthen our efforts.

In 2021, our Planning Group established a dedicated working group on wildfire and evacuation. Over the course of three years, we held meetings and engaged extensively with stakeholders—including our local fire district, Cal Fire, the Crest Fire Safe Council, representatives from the County, the Sheriff’s Department, and others—to identify the most effective ways to reduce wildfire risk and enhance evacuation capacity.

This effort culminated in a comprehensive package of seven wildfire-related resolutions, which our Planning Group unanimously adopted in the summer of 2024. Given our advisory role to the County of San Diego, each resolution is framed as a recommendation to County. You can review the full package of resolutions, along with a summary, here: Crest Planning Group Fire Resolutions.

One key takeaway from our work was the value of the Firewise USA program, which allows groups of at least eight homeowners to establish a Firewise USA site, take steps to reduce wildfire risk, and potentially qualify for homeowners insurance discounts.

Recognizing its benefits, one of our seven resolutions specifically encourages and supports the formation of Firewise USA sites throughout our subregion.

After I became Chairman of our Planning Group, we launched a website to better serve our residents by providing access to essential information. While the County’s webpage for our Planning Group exists, it is difficult to find and lacks comprehensive resources. Our goal was to create a one-stop hub where residents can find details about our Planning Group’s work, wildfire preparedness, code enforcement, defensible space requirements, and more. You can visit the site at: CrestPlanningGroup.com.

At our next Planning Group meeting on Monday, February 10 at 6:30 PM at the Crest Community Association Clubhouse, 113 North Park Drive, El Cajon we will discuss the Firewise USA program and how to establish additional sites in our subregion. I invite you to join us for this discussion—if you or members of your Planning Group plan to attend, please let me know in advance so I can ensure you are introduced. Google maps

We have made progress but we have a very long way to go before the wildfire threat in our subregion has been materially reduced.  To this end, Resolution 1 in our package established wildfire threat reduction as the top priority for our Planning Group.

I think sharing ideas and best practices at, and in between, our APG meetings can help us all in our efforts to improve our communities and make them safer. I hope you find this information useful, and look forward to hearing about the work you've done.

All the best,

Ron Nehring

Chairman, Crest-Dehesa-Granite Hills-Harbison Canyon Planning Group

body:
Hi All,

At the Board of Supervisors meeting on July 17, Sup Desmond is putting forth the recommendations below re Battery Storage Facilities.

We need as many people as possible to attend the meeting, call in or send e-comments in favor.
For instructions go to: https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/sdc/cob/bosa.html

Agenda item 8

RECOMMENDATION(S)
SUPERVISOR JIM DESMOND
1. Find that the proposed actions are not subject to the California Environmental Quality Act
(CEQA) pursuant to SCEQA Guidelines Sections 15060(c)(2) and (3), Section 15061 (b)(3), and 15378(b)(5) because the action is an administrative action that does not commit County to a specific project and will not have a reasonably foreseeable direct or indirect effect on the environment.
2. Direct the Chief Administrative Officer (CAO) to establish development standards for siting battery energy storage system (BESS) projects in the unincorporated areas. This process shall be informed by community, industry, and all other relevant stakeholder input as deemed appropriate. At a minimum, standards should include, but are not limited to the following:
a) Avoid locating BESS projects in residential areas.
b) Avoid locating BESS projects near sensitive receptors, such as schools, day care centers,
senior care centers and hospitals.
c) Incentivize locating BESS projects in commercial and/or industrial zones.
e) Specific safety requirements for thermal runaway, fire and explosion risks, emergency
response, hazardous materials, toxic gases, and noise.
f) Specific development regulations for setbacks, building height, etc.
g) Specific design standards for aesthetics, community character, lighting, and landscaping.
h) Consider exemption criteria based on project location, size, and/or other metrics as deemed appropriate and as consistent with sub-recommendations a - g (above).
Wednesday, July 17, 2024
18
3. Direct the CAO to work with applicants with BESS projects currently under review to align their submittals with today's recommendations, to the extent feasible. The CAO shall also, at the next possible meeting, prepare and bring back an ordinance temporarily (45 days)
pausing any new BESS project application from being accepted, pursuant to Government
Code Section 65858 as an urgency measure to protect public health, safety, and welfare. This pause shall include two additional one-year extensions, each to be executed until BESS
development standards have been adopted development standards have been adopted.
EQUITY IMPACT STATEMENT
Battery energy storage system (BESS) projects may pose significant health, safety, and environmental risks to surrounding communities, especially when located within or near existing residential neighborhoods. These risks range from acute noise nuisances to fire and thermal run-away hazards. To protect and buffer residential areas from these risks, and to ensure historically disadvantaged communities don't bear the brunt moving forward, the County must adopt standards and guidelines for siting future BESS projects that considers their unique operating characteristics, potential health and safety risks, and appropriateness for locating them within close proximity to existing communities and other sensitive receptors.
SUSTAINABILITY IMPACT STATEMENT
While there are many benefits of BESS facilities that contribute to the County's sustainability goals, such as strengthening grid reliability and increasing energy efficiency, there are also several potential adverse consequences. These include fire and thermal runaway risks, managing the limited lite cycle and degradation of batteries over time, and extraction of rare earth minerals that can have devastating environmental and societal consequences (unethical mining practices, etc.). The key here is striking a balance between the pros and cons of these facilities. Adopting rules for how we process and locate BESS projects in the unincorporated areas is a necessary first step.
FISCAL IMPACT
Funds for this request are included in the Fiscal Year (FY) 2024-25 Operational Plan in Planning & Development Services ($1.0 million) and San Diego County Fire ($0.25 million). If approved, this request will result in costs and revenue of approximately $1.25 million to establish development standards for siting battery energy storage system (BESS) projects, depending on the complexity of the environmental review required. The funding source is one-time General-Purpose Revenue. There will be no change in net General Fund cost and no additional staff years.

Thank you! Please forward!

Best regards,

title: Bob Figari starts the SF to LA Arthritis Foundation bike ride in just two weeks _ Help me reach my $15K fundraising goal.eml
subject: Bob Figari starts the SF to LA Arthritis Foundation bike ride in just two weeks / Help me reach my $15K fundraising goal
body:
Dear Friends and Family,

The start of the CCC/Arthritis Foundation ride is less than two weeks away. Many of you have generously helped raise almost $10K for the event. If you haven’t donated, I hope you’ll consider helping meet my goal of $15K.

Here’s the link to my donation page: https://events.arthritis.org/participant/333448

I’ve been training hard. Did a number of 50 mile+ rides in the Sierra near Pinecrest Lake in late August. Lots of altitude, but the weather was in the 70s and most riding was under the shade of pines and cedars. It was actually a wonderful way to ride and I was thrilled to be out of the San Diego heat wave. The photo below is a pano shot from Donnells lookout on Highway 108 about 12 miles before Sonora Pass. That ride was about 70 miles with a total climb of 4500’. Amazing country.

Hit a chuck hole hard on one ride which has required me to get new rims. I didn’t even notice it except for a strange little thump, thump, twang I could hear going downhill. Took my bike into the shop to have the spokes tightened, but it became clear that the rim would never be the same. That’s all spokes! (Just a little bicycle humor)

Also went on a four night backpacking trip with my son, Brennan and his husband, Ante from Croatia. We covered 50 miles exploring lakes in the Emigrant Wilderness just northeast of Yosemite. Most of the time we were backpacking or day hiking at 7000’-9000’ in elevation. Breathtaking beauty. A new lake every 4-5 miles. The second photo below is from the peak just above Rosasco Lake. Our campsite is on the opposite side of the lake in the grove of trees. We encountered 15 lakes and swam in most of them. Cold, but felt so good! The hiking was a good wake-up call for my gluts which have a tendency to doze during long bike rides. I will need them to be fully engaged on the CCC!

Please remember that the ride is really all about raising money for arthritis research. I’m especially inspired by the kids that have to deal with the disease from an early age. Every new step in research increases the odds of finding cures.

Thank you all for being a part of my life. Best wishes to everyone.

Bob

Robert Figari
figari@well.com
415 259-8153

title: Bob Figari completes 2024 Arthritis Foundation cycle from SF to LA!.eml
subject: Bob Figari completes 2024 Arthritis Foundation cycle from SF to LA!
body:
Hello dear friends and family,

My apologies for not writing sooner! I once again did complete the entire ride, all 525 miles from Fisherman’s Wharf in San Francisco to Pepperdine University in Malibu. Most importantly the event was a tremendous financial success. We raised over $1.3M for arthritis research. Also, I am the 7th place fundraiser at $12,875 thanks to all of you! Still under goal of $15K, but there is time.

The fundraising deadline is October 31, so if you haven’t donated and wish to, please go to my online link and do so now:
https://events.arthritis.org/participant/333448￼
2024 California Coast Classic Bike
events.arthritis.org

The trip was a good one for me. I actually felt stronger this year than last year. This probably due to a training change I made to fewer training rides that we longer. I averaged about 150 miles a week with 3 days of riding over 50 miles each day with a maximum of around 2500 feet of climbing. I started off the season with trying to ride every other day with a lot of elevation, but found it wore this old body down too much to sustain for the 6 months of training. The combined strategy really helped. Also, I was really re-energized riding at high altitude in the Sierras in the cool weather and then backpacking for 50 miles over 5 days. It was so stunningly beautiful and gave my legs a good cross training workout..

Our California Coastal Classic (CCC) itself was also energizing. We lucked out again with the weather. The only issue was a headwind on the first day from SF to Santa Cruz. It was a long 88 mile slog into the wind. Pretty overcast the entire trip, but what else is new about the northern California coastline!

The ride through Carmel is always stunning. As always, a highlight was sitting in the Big Sur river on Adirondack chairs at the River Inn. And I love the artichoke food truck at a rest stop before Monterey! Our ride through Foxen Canyon where the movie Sideways was filmed was perfect because the fog stayed in until about 1pm. Normally, the temperature is in the 80s the whole ride, but we got most of it done before the sun came out. The long ride from Buellton to Ventura (80 miles) wasn’t too bad this time for me. And the final ride to Pepperdine instead of Santa Monica eliminated the harrowing Hwy 1 gauntlet through Malibu. I do love seeing “Dan Blocker Beach” signs. Really dating myself but he played Hoss on Bonanza and was my favorite character.

The camp experience was fantastic. Food was even better this year. Met a lot of super people and was totally inspired by those who rode with arthritis. I mentioned in a previous email about our Team San Diego “ambassador” who is in her 20s and suffers from the disease. She rode the whole thing and gave an outstanding speech at one our camp events. Really brought the disease into perspective to hear about her grammar school experiences in trying to diagnose the arthritis. Most of her doctors thought she was just going through growing pains, until finally she was properly diagnosed. She is such a delightful and brave person!

Here’s photo from just north of Santa Cruz at Pleasure Point. Not a great shot, but it is proof that I actually did the ride! And another leaving Monterey (ARR! ARRR! ARR! ) and the Pebble Beach area.
￼￼￼
Heading into Big Sur.￼
And Paso Robles to Cambria ￼
Cayucos and leaving Morro Bay on way to Pismo￼￼
Foxen Canyon on to Buellton￼
Thru Pt Magoo to Pepperdine finish line￼￼

Some of my delay in writing to you can be blamed on the fact we’re in Maui now! It’s my reward. However, I rented a bike and did the West Maui Loop while here, a tough 60 miler with 4500’ of climb, all in the first 25 miles.
Here’s map with elevation showing start/finish at Napili Bay area.￼

This is an amazingly beautiful ride, so I’ve added a couple photos of Nakalele blow hole, road and an “average” sunset from our room on Napili Bay.
￼￼￼

Like I said, I’m well into full recovery!

Thank you all again so much for your generosity. If any of you have questions or want information on participating in next year’s ride, just ask me.

Mahalo and aloha!

Bob

Robert Figari
figari@well.com

title: BATTERY ENERGY STORAGE IN YOUR AREA.eml
subject: BATTERY ENERGY STORAGE IN YOUR AREA
body:
Hello, Chair Lyon,

Please send this e-mail to the other members of your planning group.

I saw an article on MSN that 2 BESS facilities are being proposed in your community like the ones in Escondido, Otay Mesa, and a few others, that caught fire.  Putting a BESS in a wildfire-prone area is not good, and the plan should be rejected.   You know the community best. Please do not give in the legal or other manipulation.

My latest issue with lithium-ion batteries is the danger to all of our normal ways of life:

I wrote a few months ago: “The weather has been noticeably cooler for a few days. You would think that this would help the wildfire control. Yet this morning, the 14th, the three big fires near LA and OC, are still raging virtually uncontained: the Bridge fire at 53K acres, 3% containment; the Airport fire at 23K acres, 9% containment; the Line fire at 38K acres, 25% containment. I think the huge Park fire, which we know was started by an EV, was still burning too.

Temperatures for 9/11 in San Dimas (Bridge fire) got down to the upper 50’s; San Bernardino (Line fire) and Rancho Santa Margarita (Airport fire) got down to the 60’s.

These fires should be on the way out. It is time, maybe past time, to study whether EV’s and battery storage facilites (BESS) are contributing to the fires’ staying power, especially with lithium’s ability to spontaneously combust multiple times.

AND THESE FIRES ARE STILL GOING! Depleting our water, costing money, using firefighter resources and lives.

Also, the EV truck fire on Aug. 19 in Placer County took 50K gallons of water to put out – about 4 times what a family of 4 uses each month. So in a water-poor area, flammable EV’s and battery storage (BESS) do not make sense.

Another thing that really alarms me is that the BESS companies seem to care about economics more than safety. I saw a KGTV 10 news interview on 11/24/2024 whereJason Anderson, the President of Clean Tech San Diego (a non-profit helping to ‘advance’ BESS tech) says that despite all the BESS fires at ‘older tech’ facilities, there are no plans to upgrade or replace them – it would be economically unfeasible (nothing about safety.)

I do not see why these facilities cannot be placed in non-wildfire prone areas like Borrego Springs, Ranchita (I believe) or Ocotillo Wells, or zones like near the Salton Sea, the nearby desert areas (maybe even crossing County lines.)

Another reason to reject BESS placement outside of the coastal zone is that roads in the back-country are not developed enough to handle mass evacuations. Many areas have tiny roads or just one access road which can easily be blocked and trap people and animals. Smaller communities also tend to lack shelter-in-place facilities.

In addition, the insurance cost of homeowners near a BESS facility stands to be canceled or increased in that area, which is fairly discriminatory, especially if you have livestock or agribusiness. Are we all going to have to import our food at a higher price?

Thanks to Jim at the Board of Supervisors for recognizing the need for BESS safety standards. Hope the measure gets re-introduced ASAP, so we can control these fires BEFORE they happen and not waste resources on controlling them after.

Here's what I wrote about BESS earlier:

BESS in a wildfire zone is the silliest idea I’ve heard off for a while. Here are some of my thoughts on this:

Lithium – used in EV batteries – unstable metal – causes spontaneous fires, repeat, spontaneous, you can’t put out, toxic fumes, mass evacuations, oh, and the fire just reignited draining fire department resources. And the response from the Big-BESS-Biz better technology. Isn’t that what they said about the Titanic?

I would recommend an enhancement or judicial recommendation for those who start BESS wildfires, to include those who knowledgeably situate a BESS facility in a high-risk area (including near civilization) with inadequate precautions. This should be an extra year for each death and an extra fine to make up for firefighter time and resources.

The Battery Storage (BESS) fire in Otay Mesa burned for about a week. Firemen were monitoring it even longer instead of being elsewhere, and they evacuated people within a mile.

There are proposals for larger BESS facilities in San Marcos and Poway near a major hospitals, school, and residences, within a few hundred yards in San Marcos and 1/2 mile in Poway. Lithium ion batteries put out toxic fumes like phosphorous pentaflouride and are a huge wildfire hazard and would draw away fire dept resources to monitor fire for weeks.

BoS should designate safe areas for these away from houses, schools, and hospitals and wildfire zones, environmentally sensitive areas or water sources which they would pollute.

I doubt, for instance, that the EPA and all would take it too kindly if the toxics from a BESS fire fell on a national monument after all the years and effort to plan it.

If, as I suspect the moneyed and persuasive BESS guys do get a nearby storage site, the Fire People need to get a supply of "F-500 Encapsulator Agent" to help extinguish BESS lithium fires, which cools the fire and interrupts the chemical reaction involved in the lithium battery combustion.

And for smaller BESS or EV fires, you want a supply of aqueous vermiculite dispersion (AVD) or a foam extinguisher containing powdered graphite or sodium carbonate.
And it might help to put Chickenwire or other mesh over BESS facilities to reduce the danger from floating embers or burning airborne leaves in a wildfire.

Regards,

Paul Henkin

title: Bob Figari 5th annual LA to SF ride for the Arthritis Foundation in September 2024.eml
subject: Bob Figari 5th annual LA to SF ride for the Arthritis Foundation in September 2024
body:
Hello, my dear friends and family!

I’m bicycling again for the fifth year starting September 21 from San Francisco to Los Angeles for the Arthritis Foundation. I am so grateful to all of you who have donated in the past for this event. It’s hard for me to ask you again for money, but this is the way I can help the most. And it is an easy way for you to participate without getting your rear sore! Please pardon the form letter. Often, I hear directly from some of you. I love that as it gives us both a chance to catch up in a more personal way.

For the past three years you have made me a top California Coastal Classic (CCC) fundraiser. The money we raise benefits many of us Boomers, but most importantly it helps the kids and young adults who suffer from arthritis. The CCC has been such a successful fundraising event that the Arthritis Foundation is copying our ride blueprint for similar events throughout the nation. Pretty cool that all of us are associated with such a dynamic, successful and influential philanthropic organization.

A very special thanks to Joel, Danny, Kris and Chris I, who have been incredibly generous in past donations. And to so many of you who have consistently donated for five years, I’m so grateful. You’re awesome!

The Pitch. . .  . ⚾️
Please support me with a tax-deductible donation to the Arthritis Foundation (a 501 (c) (3) charity). I’m donating $3500 from my IRA toward a fundraising goal of $15,000 and I’m hoping you will help me reach that goal.

To make your donation and get information about the ride, use this link to my CCC page:

https://events.arthritis.org/index.cfm?fuseaction=donordrive.participant&participantID=333448   Click on “Support Me” and follow the instructions.

[Special note for those of you who have IRAs that involve a Required Minimum Distribution (RMD):
You can make a charitable donation directly from your IRA to help satisfy the RMD. The donation check must come directly from your IRA and be made out to the Arthritis Foundation. I’ve attached the form to use for sending the check to the Arthritis Foundation. If you make a IRA check donation you have to use this form so that I and my team get credit.]

Trip Details       🚴🏻
For those interested in trip details, we cycle 8 days from September 21 to 28 along country roads and highways 525 miles over 8 days from San Francisco to Los Angeles. We average about 68 miles per day. We’ll travel through Santa Cruz, Monterey and Carmel, Big Sur, Cambria, Morro Bay, Pismo Beach, Foxen Canyon, Los Olivos, Santa Barbara, Ventura and Malibu, ending at Pepperdine University. All but one slide has been repaired along Highway 1, so hopefully we can ride directly from Big Sur to Cambria. If not, we have an alternative route from Los Robles to Cambria in the works.

CCC riders can camp out at specially reserved campsites or stay in hotels along the way. I’m camping again this year except for one lodge stay in Cambria which about half way. I like the fellowship and proximity to the beer and BBQ that the camping option offers! But, I do look forward to a real bed and shower in Cambria!

We are very well fed every morning and evening. SAG wagons follow us in case of either bike breakdowns or body breakdowns. So far, I haven’t had to make use of either. And we have rest stops along the way that are supported by volunteers who create an amazing spread of PBJs, dill pickles, energy drinks and supplements provided by our sponsors, and other delectable delights. Oh, and don’t forget the availability of restrooms!

The toughest day for me is the Day 1 SF to Santa Cruz ride of 88 miles. My legs do okay, but my rear end doesn’t like going past about 60 miles! Don’t feel to sorry for me though . . . we can purchase a 50 minute session at our traveling massage tent. I’m probably their best customer the entire week.

My favorite end of day spot is the Big Sur River Inn. The restaurant there provides fabulous food which you can eat while sitting in Adirondack chairs that have been placed right in the middle of the stream. The sensation of putting tired feet into the cooling waters while munching on a hamburger and drinking a beer is sublime.

Most of the trip is safe from serious traffic, but going through Malibu area on the last day feels like a gauntlet.  There is no bike lane, so we ride in-between the cars parked along the shoulders and weekend traffic racing down the winding coastal road. I wear my brightest cycling outfit and make sure my flashing lights are fully charged!

Family News  🧑‍🧑‍🧒‍🧒🇺🇸🇭🇷
On the family side of things, my wife, Chris and I had a fabulous trip to Helsinki, Norway and Amsterdam in March. Most of our time was spent on a small boat cruise through the Arctic waters north of Tromso, Norway and a Malangen lodge stay on a Norwegian bay. On the cruise we did actual dogsledding with me steering and braking while Chris was hanging on for dear life. We also rafted into hidden fjords, saw leaping sperm whales, hung out with reindeer, did two arctic plunges into the 1 deg C sea and were amazed by the Northern Lights. At Malangen, we did cross country skiing, drank incredible Norwegian gin, ate reindeer and even whale, and topped it off with hot tubbing and saunaing in a blizzard along the lakeshore. Helsinki and Amsterdam were also fabulous including ferrying through the ice filled bays of Helsinki to historic sites and dining with a couple friends at night in a tiny boat along the canals of Amsterdam. Highly recommend it all!

In April/May, we had visitors for a month from Croatia . . . the parents of our son’s husband. All six of us traveled together for two weeks for 4000 miles in my pickup truck to the Grand Canyon, Bryce, Zion, Las Vegas, Sequoia, Yosemite, Marin County and down the coast to Santa Barbara and then home. Wow! We loved every second of the trip, even riding together! We stayed in AirBnBs along the way.The sights were amazing. A standout for me was Yosemite. I climbed Half Dome a couple years ago and have spent a good deal of time backpacking just north of Yosemite. I had never seen so much water in Yosemite. On our Vernal Fall hike I was able to see both Yosemite and Lower Yosemite Falls in the distance, each with voluminous flow. Truly amazing!

We are also enjoying wonderful times with our two and a half year old grandson and his parents who happen to be our daughter and her husband! We take Grant under our wings a couple of times a week. It is so amazing to watch his development. As a grandparent you have time to observe and reflect, unlike as a parent you are so caught up in catching up there is little time to see the incremental evolution of this little soul.

We are so blessed in so many ways. I find myself sporadically weeping or chuckling out of nowhere when I think back on the people who are in or have been in my life, the places I’ve been fortunate to visit, my grandson and entire family, my times on the CCC. Each of you actually has a specific and meaningful place in my memories and in my heart.

Below are some photos below for those interested.

Thank you so, so much for your support.

Bob

￼

My grandson is a future CCC rider
￼

Northern Lights of Norway
￼

Sperm whale in the Arctic
￼

Amsterdam, just before spring bloom
￼

Mushing in Norway
￼

Family Dinner at Marin Joe’s on our road trip
￼

Robert Figari
figari@well.com
415 259-8153

Just an old man with a dream!

Happy New Year!
Our effective date for membership on the SANDAG Board of Directors was
January 1st!

Our first APG meeting of the year is an in-person meeting on Wednesday,

worked through.....

title: APG Meeting Synopsis.eml
subject: APG Meeting Synopsis
body:
Travis -

Just a quick note to let you know that I did attend today's meeting.

Synopsis:

1. Some technical difficulties delayed meeting start (10:15 ish instead of
10am)

2.  Quorum achieved

3.  Item 7 - Admitting Sponsor Groups (those that responded to the APG's
outreach) as Associate (non-voting) members:

PASSED

Associate members now include:

*Jacumba Community Sponsor Group*
*Bonsall Community Sponsor Group*
*Twin Oaks Valley Community Sponsor Group*

4.  Item 8 - SANDAG Update:

A.  SANDAG currently has no system to track money dedicated/spent
specifically for Unincorporated Area projects. Current system operates in
departments (essentially silos) and records have to be pulled manually from
each. Chair Maxson requested those figures in May and has yet to get the
data she requested.

B.  New Executive Director Mario Orso to take the reins soon

C.  SR-125 Tolling has brought to light numerous problems (there were
questions about whether this also could potentially extend to their managed
lane system tolls/FastTrak.)

5.  Item 9 - Open Discussion for Other Concerns (Informational Only, No
Action):

A.  Fire evacuation needs (67, 76, 94)
B.  CARB and potential gas tax increase next year
C.  BESS Battery storage hazards and fire insurance
D.  State-level CA Road Charge pilot program going forward
E.  Short-term vacation rentals impeding local housing supply for workers
to live nearby (Julian seems to be most impacted)
F.  Some communities have increased problems with food vendors/food trucks
popping up and causing hazards & health concerns

6.  Next meeting:  Was tentative for Wed. 1/8/2025.   NOW CHANGED TO SAT.
1/4/2025  (hoping for same location, Lakeside Library community room)

*7.  Potential Follow-up Action for You: *

*Robin mentioned during SANDAG update that she is scheduling a Wildfire
Evacuation field trip for SANDAG staff for her community in Ramona. She
wants other Chairs to let her know if there is interest in our respective
communities to have a similar field trip, so that SANDAG can see firsthand
the condition of the road and what local concerns are. *

*She asks that you email her to state interest in having/hosting a field
trip for SANDAG staff. *

That's all to report.

Thank you for this opportunity to serve.

Mary

title: Amberjack Energy LLC Battery Storage.eml
subject: Amberjack Energy LLC Battery Storage
body:
Hi Travis,
I wanted to contact you to show our extreme opposition and hope the ACPG
follows suit with not recommending this property for a major use permit.
This property is not at all a suitable location for a battery storage
facility being in close proximity to the dry brush & chaparral that
comprises the majority or the CNF nearby. This subject property is likely
zoned agricultural or residential and in no way is compatible with the
dangerous nature a facility like this would pose to the surrounding
neighbors and the Alpine/Dehesa/Harbison Canyon communities. I hope that
you & your co planning group members will Not be recommending approval of
such a facility in our community.
Best regards,
Elisa Peskin

title: Alpine Park Project Public Notice.eml
subject: Alpine Park Project Public Notice
body:
Hello Alpine Park Project Stakeholder,

In October 2023, the County of San Diego Board of Supervisors certified the Final Environmental Impact Report for the Alpine Park Project in compliance with the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). Since then, the County of San Diego, Department of Parks and Recreation has been working towards securing permits that are required for the project. This notice is to inform you that the United States Fish and Wildlife Service, as lead agency under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), has posted the Draft Environmental Assessment (EA) and Draft Habitat Conservation Plan (HCP) for the Alpine Park Project. The NEPA public review period for this project will be from January 21, 2025 to February 20, 2025.

For more information, please see the attached Notice of Public Review. The application, supporting materials, and any comments and other materials received will be available for public inspection at https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/current in Docket No. FWS-R8-ES-2024-0133.

Submitting Written Comments: You may submit your written comments using one of the following methods:

  *   Online: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/current. Follow the instructions for submitting comments on Docket No. FWS-R8-ES-2024-0133.
  *   U.S. mail: Public Comments Processing, Attn: Docket No. FWS-R8-ES-2024-0133; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, MS: PRB/3W, 5275 Leesburg Pike, Falls Church, VA 22041-3803.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Eric Porter, Fish and Wildlife Biologist, by email at eric_porter@fws.gov<mailto:eric_porter@fws.gov> or via phone at 442-287-2203.

Thank you for your continued interest in the Alpine Park Project. If you have any questions for the County of San Diego, please reach out to Jessica Montgomery.

[cid:image001.png@01DB4FCB.E1C1A000]
Jessica Montgomery, MPA
Land Use/Environmental Planner III
County of San Diego Parks and Recreation

title: Alpine Community Planning Group- Veterinary Project.eml
subject: Alpine Community Planning Group- Veterinary Project
body:
Hi Mr. Lyon,

My name is Holly Allen and I am a long time Alpine resident.  I was hoping
to connect with the Alpine Community Planning Group regarding my business
plan for the Alpine community.  A friend of mine named Mike Milligan
suggested that I reach out to you.  In addition, Brian Garmo, the landlord
of the property that I will be leasing, stated that he was recently in
contact with you regarding my project.  My plan is to open a small animal
veterinary practice in the Fall-Winter of this year.

I have practiced veterinary medicine in East county for almost 13 years and
am currently the medical director for a small animal hospital in El Cajon.
It has been my goal/dream for many years to open a private practice here in
beautiful Alpine and have the privilege to serve Alpine and the surrounding
communities.  There is a significant need for quality veterinary services
in our community.  Many of my long term clients commute to El Cajon from
Alpine, Pine Valley, Descanso, Campo, El Centro, etc for veterinary
services.

Currently, I am in the process of submitting my building plans to the
County department and have reached a few roadblocks.  I was hoping to
connect with you to discuss my project, get your advice, and clarify some
of my questions.  I sincerely appreciate your time and feedback.

Thank you,

Holly Allen

title: Alpine Community Planning Group Chair Walks like A Duck..eml
subject: Alpine Community Planning Group Chair Walks like A Duck.
body:
Travis Lyon

Chair

Alpine Community Planning Group

With blind CC's

Hello,Travis , 

I am concerned about your refusal to write the letters of support from three months ago.   Supervisor Anderson has already given them and the massive overwhelming interest in sunrise to sunset  has been demonstrated many times before your own eyes, ears, heart and mind. 

 

In fact, anyone acting like you have, independently canceling many full ACPG votes since I started going advocating at ACPG meetings in 2022, with inaction on the motion passed and the devastating consequences,   would logically be considered a person with a terrible self-serving conflict of interest. 

What would start to change my mind is the letters of support that everybody in your group, including yourself,  and  except  Darlene Cossio of Friends of Loveland voted for. Did you make a deal with Darlene or somebody else to shelf the motion post vote? Is shelving things by yourself for whatever reason part of the ACPG’s foundation? 

Why do you think those letters of support would not benefit the grass roots Loveland Defenders and Advocates who solicited them? The community including the board members who voted for them. Supervisor Anderson’s constituents? Have you performed such dedicated service to Loveland? Do you fancy yourself  working Loveland Miracles for the community behind the scenes? You never did before now. 

I have a theory of what you are up to but would not like to expend the energy to confirm them yet. However, I will say this. I imagine you like to console yourself that I am rude without concern for your own rudeness as exemplified in canceling unanimous or near unanimous ACPG votes even though you leave the meetings , time and time again, with promises to fulfill them. Does the board not monitor you for these failures? What is legitimate about your leadership and defaulting on board votes? 

Please write and send the letters of support ASAP, as promised months ago,  with proof of service to deserving advocates. The timing of now is really important. 

Russell

title: ACPG Loveland Letter's of Support; Sunrise to Sunset & SDGE Access Road Use..eml
subject: ACPG Loveland Letter's of Support; Sunrise to Sunset & SDGE Access Road Use.
cc: Jesus Arreola <jesusarreola226@gmail.com>, Carolyn McGavock <cmcgavoc@gmail.com>, David Thomas <higherglassdave@gmail.com>, Sean Walsh <walshsean63@gmail.com>, John Allen <jallen8@outlook.com>, Gregory Kazmer <gregory.kazmer@sdcounty.ca.gov>, Maggie Sleeper <maggie.sleeper@sdcounty.ca.gov>, Steve Hales <sandiegosteve@outlook.com>, Karen Wood <karensdrealestate@gmail.com>
body:
Travis LyonChair Alpine Community Planning Group

Good Morning, Travis,

I am requesting copies of the letters of support we recently discussed that were  put before the ACPG board for a successful vote. 

Some Loveland advocates and recreation users have asked me to follow up on these letters of support. Travis, I urgently need you to forward the letters of support to me. These are crucial for our advocacy efforts, especially in light of the support we have garnered from many other community leaders. Please send me, "reply all"  the letters of support for restoring sunrise to sunset and using the maintenance roads in the SDGE Powerlink easement area.

You might benefit from some follow-up I can provide regarding your recent agenda item for Loveland trails proposals: 

Last night, Sweetwater's BOD passed a motion that the 5 Loveland trails proposal items you reviewed will make up the work plan management will send to the California funding and work oversight group, the Department of Water Resources (DWR). Please see the image below for a rough version of the site plan. 

Travis, your continued involvement and the momentum we (the community) have created, including the commitment of  $75,000 for the master plan, are crucial for the success of the Loveland project. Your efforts will serve our communities on recreation and help defend Loveland wildlife and our lake user neighbors and friends in the face of potential bad ideas and acts against them by the Sweetwater Authority. We have seen the impact of such disasters in the past year, and your support and that of the ACPG is invaluable. 

Best regards,

Russell

title: ACPG Letters of Support for Loveland..eml
subject: ACPG Letters of Support for Loveland.
cc: Steve Hales <sandiegosteve@outlook.com>, Steve Hales <steve@hales.xyz>, Karen Wood <karensdrealestate@gmail.com>, Gregory Kazmer <gregory.kazmer@sdcounty.ca.gov>, Maggie Sleeper <maggie.sleeper@sdcounty.ca.gov>, Friends of Loveland Reservoir <friendsoflovelandreservoir@gmail.com>, "michael.milligan@alpinecpg.org" <michael.milligan@alpinecpg.org>, Mary Davis <sdmary33@yahoo.com>
body:
Travis LyonAlpine Community Planning Group  Chair

Hello Travis,

We may never again acheive the momentum we had at the ACPG Forest Service meeting last August for Sunrise to sunset due to retreat and compromise offered by you and Friends of Loveland Reservoir respectively. 
We know the problem. It is supression from Congressman Issa and Forest Service brass in favor of Sweetwater that trickles down to the Descanso Ranger. That is why we need any momemtum that we can possibly get. Your group has always attempted to help me and later the larger group of advocates, However, you apparently, as far as I can see, unilaterally , but defintely not with respect to the public who pushed for the vote in the first place,  cancel it.
We have not quit on what is just for Loveland lake users that brought us to ask the ACPG for help. Please follow through with the letters of support we asked for  and your group approved until we advocates tell you we that we give up on what is good for the community and region at Loveland. There is still possibly an evolution towards success occuring here. 
As you might well know. Friends of Loveland's volunteer schemes to keep the lake open have been rejected.  There never was a good reason Sweetwater can't do it. Perhaps even Friends of Loveland realizes the need for unity around the legal protections of the easement for Sunrise to Sunset.  Maybe Friends of Loveland has quit , I don't know. Either way the core of lake users still want Sunrise to Sunset and support from leaders in our Community.  Please help us restore momentum by honoring the vote we asked for and were granted by ACPG.
Thank you,
Russell

Thank you,
Russell

title: Access to Loveland Reservoir For Forest Service Constituents..eml
subject: Access to Loveland Reservoir For Forest Service Constituents.
body:
Kyle SmithUS Forest ServiceDescanso Ranger.

Hello Ranger Smith,
I spoke with Congressman Issa's staff this morning about the unanimous Sunrise to Sunset wishes of Forest Service constituents. 
Would you please tell me what the progress on this shared goal is,  or what progress could be like going forward?
Days are getting longer and use at Loveland is high while is so beautiful, including for easement protected fishing and hiking. 
Fishing isn't good most of the time , but considering the location in our relatively remote, commuter unfriendly communities, it is being used for what modest success the available  fishery can provide. User defined trails,  per the land swap easement and California  CEQA document are in better shape then ever and being used more and more due to  the social media publicity of this Forest Service partnership access. 
The best days at Loveland are ahead of us. 
Thank you,
Russell Walsh

title: 4_22_2025  Loveland Transfer Community Meeting Follow-up..eml
subject: 4/22/2025  Loveland Transfer Community Meeting Follow-up.
body:
Sweetwater Authority DirectorsChula Vista CA. 

Dear Authority Directors,

Thank you all  for expediting this topic onto your community meeting schedule. The region was well represented by a blend of Sweetwater Customers and other Loveland Stakeholders. 

It was good to see Director Ditas Yamane and several  expert management staff from your organization leading the way. 

While the last successful March Loveland Transfer was very important and you all should be congratulated on that, a more responsible accounting for the dewatering type  transfers like conducted in 2022-2023 is desirable. This is actually urgent since Sweetwater policy and possibly intentions are to repeat it as early as October of this year , possibly extending in to next year. It doesn't matter when it happens, please consider full accounting  and accountability  while promoting the policy. 

I understand that the biologist working at the time of the dewaterings no longer works at Sweetwater and that he had been allowed to incorrectly attribute the origin of these sediment sludge transfers from Loveland  by Sweetwater interdependent State and Federal Wildlife agencies. However, those pollution origin myths are no longer intact. It came from Loveland. There is much more not shown by SWA about the actual costs and hardships of dewatering Loveland. 

As you all are aware, many Loveland stake holders are under duress from the intent of your water district to dewater Loveland again. It is impossible for a few outsiders to respectfully address these concerns. 

It is a very long, high traffic impact drive from Alpine to Chula Vista at the time your meetings are offeredAs the compassionate leaders of Sweetwater Authority, please choose to  do a repeat of the Loveland Transfer meeting out here in Alpine now. I believe you all, as responsible public leaders,  will understand how the taxpayers and citizens who substantially fund your projects like Reynolds Desalination Plant, where last night's meeting was held, need to hear from you and your management/ leadership team.  

Sincerely, 
Russell Walsh

Mark and Ashley

Please find the attached support letters and emails.  These were also sent to the PC secretary, however we have not received confirmation that she has received them or forward to the commissioners. Can you check on that?

Chris

From: Dave Cieslak <dave@sandcpr.com>
Date: Tuesday, August 19, 2025 at 4:42 PM
To: Chris Brown <chris@alchemycg.com>
Cc: Dave Cieslak <dave@sandcpr.com>
Subject: FW: Letters attached re: Harmony Grove Village South (item 2 on Friday's meeting agenda)

FYI — for your records (and if you’d like to share with Mr. Slovick)...

From: Dave Cieslak <dave@sandcpr.com>
Date: Tuesday, August 19, 2025 at 4:41 PM
To: pds.planningcommission@sdcounty.ca.gov <pds.planningcommission@sdcounty.ca.gov>, georgina.gaines@sdcounty.ca.gov <georgina.gaines@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Subject: Letters attached re: Harmony Grove Village South (item 2 on Friday's meeting agenda)

Good afternoon-

Please see the attached letters to the San Diego County Planning Commission regarding Item 2 (Harmony Grove Village South) on the Friday, Aug. 22 meeting agenda. Because this is a large e-mail with multiple attachments, please confirm receipt at your earliest convenience. If copies of these letters could be provided to each Commissioner, the writers would greatly appreciate it.

Thank you very much for your assistance!

All my best,

Dave Cieslak

New eComment for Board of Supervisors
Debra ONeill submitted a new eComment.

Meeting: Board of Supervisors

Item: 4. NOTICED PUBLIC HEARING: HARMONY GROVE VILLAGE SOUTH GENERAL PLAN AMENDMENT, SPECIFIC PLAN, ZONE RECLASSIFICATION, TENTATIVE MAP, MAJOR USE PERMIT, SITE PLAN AND ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT REPORT AND ASSOCIATED DOCUMENTS

eComment: HGVS is proposed on a single dead-end road, Country Club Drive, and asks for a waiver of both State and County fire codes requiring two or more exits on a dead-end road over 800 feet long. The entire neighborhood has been deemed a Very High Fire Severity Zone by Cal-Fire Maps. Does it really seem safe to place 1000 residents in a Very High Fire Severity Zone with only one exit, especially when Fire Code says it isn’t? In a Santa Ana wind driven fire, people are going to end up trapped on the road, or they will die in their homes because they think “fire hardened” means “fire safe.” In the Coco’s fire I evacuated past 6' high flames. I was able to evacuate because only about 75 of us lived on Country Club, not the 1000 or so HGVS would bring. At a Community Meeting on 9/17/25, RSFFPD Chief McQuead stated that HGVS would not be approved by the Fire Department now because there was no secondary exit. Why is this development being held to 2018 standards and not current standards?

Mark Slovick, Deputy Director

title: August 22 Planning Commission Hearing - Harmony Grove Village South.msg
subject: August 22 Planning Commission Hearing - Harmony Grove Village South
body:
Hi Commissioners,

We wanted to reach out and offer individual briefings in advance of the August 22 Planning Commission hearing. The Harmony Grove Village South project will be presented, and we expect opposition from the community and environmental stakeholders. The project includes a General Plan Amendment to add 453 homes in north county, just south of Harmony Grove Village.

The project was originally approved by the Planning Commission and Board of Supervisors back in 2018, and after litigation, we needed to revise their greenhouse gas mitigation and add affordable housing, which has now been completed. Please let us know if you're interested in a briefing and we'll get something setup in August.

We also have a webpage setup for the project, where you can find all the project documents: https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/sdc/pds/Current_Projects/hgvs.html. It will be updated shortly with responses to public comments and the EIR.

Please let us know if you have any questions or need anything else.

Thanks,

Mark Slovick, Deputy Director

New eComment for Board of Supervisors
Debra ONeill submitted a new eComment.

Meeting: Board of Supervisors

Item: 4. NOTICED PUBLIC HEARING: HARMONY GROVE VILLAGE SOUTH GENERAL PLAN AMENDMENT, SPECIFIC PLAN, ZONE RECLASSIFICATION, TENTATIVE MAP, MAJOR USE PERMIT, SITE PLAN AND ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT REPORT AND ASSOCIATED DOCUMENTS

eComment: HGVS is proposed on a single dead-end road, Country Club Drive, and asks for a waiver of both State and County fire codes requiring two or more exits on a dead-end road over 800 feet long. The entire neighborhood has been deemed a Very High Fire Severity Zone by Cal-Fire Maps. Does it really seem safe to place 1000 residents in a Very High Fire Severity Zone with only one exit, especially when Fire Code says it isn’t? In a Santa Ana wind driven fire, people are going to end up trapped on the road, or they will die in their homes because they think “fire hardened” means “fire safe.” In the Coco’s fire I evacuated past 6' high flames. I was able to evacuate because only about 75 of us lived on Country Club, not the 1000 or so HGVS would bring. At a Community Meeting on 9/17/25, RSFFPD Chief McQuead stated that HGVS would not be approved by the Fire Department now because there was no secondary exit. Why is this development being held to 2018 standards and not current standards?

Subject: [External] terra.lawson-remer@sdcounty.ca.gov, joel.anderson@sdcounty.ca.gov, monica.montgomerysteppe@sdcounty.ca.gov, Jim.Desmond@sdcounty.ca.gov, PA@sdcounty.ca.gov, Andrew.Potter@sdcounty.ca.gov, PublicComment@sdcounty.ca.gov, Paul.Worlie@sdcounty.c...

Hello Chair Lawson-Remer and board:

When we moved into Harmony Grove, we knew there was a fire risk. The community has caught fire many times. Looking at the zoning of the area, we saw that it was zoned for lower density due to the fire risk and lack of evacuation infrastructure. For that reason we felt that the risk was acceptable. We’d learn how to evacuate quickly and get out of harm’s way at the earliest possible time.

However, at a recent community meeting we learned that a developer was seeking to undo that zoning by adding another 453 homes in the brush covered area south of the Escondido Creek. This area is notoriously flammable and has only one way in and one way out. Incredibly, we learned that the county planners are recommending approving this project without a secondary access.

And on top of that, the fire chief, who we hold in much esteem, told us that the project doesn’t actually meet today’s safety standards without secondary access. “It would not pass today” are the exact words he said. It barely meets the 2018 standards from when the project first was voted on. I don’t think I have to tell you that much has changed since 2018. We’ve seen close to 50,000 homes burn down all over California. We’ve seen hundreds of fatalities (many due to evacuation issues) and the state and local codes have tightened up considerably.

What we also learned in that same community meeting last week was that on one end of the valley, with HGV South built, 3500 vehicles will hit our narrow little roads all at once. The county never did a community-wide analysis (though we asked) of what the evacuation would look like under the fully built-out conditions, so the community had to raise funds to conduct their own study. It showed an almost-certainty of entrapment with 7 hours or more to evacuate the community (the fire arrival time is conservatively 1 to 2 hours).

The deputy chief at the very same meeting told us, in stark terms: “you better get used to sheltering in place because evacuation is not likely to be safe.” That’s sobering news because even the most fire-hardened homes burn down (45% burned down during Camp Fire and higher percentages in the Tubbs and Paradise fires). And closely spaced homes are the most at risk according to the extensive research done on California fire structure loss.

It is a terrible choice to make. This HGVS project will be the straw that breaks the camel’s back. The next fire that comes through here will likely be before some of you retire. If you vote yes, you are owning whatever the consequences are.

Please vote no on this project or at the bare minimum enforce the secondary access requirement.

Respectfully,

Greg White

Sent from my iPhone

eComment: I am generally in favor of development. I have lived in North County San Diego my entire life and I have been evacuated from my home for wildfires twice. As SoCal residents, we all know that wildfires can wipe out entire communities. Structures can be painstakingly rebuilt, but lives lost are a completely different issue. I can only support the addition of more homes in this valley if the evacuation/egress can be improved. The most recent fire approval allowed for modifications/exceptions to the existing rules, but why..? Just because they couldn't meet the requirements? This doesn't add up. It takes a lot to build a community, but let's not let this one get started on the wrong, scandalous foot. Require them to fix the fire concerns before approving this project.

Subject: [External] Harmony Grove Village South; Public Comment for 10/1/25 Meeting

Dear Chair Lawson-Remer and Members of the Board,

I am writing to express my opposition to the plan for Harmony Grove Village South, as it does not include the creation of a secondary access route. If 453 dwelling units will be added to Harmony Grove, a secondary access route is absolutely necessary to ensure that all residents can safely evacuate during a fire.

The project site for Harmony Grove Village South is located in an area designated by CalFire as a Very High Fire Hazard Severity Zone and there have been numerous fires in the direct vicinity of the project site. The Cocos Fire in 2014 burned up to the project site while the 1997 Del Dios Fire burned directly on the project site.

Additionally, the frequency and severity of wildfires in California generally have increased in recent years. Rather than a single fire, we now see regions being consumed by multiple blazes simultaneously, which overwhelm firefighting resources. Rather than assuming abundant firefighting personnel will always be available to direct evacuations, in making planning decisions, we must now contemplate what will happen when San Diego’s firefighting resources are pushed to the brink.

Given the location of the project site and the increase in wildfires generally, it is a question of when and not if Harmony Grove Village South will be threatened by wildfire. Knowing this, a secondary access route can and should be built as part of Harmony Grove Village South. Traffic gridlock during an evacuation will endanger residents and complicate firefighting efforts. A secondary access route is needed to prevent such gridlock during a fast-moving blaze.

Now is the best (and cheapest) opportunity to make sure that the right infrastructure is in place for Harmony Grove Village South when wildfires occur. Please do not approve the plan for Harmony Grove Village South without a requirement for the construction of a secondary access route.

Sincerely,

Jessie Dummer
