title: _External_ Harmony Grove.msg
subject: [External] Harmony Grove
body:
I just heard that you got that Harmony Grove development approved.  And without due consideration to traffic flow.  I understand you were somehow in charge of this project at the county?
   Yes, I read what you wrote.  But filling a page with words is very different from thinking first and writing useful information down.  You guys did not think.  And you did not go out and look at the real world.  I know you didn't because you said nothing about Via Rancho Parkway.  And a large percentage of the commuters from your new development are going to use Via Rancho Parkway to access I15.  How could you not see that?  It is already happening.
   A few years ago Citracado Parkway was widened from Auto Park down to West Valley Parkway.  So now a lot of people decided that they have a shortcut to bypass the truly awful 79 to I15 interchange during the rush hours.  They use the new Citracado Parkway.  But what happens when they get to West Valley Parkway?  The rest of Citracado does not go through to I15.  So they go west on West Valley Parkway, turn left on Via Rancho Parkway, and access I15 via that route.  I'm serious.  Since the northern part of Citracado opened, the traffic on Via Rancho Parkway has become truly awful.  Some people with driveways on that road, or who live on cross streets without street lights are effectively trapped in their homes for five hours a day.  Emergency vehicle access is almost non-existent during the busy rush "hours".  (Usually 2 or 3 hours morning and night.)  And now more people are pouring onto or off of I15 at the notoriously bad Via Rancho Parkway on ramp, which increases an already dangerous situation.
   Now, given that you din't think or look at the real world, I assume you probably have no idea what Via Rancho Parkway is like.  So let me tell you it would be REALLY expensive to widen so that it can handle the traffic that is currently being dumped onto it and the added traffic that your new development will dump onto it.  It is in rough country and would require significant excavation, retaining walls, culverts, and probably lots of eminent domain taking of land to make it work.  In short, it won't ever happen.
   So you have doomed people to die in traffic accidents or in their homes while awaiting emergency services due to your poor planning.  (And to the poor planning of whoever thought it was a good idea to finish only the one section of Citracado Parkway.)  Of course you will deny it, but you have.
   Now is there anything that can be done to mitigate the damage?  I think it's obvious:  put Citracado Parkway the rest of the way through to I15.  Go look at it.  You can do it on Google Earth if you don't want to leave your chair.  It is platted all the way through.  And it exists all the way through except for a very short stretch where it just stops abruptly.
   Look at this picture:

   The red arrow shows the end of the north section of Citracado.  Notice that the road is all widened and ready to use to that point.  The orange arrow shows the intersection on I15 that is called "Citracado Parkway".  It is there and ready to use.  The wobbly blue line that I drew shows where it appears to me that the road is supposed to continue on, eventually connecting to Gamble Lane, which I assume would then take the name Citracado as it becomes Citracado again when it passes beneath I15.  And if you look at where the yellow arrow is pointed, it looks like some clearing has even been done along this slightly curving route, though long enough ago that someone has planted a tree in the middle of it.
   Everything is in place to have Citracado extended through to I15.  So what can you do to help make that happen?  I'm sorry if you think I've been mean, but you didn't think, you did not do your due diligence, and you have created an even bigger problem than we already have by allowing this housing development.  I really do believe that people will crash and probably die due to this decision.  Or will die in their homes because emergency vehicles cannot get to them in a timely manner.  (Lest you think I'm exaggerating, it appears that my neighbor just died yesterday evening, even after calling an ambulance.  A lot of old people live off of Via Rancho Parkway.)  I think you owe it to us to at least try to mitigate the problem.

--Brian M. Godfrey
  brian@wildbirdshop.com <mailto:brian@wildbirdshop.com>

title: External Colorado Billionaire Shouldnt Decide Our Safety - Say No to HGVS.msg
subject: [External] Colorado Billionaire Shouldn’t Decide Our Safety - Say No to HGVS
to: terra.lawson-remer@sdcounty.ca.gov; joel.anderson@sdcounty.ca.gov; monica.montgomerysteppe@sdcounty.ca.gov; Jim.Desmond@sdcounty.ca.gov; PA@sdcounty.ca.gov; Andrew.Potter@sdcounty.ca.gov; PublicComment@sdcounty.ca.gov; Paul.Worlie@sdcounty.ca.gov; Kyle.LaVelle@sdcounty.ca.gov; Andrew.Hayes@sdcounty.ca.gov; Jeffrey.Yuen@sdcounty.ca.gov; Eric.Henson@sdcounty.ca.gov; Hunter.McDonald@sdcounty.ca.gov; Dahvia.Lynch@sdcounty.ca.gov; amy.harbert@sdcounty.ca.gov; Mark.Slovick@sdcounty.ca.gov; efhgtc@gmail.com; Bianca.Lorenzana@sdcounty.ca.gov; Montagne@rsf-fire.org; mcquead@rsf-fire.org; ashcraft@rsf-fire.org; hillgren@rsf-fire.org; malin@rsf-fire.org; stine@rsf-fire.org; Vince.Nicoletti@sdcounty.ca.gov
body:
Dear Chair Lawson-Remer, board members and staff:

My family and myself have lived in Harmony Grove for 40 years. I’m a retired firefighter/ captain with over 30 years of experience. We’ve been through multiple big fires. It’s just a matter of time before another event happens. During the 2014 Cocos Fire, the wind changed directions and about 30 homes burned, and it took us almost two hours just to get a few miles out. Back then, the village site was just dirt, and even that helped slow the flames. Roads were jammed even with far fewer cars.

Now Harmony Grove Village is built (the community actually testified in favor of the project back in 2011). We love our new neighbors, but evacuations are going to be seriously constricted: so many vehicles trying to get out on the same narrow roads. Years ago the County told us the safe place for growth was north of the creek, near the old egg ranch which is why we supported HGV. South of the creek was a dead-end fire-prone bowl unless there’s a second way out. County even removed a proposed road to Del Dios Highway from the road plans. It’s the main reason none of us can get insurance – we’re surrounded by brush and no way out.

HGV South would add another 1000 cars onto the same routes that were gridlocked back in 2014. And to make things worse, the County felt it was ok to give a Colorado billionaire a waiver for secondary access in a bowl that has repeatedly caught fire throughout the years. The County never modeled a full community evacuation (even though we asked repeatedly); they looked only at the immediate project area. We had to fundraise and pay for an independent expert, and the verdict was sobering: entrapment is likely. His analysis showed that it would take seven hours or more to evacuate everyone, but fires arrive much sooner.

Our fire chief also recently acknowledged HGV South wouldn’t pass today’s standards without a secondary access. Please vote no on HGV South, or at least require real secondary access. Our safety has to come first.

Respectfully,
Greg Kaczur
9033 Harmony Grove Rd

Sent from my iPhone

title: External HGVS  Gridlock Danger and Lost Lives .msg
subject: [External] HGVS = Gridlock, Danger, and Lost Lives
to: terra.lawson-remer@sdcounty.ca.gov; joel.anderson@sdcounty.ca.gov; monica.montgomerysteppe@sdcounty.ca.gov; Jim.Desmond@sdcounty.ca.gov; PA@sdcounty.ca.gov; Andrew.Potter@sdcounty.ca.gov; PublicComment@sdcounty.ca.gov; Paul.Worlie@sdcounty.ca.gov; Kyle.LaVelle@sdcounty.ca.gov; Andrew.Hayes@sdcounty.ca.gov; Jeffrey.Yuen@sdcounty.ca.gov; Eric.Henson@sdcounty.ca.gov; Hunter.McDonald@sdcounty.ca.gov; Dahvia.Lynch@sdcounty.ca.gov; amy.harbert@sdcounty.ca.gov; Mark.Slovick@sdcounty.ca.gov; efhgtc@gmail.com; Bianca.Lorenzana@sdcounty.ca.gov; Montagne@rsf-fire.org; mcquead@rsf-fire.org; ashcraft@rsf-fire.org; hillgren@rsf-fire.org; malin@rsf-fire.org; stine@rsf-fire.org; Vince.Nicoletti@sdcounty.ca.gov
body:
Dear Chair Lawson-Remer and Members of the Board,

I have been an Elfin Forest resident for 13 years. I love the beauty of our trails and wildlife and am blessed to live here. That said, wildfires are the biggest threat to our community. I survived the Cocos Fire unscathed physically, but am still traumatized. Not all my neighbors fared as well. We loaded up our three horses, two dogs, and parrot and drove off in gridlocked traffic, not knowing if we would have a house to return to. We saw the fire on the hill as we evacuated and it moved very fast down towards Harmony Grove Spiritualists and the area where HGV South is being proposed. There is nothing scarier than seeing your neighbors wrestle livestock trailers and unruly animals to try to get them out in time. The evacuation took at least 2 hours in literally crawling traffic. And that was before any developments in the community.

As a community, we’re well aware of the fire danger. We keep “go bags” at the ready. We hitch our trailers every time there is a red flag warning and do not sleep when the warm wind blows. Some of my neighbors are third generation residents and have seen the many fires (once a decade) that have ravaged this little valley. We’ve lost hundreds of homes over the years and even suffered fatalities. We are all prepared for the next wildfire. What we are not prepared for, however, is the entrapment that is in store for us with a community that continues to accept (and support) additional housing but without any major improvements in the evacuation infrastructure.

We barely made it out during the Cocos Fire and that was a few hundred cars and dozens of livestock trailers. If HGV South is built, the total number of vehicles evacuating during the next fire will number in the thousands. Nationally renowned evacuation experts have analyzed the area and estimate it will take 7 hours to evacuate, but the fire arrives within an hour or two. This can only mean entrapment.

We cannot gamble with human lives just because a billionaire from Colorado throws a bunch of money at our fire district, our unions and our elected officials. Please vote no on Harmony Grove Village South or at least require a secondary access. Put community safety ahead of development interests.

Thank you for your leadership and for protecting the people you represent.

Sincerely,
Jorgine Ellerbrock

Sent from my iPhone

title: External Prioritize Safety .msg
subject: [External] Prioritize Safety
to: terra.lawson-remer@sdcounty.ca.gov; joel.anderson@sdcounty.ca.gov; monica.montgomerysteppe@sdcounty.ca.gov; Jim.Desmond@sdcounty.ca.gov; PA@sdcounty.ca.gov; Andrew.Potter@sdcounty.ca.gov; PublicComment@sdcounty.ca.gov; Paul.Worlie@sdcounty.ca.gov; Kyle.LaVelle@sdcounty.ca.gov; Andrew.Hayes@sdcounty.ca.gov; Jeffrey.Yuen@sdcounty.ca.gov; Eric.Henson@sdcounty.ca.gov; Hunter.McDonald@sdcounty.ca.gov; Dahvia.Lynch@sdcounty.ca.gov; amy.harbert@sdcounty.ca.gov; Mark.Slovick@sdcounty.ca.gov; efhgtc@gmail.com; Bianca.Lorenzana@sdcounty.ca.gov; Montagne@rsf-fire.org; mcquead@rsf-fire.org; ashcraft@rsf-fire.org; hillgren@rsf-fire.org; malin@rsf-fire.org; stine@rsf-fire.org; Vince.Nicoletti@sdcounty.ca.gov
body:
Dear Members of the San Diego County Board of Supervisors,

I am writing to you as a concerned resident and environmentalist regarding the proposed Harmony Grove Village South project. I urge you to reject this development, as it epitomizes urban sprawl that threatens to undo all the hard work the County has done on its Climate Action Plan and its efforts to limit sprawl and encourage infill.

The project is not served by transit and will increase the county’s Vehicle Miles Traveled (VMT) as it is significantly higher than the County-wide average. And it will generate more GHGs than it is claiming it can offset. In addition, during the next wildfire, the potential for gridlock will pose a serious risk to the nearby communities. Independent experts have shown that, due to inadequate secondary egress, it poses a serious entrapment risk. This is absolutely unacceptable in view of the recent Palisades and Altadena evacuation catastrophes.

Increased VMT and driving distances will lead to greater carbon emissions, more sprawl and further contribute to climate change. The community itself is mostly rural, known for its wildlife, open space reserves, and natural beauty. We must protect areas like this from irresponsible developments that prioritize profit over public safety and ecological integrity.

Additionally, the site is listed as a Priority Conservation Area in the Multiple Species Conservation Area (MSCP) North draft. It is directly adjacent to lands supporting state and federal endangered least Bell’s vireo, federally threatened coastal California gnatcatcher, the endangered Southwestern Willow flycatcher and near the Escondido Creek which supports the proposed federal threatened status Southwestern pond turtle.

The position of this project within the wildland urban interface (WUI) flies in the face of a wide body of research that shows that these are the communities that suffer the most losses during wildfire events. This community has already experienced the devastating effects of wildfires numerous times over the years (most recently, the Cocos Fire), with limited evacuation infrastructure.

I strongly urge you to consider the long-term implications of approving the Harmony Grove Village South project.

Thank you for your attention to this critical issue.

Sincerely,

Nicole Beaurain

Sent from my iPhone

Subject: [External] Don’t repeat past supervisors’ mistakes by approving fire trap sprawl HGVS

Dear Commissioners, Chairperson Lawson-Remer, Board and staff:

In the upcoming weeks, you will be asked to take yet another look at the Harmony Grove Village South (HGVS) project that the previous, pro-sprawl and developer-funded board of supervisors approved in the face of overwhelming opposition from environmental groups like the Sierra Club, Cleveland National Forest Foundation, EHL, Climate Action Campaign as well as the communities of Harmony Grove, Eden Valley and Elfin Forest.

For some reason, County staff seem intent on adhering to the outdated desires and wishes of a past, pro-sprawl, anti-environment board and are ignoring how much the wildfire landscape has changed since the first ill-fated approval.

The Colorado billionaire seeking to get this project approved has hired a small army of consultants and lobbyists to try to gaslight decision-makers into ignoring crucial but common sense fire code requirements. They’ve been trying since at least 2015 to make the case that a large sprawl subdivision in a very high fire severity zone, surrounded by over 15,000 acres of open space and habitat, does not need the required secondary access that every other project in the state has required for decades.

After the Camp Fire in Paradise (and the many, increasingly violent and destructive wildfires since), the rules for development in high risk areas have only gotten more stringent both at the county and the state level. Instead, this developer, whose project approval was completely rescinded following a lawsuit and appellate court judgement, has opted to continue to pretend we’re still operating in 2015.

Our own Fire District (RSFFPD), according to public record documents, seems to have been illegally told by county staff (and probably pressured by the billionaire and his attorneys) that there can be no changes to the public safety plan for this project, originally developed in 2015. The district itself has been very strict about secondary access requirements, requiring them for even minor lot splits—a non-negotiable requirement that has killed numerous projects over the years. The district reminds us to “always have two ways out” when advising us to prepare for the inevitable wildfire. So it is ironic that they are being ordered by county staff to waive secondary access requirements.

As a community that has suffered through numerous major, destructive wildfires over the years, hundreds of homes lost and even the loss of life, we cannot believe that County staff is supporting a project that doesn’t have an alternate way out (in violation of state fire code). While we do not support this project for a variety of reasons, requiring a proper secondary access would at least save lives when the inevitable wildfire shows up.

Respectfully,

Lisa M. Franken-Lopez

Subject: [External] End the siege and starvation of Gaza

July 30, 2025

Black image with bold text reading, 'Stop Starving Gaza'

We, the undersigned, are writing to express our horror and outrage at
Israel's forced starvation and ceaseless bombings of Gaza.

We have all seen images of emaciated children being intentionally
starved, families crushed or burned alive in airstrikes, and heard
the desperate cries of parents pleading for the world to end their
immeasurable suffering. We have all witnessed countless acts of
unconscionable cruelty, including Israeli forces killing more than 1,000
Palestinians since May while trying to collect a bag of flour or rice from
aid distribution sites to bring back to their starving families.

With the UN secretary general warning that Gaza's “last lifelines
keeping people alive are collapsing,” and the World Health
Organization declaring Gaza's remaining hospitals to be at a "breaking
point," it is crucial for the international community to put
forth concrete steps to end Israel's U.S.-backed genocide in Gaza.

We demand an immediate ceasefire in Gaza, as well as the lifting of
the siege, and the resumption of aid deliveries to nourish and treat the
starving, ill, and wounded Palestinians who have been subjected to a
nearly complete blockade of food, medicine, and other vital supplies
since March. This blocking of food and medicine is not only immoral, it
is also a war crime under the Geneva Conventions.

We add our voices to the global outcry demanding that the killing and
forced starvation be stopped immediately, that the death traps run by
the so-called Gaza Humanitarian Foundation be dismantled,
and for the United Nations to resume the distribution of that aid, as
“only a massive scale-up in food aid can stabilize the hunger
catastrophe engulfing Gaza.”

What we are witnessing in Gaza is a stain on our collective conscience,
and we all have a responsibility to do something to end it. We invite
people from all institutions, wherever you may be located, to sign
onto this letter, or use it as a template to create your own.

Subject: [External] Happening Tomorrow! "What I Saw in Gaza: A Surgeon's Account"

Oct. 29, 2025

 
Event flier: What I Saw in Gaza: A Surgeon's Account
If you live in the Bay Area please join us for this in-person event happening
tomorrow (Thursday, Oct. 30) at 4pm at UC Berkeley to hear a first person
account from Dr. Feroze Sidhwa about the cases he encountered as a
trauma surgeon volunteering in Gaza in 2024 and again earlier this year.
This is an in-person only event.
Speaker Bio:

Dr. Feroze Sidhwa is a general, trauma, and critical care surgeon in
California. He is also a humanitarian surgeon, having worked most
extensively in Palestine, but also in Ukraine, Haiti, Zimbabwe, and Burkina
Faso. He most recently volunteered at the European Hospital in Khan
Younis, Gaza from March 25-April 8, 2024 with the World Health
Organization, and again from March 3-April 1, 2025 with American NGO
MedGlobal. Feroze has written and spoken extensively about surgical
humanitarian work, the United States’ role in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict,
and the political consequences of medical relief work. He approaches the
Israeli-Palestinian conflict as a secular American and as a humanitarian
physician.

He has given his testimony in a variety of venues across the country. These
include Harvard’s FBX Center for Health & Human Rights among other
academic settings, and numerous news organizations including CNN, ABC,
CBS, and Democracy Now!). In May, he testified in front of the UN Security
Council. His testimony can be viewed through this link.

 
Together, we can make belonging the norm, not the exception.

Sent: Wednesday, August 6, 2025 9:06 AM
To: Simmons, Taryell <Taryell.Simmons@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Subject: [External] New Visual Explainer: What's Behind the Opportunity Gap, and How to Close It

+ more news & updates from OBI
Aug. 6, 2025

 

We're excited to share with you our brand new visual explainer video that
breaks down how opportunity is structured in the United States, its
relationship to race and class, and how to level the playing field so everyone
has a fair shot at success. The video, which is a companion to the new book
on Structural Racism recently published by OBI Research Director Stephen
Menendian, shows how the pathways we encounter in life aren't only
shaped by personal choices, but also by structural forces. Stephen, who
narrates the video, explains what he means by opportunity, why it's so
unevenly distributed, and illustrates an easy-to-grasp example of how
policies can be changed to close opportunity disparities, rather than
exacerbate them. Check out this must watch video here. And read this
fantastic article and Q&A with Stephen published on Berkeley News.

 
Photo collage of 6 people holding signs that say
Letter: Stop Starving Gaza

Last week a number of OBI staff members authored an urgent letter calling
for an immediate end to Israel's forced starvation of Palestinians in Gaza.
We invited our colleagues at other departments, centers and organizations
inside and outside of Berkeley and the general public to add their names to
the letter, repost it to their websites, and speak out publicly on this moral
calamity happening before our eyes in Gaza. About 1,500 of you have
already signed onto the letter. You can still add your name to it at the
bottom of this page, and email us a photo of yourself holding up a sign
reading "Stop Starving Gaza" to share on our website and other platforms.
See coverage of this letter in the DailyCal.

Disclaimer: The ideas expressed in the letter and in this email post are
not necessarily those of the Othering & Belonging Institute or UC
Berkeley, but belong to the signers.

 
image grab showing a sample question from our survey
Take our Audience Survey!

We'd love to learn more about your backgrounds, your interests in our
work, how you found us, and what you find most useful for your work. To
that end we've developed a super quick (5-10 minute) survey we would love
you to fill out. Your responses will help us create content that’s more useful,
inspiring, and relevant—and you will help us explore new ways for our
community to connect and grow together.

 
Graphic reading
Join a Workshop to Inform the Statewide Topical
Reports of California’s Fifth Climate Assessment

The California Fifth Climate Change Assessment Team is seeking input
from community organizations, experts on the ground, and residents with
lived experiences to inform the Statewide Topical Reports. The virtual
workshop, happening on Thursday, Aug. 7 from 1pm to 2:30pm, will
include breakout discussions on housing, health, labor, and education,
which will be featured in all four reports.

 
 + EVENTS
Illustration of homes under the title
To advance housing justice for all, we need solutions at scale. Scaling just
solutions that match what our communities want and need is about more
than building more affordable housing units. It requires building a culture
and system that prioritizes people over profit, honors community self-
determination, and fosters shared responsibility to each other and the
earth. Join us for this August 13 virtual panel discussion which builds on
the frameworks and recommendations presented in Living into the Future:
Scaling Community Owned Housing in California. We pick up one of the
questions we left off with: How can the housing field transform these
dynamics, bridge across silos, and create a more cohesive housing
ecosystem, in order to live into a better future of belonging for all?

 
 + WORK WITH US

We currently have two staff and two student positions open:
Development Director
Research Associate
Network for Transformative Change Student Research Assistant
(STDT)
Climate & Agrarian Justice Student Research Assistant
Check our website regularly for the most up-to-date information on job
vacancies.

 
Colorful banner with the OBI logo and a logo reading
We are clearing out our conference merch store to make room for new
items we'll be releasing at next year's Othering & Belonging Conference.
Here's your chance to grab some merch at 50% off! Grab your swag before
it runs out.
A variety of clothing and other items from our merch store

 
Together, we can make belonging the norm, not the exception.

Dear Taryell,

Did you know that October 19 is Majdal Day?

I spent the day in dabkeh workshops with El-Fanoun, a renowned Palestinian dance
troupe. It was an honor learning from dancers who embody the creativity, strength,
and resiliency of our community.

October 19 marks one year since we hosted over 300 of you at our local library for the
launch of our arts exhibit, Homeland & Homemaking. We transformed the space into
our own through art, music, and dance.

That evening, the County of San Diego presented us with a proclamation declaring
October 19 as “Majdal Day” and welcoming us as a Live Well partner.

In honor of Majdal Day, please consider making a donation to sustain our
programs and deepen our impact. Your support helps us continue building spaces
where culture, community, and belonging thrive.
Relive the day with us by watching the recap video! Thank you for ongoing support!
With gratitude,
Ramah Awad
Executive Director

Dear Taryell,

It’s been a busy summer at Majdal — with new staff, advocacy wins, and youth
workshops!

This past month, we co-hosted an Organizing 101 Bootcamp with CTWO and Youth
Organize California, where youth and community members came together to build
skills, connect, and grow their leadership.

We also saw a major advocacy win: AB-91, the MENA Inclusion Act, passed its
final policy committee hearing! This is a huge milestone for recognition and equity
in our communities. Next up is the Senate Appropriations Committee. We’ll keep
pushing to ensure MENA communities are counted and served.

As our communities face widespread budget cuts, critical services are at risk. We
are partnering with MTS to host a  community forum July 31st at Majdal Center to
gather feedback on how transit systems are used and public funds should be
prioritized.

I invite you to continue reading below for more updates, highlights, and ways to plug in
this summer.Thank you for your ongoing support.
Sincerely,
Subrein Damanhoury
Programing & Communications
Majdal: Arab Community Center of San Diego

Youth Organizer
We’re excited to welcome Rima to the team!
Rima has been a long-time youth member
with us at Majdal ! Rima will now be taking
on the role of Youth Organizer— leading our
Arab Youth Collective, hosting youth events,
and advocating on broader youth issues.

Read more about Rima!

Youth Fellowship Showcase
 Join Us for the "Scene and Heard" Summer
Fellowship Showcase!

As members of the SDRCC, we’re excited to
announce this upcoming showcase featuring
powerful films created by youth during their
summer fellowship. These films explore
themes around breaking the stigma of mental
health and substance use in immigrant and
refugee communities.

 Saturday, August 2 | 3PM – 6PM
5555 University Ave, San Diego 92105
RSVP here: tinyurl.com/AMEAaug2

El Cajon Solidarity March
As ICE presence continues to rise in
our communities, we joined other
organizations in El Cajon to stand in
opposition. We must remain united in
protecting the safety, dignity, and rights
of our immigrant and refugee
communities.

From Your Future Self To Your Past Self
Join us for a summer workshop series
with the AJA project!

Youth will make personalized postcards
through storytelling, photography,
Arabic calligraphy, and design. Open to
Arabic-speaking community members
ages 15 and up. Final works will be part
of a public art project this fall.

Majdal Center – 329 E Main St
  July 28 – August 9
⏰ 2–4 PM
 https://bit.ly/majdalsummer

Volunteer with our English Class
We’ve relaunched our English
Conversational Class. If you’re looking
to get more involved, we’re looking for
volunteers to support the class. Sign up
here!

Contact subrein@majdalcenter.org with
any questions.

San Diego for Palestine
As the attacks on Gaza continue, we urge
your solidarity. Follow the San Diego for
Palestine Coalition on Instagram to
receive local action and campaign
updates.

Dear Eric,

I hope this message finds you well! Michael Ogbeiwi in Supervisor Anderson's office
provided your information as Acting CIO and recommended I reach out to you directly
regarding the implementation of the new Middle Eastern and North African (MENA) data
category.

My name is Dr. Ryan Fan, and I serve as Advocacy & Campaign Manager at Majdal, the Arab
Community Center of San Diego. Based in El Cajon, we support hundreds of Arab and MENA
families throughout San Diego County. We are also part of the CA MENA Civil Rights
Coalition, comprised of dozens of MENA community organizations and elected officials
across the state that have been advocating for data equity for years.

I'd like to share the great news that Governor Newsom just signed our bill AB 91 "The MENA
Inclusion Act" into law this week! This will create detailed categories that more accurately
represent our state's diverse MENA populations than OMB SPD 15's minimum categories.
We've also heard concerns from our national partners that the federal government may not
implement OMB SPD 15, which is all the more reason for us to ensure the implementation of
AB 91 in California.

I'm eager to meet with you to learn more about the status of the County's initiative, to share
about our campaign, and to discuss ways to engage community partners in the
implementation of San Diego County's MENA categories. Would you be available for a virtual
or in-person meeting on Thursday 10/23 or Monday 10/27?

For reference, I've attached Supervisor Anderson's letter of support, the chaptered text of AB
91, and the MENA category BoS letter and update memo. Please let me know if I can provide
any additional information. Thanks for your time and consideration!

With gratitude,

Over the past five years, communities have persevered, organized and
reimagined new possibilities in the face of a global public health crisis. We Were
Who We Were Waiting For is a new art exhibition that reflects on the resilience
and creativity that emerged throughout California during the COVID-19
pandemic, centering the artists, nonprofit organizations and public-private
partnerships providing critical information, resources and care to communities in
need.

Through multiple mediums, this exhibition honors the collective work of these
cultural stewards, who turned uncertainty into action and isolation into
connection. It is a testament to the power of art and community in times of crisis
and a call to recognize that we have always been our own catalysts for change.

Join us Friday, March 28, for the opening of this reflective exhibition and a
timely conversation with community-based partners and featured artists about
the crucial roles of community knowledge and coordinated action in a healthier,
more equitable future.

title: Chiara_CAIR_Email 03.pdf
subject: [External] Let"s build a world based on belonging
body:
From: Othering & Belonging Institute
To: Leroy, Chiara
Subject: [External] Let"s build a world based on belonging
Date: Wednesday, October 9, 2024 4:28:34 PM
October 9, 2024
OBI News with organic circles in background
Hi Chiara,
As election day approaches, you can expect to hear more and more
political speech that pushes boundaries and fuels longstanding
divisions. The losers? All of us. But especially those who are members
of groups routinely scapegoated by majorities because of things like
where we were born, the color of our skin, or who we love.
The Othering & Belonging Institute has long been a home for people
like you who are looking to make sense of these processes of
marginalization—what we call othering. More important, we’re here
to align efforts to build a world based on inclusion, fairness, justice,
and care for the earth—what we call belonging.
The need for our collective courage, contributions, and commitment
to bridging, has never been more pressing.
 
+ BUILDING COMMUNITY
Last month, OBI staff and faculty spent a few days at Asilomar to
relax, renew, and prepare for the upcoming year. Surprisingly, beach
volleyball was the most popular activity.
Three people carve ''OBI'' into sand on the beach
Four members of OBI smile
 
+ PROGRAM SPOTLIGHT
Allow us to reintroduce the Belonging Resident Company (BRC), a
groundbreaking performance ensemble spotlighting BIPOC and
LGBTQIA+ artists, facilitators, and musicians to make the revolution of
belonging irresistible. Using radical imagination, contemporary and
hip-hop dance, movement theater, and playback theater, we create
embodied experiences of belonging and actively work to dismantle
oppressive systems.
The Belonging Resident Company is offering in-person fall dance
workshops in Berkeley to anyone who loves dance, theater,
belonging and co-creation. They will offer two workshop series:
BRC Director Sarah Crowell will lead Dance and Theater
workshops. These free, two-hour workshops are on Mondays
from October 21 to December 9.
Sangita Kumar will instruct Playback Theater workshops on
Sundays, November 3 and 10. Each session costs $25 and
participants are encouraged to register for both sessions!
Register for the workshops!
Learn more about the Belonging Resident Company here and the
Fall workshops here.
“Movement is our superpower,” said BRC Director Sarah Crowell.
“Connecting with each other across movements through our
movement.”
 
+ OBI IN THE NEWS
OBI scholar Shadrick Small was quoted in KQED’s story “Alameda
County Reparations Commissions Extended 2 Years with Slashed
Budget.” During a board of supervisors meeting, Small urged the
commission to grant funds for a community survey that would
inform potential reparations policy.
Senior researcher Basima Sisemore was quoted in the Seattle
Times story “8 in 10 Muslims experienced discrimination in the past
year.” Sisemore said: “It’s surprising and also not surprising at the
same time. … A lot of it is unfortunate and reaffirms the reality of
discrimination and Islamophobia that Muslim-Americans face,
specifically within Washington state.”
OBI scholar Professor David
Harding, shared his
expertise in a Courthouse
News Service story, “Real —
or imagined — crime spike
spurring California voter
interest in November ballot.”
Harding gave his
perspective on California
propositions 36 and 6, both
linked to potential crime
policies around the state.
David Harding's headshot
Professor David Harding photographed in his office
Lastly, research director Stephen Menendian’s Q&A story “What
good is free speech when no one is listening” was republished in
NJ Today, and Equity Metrics’ California single family zoning
research was once again referenced in affordable housing
coverage in the Los Angeles Times and LAist.
 
+ GETTING TO WORK
Last month, as part of her Revolutionary Love Tour, award-winning
writer and activist Valarie Kaur invited our john a. powell and
immigration rights activist and journalist Jose Antonio Vargas to a
joyful discussion at Berkeley’s La Peña Cultural Center. Our OBI staff
showed out, too.
Watch a recap of their discussion here!
 
Big congratulations to Hossein Ayazi, Senior Policy Analyst at OBI’s
Global Justice Program, and Betsy Popken, Executive Director of the
Human Rights Center at UC Berkeley School of Law, who have been
selected by the Governor’s Office of Land Use and Climate Innovation
(formerly the Office of Planning and Research) to be the Coordinating
Lead Authors of California’s 5th Climate Change Assessment Topical
Report on Climate-Induced Human Displacement & Migration.
You can contribute to the report here.
Hossein Ayazi presents to a group of youth in a conference room.
Dr. Hossein Ayazi presents “Towards Climate Justice: Transformative Approaches to Climate Migration Research
and Learning” at the 2024 Bay Area Youth Climate Summit on September 28, 2024.
 
The groundbreaking Washington Muslim Survey 2024 Report was
recently released by the Washington chapter of the Council on
American-Islamic Relations. Sisemore and Global Justice Program
Director Elsadig Elsheikh consulted CAIR to create the report and
co-authored a guest essay here.
For more nuanced background around this research, check out our
2021 survey Islamophobia Through the Eyes of Muslims.
 
As part of a new interview series, Lara Habboub of OBI’s Democracy
and Belonging Forum recently spoke with Forum Advisory Board
member Sanam Naraghi Anderlini, a renowned peace strategist and
CEO of the International Civil Society Action Network (ICAN),
spearheading the Women’s Alliance for Security Leadership (WASL).
Sanam’s journey into peacebuilding tells a powerful story where the
personal and political intertwine, as often happens when one
witnesses their country in turmoil. Read the full interview here.
“Understanding our multiple identities allows
us to push past the prejudices and
assumptions we’re conditioned to have about
each other. ... This fluidity is key—it’s about
recognizing that our identities are not static;
they can evolve and adapt as we navigate
different contexts and stages of life.”
 
+ PLACES TO BE
As part of OBI’s scholarship,
professor Sunaura Taylor will
host a discussion on her new
book, Disabled Ecologies:
Lessons from a Wounded
Desert — a powerful analysis
and call to action that reveals
disability as one of the defining
features of environmental
devastation and resistance.
The event will be held at the
Toll Room in Alumni House on
Tuesday, October 15 at 4pm. It
is free and open to the public.
Join us to celebrate the launch
of Trans Hirstory in 99 Objects
with co-author and artist Chris
E. Vargas alongside two artist-
activists and contributors to
the book, Ralowe Ampu, and
Craig Calderwood. OBI
Scholar Eric Stanley will
moderate this fantastic panel.
The event is free and open to
the public and will be held at
the Multicultural Community
Center in the MLK Jr. Student
Union building tomorrow,
October 10, at 4 pm.
Our transportation analyst Jose Richard Aviles has a message for
all who have attended their monthly Reimagining Urban Planning
series:
“THANK YOU! Whether you've only had the chance to make it to
one webinar or if you've made it to the entire series, we wanna say
thank you for participating! But the series is not over yet! We have
two more sessions planned. On October 11, we have ‘Belonging and
Urban Planning’ where I will be conversing with john a. powell and
Aimée Okotie-Oyekanand. We culminate the series in December
with ‘Planning for (dystopic) Futures’.”
Please register here for the two conversations.
Flyer for Reimagining urban planning for belonging
On October 15 from 5 to 6 p.m. CET, the Democracy and Belonging
Forum will hold a virtual event with john a. powell and Hans
Kundani, “From ‘Eurowhiteness’ to Belonging without Othering:
Crafting New Identities in a Changing Europe.”
This event is free and open to the public. Register here now!
Flyer for From ‘Eurowhiteness’ to Belonging without Othering''
 
+ OFFERINGS
As the final month of the U.S. elections ends, regardless of the results,
belonging and bridging will be necessary practices for all of us to
connect and move forward together.
john a. powell’s upcoming book The Power of Bridging: How to build
a world where we all belong aims to provide a narrative and
framework for us all to understand and use in our daily lives.
You can pre-order it here!
Promotional graphic for The Power of Bridging
 
Together, we can make belonging the norm, not the exception.
– The Othering & Belonging Institute

title: Chiara_CAIR_Email 06.pdf
subject: [External] Thank you for making this event so memorable!
body:
From: CAIR San Diego
To: Leroy, Chiara
Subject: [External] Thank you for making this event so memorable!
Date: Wednesday, October 29, 2025 1:55:51 PM
View in browser
On behalf of the entire team at CAIR-SD, thank
you for joining us at our 18th Annual Gala! Your
presence made the evening truly special as we
celebrated our shared commitment to justice,
faith, and community empowerment.

Your support helps us continue to defend civil
rights, challenge Islamophobia, and uplift the
voices of our community. Together, we are
building a more just and inclusive future for all.

If you haven’t had the chance to donate yet, it’s
not too late to make an impact. Your
contribution, no matter the size, helps
sustain our vital work throughout the year.
Support CAIR-SD
Thank you once again for being part of this
inspiring night and for standing with CAIR-SD.
We look forward to seeing you at future events
and continuing this important work together.

With gratitude,
The CAIR-SD Team
Council on American-Islamic Relations
California San Diego

title: Chiara_CAIR_Email 10.pdf
subject: [External] Join us March 28 to explore art and community as
body:
From:                                                       Sierra Health Foundation <communications@send.shfcenter.org>
Sent:                                                         Tuesday, March 11, 2025 4:16 PM
To:                                                            Leroy, Chiara
Subject:                                                   [External] Join us March 28 to explore art and community as
critical drivers for change

Pictured above: Artwork by Jessica Wimbley, Sunroop Kaur, Robin Lasser and Adrienne Pao, created
for the statewide COVID-19 public arts project featured in the upcoming Speaker Series event.
Not able to view the images in this email? Try clicking "Show blocked content" and adding
communications@shf.ccsend.com to your contacts.
Over the past five years, communities have persevered, organized and
reimagined new possibilities in the face of a global public health crisis. We
Were Who We Were Waiting For is a new art exhibition that reflects on the
resilience and creativity that emerged throughout California during the COVID-
19 pandemic, centering the artists, nonprofit organizations and public-private
partnerships providing critical information, resources and care to communities
in need.

Through multiple mediums, this exhibition honors the collective work of these
cultural stewards, who turned uncertainty into action and isolation into
connection. It is a testament to the power of art and community in times of
crisis and a call to recognize that we have always been our own catalysts for
change.

Join us Friday, March 28, for the opening of this reflective exhibition and a
timely conversation with community-based partners and featured artists about
the crucial roles of community knowledge and coordinated action in a healthier,
more equitable future.

Speaker Series: We Were Who We Were Waiting For
Art Exhibition and Discussion
Friday, March 28, 2025, from 6 to 8 p.m.
CAIR Art Gallery, Sacramento
Register now for this in-person event

Hi ABMoC partners,
I am writing to request your support to join a sign-on letter to California Members of Congress demanding the
release of Mahmoud Khalil.
More information below. Thank you for your consideration.
In solidarity,
Bruno
---------- Forwarded message ---------
From: Shiu-Ming Cheer <smcheer@caimmigrant.org>
Date: Thu, Mar 13, 2025 at 1:56 PM
Subject: Sign On Request: Letter Demanding Release of Mahmoud Khalil (deadline Tuesday 3/18 12pm)
Hi everyone,

CIPC is outraged at ICE’s baseless arrest of Mahmoud Khalil, a lawful permanent resident, on March 8th because of
his activism. We are working with CAIR, who has been leading on efforts related to the suppression of dissent,
profiling, and state violence, to uplift some asks related to his case.

As organizations committed to the values of equity and justice for all, regardless of status, please sign-onto this
letter to California Congressional Members by Tuesday, March 18th at Noon, to Demand Justice For Mahmoud
Khalil.

The letter asks the California Congressional delegation to join in publicly demanding Mahmoud Khalil’s immediate
release, and to take other actions to protect free speech and oppose detentions and deportations.
Here’s the sign on form: bit.ly/signon4mahmoud. And the letter: bit.ly/justice4mahmoudk.

Thank you and please circulate this to your networks.

In Solidarity,
Shiu-Ming

Hello Dear Jaine, Chiara and Brandon,
I am Mohammad Rahimi from CAIR-SD. Since 2007, CAIR-SD has worked tirelessly
to uphold the civil rights of American Muslims, foster a better understanding of the
Islamic faith and its followers, and help find avenues for Muslims to integrate more
fully into the broader society. By sponsoring our annual gala, not only are you
advertising directly to over 500 community leaders, business owners, young
professionals, and other attendees, you are also supporting an organization
committed to the defense of civil rights and immigrant rights and the promotion of
justice for all Americans. This is a once-a-year opportunity to directly reach our largest
in-person audience, as well as tap into the more than 120,000 Muslims living in San
Diego County, through community announcements, emails, social media, and
professionally designed flyers and mailers. Our diligent outreach at more than 20
mosques and community centers will bring increased attention to your sponsorship.
This year, we are hosting our annual gala on September 14th, and we are excited to
invite the Office of Equity and Racial Justice to become our sponsor. Sponsorship
packages can be purchased online at CAIR-SD 17th Annual Gala Sponsorship

title: Chiara_Gaza_Email 03.pdf
subject: [External] ? The courage to be bold, the boldness to take action
body:
From:                                                       Center on Policy Initiatives <cpi@cpisandiego.org>
Sent:                                                         Friday, October 31, 2025 3:09 PM
To:                                                            Leroy, Chiara
Subject:                                                   [External] ? The courage to be bold, the boldness to take action

 
October 2025
In This Issue
Chris Smalls In San Diego!
Protecting Workers From Attacks On Our Communities
Picture Me, Free - A Student Art Zine
San Diego Stands Up For Our Civil Liberties
Vacation Home Tax
 
Chiara,

There have been so many instances lately of people having the
courage to be bold and take action.
Whether you’re a CPI volunteer talking to businesses about how
to protect workers from ICE raids or a high school student using
art to encourage others to envision a world beyond policing,
people like you and I are leaning into building power.
If you’re not currently organizing with us but want to get involved,
respond to this email and we’ll connect on working together!
HUGE NEWS: Chris Smalls is coming to San Diego!

Join us at City College on November 10th at 9:40am for a special
event organized by Students for Justice in Palestine and the World
Cultures Program. We are proud to be co-sponsors of this event
and hope to see you there!

📍Address: Saville Theater, 14th St & C St, San Diego 92101
“Solidarity with historically oppressed communities is at the core of
all social justice movements.
Chris Smalls led the efforts for the first successful Amazon Union in
New York and was one of the activists on the Handala Flotilla on a
mission to deliver food and aid to Gaza.
The event, which also features local labor and CalSTRS divestment
campaign organizers, will explore the interconnectedness of racial,
labor, and international organizing.”

- Students for Economic Justice intern Keila Menjivar Zamora
Lead Organizer Rocío led us in a campaign with partners
throughout the state to educate businesses about their rights and
what they can do to protect their workers from ICE raids and
kidnappings. Knowing this would require a group effort, we trained
volunteers to hit the streets and canvass local businesses.

Retired attorney and CPI volunteer, Dorothy, said this of the
campaign:

"I volunteered to do the small business outreach program because
it was time for me to put down my phone, stop doomscrolling and
get to work. Each of us can contribute in some way to push back on
this administration’s attacks on our Constitution, our country and
our communities.
I learned that most folks had no idea that ICE did not have the
right to enter non-public areas of their business without a valid
judicial warrant. Most had no idea what a valid warrant looked
like.
Because of the information we provided, there will be more
conversations at the workplace, and business owners may have
more conversations among themselves. I think that’s important, and
I’m glad to be part of this CPI campaign."
A Student Art Zine
ICE attacks are just one way that workers and working-class
families are criminalized and dehumanized. Policing young
students in schools and in their communities is just another form of
this repression.
Over the summer, CPI organizer, Abeeha, and CPI communications
specialist, Nelly, collaborated with a group of students to create art
that delved into what community safety means to them. Student
artists participated in weekly sessions with teaching artist Delana
Delgado where they explored symbolism, prose and poetry, and
used photography and other mixed media.
The art project culminated in a zine and art show that presented
their vision of safety with freedom and without policing. Check out
this video from Sophia sharing her poetry piece that was included in
the zine! Keep an eye out for the zine, which will be featured on our
website.
In the face of federal agents terrorizing our communities and getting
access to our private information, CPI and other partners in the
community mobilized around two measures that could protect us
from these attacks.

Thanks to this hard work, we won both proposals!
On October 20th, the San Diego City Council voted unanimously to
adopt City Councilmember Sean Elo-Rivera’s “Due Process and
Safety" ordinance. The ordinance restricts collaboration with ICE at
a time when San Diegans are being disappeared off the streets in
direct violation of their right to due process.
On October 21st, the Board of Supervisors voted to draft similar
legislation at the County.
As attacks from the federal government continue, local fights like
these will only become more important. Stay tuned for updates on
how you can join this fight!

On October 22nd, the San Diego City Council Rules Committee
began a conversation about a tax on businesses operating full-time,
whole home vacation rentals and on people who own second
homes in San Diego.

Working people are struggling to survive the housing crisis of
limited available units and skyrocketing prices. Meanwhile, people
rich enough to own multiple homes, and corporations, benefit from
city services that we can’t afford unless everyone pays their fair
share. If the full City Council agrees, San Diegans will vote on this
in the 2026 election.
This is going to be a fight! If it’s your fight, get in touch to get
involved.
 
Fighting for economic justice takes a village. Your donation to CPI will
help sustain the fight for workers' rights, education justice, housing for
all, and a healthy environment.

Oct. 22, 2025
 
Our latest Inclusiveness Index is out, with new tools and
features

We are excited to unveil our 2025 Inclusive Index today, which includes an updated look
and new features to make the user experience more intuitive and easier to find the data
you're looking for. There is nothing shocking about this year's results, which again saw New
Zealand and Hawaii top the rankings as most inclusive country and US state, as they did last
year. But now our interactive tables include a column showing how much better or worse
each state and country is doing compared to the previous year. It also includes a brand new
tool allowing the user to select two countries or states for comparison. Our annual
Inclusiveness Index, now in its tenth year, ranks countries and US states by their levels of
inclusion based on a handful of indicators, including how well they respect the rights of
different groups based on their race, gender, dis/ability, religion, and the general population.
 
Listening to the Listeners: Lessons from Long Bridge
Canvassing

Could you knock on the door of someone that you disagree with and have an open,
connecting conversation? In 2024, canvassers across five states set out with this very
question in mind. This wasn’t your typical political canvassing. Instead, it was a new form
of canvassing called long-bridge canvassing– a method designed not to persuade, but to
connect. Black, working-class canvassers knocked on the doors of affluent, white voters;
urban canvassers knocked on the doors of rural residents; and progressive canvassers
knocked on the doors of conservative counterparts. Read more about this project in this
new blog post by Ella Streng, OBI's video producer, who spent six months
researching this pilot as part of her master’s thesis.

Disclaimer: The ideas expressed in this blog are not necessarily those of the Othering &
Belonging Institute or UC Berkeley, but belong to the author.
 
Is Civil Society the New Battlefield for Democracy?

Changes in the political order—globally and nationally—are part and parcel of human
history. In 2025, the process of becoming less and less inclusive and democratic is
seemingly leaving no country unscathed. The arc of history is bending in the direction of
othering and continued oppression. According to V-Dem, 2025 marks the 25th consecutive
year of autocratization (that is, of the world becoming even less democratic). For the first
time in 20 years, there are more autocracies than democracies... Read more from this latest
blog post by Míriam Juan-Torres González, Head of Research at OBI's Democracy &
Belonging Forum.

Disclaimer: The ideas expressed in this blog are not necessarily those of the Othering &
Belonging Institute or UC Berkeley, but belong to the author.
 
We now have racial disparity data for San Francisco and
Philadelphia

We have just updated our Racial Disparities Dashboard with city-level data for the first time
showing progress and setbacks for Black-white equity at the city level in San Francisco and
Philadelphia. The dashboard highlights disparities in key areas such as education, income,
health, and other critical life outcomes. The data is displayed on a few interactive widgets
that allow the user to dig deeper into the circumstances surrounding the disparities for any
given issue.
 

Register for our 2026 Othering & Belonging Conference!

We have opened registration for our next Othering & Belonging Conference happening in
Louisville, Kentucky on March 31-April 1, 2026! Whether this is your first
O&B conference, or fifth, we invite you to come to Louisville and take an active role in
shaping this dynamic two-day conference alongside us. Our conferences are designed to be
fully immersive spaces that bring together leading thinkers, doers, and visionaries to share
strategies and purpose on building societies rooted in care and the fundamental belief that all
people have the unconditional right to belong.
 
Hossein Ayazi, Senior Policy Analyst from OBI's Global Justice Program, was invited to be
part of an expert panel on September 26th for the launch of the Kühn Initiative for Post-
Conflict Development Studies as part of the Center for Middle East Studies at UC Berkeley.
 
 + EVENTS
Oct. 29: Structural Racism Book Talk

Join us in person at UC Berkeley on Oct. 29 at 4pm for a dynamic conversation featuring OBI
Assistant Director Stephen Menendian and other Berkeley scholars to discuss the nature and causes
of racial inequality in the United States. Stephen will open the event by summarizing the themes of
his recently published book, Structural Racism: The Dynamics of Opportunity and Race in America,
before engaging with panelists john a. powell, Director of OBI; and Anna Livia Brand, associate
professor of Landscape Architecture & Environmental Planning, about how they think about racial
inequality and pathways to build a more just society. The event will be moderated by Tina Sacks,
associate professor at UC Berkeley’s School of Social Welfare.
 
Oct. 30: What I Saw in Gaza: A Surgeon's Account

Dr. Feroze Sidhwa volunteered with the World Health Organization at the European
Hospital in Khan Younis, Gaza, March 25 – April 2, 2024, and again from March 3 – April
2, 2025, with MedGlobal, an American Non-governmental Organization (NGO). In “What I
Saw in Gaza: A Surgeon's Account,” Dr. Sidhwa will provide eyewitness testimony of the
genocide against Palestinians through a series of cases that he encountered as a trauma
surgeon serving in the Gaza Strip. This is an in-person only event.
 
Nov. 8-16: Cultural Week of Action

As our communities fight against erasure of their histories, we must all come together to
celebrate ourselves, protect our cultures, and reclaim our narratives. We’re proud to
partner with Race Forward for the Cultural Week of Action on Race and
Democracy, November 8-16. This is an opportunity to deepen commitments to
racial justice and inclusive democracy through music, storytelling, movement,
and collective learning in communities across the nation. Learn more and see
how YOU can take action!

Míriam Juan-Torres González, Head of Research at OBI's Democracy & Belonging
Forum, was interviewed for this Berkeley News Q&A about her recently published "
(En)Gendering Authoritarianism" report, co-authored with others.

Turning fragmentation, polarization, and
fear into solidarity, partnership, and hope.
Since the October 7th Hamas-led attacks on Israel and the ensuing conflict in Gaza,
polarization has fractured faith communities all across the country. People of faith no longer
feel safe practicing their own religious freedoms or connecting with others across differences.
We are losing the richness and grounding influence of these communities.
This year, Essential Partners collaborated with LIFaith, a project of the UJA-Federation of
New York, to support healing interfaith dialogues across Long Island. The initiative’s mission
is to help Long Island clergy from different faith traditions cultivate the necessary skills for
interfaith collaboration, to build resilience in advance of flashpoint conflicts, and to imagine
what a thriving interfaith community might look like moving forward.
“The aftermath of October 7th was felt far beyond the borders of Israel and Gaza,” said Sepi
Djavaheri, Community Mobilizers Director for UJA-Federation of New York. “Communities
that had long lived side by side suddenly found themselves facing fear, mistrust, and
increasing pressure from external narratives that were pulling neighbors apart. What became
clear in those early days was that the global had become local—and that we could no longer
treat international conflict as something separate from our own community fabric.”
LIFaith wanted to respond with something new—a dialogue series that would allow genuine
friendship and deeper interfaith collaborations to emerge.
“This is a blueprint for how faith leaders
everywhere can respond to global events in
ways that strengthen, rather than fracture,
their communities.”
Would you consider donating $35 to help us strengthen initiatives like this one, with interfaith
groups all across the country?

Many of the clergy members had participated in interfaith dialogues previously. They were
often less in-depth engagements, though, and even those had been disrupted, according to
Kenis. “There was a break in efforts trying to do that after October 7th, so we were trying to
close that gap—to do it more intentionally and less at a surface level.”
UJA Federation and LIFaith selected Essential Partners because they were looking for a style
of facilitation that would, in Kenis’s words, “help break up the regular power dynamics that
happen in a lot of these dialogue groups [between clergy]” and invite deeper relationship-
building.
The hand-picked LI Faith Planning Committee—comprising experienced community
members—forged an unprecedented coalition. By uniting leadership from councils
representing synagogues, churches, mosques, and temples, we now represent more than 100
houses of worship across Long Island, fostering collective action and shared responsibility at a
scale never before possible.
On February 4, 2025, LI Faith hosted its first Dialogue Across Faith Symposium. 65 clergy
members from 14 different faith communities convened to repair interfaith relationships in the
wake of October 7th.
“The audience was split into groups of eight to ten people each,” said Kenis. “Each group was
facilitated by a clergy member from the planning committee who was trained in RSD over a
period of three ninety-minute dialogues.”
“What began as an urgent response to
October 7th has become something
enduring, a coalition that embodies the
very best of what interfaith work can
achieve—to transform a moment of
fragmentation, polarization, and fear into
solidarity, partnership, and hope.”
Can you consider a gift of $35 to support more transformative initiatives like this one?
The feedback from this event was overwhelmingly positive, with clergy members reporting a
new, unique connection across faith traditions. Kenis reflected on a powerful moment when a
retired Buddhist priest shared that he finally felt connected in an interfaith space,
understanding the similarity with other faiths after hearing God described as a “creative
force.”
Djavaheri noted that this unprecedented coalition is more than a reaction to one crisis; it is a
“blueprint for how faith leaders everywhere can respond to global events in ways that
strengthen, rather than fracture, their communities.”
The coalition's work is ongoing, focusing on deep, authentic dialogue to create structural shifts
that build resilience across faith communities. The Symposium has already propelled the
launch of two new locally-led initiatives, with the coalition serving as a permanent platform
for joint action.
“In short, what began as an urgent response to October 7th has become something enduring,”
Djavaheri said, “a coalition that embodies the very best of what interfaith work can achieve—
to transform a moment of fragmentation, polarization, and fear into solidarity, partnership, and
hope.”
Hope is the cornerstone of our work at EP. We are committed to nourishing hope among the
thousands of people—including faith leaders of every tradition—who do the hard, deliberate
work of healing divides and building stronger communities. That's what our Community of
Practice is all about: to empower, inspire, and support the peacemakers in our movement.
Can you donate $35 today to support our commitment to the Community of Practice and these
crucial leaders?
In community,
John Sarrouf & Katie Hyten
Co-Executive Directors

Trenchard is a double threat -- not only a gifted photographer but a talented

Reflecting on his time spent covering this story in Zambia, Trenchard was
impressed with the humans who volunteer to defuse conflicts with

"Judging by the body language of the volunteers, who had a deep
understanding of elephant behavior, we were never in any actual danger. But
not being an elephant expert myself, I persistently failed to tell the difference

Malaka Gharib/NPR
The other day I took the metro to work. When I exited the station to walk up
the street to NPR, I saw a man lying flat on the sidewalk -- and two young
men who'd gotten off their bicycles and were kneeling by his side. One of
them was cradling the man's head. The man was barefoot so it seemed he
was living on the street.
"Is there anything I can do?" I asked. One of the young men said they'd seen
this fellow sprawled out on a hot day and seemingly unwell. They called an
ambulance. And they were waiting with him and talking with him until the
vehicle arrived.
I was so touched by their act of kindness. All I could think to say was "thank
you." Thank you for caring for this stranger. And thank you for reminding me
that in a world full of conflict and tension, it's important to remember that we
all have the capacity to do good.
Dear readers: Do you have any memories you'd like to share of a moment
when you saw a random act of loving-kindness? Or perhaps an instance
where you were the altruistic soul who helped a stranger? Please send your
thoughts to goatsandsoda@npr.org with the subject line "kindness." We'd
love to publish a collection of stories to inspire others.
Marc Silver
Editor, Goats and Soda

To speak out or not to speak out? That is the question being debated at aid
groups as they face funding cuts during this Trump administration. Our global
health team noticed this as charities would ask us to write about programs in
jeopardy due to the cuts -- but then ask us not to quote any staff people from
their group.
There's even a phrase to describe this reaction: "anticipatory silence."
That's what Thomas Weiss, a professor of international relations and global
governance at the Graduate Center at the City University of New York, is
calling it.
Correspondents Fatma Tanis and Gabrielle Emanuel spoke to many
representatives of charities (most of whom asked not to have their names
used) and other analysts to see what's behind the silence -- and whether it's
an effective strategy in the effort to save programs from the ax.
Read the story here.

Dear readers,
Over the years, Goats and Soda has covered the extraordinary effort led by
President Jimmy Carter to eradicate a terrible ailment -- Guinea
worm disease. It's a neglected disease caused when the worm itself is spread
From:                                                       Goats and Soda <email@nl.npr.org>

When Carter began his campaign in the mid-1980s, the World Health
Organization estimated 3.5 million cases of the parasitic infection in Asia and
Africa. Thirty-eight years later — at the time of Carter's death in 2024 — the
late president's Guinea worm eradication program counted a mere 14 cases.
The President and the Dragon is a new documentary about this campaign. We
interviewed the writer, producer and co-director, Waleed Eltayeb, who's from
Sudan, one of the countries afflicted. "For me, this film is basically about one of
the most important things that we as human beings cannot do without, and
that's hope," he says. "It showcases very clearly the power of us when we come
together."

Dear Chiara,
As I have been planning the 35th Anniversary Virtual Gala (in only two weeks!), I've been
thinking about the phrase “coalition of the willing.” Not every person is willing to take
responsibility for the health and cohesion of their community, college, school, or institution—
but you do.
You are part of a movement that grows stronger every year, reaching more communities,
transforming classrooms, and changing hundreds of thousands of lives. We are so grateful for
you. But the world is not well. We need to find and equip many more changemakers just like
you.
Can you consider a donation of $35 to support the hard work of connection,
community, and hope in the coming year?
In more than 400 local communities, 350 college campuses, 140 nonprofits and companies,
and 100 secondary schools around the globe, the impact of our work speaks for itself:
“The Israel-Hamas war in Gaza has hit our community particularly hard, and we
have had to navigate many difficult conversations on the issue.… the EP model
gets to the core of the issue in a way that creates empathy and moves the
conversation forward.”
“RSD has made me realize that safe, thoughtful communication can happen in a
world where these things can no longer be taken for granted.”
“Dialogue enables our community to come together, across differences, to hold
space for various beliefs and to cultivate spaces where people feel seen, heard,
and valued.”
These are just a few real testimonials from the past year. In the year to come, thousands more
local leaders will look to us for thought partnership and expert guidance.
Can these inspiring leaders count on your gift of $35 to support and empower
them in 2025 and beyond?
Thank you, once more, for being part of this movement—as a local changemaker, as a
supporter of EP’s mission, and as a person deeply invested in your community.
With gratitude,

body:

Subject:                                                   [External] New Visual Explainer: What's Behind the Opportunity
Gap, and How to Close It

Aug. 6, 2025
 

We're excited to share with you our brand new visual explainer video that breaks down how
opportunity is structured in the United States, its relationship to race and class, and how to
level the playing field so everyone has a fair shot at success. The video, which is a
companion to the new book on Structural Racism recently published by OBI Research
Director Stephen Menendian, shows how the pathways we encounter in life aren't only
shaped by personal choices, but also by structural forces. Stephen, who narrates the video,
explains what he means by opportunity, why it's so unevenly distributed, and illustrates an
easy-to-grasp example of how policies can be changed to close opportunity disparities,
rather than exacerbate them. Check out this must watch video here. And read this fantastic
article and Q&A with Stephen published on Berkeley News.
 
Letter: Stop Starving Gaza

Last week a number of OBI staff members authored an urgent letter calling for an immediate
end to Israel's forced starvation of Palestinians in Gaza. We invited our colleagues at other
departments, centers and organizations inside and outside of Berkeley and the general public
to add their names to the letter, repost it to their websites, and speak out publicly on this
moral calamity happening before our eyes in Gaza. About 1,500 of you have already signed
onto the letter. You can still add your name to it at the bottom of this page, and email us a
photo of yourself holding up a sign reading "Stop Starving Gaza" to share on our website
and other platforms. See coverage of this letter in the DailyCal.

Disclaimer: The ideas expressed in the letter and in this email post are not necessarily
those of the Othering & Belonging Institute or UC Berkeley, but belong to the signers.
 
Take our Audience Survey!

We'd love to learn more about your backgrounds, your interests in our work, how you found
us, and what you find most useful for your work. To that end we've developed a super quick
(5-10 minute) survey we would love you to fill out. Your responses will help us create
content that’s more useful, inspiring, and relevant—and you will help us explore new ways
for our community to connect and grow together.
 
Join a Workshop to Inform the Statewide Topical Reports of
California’s Fifth Climate Assessment

The California Fifth Climate Change Assessment Team is seeking input from community
organizations, experts on the ground, and residents with lived experiences to inform
the Statewide Topical Reports. The virtual workshop, happening on Thursday, Aug. 7 from
1pm to 2:30pm, will include breakout discussions on housing, health, labor, and
education, which will be featured in all four reports.
 
 + EVENTS
To advance housing justice for all, we need solutions at scale. Scaling just solutions that
match what our communities want and need is about more than building more affordable
housing units. It requires building a culture and system that prioritizes people over profit,
honors community self-determination, and fosters shared responsibility to each other and the
earth. Join us for this August 13 virtual panel discussion which builds on the
frameworks and recommendations presented in Living into the Future: Scaling
Community Owned Housing in California. We pick up one of the questions we
left off with: How can the housing field transform these dynamics, bridge across
silos, and create a more cohesive housing ecosystem, in order to live into a
better future of belonging for all?
 
 + WORK WITH US

body:

Subject:                                                   [External] Introducing our Narrative Resource Library!

Sept. 3, 2025
 
Narrative Strategies for Belonging

Narratives shape how we understand the past, make sense of the present, and imagine the
future. But what exactly is narrative, and how does it influence feelings of belonging or non-
belonging? A new digital library —created by a Narrative Community of Practice co-led by
OBI and the Center for Inclusion and Belonging at the American Immigration Council—
offers a curated collection of resources exploring narrative change. Whether you’re just
beginning to explore how narratives shape our world or are a seasoned practitioner, this
collection provides essential tools and insights to strengthen your work and support a more
inclusive, pluralistic democracy.

Image credit: Artwork by Nina Yagual for Amplifier.org and Belonging Begins with Us
 
Normalizing the Exceptional: Migration Governance and the
Authoritarian Turn

Migration debates may feel repetitive, but beneath the surface, profound changes are
underway. Policies justified in the name of “control” are reshaping rights and governance in
ways that echo democratic erosion worldwide. At the same time, public opinion is fluid—
shifting between fear and opportunity, challenge and benefit. Míriam Juan-Torres' latest
Connecting the Dots piece unpacks how migration is not a temporary issue to be
managed, but a defining reality shaping democracy—past, present, and future.

Disclaimer: The ideas expressed in this essay are not necessarily those of the Othering &
Belonging Institute or UC Berkeley, but belong to the author.

 

Get ready for our 2026 Othering & Belonging Conference!

We'll soon be announcing registration for our 2026 Othering & Belonging Conference
happening in Louisville, Kentucky on April 1-2, 2026! Check our our website for the latest
updates on our conference.
 
Impact Story: Bridging in the biosciences by building a better
environment

This coming Friday, Sept. 5, our Campus Bridging Project and Berkeley's Graduate Division
will host a Biological Sciences Bridging event in the Valley Life Sciences Building. From
noon to 3 p.m., the lunch gathering will bring together students, faculty, and staff to share
stories of their experiences in science and to build a culture of collaboration across
departments. Our latest impact story profiles this initiative from the perspectives of the
people behind it.
 

Structural racism explained in 101 seconds

Berkeley News recently produced this short explainer video featuring OBI Assistant
Director Stephen Menendian breaking down structural racism, which is the topic of his
new book. In this 101 in 101 video, a series that challenges UC Berkeley scholars to explain
their field in 101 seconds, Stephen explains how most of the mechanisms that form
structural racism –– like mass incarceration –– have taken shape in the post-Civil Rights era.
Watch this video here, read a related Berkeley News interview with Stephen here, and learn
more about his new book here.
 
Impact Story: Renewing my commitment to the power of
connection

We recently wrapped up our 2025 summer fellowship program with an outstanding cohort of
inspiring young changemakers. One of the fellows, Anjali Pajuri, summed up her
experience and collected testimonies from others in her cohort in this recent impact story we
published. "Far from the silent summer I envisioned, the last 14 weeks have
served as a constant source of inspiration, and I’m truly looking forward to
applying the skills I’ve gained in research and community-building to my life
post-fellowship," Anjali writes.
 
Letter: Stop Starving Gaza

A few weeks ago a number of OBI staff members authored an urgent letter calling for an
immediate end to Israel's forced starvation of Palestinians in Gaza. We invited our
colleagues at other departments, centers and organizations inside and outside of Berkeley

out publicly on this moral calamity happening before our eyes in Gaza. The letter remains

body:
Goats and Soda
editor's note
Claire Harbage/NPR
Dear readers,
For Meridah Nandudu, sipping a medium roast is symbolic of something more
-- how the humble bean has transformed her life and the lives of many
women in her village in Uganda.
From:                                                       Goats and Soda <email@nl.npr.org>
Sent:                                                         Saturday, October 18, 2025 9:22 AM
To:                                                            Leroy, Chiara
Subject:                                                   [External] How coﬀee beans are changing lives

"It is the gold that is seated on our trees," she says.
The daughter of coffee farmers, she had dreams of a career in the big city. She
earned degrees in social work and project management, but the country's high
unemployment rate left her jobless. When she was 30, her husband left her and
their two children. She didn't know how she'd make a living.
Then it dawned on her -- maybe her coffee knowledge from her childhood plus
her academic skills could enable her to turn her life around. Now she is the
owner of a coffee company that has given her a new course and also inspired
her to help women in the community find a way to earn a living through coffee
farming, giving them independence from partners who were often controlling
and even abusive.
Nandudu told NPR's Fatma Tanis that even though she grew up with zero
interest in coffee, today the drink is a source of strength -- and enjoyment.
"Medium roast is my favorite," she says, taking a deep inhale of her full cup. "It
brings out the caramels, the body of the coffee, the chocolate flavors."
Read the story here.
Marc Silver,
